## 406. Coverage floors recorded where LocalStack ran would have failed every CI run, and every `make ci` without a token

**Symptom.** Found 2026-09-30 by reading, before the first pull-request run of Phase 118's workflow, while
recording floors for new packages. `internal/catalog/cloud/aws/ec2` has a floor of 96.7% and
`internal/catalog/cloud/aws/s3` one of 98.0%. With `LOCALSTACK_AUTH_TOKEN` unset they measure 37.6% and 47.1%,
and the workflow never sets it, so the `coverage` job would have failed on every pull request. So would `make
ci` on any contributor's machine without a LocalStack account, for a reason unrelated to their change. Every
local gate passed, because the developer's shell had the token.

**Root cause.** A floor is a number measured on one machine, and a skipped test lowers a package's number
without saying why. The floor check could not tell "this code lost its tests" from "this run could not run
them", so it could only fail both or pass both. The LocalStack tests skipped with a bare `t.Skip`, which the
skip ledger listed but nothing else read.

**Fix.** Every LocalStack test stops through `testsupport.LocalStackToken`, which calls `Require("localstack")`,
so its skip reads `needs localstack: ...`. `testgate` records each package's missing requirements beside its
coverage (`flakegate.Missing`, `flakegate.Measurement`), and `coverage-check -measured` names a package below
its floor that lacked something as unchecked, neither pass nor failure. `TestMissing_ReadsTheReasonRequireGives`
holds the skip format and the parser to one another. Proved through the real tools: `testgate` over `ec2`
and `s3` without the token, then `coverage-check` over the real `coverage-floor.json`, passes naming both,
and the same numbers without the missing record fail as before. The workflow passes an optional
`LOCALSTACK_AUTH_TOKEN` secret and, when it is set, requires LocalStack, so a dead token fails the job
instead of skipping.

**Lesson.** A measurement is only comparable to a threshold taken under the same conditions. When a check
compares numbers from two machines, record the conditions with the number, or the check will be wrong on
whichever machine the threshold was not set on, and it will be wrong silently on the one where it was.

## 407. The view reachability check hand-listed 8 of 22 views, so dropping any of the other 14 passed

**Symptom.** `TestViewConformance_RegisteredAndReachable`, the gate for FAILURE_PATTERNS 52 (a view package
nothing imports), checked a literal list of eight view names. Fourteen views were added after it was written,
none to the list. Replacing `labels.Register()` in `internal/ui/resources/registrars.go` with a no-op left the
test green.

**Root cause.** The check moved the gap it was written to close one step along: a view had to be added to
`registrars.go` to be reachable, and then to a test's list to be checked, and nothing required the second.

**Fix.** The list is read from source: `viewPackageNames` parses each package under `internal/ui/resources`
for its `Name` constant, and a package without one fails. The same mutation now fails naming `labels`.

**Lesson.** A completeness check that works from a hand-kept list is only as complete as the list. Derive the
list from the thing being checked, so that adding the thing adds it to the check.

## 408. A Vault container was "ready" on a log line before Docker forwarded its port, so the first write was refused

**Symptom.** 2026-09-30, `make push-gate` on the Phase 118 tip: `TestReleaseGate_AnInputResolvesOutOfARealVault`
failed with `writing the secret: Post "http://localhost:43674/...": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:43674: connect:
connection refused`, 2.00s into the test, and passed when re-run alone. `flaky-packages.json` had carried the
package since 2026-08-26 as contention. This was the first run that printed a tolerated failure's own output
(FAILURE_PATTERNS 402's fix), and the output said it was not a lost race at all.

**Root cause.** The container waited for `wait.ForLog("Vault server started!")`, which proves the server is
listening inside the container. It does not prove Docker is forwarding the mapped host port, and under load
the gap between the two is long enough for one request to land in it. The test's first request is a single
`http.DefaultClient` POST with no retry, so it found the gap; the sshd containers that wait on a log line the
same way reach their port through the SSH dial's retry, which hides the same gap.

**Fix.** The wait is `wait.ForAll` of the log line and an HTTP 200 from `/v1/sys/health` through the mapped
port, both under `testsupport.ContainerStartupTimeout`. Health answers 200 only once Vault is initialized,
unsealed and active, and it goes through the same port the test then writes to. The same wait cannot finish
before the mapped port exists, which also closes the 2026-08-26 symptom (`port "8200/tcp" not found`), so the
package's `flaky-packages.json` entry, which called both a lost race rather than a defect, is removed.

**Lesson.** A readiness check proves the path it checks. Wait on the path the test will use, through the host
port it will use, rather than on something the server says about itself inside the container. About fifteen
other containers here still wait on a log line alone; they are not failing because their callers retry, which
is luck rather than design.

**Follow-up, the same day.** The pattern is now shared: `testsupport.ForGreeting` (and `SSHGreeting`) reads a
server's first line through the mapped port, generalizing the NATS greeting wait FAILURE_PATTERNS 353 added,
and stops at once when the container exits. Every sshd and netopeer2 container that publishes a port waits for
its log line and then its banner; the generic gRPC device waits for its listening port too, and the ServiceNow
mock for an HTTPS answer. The Ansible gate's sshd publishes no port and is reached from another container, so
it keeps its log wait.

## 409. A roadmap item cited `TestCheckCmdEnvReads`, which was never written, and the refusal it named was tested only by a lab gate

**Symptom.** 2026-09-30, the roadmap tracker's missing-test check flagged a finished Phase 75 item, "pass
runbook data into a shell as data", for citing `TestCheckCmdEnvReads`. No commit ever defined it.
`checkCmdEnvReads` is the refusal that keeps a cmd script from reading its own environment value as `%NAME%`,
which cmd.exe expands before it parses the line: measured on Windows 11, a value `a & echo INJECTED` ran the
echo. The only test that reached it was the WinRM modes Release Gate, which skips on every machine without the
lab's Windows host.

**Root cause.** The item's evidence was written from the plan when the item closed, not read from the tree,
and a gate that needs a lab host is green everywhere else by skipping. Nothing compared the two until the
tracker's check.

**Fix.** `TestCheckCmdEnvReads` exists now: both expansion forms (`%NAME%`, `%NAME:...%`), any case, the
`!NAME!` form that stays text, a variable the command does not set, and a longer name sharing the prefix.
`TestRun_RejectsBeforeTouchingCredentials` gained the case through `Execute`, so the refusal is shown to come
before any credential is read. Dropping the substring branch fails two cases. The tracker's other stale
citations (a file moved to `pkg/breaker`, three renamed tests, a report built as two files) now name what
exists, with the history in prose.

**Lesson.** A security refusal proved only by a gate that needs a lab is unproved on every other machine. Give
it a unit test that runs everywhere, and let the lab gate prove the part only the lab can: that the real shell
agrees.

## 410. `tools/doctor`'s coverage was a property of whichever machine ran its tests

**Symptom.** `tools/doctor` measured 71.1% here with no floor. Its tests ran the real checks, so a machine with
Docker, every pinned scanner and pywinrm covered the "ok" branches and none of the "fix" ones, and a bare
machine the reverse. A floor recorded on one would fail or pass on another for no change at all, and nothing
proved the fix lines a new contributor most needs.

**Root cause.** Code that asks the machine was only ever tested against the machine running the test.

**Fix.** The checks ask through four replaceable seams (`run`, `lookPath`, `getenv`, `goVersion`), and
`checks_test.go` describes a machine with everything and one with nothing, plus a scanner at the wrong or an
unreadable version and a toolchain older than go.mod asks for. Coverage is 82.2% on any machine; the live test
still asks the real one.

**Lesson.** A test of code that reads its environment has to run against an environment it describes too, or
its coverage, and any floor set from it, belongs to whoever ran it last.

## 411. Schedule pages were ordered by name and resumed by id, so following Next skipped schedules

**Symptom.** Found 2026-09-30 by a subagent seeding a second schedule for the view conformance suite, and
confirmed with a test written before the fix: five schedules named `zulu` through `victor`, created in that
order and paged one at a time, returned `victor` and then nothing. Four of the five could not be reached by
paging, through the Schedules view or `GET /schedules`, which share `schedule.Store.List`.

**Root cause.** `List` ordered by `(name, schedule_id)` and resumed with `schedule_id > after`. Schedule ids
are time-ordered, so any schedule whose name sorted before a newer one's fell behind the cursor. The store's
own paging test created `sched-0` to `sched-4` in name order, where the two orders agree, and checked only for
a schedule on both pages, never for one on neither.

**Fix.** The cursor stays a schedule id, which is what an API client passes back, and the page resumes after
that schedule's place in the order: `name > n OR (name = n AND schedule_id > after)`. A cursor whose schedule
was deleted is refused with `ErrNotFound`, since its place is unknown and resuming anywhere else would skip or
repeat without saying so (`TestListFollowsTheCursorInNameOrder`, `TestListRefusesACursorThatNoLongerExists`);
`GET /schedules` answers that with a 400 naming the cursor rather than a 404, which a client asking for a list
would read as an empty collection.

**Lesson.** A keyset cursor must compare the same columns the query orders by. A paging test has to create
records whose orders disagree, and check that every record appears once, not only that none appears twice.

## 412. The Access list linked every row to its team and none to its grant, and the drill-down test skipped it

**Symptom.** Found the same way. `/ui/access` rendered six grants, and every row's links went to `/ui/teams/<id>`;
none reached `/ui/access/<id>`, the grant's own page, which holds its Edit and Delete. The conformance drill-down
and edit-form tests reported "no seeded record to walk into" and skipped.

**Root cause.** The grant's primary field was `team`, which references the Teams view, and a referencing cell
links to what it names before a primary cell links to its row (`TableModel.CellHref`). The drill-down test
treated "no record link on the page" as "no records", so the one outcome it exists to catch read as a skip.

**Fix.** `granted_at`, the view's own id field, is the primary field; the team column still links to its team.
`view.Register` refuses a view whose records open and whose primary list field references another view, and
the drill-down test fails when the list returns rows and links none of them. The paging test now says when a
reader does not page at all rather than blaming the fixture.

**Lesson.** A test's skip has to distinguish "nothing to check" from "the check found nothing", or its most
important failure reads as a missing fixture.

## 413. A dependency update moved grpc from a patched release to one that reintroduced a vulnerability, and the gate passed

**Symptom.** 2026-09-30, `chore/dependency-updates` moved every direct module to its latest, grpc among them
(1.83.2 to 1.84.0), and `make push-gate` passed. Its `govulncheck` summary had changed from 0 to 1
"vulnerability in packages you import": GO-2026-6443, a server panic in grpc's HTTP/2 transport and xDS routing
on a request with neither `:authority` nor `Host`. The advisory's ranges: fixed in 1.83.2, reintroduced in
1.84.0, and since fixed only in an unreleased 1.85 build. Nothing here calls the vulnerable functions; the
package came in through `internal/inventory/onboard`'s gRPC probe.

**Root cause.** Latest is not the same as fixed: a newer release can lack a patch an older point release
carries. And `make govulncheck` fails only when this module calls a vulnerable function, so a vulnerable
package newly imported is a changed number in a summary no step compares with anything.

**Fix.** grpc stays at 1.83.2, with the reason in the commit; the imported count is 0 again.

**Lesson.** After a dependency update, compare `govulncheck`'s imported and required counts with the base
branch's, not only its exit status. A count that rises is a regression even when nothing calls it yet.

## 414. A tolerated failure's printed output was fifteen lines of teardown and not one word of why

**Symptom.** 2026-09-30, the dependency branch's gate tolerated `internal/topology`'s
`TestLockBucketReaderNeverReshapes` (121s under load, 1s alone) and printed "why it failed under load": a NATS
broker's startup log and four lines of container teardown. The line saying what failed was among the "24 earlier
line(s) left out".

**Root cause.** FAILURE_PATTERNS 402's fix kept a failure's last lines, and the last lines of a container test
are what ran after the failure: cleanup, teardown and a helper's log dump.

**Fix.** When none of the kept lines came from the test's own `_test.go` file, `FailureOutput` also keeps the
last line that did, marked as such (`TestFailureOutput_KeepsTheReasonBehindATailOfTeardown`); a tail that already
has one is left alone.

**Lesson.** A summary that trims output has to trim toward the evidence, not toward the end; for a test, the
evidence is what the test's own file said.

## 415. Phase 118's Documentation Gate was ticked while most of what it named still described the old gate

**Symptom.** 2026-09-30, asked "are you updating IMPLEMENTATION.md accurately?", an audit of Phase 118's ticked
items against the code found the Documentation Gate ticked since 2026-09-29 over documents that still described
the gate Phase 118 replaced. The Makefile said the pre-push hook runs the gate, that the workflow runs no tests,
and that `push-gate` swaps in three tolerant targets nothing called any more; `flaky-packages.json`'s header said
a listed package's failure is a warning; `testgate`'s and `flakegate`'s package comments described the same rule;
docs/11 listed part of `make ci` as all of it. Three pushes went out on that tick. The same audit found two
items describing their plan rather than what was built (a `-tier` flag and a `ci-coverage` target, neither of
which exists), a secrets claim made false by a later change, and a clean-room pass a day older than the code.

**Root cause.** The item was ticked after editing some of the documents it names, not after reading each of
them against what the code runs. The one phrase changed in the flaky list's header was the one being looked at.
And nothing re-read a ticked item when later work changed what it claimed.

**Fix.** Every named document was read against the targets and code it describes and corrected
(`b755584f`, `15b1dba1`); the dead targets and `coverage-check -tolerant` were removed rather than re-described;
the deviations were written into their items; the clean room was re-run on the committed tip; the Documentation
Gate was unticked until then and re-ticked with that evidence.

**Lesson.** Tick a documentation item after reading every document it names against the code, not after editing
the ones in view. Before a push, re-read the ticked items later work touched: a tick records one moment, and a
push asserts the present.

## 416. The first pull-request run failed at steps no local gate runs, and reading them against the pinned actions found two more

**Symptom.** 2026-10-01, Phase 118's pull request (#48): every `containers` shard and the Ubuntu `fast` job failed.
Shard 2's pull step asked Docker Hub for a repository called `65532`. Shards 1, 3 and 4 failed at their upload
with `No files were found with the provided path: .coverage/*.json`.

**Root cause.** Three CI-only steps no local gate had run. `tools/testimages` keeps the value of any constant whose
name contains `Image`, and `tests/e2e`'s `packagingImageUID = "65532:65532"` has the shape of `name:tag`.
`upload-artifact` 4.6.2 skips hidden paths unless told otherwise, and its glob for `.coverage/*.json` starts its
search at the hidden directory and skips it whole (read in its bundled code at the pinned commit); the single-file
path in the `fast` job would have worked. And macOS ran as an advisory leg of the `fast` matrix that `coverage`
needs, so its first failure could keep the ratchet from running. The workflow had been linted, and `actionlint`
checks a workflow's shape, not what each pinned action does with its inputs.

**Fix.** A reference whose repository has no letter is not an image; every shard's pull and cache save were run
here as the job runs them. Both uploads set `include-hidden-files: true`. macOS is its own job, which nothing
needs. The Linux jobs run on `ubuntu-24.04` by name, since `ubuntu-latest` becomes Ubuntu 26 on 2026-10-19 and the
user-namespace step is 24.04's, and the container and nightly jobs free the disk a runner is promised only 14 GB
of before pulling up to 4.8 GB of images and writing them again as a cache tar. `make ci-fast` and
`make ci-containers SHARD=2/4` were run here with CI's environment and wrote the files the uploads expect.

**Lesson.** A step that only CI runs is unverified until it has run somewhere. Run each one locally the way the
job runs it, and read each pinned action's handling of the inputs the step relies on, before the first run is
the one that finds out.

## 417. A failed run wrote no job summary, and the summary would have carried test output unmasked

**Symptom.** The same run's Ubuntu `fast` job failed in `make ci-fast` after 13 minutes, and nothing readable said
why: the job's log needs admin rights on a public repository, and `testgate` returned before writing the summary
on any failing path, so the summary page was empty exactly when it mattered. Asked whether the summary could leak
secrets, the answer was that it could: it carries each failure's own output, and the container jobs hand their
tests `LOCALSTACK_AUTH_TOKEN`.

**Root cause.** The summary was written as the last step of a passing run, and its content was never considered
as a place a secret could land, because GitHub masks the secrets it was given.

**Fix.** Every outcome writes the summary, failures first with their output. Everything `testgate` prints or writes
is masked through `internal/redact`, by the value of every secret-named environment variable and by shape;
`TestRun_MasksASecretATestPrints` runs a failing test that prints the token, and the value reaches neither output
while the failure is still named (with masking disabled the test fails, token visible).

**Lesson.** A report is most needed by the run that failed, so write it on every path. And a new place that
shows a test's output is a new place a secret can land: mask it there with this repository's own ruleset, not on
the strength of someone else's.

## 418. A pull request's checkout had no `main`, so the upgrade gates could not find the previous release, and test-repeat failed where nothing could read it

**Symptom.** The second GitHub run of pull request #48: containers shard 2 failed both upgrade gates on
`git merge-base HEAD main: fatal: Not a valid object name main`. In the same run Ubuntu `fast` passed every
package through `testgate` and then failed, and nothing said where: `make ci-fast`'s last step, `test-repeat`,
was a bare `go test -count=3` outside `testgate`, so its failure reached no job summary, and the log needs
admin rights to read.

**Root cause.** `actions/checkout` fetches one commit, detached, with no local `main`, and the gates asked for
`main` by name; a developer's clone always has one. And `test-repeat` predated `testgate`, so it was the one
test step whose output had no path to the summary.

**Fix.** `tests/e2e`'s `mainBranch` uses `main` where it exists and `origin/main` otherwise, with a message
naming `fetch-depth: 0` when neither exists, and the containers and nightly jobs fetch full history
(`1a35d0a6`, proved in a clone shaped like CI's checkout). `testgate -repeat n` runs the repeats and `make
test-repeat` is `go run ./tools/testgate -repeat 3 -strict` (`3070a8f1`), so the next run's summary named the
failing test (419).

**Lesson.** A CI checkout is not a clone: it has one commit and no branches, so anything that names a ref by
its local name has to be proved in a checkout shaped like CI's. And every test step belongs behind the one
reporter, because the step outside it is the one that fails unreadably.

## 419. The dispatcher gate's own watcher starved the fan-out it was waiting on

**Symptom.** Ubuntu `fast`'s `test-repeat` failed `TestDispatcher_ReleaseGate`: the job was still
`fanning_out` after 60 seconds. The same test had passed in the same job's `-race` pass minutes earlier, and
passes here in 7 seconds on four cores.

**Root cause.** `pollJobUntilTerminal` called `store.Get` every 5 ms, and `Get` eager-loads every JobTask row
recorded so far through the single SQLite connection `newSerializedSQLiteClient` allows. Each poll held the
connection the Worker needed for its next insert for as long as reading thousands of rows took, so the
watcher was most of the gate's cost, and on a hosted runner sharing four slow cores with three other test
binaries it was more than the budget. The race pass passed only because `raceTimeScale` gave it ten times
the budget.

**Fix.** The poll is 250 ms apart (3.2 seconds for the fan-out on the same four cores, identical across
three repeats), the failure message counts the rows recorded so far, and the budget is 120 seconds, written
for the slowest machine that judges it (`1ec9bd39`).

**Lesson.** A watcher that shares a resource with the work it watches is part of the work. Poll at the pace
the answer matters, not the pace the loop can run, and when a liveness bound fails, print how far the work
got.

## 420. The fast tier assumed Linux, and the first macOS run failed 43 tests that had nothing wrong

**Symptom.** `fast-macos` failed 43 tests across five packages: 35 in `internal/loader`, every one that loads
a program; 5 of `internal/catalog/http`'s device tests, each failing a TLS handshake with an unknown
authority; and one each in `internal/catalog/facts`, `internal/inventory/onboard` and `pkg/remotefile`. The
skip ledger told the macOS run to install `unshare` and change an Ubuntu sysctl.

**Root cause.** Each was a Linux fact assumed as a universal one. `Load` refuses every program where there is
no Landlock, so a test that loads one can only run on Linux, and said nothing about it. The test authority
was trusted through `SSL_CERT_FILE`, which Go's verifier reads only on Linux and the BSDs; macOS and Windows
ask the platform's store, so the variable did nothing. The facts and onboard harnesses run the method
against this machine and assert Linux's answers. Linux keeps a directory's setgid bit through a chgrp, which
POSIX leaves to the implementation. And `UserNamespaces` diagnosed a missing Linux tool on a kernel that has
no namespaces.

**Fix.** `b947d97a`: the loader's tests require `landlock` through `testsupport.Require` wherever `Load` is
called (`loadOne`, `tryLoad` and the tests calling it themselves, not `programDir`, which the approval tests
use without loading); the http tests pin the authority as the device's own `tls_ca_pem`, the product's way to
trust a private authority on any platform, and the full-URL test takes the old path's `validate_certs:
false`; facts and onboard require `linux`; the remotefile case is marked `linuxOnly`; and off Linux
`UserNamespaces` says the kernel has no such thing. Reasoned from the code and the pasted failures, since
macOS cannot run here; the fourth run is the test.

**Lesson.** "Works for others" includes the developer on a Mac. A test that needs the host to be Linux says
so through `Require`, so the ledger shows the want, and a fixture's trust should go through the product's own
mechanism, which is portable because it has to be.

## 421. Docker's port map lists an exposed port with no binding, and the mesh gate read every key as "published"

**Symptom.** Containers shard 2's mesh WSS gate failed, alone and again when re-run alone: "the broker
container published 4222 (the plain NATS client port) on []". The same gate passed here on every run.

**Root cause.** The gate asserts that this host has no route to the broker's plain client port by scanning
`Container.Ports` for forbidden keys. The runner's Docker 28.0.4 lists every port the image EXPOSEs in
`NetworkSettings.Ports`, bound to the host or not, so 4222 appeared with no bindings; Docker 29.8.0 here
lists only bound ports (checked by inspecting a `nats:2.14.4` container started with one `-p`: four exposed,
one listed). A key with an empty binding list is the image's EXPOSE, not a route.

**Fix.** A port with no binding is skipped, and the positive control still demands the websocket port with
a binding (`5e959438`; the gate passes here in 44 seconds).

**Lesson.** The shape of a daemon's inspect output is a version-dependent fact, and "exposed" and
"published" are different things. Assert the property (a binding exists), not the presence of a key.

## 422. Two tests measured once and failed a pull request whose change was one handoff document

**Symptom.** Pull request #50's second run, on a commit that changed only `HANDOFF_DOCUMENT.md`, failed both
`fast` jobs in `test-repeat`, the strict three-times-over pass. Ubuntu: `TestSecureCompare_ConstantTime`, "early-diff
took 2.617566ms, late-diff took 8.594473ms (ratio 3.28); want within 3x". macOS: `TestProcess_StreamsInBoundedMemory`,
"heap in use grew by 34504704 bytes while streaming 67108864, want at most 33554432", on the third repeat after two
passes. The previous run, on the same code and dependencies, passed both.

**Root cause.** Each test took one measurement of a noisy quantity. The timing test compared one round of each
side, and a shared runner that stops the process during one round adds milliseconds to that side alone. The memory
test sampled `HeapInuse`, which counts garbage not yet collected and spans not yet swept alongside live data, so it
measured the collector's pacing on a slow runner as much as the code; its bound had already been loosened once for
the same reason (25.8 MB against 24 MiB).

**Fix.** The timing test takes each side's fastest of 15 rounds, the two sides alternating: a stop only adds time,
so the minimum is nearest the code's own cost, and alternating puts a slow stretch on both sides. The memory test
samples runtime/metrics' `/gc/heap/live:bytes`, what the collector found reachable, which is what buffering would
inflate and garbage does not, and logs the growth it saw. Each was held to its defect by planting it: a first-byte
shortcut in `SecureCompare` fails the timing test at a ratio of 890, and reading the whole stream into memory fails
the memory test at 102 MB against the 32 MB bound. The real code grows the live heap by about 6 MB (under 1 MB with
`-race`), 15.5 MB at most with 24 busy loops on 20 CPUs, and both tests passed every run under that load (30 and 15).
A sweep found no other test comparing two timings or asserting on a raw heap counter outside a forced collection.

**Lesson.** On a shared machine, a single measurement is a sample of the machine. Take the minimum of interleaved
rounds for time, and measure the quantity the claim is about (live data, not heap in use) rather than loosening a
bound until the noise fits under it.

## 423. A failed container start was never terminated, in 47 places, and in production it left Ansible running past its job's timeout

**Symptom.** A `make push-gate` on the dependency branch (`02b4fff3`) tolerated thirteen `tests/e2e` failures between
17:41 and 17:56, each passing when re-run alone. The mesh WSS gate failed first, after 122 seconds, and every
`TestUI_*` harness test after it failed the same way: `harness_test.go:295: found unexpected goroutines`, naming one
goroutine in `testcontainers-go.(*Reaper).connect.func1`, "2 minutes" old at the first failure and "15 minutes" at
the last.

**Root cause.** Ours, not the library's. When a container's start fails partway (a wait strategy gives up, or the
context ends), testcontainers-go returns the container alongside the error, and the container keeps running, with
its reaper connection's goroutine alive, until the caller terminates it; the library's documentation says to
schedule the cleanup before checking the error. 47 of this repository's 49 container starts checked the error first
and stopped, so a failed start leaked both. In the gate, a start in the mesh WSS gate timed out during a Docker port
stall (the shared startup timeout is two minutes). The leak then failed twelve more tests because their leak check
had no baseline: each answered for every goroutine in the process. The same omission was in production:
`internal/adapters/legacy`'s orchestrator, through which the Runner runs `ansible-playbook`, returned the start error
without terminating the container, so a run whose context ended (a launch's `timeout`) was reported failed while the
playbook kept running against its devices. A first reading blamed the library (its reaper spawner discards a parked
connection without releasing it); the library hands that connection to the new container on the next line, so that
gap has no realistic path, and the user's rule to prove a fix before calling it out caught the claim before it went
anywhere.

**Fix.** Proved before changing: a start made to fail leaves 1 reaper goroutine, and 0 once terminated (a
temporary test, not kept); `TestDockerOrchestrator_ACanceledRunLeavesNoContainerRunning` failed on
the old orchestrator with the container still running after `Run` returned. Every failing-start branch now calls
the nil-safe `testcontainers.TerminateContainer`, the orchestrator with a comment saying why, and
`internal/testsupport`'s `TestEveryContainerIsTerminatedWhenItsStartFails` parses every Go file and fails on a start
whose failure path does not terminate its container (47 reported on the old tree, 0 now; six-case positive control).
At the mesh gate's own proxy, a start made to fail now fails on the start error alone, and with the fix removed it
also reports the gate's exact goroutine. Every per-test leak check now verifies against a snapshot taken when its
test starts, as `internal/backup` and `internal/transport/ssh` already did, so a leak is charged to the test that
made it.

**Lesson.** A start that fails is a container that exists. Read a library's error contract before blaming the
library, and reproduce the symptom with and without the fix before naming a cause; and a leak check without a
baseline turns one leak into a dozen failures.

## 424. The nightly job never installed socat, and a bare `t.Skip` made six missing tests read as a coverage regression

**Symptom.** The first scheduled `nightly` run (2026-10-02, run 37007388376, `main` at `6b5ff333`) passed the strict
`make test-full` and then failed `make coverage-measured`: `internal/transport/serial` at 87.5% against a floor of
100.0%, and `pkg/serialexec` at 70.4% against 95.5%. The same commit's pull-request `coverage` job and a local `make
ci` measured both at or above their floors.

**Root cause.** Two gaps, each harmless alone. The `nightly` job was written without the `fast` job's step that
installs `socat`, so the six PTY-backed serial tests skipped there. And they skipped through a bare
`t.Skip("skipping PTY-backed test: socat is not on PATH")` rather than `testsupport.Require`, which CONTRIBUTING.md
asks for. A bare skip names no need, so the run recorded nothing missing, and `coverage-check` could not tell a run
without `socat` from a package whose coverage fell. It also meant no job could require `socat`: the `fast` job losing
its install step would have quietly tested six fewer tests.

**Fix.** Both copies of `testPTYPair` (`pkg/serialexec`, `internal/transport/serial`) stop through
`testsupport.Require(t, "socat", ...)`. The `nightly` job installs `socat`, and both `fast` and `nightly` set
`PLEIADES_TEST_REQUIRE: userns,socat`. Proved with `socat` hidden from `PATH`: `tools/testgate` reproduces CI's 87.5%
and 70.4% and records `missing: socat` for both packages; `coverage-check -measured` over those numbers names both
floors unchecked and exits 0, while the same numbers without the missing record (what the old skip produced) fail
exactly as the nightly did. With `socat` required and hidden, both tests fail naming it; with it present, every test
runs and passes under `-race`.

**Lesson.** A second job that runs the same tests needs the first job's setup, and a test that skips for a missing
tool must say so in the form the gates read, or a gate cannot tell absence from regression.

## 425. GitHub's Windows runner ships its own HTTPS WinRM listener, and the lab script refused to replace it

**Symptom.** The experimental `winrm` job failed at its setup step on both of its first runs (2026-10-02, runs
37007388376 and 37012407427): "This host already has an HTTPS WinRM listener that this script did not create, and
WinRM allows only one." The WinRM gates never ran.

**Root cause.** The `windows-latest` image comes with an HTTPS WinRM listener already configured (certificate
`03330B472C89B63CBBEBE69B585EA1FA7D2989D3` in that run). `examples/windows_lab/winrm-cert-setup.ps1` refuses to
replace a listener it did not create unless given `-ReplaceExistingListener`, because its teardown cannot put a
foreign listener back. That is the right default on a real host. The job was written for a clean machine.

**Fix.** The job passes `-ReplaceExistingListener`, with a comment saying why: the runner is discarded after the job,
so there is nothing to put back. The script's default is unchanged. Whether the gates themselves pass on the runner
is still unproven until the job's next run.

**Lesson.** A hosted runner is not a clean machine. Before a setup script that refuses to overwrite runs there,
check what the image already configures.

## 426. The Podman fixture's passwords were refused on the CI runners and accepted under Docker Desktop

**Symptom.** PR #54's `containers (1)` shard failed `TestEngineProbe_Podman` and
`TestPodmanService_ADroppedSessionLeavesNothingRunning` with "ssh: unable to authenticate", and both failed again
when re-run alone (2026-10-14, run 38587017209). The fixture's sshd log, printed on failure since bde456d0, said
"Failed password for podman" and "Failed password for root". Both tests passed on the WSL machine against the same
`quay.io/podman/stable:v5.8.7` digest, and the runners' image cache had been built from that digest the same day.

**Root cause.** Somewhere in Fedora 44's PAM password path on the CI runners (Docker Engine on Ubuntu 24.04), and
not under Docker Desktop. Which module refused is unproven: `pam_unix` logs to syslog, which the container has
none of, so sshd's own line was all there was.

**Fix.** 7a6599e7: the fixture's sshd checks the password against `/etc/shadow` itself (`UsePAM no`), and the
next run passed both tests with no re-run. A failed test now also logs the fixture's effective login settings
(`sshd -T`), each account's password scheme (the hash's prefix only) and sshd's capabilities, so a refusal on a
machine nobody can log into names its reason.

**Lesson.** A fixture's login stack is part of the environment it is tested in. When a CI-only refusal cannot be
reproduced, take the variable component out of the fixture's path and make the fixture report its decisive state
when it fails.

## 427. Code moved between packages left its tests behind, and eight coverage floors failed at once

**Symptom.** PR #54's coverage job (run 38590937755) reported eight packages below their floors:
`internal/inventory/record` 78.5% (floor 100), `devices/container` 77.8% (91.5), `onboard` 84.6% (91.9),
`credential` 91.5% (93.0), `validate` 95.4% (100), `pkg/capability` 97.6% (100), `devices/linux` 98.5% (100) and
`pkg/remoteexec` 94.3% (94.5). `devices/engines` had no tests at all.

**Root cause.** 119a and 119b moved the discovery rules from `devices/generic` into `record`, and added engine
accessors, a route planner, a registry store and probers whose behavior was tested only from other packages
(`cmd/pleiades`'s release gates, the generic types' tests). A floor counts the package's own tests. Nothing local
measured it, since the gate now runs in Actions.

**Fix.** 35a07941 tests each in its own package: records with recorded discoveries, fake engines on real Unix
sockets and a real TLS server, a failure-injecting repository, a real loopback SSH server. Every package is at or
above its floor (`onboard` 92.9%, `remoteexec` 95.3%, the rest 93.5% to 100%).

**Lesson.** When code moves, its tests move with it; a release gate elsewhere proves behavior, never the floor.

## 428. probe_linux.go's file name built the Linux server prober on Linux only

**Symptom.** PR #54's `ci` jobs on macOS and Windows failed vet on a new test: "undefined: linuxProber"
(run 38600372480). The Linux jobs and the WSL machine passed.

**Root cause.** Go reads a `_linux.go` suffix as a build constraint. 119b's Linux server prober probes a remote
server over SSH, but sat in `probe_linux.go`, so it compiled only into Linux builds, and on macOS or Windows
`pleiades onboard <linux_server>` answered that the type has no prober. No Linux build could notice.

**Fix.** 7016137a renames it `probe_linux_server.go`, and `internal/archtest`'s
`TestFileNamesConstrainBuildsOnlyOnPurpose` refuses a Go file whose name implies an OS or architecture unless a
`//go:build` line names it; it fails on the old name.

**Lesson.** A file name can decide a build silently; a portable file never ends in an OS or architecture.

**Repeat.** This is 303 again (2026-09-23): a file constrained to Linux left a symbol undefined on macOS and Windows.
303's lesson was to vet for every operating system CI builds before calling a change verified, and on PR #54 that
was not done, so the fix lived in a sentence and the failure came back. What holds it now is mechanical: the
archtest against file-name constraints (this entry's fix), and `make pr-check-vet` inside `make pr-check`, whose
receipt the pre-push hook requires for a branch (LESSONS 271).

## 429. A refused SSH host key was retried three times and opened the address's circuit

**Symptom.** Onboarding a cluster through a bastion whose key `known_hosts` did not hold reported "retry:
exhausted 3 attempt(s) ... knownhosts: key is unknown". A test against a real loopback SSH server showed three
handshakes per call, and the second call refused with "circuit open" without dialing.

**Root cause.** `pkg/remoteexec`'s `dialWithRetry` treated only "ssh: unable to authenticate" as the far side's
answer. A `knownhosts.KeyError` or `RevokedError`, this side refusing the server, counted as a network failure:
retried, and recorded against the address's breaker, so one stale `known_hosts` entry refused every other task
on that host.

**Fix.** `hostKeyRefused` (`errors.As` on both types) is neither retried nor counted, like a refused credential;
`TestConnect_ARefusedHostKeyIsNotRetried` and `TestConnect_ARefusedHostKeyDoesNotOpenTheCircuit` fail without it.

**Lesson.** An answer is not an outage, whichever side refused.

## 430. Kubernetes discovery recorded only preferred versions, which would have refused valid manifests

**Symptom.** Found while writing the manifest kind rule (Phase 119c): discovery recorded
`autoscaling/v2 HorizontalPodAutoscaler` but not `autoscaling/v1`, so a manifest at `v1`, which the cluster
serves, would have been refused as unserved.

**Root cause.** `ServerPreferredResources` lists each kind at the version a client would pick, not every version
the server serves.

**Fix.** Discovery uses `ServerGroupsAndResourcesWithContext`, records `kinds_truncated` when it keeps fewer than
the server named, and the live test asserts both HPA versions against k3s 1.35 and 1.37.

**Lesson.** A record of what a server serves holds everything it serves, not what one client would choose.

## 431. A hostile API server could make discovery unbounded, and its whole answer reached an error

**Symptom.** `FuzzDiscover`'s first run: an undecodable rules review came back as an error quoting the entire
body ("Object 'Kind' is missing in '...'"). Reading the code for the harness showed one rule's groups times its
resources listed as their product, so 2,000 of each would be four million entries.

**Root cause.** client-go quotes an undecodable body into its error, and nothing bounded the discovery's bytes,
the entries per rule, or the error text.

**Fix.** Discovery reads through one 128 MiB budget for all its answers, keeps 64 entries per rule and marks the
rules incomplete when it cuts one, and `kubeapi.Explain` keeps 512 bytes of error text with every non-printable
rune escaped.

**Lesson.** Text a remote system wrote is bounded and escaped before it reaches an error.

## 432. A replacing kubeconfig import over the API reported success and wrote nothing

**Symptom.** `TestImportKubeconfig_Replace`: the replacement answered 200 and the stored record still had the old
`api_server`.

**Root cause.** `entRepository.Save` writes only the revisions an item recorded beyond its loaded version. A record
rebuilt by the factory with new properties records none, so `Save` returned nil without writing.

**Fix.** The replacement changes the loaded record through `AddInfo` and `RemoveInfo` for the four properties an
import owns, checks the result through the factory, then saves; the test also proves a property the operator set
survives.

**Lesson.** Change a stored device through its loaded record's change methods; a rebuilt record saves nothing.
This is FAILURE_PATTERNS 261's defect again, in a new handler: `DeviceHandler.Update` had the same shape and the
same fix.

## 433. A branch checkout in an auxiliary worktree moved the main worktree's branch

**Symptom.** After work in a second worktree that switched branches, the main worktree's index showed every staged
change reversed.

**Root cause.** Worktrees share branch refs. Checking a branch out and committing in another worktree moved the ref
the main worktree had checked out beneath it.

**Fix.** `git reset --mixed HEAD` in the main worktree. Since then an auxiliary worktree is created detached at a
commit (`git worktree add --detach`), and its work is pushed with `git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/<branch>`, then
fast-forwarded into the main worktree.

**Lesson.** Never switch branches in an auxiliary worktree.

## 434. The moby client's hijacked connections bypassed the engine guard's dialer

**Symptom.** Phase 119b: an exec through the engine port skipped the guard's operation table.

**Root cause.** The moby client dials a hijacked request (exec, attach) itself whenever its transport has a TLS
config, and cloning a default transport gives it one, so the hijack never went through the dialer the guard wraps.

**Fix.** `newAPI` builds an HTTP/1-only transport; `TestSession_HijackedRequestsPassTheGuard` fails without it.

**Lesson.** A guard on a dialer guards only the connections that dial through it; prove each path does.

## 435. No stdio login was ever pooled

**Symptom.** Phase 119b: every engine session over the stdio carrier logged in anew, though the pool was meant to
lend the login to the next task.

**Root cause.** Each enough alone: `Conn.Start` tainted the lease for the `dial-stdio` process; the dial's context
ended the process when the dial returned; and the HTTP transport closes a finished request's connection on its own
goroutine, after the session had released the login.

**Fix.** A lease counts its streamed processes (`lease.running`) and a `Wait` that sees one exit counts it out;
`dial-stdio`'s life is detached from the dial context; the carrier closes its processes before releasing the login.

**Lesson.** A pool's reuse is a claim to measure, not to assume: count the reuses.

## 436. Two checks passed vacuously against the Docker fixture

**Symptom.** Phase 119b: a check over the dind fixture's files found nothing and passed.

**Root cause.** busybox `find` refused the size `64M` and the error was swallowed, and `-xdev` skipped the volume
the files were on.

**Fix.** The command's error is checked, and a canary file the check must find proves it looked.

**Lesson.** A check that can find nothing must prove, with a canary, that it looked.

## 437. OpenSSH applies AllowTcpForwarding to Unix-socket channels and answers every refusal "connect failed"

**Symptom.** Phase 119b: a channel to the engine's socket was refused on an sshd whose forwarding settings looked
irrelevant to Unix sockets, with the same "connect failed" a missing socket gives.

**Root cause.** OpenSSH applies `AllowTcpForwarding` to `direct-streamlocal` channels too (Alpine's default is
`no`), and `DisableForwarding`, `AllowStreamLocalForwarding no`, a key restricted with `no-port-forwarding`, an
absent socket and an unreadable one all come back as the one answer; only sshd's log says which.

**Fix.** The refusal names every cause the answer allows rather than guessing one
(`remoteexec.describeChannelRefusal`), and the fixtures set `AllowTcpForwarding local`.

**Lesson.** When a server gives one answer for many causes, the message lists them all.

## 438. The engine guard judged a decoded path when the target held an invalid character

**Symptom.** Phase 119b, `FuzzGuard_RequestLine`: a request target holding a character not valid in a path was
judged by the operation table as a path the engine never received.

**Root cause.** The URL parser dropped such a target's raw form, so the guard decided on a decoded path while the
engine would parse the string as sent.

**Fix.** The guard decides on the target exactly as written and refuses one that is not its own canonical escaping
(an encoded slash, a dot segment, an invalid character, a non-canonical escape); Docker's own client sends only
canonical targets, so nothing it sends is refused.

**Lesson.** A guard decides on exactly the bytes the far side will read.

## 439. Closing an SSH exec channel did not stop the remote process

**Symptom.** Phase 119b: the Podman API service a session started was still running after the session's `Close`.

**Root cause.** Closing the channel ends the client's side; sshd does not signal the process on the far side.

**Fix.** The service is started with an idle timeout and stopped explicitly on `Close`;
`TestPodmanService_ADroppedSessionLeavesNothingRunning` proves a dropped login leaves nothing running within the
idle time.

**Lesson.** Over SSH, closing a channel is not stopping a process; stop it, and bound how long it can outlive you.

## 440. A test asserted on `ps` in an image with no `ps` and passed vacuously

**Symptom.** Phase 119b: a check that no process was left running passed, and kept passing when one was.

**Root cause.** The image has no `ps`; the command failed, its output was empty, and "nothing matched" read as
"nothing running".

**Fix.** The fixture installs `procps-ng`, and the check fails when its command fails.

**Lesson.** A check that looks for absence must fail when it cannot look.

## 441. container_host parsed its TLS settings and never exposed them, so a pinned authority was ignored

**Symptom.** Phase 119b: the TLS carrier verified an engine against the system's roots although the record pinned
`tls_ca_pem`.

**Root cause.** `NewHost` parsed the settings but the type did not implement `devicetls.Configured`, so
`devicetls.For` returned the defaults.

**Fix.** `Host.TLSSettings` implements it; a test reads the pinned authority back through it.

**Lesson.** A parsed setting nothing exposes is a setting nothing uses; test it through the reader.

## 442. trust-host --first-connect wrote a fixture's key into the real ~/.ssh/known_hosts

**Symptom.** Phase 119b: a test run left an ephemeral fixture's host key in the developer's own `known_hosts`.

**Root cause.** The test resolved `known_hosts` from the home directory, as production does.

**Fix.** Tests point `PLEIADES_KNOWN_HOSTS` at a file of their own.

**Lesson.** A test never writes to a file the developer owns.

## 443. A fixture's SSHDConfig option replaced its default AllowTcpForwarding instead of adding to it

**Symptom.** Phase 119b: a stress test meant only to raise `MaxStartups` lost every socket channel.

**Root cause.** `testsupport.EngineHostOptions.SSHDConfig` replaces the default drop-in (`AllowTcpForwarding
local`) rather than adding to it, so forwarding fell back to Alpine's `no`.

**Fix.** The stress tests pass both settings, and the option's documentation says it replaces the default.

**Lesson.** An option that replaces a default says so where it is set.


## 444. The SSH test fixture's forwarder never ended a connection its destination kept open

**Symptom.** Two new tests passed their bodies and then hung in cleanup until the test timeout (10 and 8 minutes):
the bastion's `remoteexectest.Server.Close` waited forever on a forwarded connection.

**Root cause.** `forwardDirectTCPIP` copied both directions and waited for both, and its comment said either side
closing ended both. It did not: when the client's side ended, the copy back from the destination stayed blocked
reading from a destination that keeps an idle connection open (an echo that waits for more, client-go's HTTP/2
connection to an API server). OpenSSH's sshd half-closes the destination socket when the client's side ends.

**Fix.** The forwarder half-closes the destination (`CloseWrite`) when the client's side ends, as sshd does, so an
HTTP server reads the end of the stream and closes. Every package using the fixture passes with it.

**Lesson.** A fixture standing in for a real server copies that server's connection lifecycle, not only its bytes.

## 445. Pull request #55 failed CI twice on checks that run locally in minutes

**Symptom.** PR #55's `ci (ubuntu-24.04, true)` failed `tidy-check` (`k8s.io/klog/v2` marked indirect though
imported directly), and its `coverage` job failed eight floors and nearly a ninth, after a local run of every
touched package's tests had passed.

**Root cause.** Tests passing is not the gate. The PR was pushed without `make ci-remote` (about three minutes
here) and without measuring each touched package's coverage against `coverage-floor.json`, so both failures were
first seen in CI, the same way PR #54's coverage failure was (427).

**Fix.** `go.mod` tidied; each package's gaps tested in its own package (99 to 100% where the floor is 100); every
floor and `make ci-remote` verified locally before the next push.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 270.

**Repeat.** In kind, this is 427 eight hours earlier: a push whose checks had not been run here, each failure first
seen in CI. LESSONS 270 answered it with a procedure, which 449 then shows being followed narrowly the same day.

## 446. k3s died at startup in CI because the fixture's readiness exec raced its cgroup move

**Symptom.** PR #55's `fast` job failed three `pkg/kubeapi` tests with `starting the k3s fixture ...: container
exec create: ... is not running`, and the server's last lines were kubelet's `Failed to start ContainerManager ...
cgroup ["kubepods"] has some missing controllers: cpu, cpuset, hugetlb, memory, pids`. The same tests had passed
in the PR's previous run and pass alone.

**Root cause.** k3s, as pid 1 on cgroup v2, starts by reading its root cgroup's process list once, moving those
processes into `/init`, and then writing each controller into the root's `cgroup.subtree_control`
(`rootlesskit/pkg/parent/cgrouputil.EvacuateCgroup2`, called from `pkg/cli/server/server.go` line 70, before logging
starts). A process entering the root cgroup between the read and the writes makes every write fail with EBUSY, and
k3s only logs `failed to enable controller` and carries on; kubelet then dies on the missing controllers. A `docker
exec` enters exactly that cgroup, and `testsupport.StartK3s`'s readiness wait was two `wait.ForExec` probes sent the
moment the container started. On an idle machine k3s finishes the move first; on a loaded runner it does not.
Reproduced here: with the container's CPU at `--cpus=0.05` and execs from the start, 2 of 3 starts logged `failed to
enable controller ... write /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.subtree_control: device or resource busy` for all seven
controllers, against 0 of 2 with no execs and 0 of 3 unthrottled.

**Fix.** The wait now begins with `wait.ForLog("Starting k3s")`, which k3s logs at `server.go` line 512, after the
move, in both pinned images (`wait.ForAll` runs its strategies in order); under the same throttle and exec storm 0
of 4 starts warned. A failed start's message leads with any `failed to enable controller` line (`k3sLastWords`),
since kubelet's own last words never name it, and the fixture's test asserts no such line.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 272.

## 447. The container-list guard read a proxy, so pkg/kubeapi reached CI unlisted

**Symptom.** `pkg/kubeapi` starts k3s in its tests but was missing from the Makefile's `DOCKER_DEPENDENT_PACKAGES`,
so CI's fast tier ran it beside every other package and three times over in `test-repeat`, where 446 killed it.
`TestEveryContainerPackageIsListed`, which exists to catch exactly this, passed.

**Root cause.** The guard read whether a package's test files import testcontainers-go, a proxy for "starts a
container". `pkg/kubeapi` starts k3s through `testsupport.StartK3s` and imports no testcontainers-go itself. The
Makefile's own comment already named the hole (`pkg/sftpxfer` and `pkg/scpxfer` were listed by hand for the same
reason), so the guard was known to miss this shape and nothing stopped the next package from having it.

**Fix.** The guard now reads the property: `scanForContainers` parses every Go file in the module, records each
function's calls, seeds the functions that create a container (testcontainers-go's `GenericContainer`, a module's
`Run`, `network.New`, or `docker`/`podman` run, create, start, build or compose), and follows calls to a fixed
point, so a test reaching a starter through any helper counts; it takes 1.5 seconds. It found `pkg/kubeapi`, and
`internal/engine` and `internal/forge/playbook`, which run a one-shot `docker run --rm` of the Ansible image; those
two stay in the fast tier through `oneShotContainerPackages`, each with its reason, and only while they start no
testcontainers-go fixture.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 273.

**Repeat.** This is 239 again. 239's guard was the fix for a container package missing from the list, and it read the
import that had just failed, which is exactly what LESSONS 114 had warned about months before: a guard written after
an incident is written against its literal. The Makefile's comment then recorded the miss as two hand-listed
exceptions instead of a defect in the guard, so the third package of that shape went to CI unlisted.

## 448. pkg/tftpxfer's Get timed out on macOS twice running, and the cause is still unknown

**Symptom.** `fast-macos` failed on PR #55's runs 38636093862 and 38651908450, both times in
`TestLongestAcceptedFilenamesCrossARealServerWhole` during the strict `test-repeat`, in different subtests
(`largest_blocksize/a_space`, then `smallest_blocksize/exactly_the_limit,_nested`): the Put succeeded, then the Get
failed after about 61 seconds with `read udp [::]:<port>: i/o timeout`. The first of three repeats failed and the
other two passed in milliseconds. Every earlier `fast-macos` run passed, including #55's first.

**Ruled out.** This branch changes nothing `pkg/tftpxfer` depends on (its dependency set intersected with
`tools/prscope`'s list is empty, and no module it uses moved), and all three runs used runner image 20260828.587. One
lost datagram is not enough: pin/tftp v3.2.0 retransmits at every step, so 61 seconds is six unanswered attempts.
Not reproduced on Linux: 40 runs of all 18 subtests under `-race` passed.

**Root cause.** Unknown. One hypothesis, unproven: pin/tftp's client listens on the dual-stack wildcard `[::]`, the
server answers from a socket bound to `127.0.0.1`, and XNU's search for a free port for an IPv6 socket skips IPv4
sockets (`in6_pcblookup_local` continues past any pcb without `INP_IPV6`), so the client could be handed a port an
IPv4 socket on `127.0.0.1` holds, which then receives the replies. XNU's netns reservation may already prevent that,
and the source does not settle it.

**Fix.** None yet, deliberately. The test server now records every transfer it finished (client address and port,
options, datagrams sent and acknowledged, duration, outcome) and prints them when a test fails, proven with a
deliberate failure, so the next occurrence says whether the server answered the client's port or never saw the
request. `fast-macos` is advisory, so this does not block a merge.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 269: when a failure happens only where nobody can log in, make the fixture say why.

**Third occurrence, 2026-11-04 (still open).** PR #112's advisory job `fast-macos (1)`, Actions run 41904826019 at
`04756356`, in the strict `test-repeat` pass: `TestLongestAcceptedFilenamesCrossARealServerWhole/largest_blocksize/non-ASCII`
failed in a Put this time, not a Get. The request to send `"配置.txt"` at blksize 16356 timed out (`filename_test.go:160:
Put: tftpxfer: requesting to send "配置.txt": read udp [::]:57863: i/o timeout`). The server dump this entry's fix added
is the first evidence from inside a failure: 6 attempts, each `sent=6 acked=0` and about 32 seconds long, with the
server sending to `127.0.0.1:<client port>` and receiving no reply. So the request reached the server each time, and
the client, listening on the dual-stack `[::]:57863`, never read the server's replies. Resources were not short
(3780 MB free, no swap growth). It is not PR #112's code. This fits the unproven hypothesis
above (client on `[::]`, server answering from `127.0.0.1`) but does not prove it. The real fix is still open; the
candidates are to pin the client to `udp4` and `127.0.0.1`, or a recorded, counted retry on darwin (CI_LESSONS 24).
The ledger entries are annotated with this pattern.

**Resolved 2026-11-06 (fixed on `fix/open-patterns-batch2`, `8a7b91fd` and `07929043`).** **Cause, measured** on the
owner's Mac (macOS 27.0.1, XNU arm64) through `pleiades`: pin/tftp's client opens `net.ListenUDP("udp",
&net.UDPAddr{})`, a dual-stack IPv6 wildcard socket. XNU can give that socket an ephemeral port that an IPv4 socket
bound to `127.0.0.1` already holds, with no error, and a datagram sent to `127.0.0.1` on that port then goes to the
IPv4 socket. A probe on the Mac: of 2,000 dual-stack sockets, 253 shared a port with an IPv4 loopback socket, and 253
of 253 datagrams sent to such a port reached the IPv4 socket. With the sockets bound to `127.0.0.1` instead, none
shared a port; on Linux, none did either way. This is the hypothesis above, now measured, and it matches the third
occurrence's dump: the server sent to `127.0.0.1:<client port>` six times, about 32 seconds each, `sent=6 acked=0`,
and the client never read a reply because another socket received them. Linux runs could never have shown it.

**Fix.** `newClient` (`pkg/tftpxfer/tftpxfer.go`) resolves the server through `net.DefaultResolver` with the task's
context (`net.ResolveUDPAddr` takes no context, so a lookup used to run past a cancelled task), and for an IPv4
server binds the client socket to the source address of the route to the server (`pkg/tftpxfer/localaddr.go`). An
IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal takes the IPv4 path. An IPv6 server keeps the library's own socket; that this is safe is
reasoned, not measured.

**Tests.** `TestAnIPv4ClientSocketLeavesItsPortFreeOnIPv6`, `TestTransfersSurviveIPv4SocketsHoldingManyPorts` (on the
Mac with `main`'s code, 9 of 40 Gets timed out with the CI signature) and `TestResolveServer_EndsWithItsContext`, each
red on the old code. `TestResolveServer_TakesTheIPv4Address` and the mapped-literal subtests guard against a regression
only. The first version of the bind test could pass with the fix reverted (958). A second model's research (r448)
agreed with the cause. The ledger entries are annotated with it.

## 449. A touched package CI could not floor-check was left out of the pre-push measurement

**Symptom.** `make pr-check`'s first full run found `pkg/awscloud` at 94.9% against its 95.8% floor. 119c had added
`eks.go` with two untested error branches, and the measurement taken before pushing `0d2b11aa` had not included the
package.

**Root cause.** LESSONS 270 says to measure every touched package; the measurement covered the packages CI's
coverage job had named. CI runs without LocalStack, so it reports `pkg/awscloud` as unchecked rather than failed,
and a list copied from CI's failures can never contain it. The rule was followed narrowly, in the shape of the last
failure, which is 445's pattern repeating within the day.

**Fix.** A nil context is now tested (reachable) and the Windows platform branch of `instanceFrom` is covered as a
pure unit test, since the signer's error cannot happen with this SDK; 131 of 136 statements, 96.3%. The procedure is
now a target: `make pr-check` measures every package the branch changes itself (`tools/prscope`), and its receipt is
required for a branch push.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 271.


## 450. The docker CLI methods passed names and images unchecked, so an image of `--privileged` ran a privileged container (a repeat of 148)

**Symptom.** A verification sweep of the container methods (2026-10-14) found `container.docker.run`, `stop` and
`remove` building `docker run -d --name NAME ... IMAGE CMD` with every value quoted and none checked, and no `--`
before the operands. `image: --privileged` with `command: [alpine, sh]` created a privileged container; a name of
`--help` made `docker inspect` exit 0, read as "exists".

**Root cause.** Quoting stops a shell, not option parsing (LESSONS 137). 148 fixed the one `cd` in
`internal/catalog/exec`'s command line and 137 stated the rule, but the sweep that followed looked at shell
commands, and these methods build an argv for `remoteexec.QuoteCommand`, which reads as already safe.

**Fix.** `eff5b82d`: names through `containerengine.ValidName`, images through the new `containerengine.ValidImage`
(the distribution reference grammar), restart policies against docker's set, ports and volumes refused with a
leading `-` or a control character, all before connecting; every flag in its equals form and `--` before the
image and the name. Hostile-value table tests fail on the old code.

**Lesson.** A repeat of 148: its fix covered the instance, and the rule's sweep searched by the instance's shape
(a shell string) rather than by what the code does (put a caller's value where a program reads options).

## 451. docker inspect read any non-zero exit as an absent container, so an unreachable daemon let run create one elsewhere

**Symptom.** `queryContainer` treated every non-zero `docker inspect` exit as "no such container". Docker 29.8
exits 1 for a missing container ("No such container") and also for a daemon it cannot reach ("failed to connect to
the docker API"), measured 2026-10-14. With the daemon unreachable, `run` went on to `docker run`, and `stop` and
`remove` reported success for a container they never saw.

**Root cause.** LESSONS 138's second half, "I could not look" collapsed into "it is not there", in a module 138
never reached.

**Fix.** `eff5b82d`: only docker's own "No such container" (or "No such object") is absence; anything else is an
error naming the exit and the bounded text.

**Lesson.** A predicate that can fail to evaluate has three answers, and the message is the only place docker
gives the third.

## 452. The engine drops a failed task's undo, so a docker run that created a container and failed to start it left it unrecoverable

**Symptom.** `docker run -d` creates a container before starting it. A start that failed (a host port already
taken) left it "created" under the name, and the method returned the error. A second inspect failing after a
successful run did the same. The engine keeps a method's stats only when it succeeds (`collection_action.go`), so
no undo was journaled, and the next `container.docker.run` found the name, reported no change, and never started
it. An inspect that failed after the create also recorded an empty id, which disables the remove's guard.

**Root cause.** The method assumed an inverse recorded before returning an error would survive.

**Fix.** `921047c8`: a failed run removes the container it left "created", by id, never one docker said was
already in use and never one in another state, and says so; the undo is pinned to the id `docker run -d` printed,
validated as 64 hex digits, and a failed read back after a successful create is a warning, not a failure.

**Lesson.** Whatever a method records is dropped with its failure: a change it cannot undo by returning success
must be undone, or completed, before it returns the error.

## 453. The docker CLI methods buffered whatever the device wrote and copied all of stderr into their errors (a repeat of 431)

**Symptom.** `remoteexec.Conn.Run` buffers a command's output without limit, and `runDockerCmd` quoted all of
stderr, control characters included, into the error.

**Root cause.** LESSONS 266 (from 431) bounds and escapes remote text at the port it comes through; 431's fix was
the Kubernetes port, and the SSH output port was not swept for the same class.

**Fix.** `43f7ad70`: `remoteexec.RunWithStdinBounded` cuts a command off past its bound, taints the connection and
fails with `ErrOutputTooLarge`; `remoteexec.Excerpt` bounds and escapes text as `pkg/kubeapi` does; the docker
methods use 1 MiB per stream and 512 bytes of escaped failure text. Every other SSH method still uses the
unbounded `Run`, listed for the owner as a contract change.

**Lesson.** A repeat of 431: the rule names every port remote text comes through, and the fix covered one.

## 454. The docker CLI methods skipped the engine identity pin container.docker.exec checks

**Symptom.** `container.docker.exec` compared the engine it reached with the identity onboarding pinned; `run`,
`stop` and `remove` ran whatever engine the login's own docker configuration pointed at (`DOCKER_HOST`, a context).

**Root cause.** The sibling-guard class (LESSONS 244, FAILURE_PATTERNS 352): one path of two carried the guard.

**Fix.** `a1c248f7`: each asks `docker info --format={{.ID}}` and refuses an engine that is not the pinned one, and a
device with no pin, naming `pleiades onboard`.

**Lesson.** When a guard lands on one method of a family, the family is the unit to check.

## 455. A registry account a method obtained was never masked on the command line, and its encoded header nowhere (a repeat of 394)

**Symptom.** The Crawl tier masked what `InjectSecrets` handed a method; a registry account a method asked for
(`sdk.RegistryCredentials`) was not in that set, and the Runner masked the password but not the `X-Registry-Auth`
value, which carries it base64-encoded.

**Root cause.** 394 fixed the credential a method is handed at the start; a secret obtained during the run had no
way into the mask (LESSONS 29: the check belongs at the call site that adds the value).

**Fix.** `26c89fe2`: `sdk.SecretRegistrar`; the engine's context registers the password it answers with,
`containerengine.RegistryAuth` registers the header, and the executor masks both on failure and on success; the
Runner computes the header with `containerengine.EncodeRegistryAuth`.

**Lesson.** A repeat of 394 for secrets that arrive after the run starts: every way a secret reaches a method is a
way into the mask.

## 456. Controller onboarding lent any organization's Kubernetes credential to a record naming its address, under the record's authority and route

**Symptom.** A cluster with no credential of its own onboarded with the one stored Kubernetes credential whose host
matched its `api_server`, searched across every organization; the record's pinned authority won over the
credential's, and its route carried the connection. Whoever could write and onboard a device could read another
organization's cluster facts, and with their own authority and a hop they controlled could receive its token.
Reasoned from the code, not reproduced; the template-bound native path had the same authority rule.

**Root cause.** The facts that decide where a lent secret goes (organization, authority, route) were read from the
record, whose writer is not the secret's owner. Devices also carried no organization in practice (the import
created them without one).

**Fix.** `cab66aef`: `resolve.BorrowedKubernetesSecrets` lends only within the cluster's organization and refuses a
cluster in none, behind a route, or pinning another authority; the import puts the cluster in its credential's
organization (`AssignDeviceOrganization`, which never moves a device between organizations); a template's
credential is checked only against its own authority, the record's being dropped from the dispatch.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 276.

## 457. A refused server address was quoted, password included, into the import API's response

**Symptom.** `kubeapi.checkServer` quoted the address in every refusal but one and wrapped `net/url`'s parse error,
which repeats the raw address, so `http://user:pass@host`, an unparsable address with a password, or a token in a
query came back in `POST /inventory/kubeconfig-imports`' 422 and the CLI's message.

**Root cause.** The class of 298 and LESSONS 266: a refusal that quotes the input it refused.

**Fix.** `ca204d1f`: the user name is refused first, a parse failure gives only the parser's reason, and no other
refusal quotes the address.

**Lesson.** A validator's error quotes what it judged; when the input can carry a secret, it names the problem
instead.

## 458. HasEmbeddedSecret checked only a URL's password, so a token in the user position passed

**Symptom.** `https://<token>@github.com/org/repo.git` passed the project write check, was stored in the plain
`scm_url` column and returned by the API and the web UI; git sends the user as Basic auth and a forge accepts a
token there. go-git also reads an scp-like `git:password@host:path` userinfo whole, so its password arrived in the
user and passed too (probed 2026-10-14).

**Root cause.** The check asked where the parser files a password, not where the protocol accepts a credential.

**Fix.** `f5512ff5`: any password, any user over http or https, and a colon in an ssh user count; stored rows keep
syncing with a warning, and the API and UI show them through `RedactedSourceURL`.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 277.

**Note 2026-11-09 (`fix/patch-projects-partial`, `b9395276`).** This fix did not hold. It kept the detector a list of
credential shapes, and review on that branch found many more it missed (1089). Both functions were rewritten as an
allowlist in `internal/project/secret_url.go`. The check also ran for git projects only (1088).

## 459. The README and start-here counts drifted 22 methods behind the registry with nothing to notice

**Symptom.** Both said 82 registered, 79 implemented, 16 namespaces and 70 checkable; the registry had 104, 101,
17 and 91, and the start-here page's per-namespace list had no `virt`.

**Root cause.** Prose counts with no test (LESSONS 99: anchor one side outside the implementation).

**Fix.** `a7b36716`: corrected, and `TestStatusCounts_MatchTheRegistry` reads every count both documents state.

**Lesson.** A number a document states about the code is a claim the build can check.

## 460. Session-budgeted tests kept passing after a new first command, now testing the step before the one they name

**Symptom.** The docker tests cut the SSH connection at the Nth session to fail a named step
(`TestRun_ConnectionDiesRunning` at session 1). Adding `docker info` as the first command moved every cut one step
earlier; three tests still passed, now failing the step before the one their names say, and one failed.

**Root cause.** A test indexed by a count tests whatever step that count lands on.

**Fix.** `a1c248f7`: each budget moved by one, and a test of its own for the new step.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 275.

## 461. The local engine probe's unit tests read the developer's real Docker socket first

**Symptom.** `probeLocalEngines` tried `/var/run/docker.sock` and `/run/podman/podman.sock` before the test's own
sockets, so its tests read this machine's daemon whenever one ran, and asserted loosely enough to pass either way.

**Root cause.** A system path as a constant in code a unit test drives (LESSONS 148's shape).

**Fix.** `42ec10bf`: the local system sockets are a variable the tests point at absent paths, and the tests assert
the rootless engine they served is the one found.

**Lesson.** A test that passes on any machine's state is not testing the state it set up.

## 462. A failed Podman start's cleanup ran on an unbounded context while close() bounded the same script

**Symptom.** Two cleanups ran one stop script; `close()` held it to ten seconds, the failed-start path to
`context.Background()` with no deadline.

**Root cause.** The sibling-guard class again (LESSONS 244).

**Fix.** `42ec10bf`: one `stopService` with one bound, tested with a hanging `rm` on the harness shell's PATH.

**Lesson.** Two copies of a cleanup drift; one helper cannot.

## 463. Generated packages written into the module tree failed a new reader of it (a repeat of 53 and 55)

**Symptom.** `make devtools` failed `tools/internal/flakegate`'s `TestRepeatGate` with "open
../../../internal/catalog/test/gencatalogtest26309/check.go: no such file or directory": its container scan walked
the module while `tools/gencatalog`'s dogfood test, in a parallel package, removed the collection it had generated
there. Passed alone, every time.

**Root cause.** Five tests wrote generated source into the module tree: `tools/gencatalog`'s dogfood test,
`cmd/pleiades`'s two forge end-to-end tests, and the collection and device scaffold release gates. The filter
scaffold's gate added files to `pkg/filters` itself, so every package importing it that another test built
meanwhile compiled them. Why 53 and 55 did not hold: 53 was left unfixed as disproportionate, 55 fixed only the
deletion of the shared parent, and LESSONS 91 had each *reader* tolerate the writes (`go list -e`) on the premise
that the writes could not be removed, because a throwaway module cannot import `internal/`. The premise was wrong,
and a tolerance added to one reader protects no reader written later; flakegate's scan was one.

**Fix.** `0bef18a4`: `internal/testsupport/gooverlay` keeps generated files in a temporary tree laid out like the
module's and hands them to the go command with `-overlay`, so they build and test as members of the module,
internal imports included, while nothing in the module changes. All five tests use it. Proof: with every directory
under `internal/catalog`, `internal/inventory` and `pkg/filters` read-only, all five pass, and the old gencatalog
test fails with "mkdir internal/catalog/test: permission denied". Given up: `go vet` on the generated packages,
which runs in a directory that exists only in the overlay.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 278.

## 464. A second switch for one fact let onboarding grant a reach the engine port then refused (the sibling-guard class, LESSONS 244)

**Symptom.** `make pr-check` failed `TestKubernetesOnboard_NodesAndRoutes` after `0e1d51db`: "the node engine host
"engine": onboard.nodes: device engine is reached through this machine's own engine socket (engine_local), which
only the pleiades command line may use". Onboarding's coverage fell from its 91.9% floor to 85.5% with it.

**Root cause.** `0e1d51db` gave `pkg/containerengine` a process-wide switch for "this process is the command line"
(`AllowLocalCarrier`) beside the one onboarding already had for the same fact (`onboard.AllowLocalEngine`). The CLI
set both; the test, standing in for the CLI, set only onboarding's, so it onboarded an engine and then could not
search it. Two switches for one fact is LESSONS 244's sibling guard in another shape, and nothing held them
together. It got past the commit because only the edited packages were run, not the packages of every caller of
the seam the refusal sits in.

**Fix.** `882a637c`: one switch. Onboarding reads `containerengine.LocalCarrierAllowed`, and
`onboard.AllowLocalEngine` is gone; `TestLocalEngine_IsTheEnginePortsOneSwitch` fails when onboarding keeps its own.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 281.

## 465. CI's pull step asked Docker Hub for a fake image ID a test had named (a repeat of 416)

**Symptom.** Pull request #56's `containers (2)` job failed before any test ran: "pull access denied for sha256,
repository does not exist", three times, for `sha256:9f2c0e6a...`.

**Root cause.** `tools/testimages` keeps the value of any constant whose name contains `Image`, and
`internal/catalog/container/docker`'s tests name a fake image ID `fakeImageID`; an image ID has `name:tag`'s shape
(a repository called `sha256`, a 64-character tag). Why 416's fix did not hold: it refused one shape a non-image
can take (a name with no letter, after a uid:gid pair) and left the class open, a guess from a variable's name; and
the step that would have caught either, the pull, ran only in CI, so `make pr-check` passed both times.

**Fix.** `0a364b4b`: an image ID (`sha256:<64 hex>`, `sha512:<128 hex>`) is refused by the scanner, since no
registry serves one under any name. `89f7ad2a`: `make pr-check` runs `tools/testimages -served` over every container
package, asking a registry for the manifest of each image this machine's engine lacks, so the next shape the guess
admits fails before a push. With the scanner's fix reverted, that step names the fake ID on the real list.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 282.

## 466. A result that beat its dispatch's row was acknowledged as a message about nothing, and the job never finished

**Symptom.** `make pr-check` tolerated `TestRollbackReleaseGate_AControllerJobIsUndoneOnItsDevice` as contention:
it failed under load and passed alone. Its own output said "job ... never completed; rb-walk-1 dispatched
result=""": the rollback's check job had failed in two seconds, and its result never reached the job in two
minutes. Eight runs under CPU load, with and without `-race`, and a whole-package run all passed.

**Root cause.** The fan-out publishes a device's dispatch and only then writes its row
(`internal/dispatch/worker_devices.go`), to stay crash-safe; `RecordResult` records only against a dispatched row,
and the result consumer acknowledged any result without one as permanent, on a comment saying the row always came
first. A Runner that answers before the row write (a check failing at once, a Controller slowed by load) lost its
result for good, since every redelivery is the same message. Related to 222 (results discarded as duplicates), not
a repeat: there the publish key collided, here the order of two writes did.
