## 527. virt.vbox.vm.delete took a saved VM for one it could change, and failed at its first step (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-19, rebuilding the lab domain: `dc-00-teardown` stopped at "delete lab-lin1 and its disks",
`VBoxManage storageattach lab-lin1 ... --medium none exited 1: The machine is not mutable or running (state is
Saved)`. Nothing was deleted. Both lab VMs were saved, the state `virt.vbox.vm.stop mode: save` (#73) leaves them in.

**Root cause.** The delete's guard was `Machine.Off`, which answers "does guest code run" and is right to count a
saved VM as off. The delete then asked a second question the guard does not answer, "may this VM's media be
changed", and VirtualBox's answer for a saved VM is no. The test model let a saved machine's media change, so every
test of the delete passed on a VM in a state the real host refuses.

**Fix.** `vboxmanage.Host.DiscardState` (`VBoxManage discardstate`), called by the delete for a saved VM before it
detaches anything; the delete throws that memory away anyway. The model now refuses a saved machine's
`storageattach` in the lab host's own words and answers `discardstate`. TestDelete_ASavedVMIsDiscardedFirst failed
on the old code with the lab's error.

**Lesson.** A predicate named for one question (off: no guest runs) gets used for a neighbouring one (mutable).
When a new state appears (saved, from #73), every caller of the predicate needs reading, and the model needs the
host's refusal for that state, or the tests prove the method against a host that does not exist.

## 528. The file inventory's reads took no lock, so a read could straddle a Save (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-19, the Windows lab check's first run of `internal/inventory` with cgo on:
TestFileRepository_ConcurrentSaveDifferentHosts failed alone, "failed to read inventory file ...hosts.yaml: The
process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process." The test had passed on Linux and macOS
for months; no branch had put the package on Windows before.

**Root cause.** `fileRepository.GetByName` and `GetGroup` read hosts.yaml and then the sidecar with no lock, while
Save, Create and Retire hold `mu` and rename new files over both. On Windows an open and a rename of the same file
refuse each other, which is the error. On every OS the read could take hosts.yaml from before a Save and the sidecar
from after it: an item with the old properties at the new version, whose own Save then passes the version check and
overwrites the change it never saw, the lost update Save's version check exists to prevent.

**Fix.** `mu` is a `sync.RWMutex`, and both reads take both files under its read lock.
TestFileRepository_AReadTakesBothFilesFromOneMoment runs a Save between a read's two files (a test seam,
`afterHostsRead`) and failed on Linux with the lock removed: "the read holds version 1 without the change version 1
made". Two pleiades processes on one project are still kept apart only by `.pleiades/run.lock`.

**Lesson.** A test passing on one OS for months says nothing about another; the Windows leg found this the first time
the package reached it. And a version check guards a write only if the read it compares against was whole.

## 529. win.firewall.rule's undo carried lists the journal cannot keep, and only a real rollback said so (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-19, proving the new method on lab-dc1: widening OpenSSH-Server-In-TCP's profiles worked, and
`pleiades rollback` of that run refused before contacting anything: "win.firewall.rule's undo through
win.firewall.rule was not recorded in full (profiles kept out of the journal), so it cannot be replayed". Every unit
test passed, including the one replaying the undo, because it replayed it from the method's own stat, not from the
journal.

**Root cause.** The undo restored `profiles: [private]`, a list. The run journal keeps a recorded parameter only as a
single string, number or boolean (`engine.InverseParam`, held by TestJournalEntryHoldsNoValue), so a list was dropped
by name, whatever the manifest's `Record` said. The method also listed display_name and description as recorded,
which are text the device holds and belong in `Withhold`.

**Fix.** Every list parameter also takes one comma-separated string (no port, address or profile holds a comma), and
the undo writes lists that way; display_name and description are withheld. TestFirewallRule_UndoIsJournalable holds
every undo value to a single value. Proven live: widen, `pleiades rollback`, port 22 closed again, widen again.

**Lesson.** A test that replays an undo from the stat it was written to skips the journal, the one step a real
rollback goes through. An undo's values must fit what the journal keeps, and only a rollback through the journal
proves it.

## 530. A PowerShell script's helper named R ran Invoke-History instead, since an alias wins over a function (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-19, `win.firewall.profile`'s first live call on lab-dc1: "R : Cannot locate the history for
command line PersistentStore", CategoryInfo Invoke-History. Every unit test had passed: the stand-in for WinRM answered
the script's JSON without running the script.

**Root cause.** The script defined `function R($store)` and called `R 'PersistentStore'`. `r` is a built-in alias for
`Invoke-History`, and PowerShell resolves an alias before a function of the same name, so the function never ran.
The rule script's `D` worked only because no alias is named `d`.

**Fix.** Both helpers have verb-noun names (`Read-Profile`, `Read-Rule`), and TestScripts_NameNoFunctionAfterAnAlias
refuses a helper name that is not verb-noun or is a short built-in alias; it failed with the old name.

**Lesson.** A stand-in that answers a script's input never runs the script, so a PowerShell name resolution problem
reaches only a real host (or the parse test, which cannot see it either). Name a script's helpers as cmdlets are
named.

## 531. The repository taught the task form its owner had refused, so every copy brought it back (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-19: a converted Windows playbook came out with every task as `fqcn:` and `params:`, the form the
owner has refused at least 22 times across sessions ("How is fqcn sneaking back in all of the time?"). The same day the
agent had edited `pleiades init`'s sample runbook to give it a header comment and left `fqcn: noop` in it.

**Root cause.** The rule lived only in memory, and the repository taught the opposite. The converter's emitter wrote
`fqcn:` and `params:`; `pleiades init`'s sample used it; the `upgrade_ios` example was written that way, with a README
calling it one of "two syntaxes supported forever" and the migration guide calling module-as-key the "sugar"; the
`external_collection` README and a developer tool's runbook did the same. Nothing checked any of it, since the engine
still reads the old form, so every runbook copied or generated from those sources validated cleanly and carried it on.

**Fix.** The converter rewrites each task into module-as-key after encoding, and its round trip proves the file still
builds to the same runbook (TestEmit_ModuleAsKey). The init sample, the examples and the docs use and teach only the key
form, mentioning `fqcn:` as something older runbooks may hold. `pleiades validate` warns on each task written the old way
(validate.TaskFormWarnings), and internal/archtest's TestShippedRunbooksNameTheirMethodAsKey refuses it in docs/,
examples/, the root documents, every method's documented examples and the init sample; it failed on a planted task.

**Lesson.** A rule kept only in a person's or an agent's memory loses to a generator and an example that teach the
opposite, every time something is copied. Enforce a style rule where the copies come from: the generator, the scaffold,
the shipped examples, and a check on all of them. And a file being edited for one reason is fixed for the known rule in
the same edit.

## 532. WinRM over HTTP sent a message unsealed whenever its NTLM handshake failed (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-19, twice on the lab: a WinRM call failed with "http response error: 401 - invalid content type"
after its command had been running (the GCC download on win-check had finished; a win-check tree upload through
win.file.copy), and passed when retried. Nine long silent commands did not reproduce it, which pointed away from
timeouts and at the handshake.

**Root cause.** On plain HTTP with a password, pkg/winrmexec used masterzen/winrm's `Encryption` transport. Its `Post`
runs an NTLM handshake on an empty request before each message and seals the message with the session it gets, but when
that handshake fails for any reason (a 401 from three handshake requests split across two pooled connections, a
connection the host closed under load, a 503), it discards the error and posts the message through plain NTLM,
unsealed. The whole SOAP envelope crossed the network in the clear (a script's text, its environment values, which
carried the CA build's one-time domain-join password; a stdin chunk of a copied file), and Windows, which refuses
unencrypted WinRM by default, answered 401 with a non-SOAP body: "invalid content type". The transport also used the
process-wide `http.DefaultTransport`, so another exchange's traffic to the host could take a handshake's connection.

**Fix.** pkg/winrmexec's `sealedNTLMTransport` (ntlmtransport.go) replaces it: the same empty-request handshake through
bodgit/ntlmssp, its own connection pool held to one connection, the message sealed with that session in the WS-MV
framing Windows reads, and no unsealed path; a handshake that does not complete is an error saying nothing of the
message was sent, a refused login is `errLoginRefused`, and a sealed message the host refuses with 401 (unprocessed) is
sent once more after a fresh handshake. TestSealedTransport_AFailedHandshakeSendsNothing failed on the library's
transport with the envelope arriving in cleartext; proven live on lab-dc1 (commands, a 70-second silent command, and a
2 MB upload whose digest matched on both ends). Found by tracing the library after the 401 recurred, not from a scan.

**Lesson.** A transport that falls back to a weaker mode to keep working hides the fault as a confusing error and
spends the protection the caller asked for. An error the protocol layer swallows is worth reading in full when an
intermittent failure keeps passing on retry.

## 533. The sealed transport's header timeout raced Execute's deadline, and a silent host lost its name again (a repeat of 400) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-19, make pr-check on feat/win-firewall-rule: TestExecute_ADeadlineBeforeAnyShellIsNotStarted
failed all three of FreeBSD's repeat runs, and 5 of 200 runs under -race here. The error was a *NotStartedError, but its
text was "net/http: timeout awaiting response headers", not "the command was never sent", and it did not name the bound.

**Root cause.** Entry 532's sealedNTLMTransport bounded each reply's headers by endpoint.Timeout, the same value
Execute's own deadline uses. A host that never answers then fails the request and expires the deadline at the same
moment, and Execute's select took whichever arrived first. The library's `Encryption` client it replaced had no header
timeout at all, so entry 400's test never raced before; a check of ctx.Err() on the result path did not close it either,
because the timer can fire a moment before the context records its deadline.

**Fix.** The header timeout is the bound plus headerGrace (five seconds): Execute's deadline always names the failure,
and the timeout remains only to release a request Execute abandoned. 200 of 200 runs pass, against 5 failures before.

**Lesson.** Two timers set to one value are a race, not a redundancy. A replacement for a library component inherits
the tests written against the old one's timing, and a backstop timer has to sit clearly past the bound it backs.

## 534. A value of the wrong type reached a method as absent, literal or rendered, and nothing compared it with the declared type (a sibling of 324) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-19, writing the lab's bsd/check-05-disk-cleanup.yaml: `stdin: "{{ vars.min_free_gb | default(4) }}"`
reached `exec.shell` empty, with `-e min_free_gb=7` too, and the script's own guard refused the empty value. A literal
`stdin: 4` was dropped the same way.

**Root cause.** Two layers. A parameter that is one expression keeps its rendered type (renderValue, through
`render.Template.Value`), so 7 stayed a number; and `sdk.StringParam`, which most methods read text through, takes any
non-string for absent. `collection.Param.Type` was documentation only: no rule held a value to it, at validation or at
dispatch. Entry 324 closed the undeclared key; a declared key of the wrong type was the same silence one step on.
Checking the catalog against the rule found file.json and file.yaml's `key` declared a string while documented (and
used by a shipped example) as a string or a list of segments, and five win.firewall.rule parameters declared lists while
taking a comma-separated string, the form their own undo records.

**Fix.** `collection.ParamFits` (pkg/collection/paramtype.go) is the one rule, accepting every number shape the tiers
produce and converting nothing; `Register` refuses a type outside its vocabulary; validate's `param-type` rule refuses a
literal of the wrong type with how to write it; the engine renders a string parameter, and each item of a list of
strings, as text, and holds every other rendered value to its declared type, naming the parameter and never the value.
The seven parameters take a new type, `scalar or list`. TestRenderedParams_AStringParameterReceivesText failed on the
old rendering with `stdin = 7`; every shipped example and the lab's 149 runbooks pass the new rule; the cleanup runbook
ran on bsd-check without its workaround.

**Lesson.** A declared type that nothing checks is a comment, and a reader that takes the wrong type for absent turns
every mismatch into a silent pass. Hold values to declarations at the boundary, both where they are written and where
they are computed.

## 535. A resumed Windows box missed connections for up to two minutes, after the streak entry 516 added had passed (a repeat of 516) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-19, `make pr-check` on e2161c72: wincheck resumed win-check, `Box.Up`'s three-login streak passed,
and Ready's first WinRM call failed to connect ("dial tcp 192.168.56.31:5985: i/o timeout"). Started again by hand, it
answered at once.

**Root cause.** Measured through Pleiades: after `virt.vbox.vm.start` began, win-check (one vCPU) missed TCP
connections and WinRM calls from about 30 s to 90-130 s on three resumes of three, answering in between; at two vCPUs,
one resume of two stalled to 87 s. Entry 516's streak (three logins ten seconds apart) spans about 20 seconds and can
pass on those answers. FreeBSD on the same host and network answered every probe from the start; no adapter or DHCP
event, and the guest clock ran at the host's rate (a Get-Counter logger that stalled after the resume misled for a
while), so what the guest is doing in the window is not proven, only its length. The guest clock also stayed minutes
slow across resumes.

**Fix.** oscheck tries any call again while the run report says its device never answered (entry 536's mark), within
three minutes of waits and never after an answer; a Windows box waits for six logins twenty seconds apart
(`oscheck.WindowsWait`); wincheck sets the guest's clock (w32tm, else the host's time); win-check runs at two vCPUs.
Unit tests for every retry boundary.

**Lesson.** 516 was right that one answer is not a box that is up, and wrong about how long "steady" has to last: a
streak shorter than the window it guards proves nothing. Measure the window, then size the wait from it, and let the
steps after it survive a miss anyway.

## 536. A run report could not say a task never reached its device, so nothing could retry it safely (fixed)

**Symptom.** Found 2026-10-19 planning entry 535's fix: wincheck reaches its machine only through `pleiades adhoc
--json`, whose report gave a failed task's error text and nothing a caller could act on without matching words.

**Root cause.** The distinction existed inside the transports (winrmexec.NotStartedError, internal/transport/winrm's
networkNotStarted, remoteexec's authRejected) and stopped at the engine's error string.

**Fix.** `pkg/remoteexec.DialError` and `winrmexec.NotStartedError` each carry `Unreached()`, false for a refused
login, a refused host key or a TLS alert, which are answers; `run --json` and `adhoc --json` mark such a task
`unreached: true`; internal/transport/winrm's rule is now NotStartedError's own. Tested through the real binary against
a closing listener, a silent one, and a real sshd refusing the password.

**Lesson.** A property a caller needs to decide safely (did anything run?) belongs in the result's model, not in the
text of an error a caller would have to parse.

## 537. A package that failed to build was reported without the compiler's words, so a full disk read as 169 unexplained build failures (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-19, `make pr-check` on e2161c72: the FreeBSD leg failed 169 packages, the standard library's
among them, each "(the package: build) [failed]" with no output, and the same code had passed there half an hour
before. The cause, bsd-check's / at 99% with a 7.8 GB Go build cache nothing trims, was found only by logging in.

**Root cause.** `go test -json` gives a compiler's message only in build-output events named by ImportPath ("pkg
[pkg.test]"), and flakegate.FailureOutput read output events named by Package, so every build failure carried
"[build failed]" or nothing, locally and on every leg. The plan for this fix guessed the output was lost on the remote
leg's way back; the captured event stream showed it was never read.

**Fix.** FailureOutput includes a build failure's build-output events, the package's own and a dependency's
(TestFailureOutput_ABuildFailureCarriesTheCompilersWords, from a captured stream, failed first). Each check's readiness
now refuses under 4 GB free where its tests unpack and build, naming the fix, and the lab has
bsd/check-05-disk-cleanup.yaml.

**Lesson.** When every failure in a report has the same empty reason, the reader of the report is broken before
anything else is. Test a report with the real event stream of the failure it must explain.

## 538. A new CLI test read the developer's own known_hosts, passed here and failed on CI's runner (a repeat of 520) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20, PR #79's `containers (1)` job: TestCLI_ADeviceThatNeverAnsweredIsUnreached/ssh failed, alone
too, with the task refused before any dial: "host key verification unavailable for 127.0.0.1:...: known_hosts file
/home/runner/.ssh/known_hosts not found". `make pr-check` had passed it on this machine.

**Root cause.** The test ran the binary with this process's HOME, and this machine's `~/.ssh/known_hosts` exists, so
the dial reached the handshake and failed there as the test meant; the runner has no such file, and Pleiades refuses an
SSH dial with no known_hosts (entry 150's rule), a local mistake rightly not marked unreached. Entry 520's class: a
test whose result depends on the home of whoever runs it.

**Fix.** The test gives the binary a home of its own with an empty known_hosts (emptyKnownHostsHome). Reproduced first
by running the old test with HOME pointed at an empty directory, which failed as CI did; the new one passes there.

**Lesson.** A test that reaches SSH through the real binary owns its home, as the release gates already do with
runPleiadesWithHome. Running a new CLI test once with an empty HOME is the cheap way to find out whether it does.

## 539. A block's always: was parsed and never run, so a failed lab run left a domain account enabled (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-18, building the lab's Linux domain member: a block's `always:` disabled the logon test account,
the block failed, and the account stayed enabled. `pleiades validate` reported no issues, and a block that succeeded
printed `run complete` and exited 0 with its `always:` skipped.

**Root cause.** The builder registered rescue and always tasks as DAG nodes for validation's sake and kept them off the
chain; the executor walked the chain and stopped at the first failure. The schema, validate and the plan view all
accepted both, so nothing said they did not run. docs/03 said so; the plan view printed them as if they would.

**Fix.** They run (docs/design/block-rescue-always.md): one chain, a block's tasks then its rescue then its always,
with a per-device stack of failures deciding what runs where, a block that reaches other devices running as one unit,
a rescued run ending `rescued` (exit 4 under `--fail-on-rescue`), `error` in a rescue, and a run that has to end still
running the always of every block it is inside. Proven against an independent interpreter over generated nestings,
by a release gate on a real sshd, and on the lab, where each `# TODO(always):` task now sits in an `always:` proven by
failing a task inside its block.

**Lesson.** A keyword the parser accepts and the executor ignores is the most dangerous kind of unbuilt feature: it
validates, it prints, and it reads as working. Refuse it, or warn on it, until it runs.

## 540. A tag selection dropped the runbook's reversible: flag, so --tags turned the reversible rule off (fixed)

**Symptom.** Found 2026-10-20 adding block scopes to `engine.Select`: the copy it makes of a DAG listed every field but
`Reversible`. A runbook declaring `reversible: true`, run with `--tags`, was validated as though it declared nothing,
so a task that cannot be undone passed.

**Root cause.** `Select` builds its DAG with a struct literal naming each field to carry over; `Reversible` was added to
`DAG` later and never to the literal. Nothing compared the two.

**Fix.** The literal carries it; TestSelect_KeepsReversibleAndHandlers failed without the line.

**Lesson.** A copy written as a field-by-field literal goes stale silently whenever the type grows. Copy the struct and
change what differs, or test that a selection keeps every flag the runbook sets.

## 541. A rescue that answered a chain of failures cleared only the first, so the run still read failed (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20, the rescue oracle test (seed 99): the executor and the independent interpreter ran the same
tasks in the same order, but the executor reported the run failed where the interpreter reported it rescued.

**Root cause.** A failure that passes outward (an inner block's rescue that also failed, an always task that failed)
carries the failures before it as causes. When an outer rescue answered the chain, only the frame's first failure was
marked rescued; the causes still counted as errors.

**Fix.** Every failure a rescued frame carried is marked with the rescue. The oracle agrees over 400 seeds on one
device and two, and the fuzzer over 160,000 runs.

**Lesson.** A state machine checked only by hand-picked cases is checked where its author looked. An independent
interpreter of the same rules, run over generated inputs, finds the case nobody wrote.

## 542. One device's failure ended the run before another device had run its always: (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20, TestAlways_AFailureSkipsTheRestOfIt: a failure inside `always:` on web1 ended the run at once,
and web2 never ran the rest of its own `always:`.

**Root cause.** A failure no handler is left for ended the walk at its level, as a failure outside any block always
has. That is right for the failed device, and wrong for the others: their cleanup is what `always:` exists for.

**Fix.** A run that has to end still runs the `always:` of every block it is inside, on every device, and nothing else,
then stops (`whileEnding`). A runbook without `always:` still stops at its first failure.

**Lesson.** "Always" is a promise to every device, not to the one that failed. Test the guarantee from the device that
did nothing wrong.

## 543. A domain controller resumed from its saved state was 90 minutes slow, and a member's Kerberos join failed (a repeat of 535's clock) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20, proving dc-04's `always:` on the lab: the join failed with "Ticket expired" before the run
reached the block. lab-dc1's clock read 90 minutes behind the host; lab-lin1, on NTP, was right.

**Root cause.** A VM resumed from its saved state keeps the time it was saved at (entry 535 measured win-check 567 s
slow), and lab-dc1, as the forest root, took its time from its own clock, so `w32tm /resync` reported success and
changed nothing. Kerberos refuses more than five minutes of skew.

**Fix.** lab-dc1 takes its time from time.windows.com, applied through Pleiades and added to dc-01-build, so a resume
is corrected at its next sync.

**Lesson.** The forest root's time source is part of building the forest. A lab that saves and resumes its machines
has to give each one a clock that corrects itself.

## 544. The journal reader's symbolic-link refusal read as Linux's errno, and two owner-only mode tests assumed Unix (a repeat of 505) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20, `make pr-check` on the rescue/always branch, the first to bring `internal/journal` into
scope: on the FreeBSD box `TestReadRun_RefusesWhatNoRunWrote/a_symbolic_link` got "too many links" where it wanted
"symbolic link", and on the Windows box `TestNewFileStoreCreatesBothDirectoriesOwnerOnly` and
`TestSealWritesAnOwnerOnlyFileBesideTheJournal` read modes 0777 and 0666.

**Root cause.** The reader passed `O_NOFOLLOW`'s error through unchanged, so its refusal said only what the kernel
said: ELOOP's "too many levels of symbolic links" on Linux, EMLINK's "too many links" on FreeBSD. The test had
special-cased Linux's wording rather than the reader naming what it found. The two mode tests lacked the Windows
skip their siblings in the same files have. 505's fix covered the packages its branch touched; pr-check runs a
system's leg only over the packages a branch changes, so a package meets FreeBSD or Windows the first time a branch
edits it.

**Fix.** The reader maps ELOOP and EMLINK to "is a symbolic link", keeping the kernel's error wrapped, and the test
asks for that wording everywhere. The two tests skip only their mode check on Windows; the seal's content is still
checked there.

**Lesson.** A refusal names what it found in its own words; a test that accepts one system's error text is a test
of that system. When a branch first brings a package into a system's leg, expect that package's host assumptions to
show up there.

## 545. Every CI job's Go cache restore failed, because setup-go installed go.mod's go line and Go then fetched the toolchain line's release into the module cache (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20, reading PR #80's container shard logs for the e2e hang: setup-go's step downloaded a
1.66 GB cache in ten seconds, then warned "Failed to restore: /usr/bin/tar failed with exit code 2" after a page of
"Cannot open: File exists" lines under `golang.org/toolchain@v0.0.1-go1.26.9`. The `fast`, `ci` and every container
job showed it: each compiled from nothing, and paid for downloading the cache anyway.

**Root cause.** go.mod says `go 1.26.0` and `toolchain go1.26.9`. setup-go v5's `go-version-file` reads the `go`
line, so it installed 1.26.0; its first `go` command then switched toolchains and fetched 1.26.9 into the module
cache, before the cache was restored. The cache held its own copy of that same toolchain directory, so extracting
it collided, and the restore failed whole. The cache key carried `go-1.26.9` (setup-go names it from `go version`
after the switch), which made the entries look right.

**Fix.** `.github/actions/setup-go` reads the toolchain line (stripping a carriage return, for a Windows checkout)
and installs that release, so Go has nothing to fetch. Every job uses it.

**Lesson.** A cache step that warns and carries on fails silently in every run; read a step's warnings, not its
color. A toolchain switch inside a setup step changes what the step writes before anything restores over it.

## 546. tests/e2e's per-test times came from a local run, where the compose gates' image builds hit a warm cache, so one CI shard got both builds (a repeat of 503) (fixed before merge)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20, PR #80's first run with tests/e2e divided: one e2e part took 855 s where 393 were expected,
the other 368. `TestPackagingReleaseGate_ComposeStack` took 323 s in CI against 32 recorded, and
`TestUpgradeReleaseGate_ComposeUpgradesAndRollsBack` 322 against 138, and both had been dealt to the same part.

**Root cause.** 503's class: a table holding times from a different source than the check and the runners. No CI
run had recorded per-test times yet (they are recorded only for a package durations.json divides), so the seed came
from a local run scaled to CI's package total. The compose gates build images, which a developer's warm Docker build
cache makes cheap and a fresh runner does not, so scaling by one factor ranked them wrong. 503's fix (regenerate from
CI's own measurements) holds for packages; per-test times had no CI measurement to regenerate from until this run.

**Fix.** durations.json is regenerated from this run's own Seconds and TestSeconds, as 503 said. With CI's times the
two compose gates go to different parts and the six shards come to about 650 s each, except cmd/pleiades alone.

**Lesson.** A seed from another machine is a guess even when scaled, and worst for tests whose cost is a cache; take
the first real measurement before trusting the dealing, and expect the check's drift warning on the first run.

## 547. After rescue and always ran, the generated task-key reference still said they never run, and that rollback was refused in them (a repeat of 539's documentation) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20, mapping the rollback code for `rollback_on_failure`: docs/reference/task-keys.md, regenerated
and merged in #80, opened by saying "`rescue` and `always` validate and never run", and its `rollback` row said the key
is refused on a `rescue` or `always` task, though #80 made both run and lifted that refusal. The design note also said a
failed task contributes the undo it recorded, where the engine drops it.

**Root cause.** #80's sweep rewrote every rescue and always statement it found in the docs' prose and in the key table's
rows, which are data; the page's opening sentence is a string literal in the generator's own code
(tools/gendocs/taskkeys.go), and a search of the docs reads its output, not the sentence's source, which it found only
after regenerating had already copied it back. 539 recorded that the docs said the keys did not run; its fix changed
what ran and the statements it looked for, not every place a statement could live.

**Fix.** The sentence and the row are corrected at their source and regenerated; the design note says what the engine
does with a failed task's undo.

**Lesson.** When a feature stops being "not yet", search for the old claim in the generators' code too: a generated
page's fixed text is written there, and regenerating restores whatever it says.

## 548. The upgrade_ios example validated clean and could not run past its first task (a repeat of 324) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20, rewriting examples/upgrade_ios so a model could handle the switch's questions. Reading the
code each task reaches, before any run, found five defects `pleiades validate` passed:
- `sw1` set no `cli_prompt`, which `net.cli.command` needs, so its first pretask was refused at session open.
- "Back up the running config" called `net.ios.config` with `backup: true` and no `lines`, which the method refuses.
- `net.cli.command` cuts each line at 30 seconds, and a task's `timeout:` can only shorten that, so a real image copy
  failed even with `file prompt quiet`, which the README said made it work.
- The post-reload wait was `pleiades.builtin.wait.port`, which dials from the device itself over SSH: not something a
  switch can run, least of all mid-reload.
- A failed copy or checksum prints `%Error ...`, which neither the generic dialect nor `netcli.IOS` read as a failure
  (549), so the block never failed and its rescue never ran.

**Root cause.** 324 put every example through `pleiades validate`, which checks what a runbook says, not what its
methods need from the device (a property, a runtime bound, a place to run), and, it turned out, not even the parameters a
method marks required (550). The example had never been run against anything that answers as a switch does, so nothing
reached the steps that could not work. 324's fix held for what validate reads and could not reach the rest.

**Fix.** Both runbooks now use `net.ios.command` (no `cli_prompt` needed, paging off, `%Error` fails the task, the task's
`timeout:` the only bound), answer IOS's questions through `prompts:`, back up in the boot change itself, and wait with
`wait.connection`, whose try on an IOS device now logs in and waits for the prompt. `cmd/pleiades`'s
`TestCLI_UpgradeIOSExamplesAnswerRefuseAndRecover` runs both through the real binary over real SSH against a scripted
switch that asks IOS's questions, drops the session on reload and answers the new version afterwards; the examples test
defers `upgrade_ios` to it.

**Lesson.** An example passing validate says it is well formed, not that it runs. An example that changes a device is
done when a test runs it through the binary against something that answers as that device does.

## 549. netcli.IOS read IOS's "%Error ..." as output, so a failed save could report success (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20, found by design review of the upgrade example, not observed on a device. `netcli.IOS`'s error
pattern was `(?m)^% `, IOS's form for a rejected line ("% Invalid input ..."). A failed file operation prints
`%Error opening ...` with no space, so `net.ios.save` would report a save IOS refused as made, and a copy or checksum
failure read as output.

**Root cause.** The pattern was pinned against the device's answer to an invalid configuration line, the only error the
first live probe provoked. No probe asked for a file operation's failure.

**Fix.** The pattern also matches `%Error` (`(?m)^%(?: |Error\b)`), and still not a `%Warning:` or a syslog line
(`TestIOSErrorPattern_ReadsBothErrorFormsAndNothingElse`); `TestSave_AnIOSFileErrorIsNotASave` and
`TestCommand_AnIOSErrorFailsTheTask` fail with the old pattern (run as a negative control). `TestLiveIOSDialogs` checks
the form against a real device when its credentials are set.

**Lesson.** Pin an error convention against every kind of failure a method can meet, not the first one a probe found.

## 550. pleiades validate did not refuse a task missing a parameter its method marks required, and three runbooks left one out (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20, confirming 548: a runbook calling `net.ios.config` with `backup: true` and no `lines`, which
the method's documentation marks required, validated with "no issues found" and failed only at run time. Once the
rule below existed, its first runs found three more runbooks that could not run:
- `net.catalyst.reachability`'s documented example called `net.ios.config` with no `lines`;
- the lab's `runbooks/win/10-install.yaml` (outside this repository) called `virt.vbox.vm.install` with no
  `installer`, which the method requires and never infers from `os_type`;
- and `exec.winrm.shell` documented `shell` both required and defaulted to `powershell`, a default no task could get,
  since the method reads it with `RequiredStringParam`.

**Root cause.** `ParamsRule` (324) refuses a parameter a method does not declare; nothing compared a task's parameters
with the ones its method marks `Required`. The method checks at run time, after the tasks before it have run.

**Fix.** `RequiredParamsRule` (`internal/validate/required_params_rule.go`, rule `param-required`) refuses a call
leaving out a parameter its method marks required, in its own parameters or a fragment's; null does not count and a
template does. `RollbackRule` holds a `rollback:` step to it too. A parameter can now name the one it is a second name
for (`collection.Param.AliasOf`): `file.symlink`'s `dest`, Ansible's name for its required `path`, gives `path`.
`collection.Register` refuses a parameter both required and defaulted, and an alias that names nothing, another alias,
a parameter of another type, or is required itself. The three runbooks give what they lacked, and `shell` lost its
default. Proven by `TestRequiredParamsRule`, `TestRequiredParamsRule_RunsInValidateAndOverRollbackSteps`,
`TestRegister_RefusesARequiredParamWithADefault`, `TestRegister_HoldsAnAliasToTheParameterItNames`, and
`TestEveryDocumentedExampleValidates` over all 248 documented examples; every lab runbook validates.

**Lesson.** A declared contract is checked at plan time or it is checked at task 47. The first run of a new plan-time
check over everything that exists is a census: read every finding before deciding the rule is wrong.

## 551. The rollback gate's "beneath a later run" check let a rollback run, intermittently, on the commit before this work too (open)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20, running `cmd/pleiades`'s whole suite after 550: `TestCLI_RollbackReleaseGate`'s G2 case
expected `pleiades rollback <run> --leave tasks[1]` to be refused because a later run changed the same container, and
the rollback ran instead (exit 0, "undo tasks[0] ... changed"). It failed once in six runs alone, once in eight on a
pristine copy of the branch's last commit (`git archive HEAD`), so it predates this session's work, and then passed
thirty runs in a row.

**Root cause.** Not proven. Journal times are nanosecond-precise, so a same-second comparison in `laterRunProblems`
(`internal/rollback/history.go`) is not it. The gate discarded the later run's exit status, and a later run that failed
before its task acted (a refused SSH login under the gate's rapid logins, say) records no change, so the planner is
right to ignore it; that fits the symptom and is unconfirmed. The other reading, a later change the planner missed,
would let a rollback undo beneath another run's change, so it matters which.

**Fix.** Open. The gate now fails naming a later run that failed, with its journal, so the next failure says which of
the two it is.

**Evidence since (2026-10-21, after #81 merged).** On a quiet machine, under `-race` with `GOMAXPROCS=4`, G2 alone
passed 30 runs in a row and the whole gate 20, on top of the 30 before: 80 with neither failure, against 2 in 14
while another session's gate was loading this machine. Reading `laterRunProblems` (`internal/rollback/history.go`),
the planner lets a rollback run beneath a later run that changed the same device in two ways only: the later run
recorded no change (it failed before acting, which the gate now names), or its last finish is not after the
target's first start by the wall-clock times the journals hold. The second is a gap whatever caused this entry: a
clock stepped back between two Crawl runs hides the later one, and on the Walk tier the comparison is between two
Runners' clocks (`journal.EntStore.onDevicesSince` filters on `FinishedAt` against the target's earliest
`StartedAt`, and the planner compares again), so skew between Runners hides a later job. Phase 40a plans ordering
by a logical clock instead: the device lease's fencing revision on the Walk tier, a project counter on the Crawl
tier. Not built here, since it reaches the lock, the Runner, the journal schema and both dialects' migrations.

**Lesson.** A gate step whose outcome it ignores turns a flake in the setup into a wrong verdict on the product. And
a safety check that compares two clocks is only as safe as their agreement, which nothing here bounds.

**Update (2026-11-01, Phase 40a, on `feat/c2a-rollback-ordering`, not yet on `main`).** The second reading is closed:
the planner no longer decides "later" by wall-clock times wherever the journals carry an order. On the Crawl tier,
`.pleiades/clock` (`internal/journal/clock.go`) is ticked under a lock of its own as a run begins and as it ends; every
entry carries the start tick (`RunTick`) and the seal the end tick, and another run is later when its end tick is above
the target's start tick. A run that died before its seal takes as its end tick the start tick of the next run that
found it gone (797); one with neither counts as later. On the Walk tier, each entry carries the fencing token of the
exclusive device lease its Runner held (`lock.Fenced`, the JetStream sequence of the acquiring write), stamped by the
Runner's journal publisher (`internal/adapters/native/journal.go`, from the context `internal/runner/agent_exec.go`
sets), and `EntStore.OnDevicesSince` and the planner compare it per device, within one epoch of the lock bucket (799),
and only while the lease was held (798). Journals from before either, and jobs on a shared lease (793), are still
ordered by clock; a refusal says so, and the CLI names each such run that changed a device it undoes on
(`Plan.OrderedByClock`). Commits `4250e101` to `abd1be84`, `ff46edb8`, and the review's fixes `6590317e` and `43613be4`;
`internal/rollback/order.go`. The planner had a second clock comparison of its own, an undo step's latest
attempt (794). Proof: `TestCLI_RollbackReleaseGate`'s G2 now rewrites the later run's journal times a day back, exactly as a
clock stepped back would have written them, and is still refused without a word of clocks; the new
`TestRollbackReleaseGate_ALaterJobFromASkewedRunnerStillRefuses` (`cmd/runner`) runs two jobs through two Runners, each
with its own NATS lock manager, moves the later job's stored times a day behind, and the Controller still refuses. Both
were checked to fail (exit 0, no refusal) with the planner forced to order by clock alone. The first reading, a later
run that failed before it acted and so recorded no change, is unchanged: the gate still fails naming such a run with
its journal. The entry stays open for that reading.

**Resolved 2026-11-06 (fixed on `fix/open-patterns-batch2`, `4f8a30fe`, with `b39700eb` and `b4a32d91` from review),
except for one case left to the owner.** **Cause, measured:** the first reading above, that the planner was right to
ignore such a run, was wrong. `laterRunProblems` (`internal/rollback/history.go`) dropped a later run's failed tasks, including those that
failed during their action, not only those that failed before the run reached the device. A refused SSH login inside a
method is a failure during the action, which fits the gate's first symptom under its rapid logins. Proven through the
real binary: on `main`, a later run whose task was `exec.shell: mkdir ... && exit 3` (it changed the device, then
failed) let `pleiades rollback` of the earlier run exit 0.

**Fix.** A later run's task that failed during its action, on a device the rollback undoes on, refuses the rollback
unless `--despite-run` names that run, as a failed task in the run being undone already does. A failure before the run
began (a lock not taken, a parameter that would not render) does not refuse. A later run that recorded no change there,
or whose changes there its own rollback undid, but has such a task, is the new kind `unknown_effect`. The new field
`Problem.UnknownEffects` (`unknown_effects` in `--json`, additive within the run-report schema) names the methods that
failed, whatever the kind. The Controller's `RollbackProblem` now carries `kind` and `unknown_effects` too, and the
OpenAPI document is regenerated (958). The "cancels out" case this fix first left is 957.

**Tests.** `TestBuild_ALaterRunThatFailedDuringItsActionRefuses`, `TestBuild_AFailureBeforeTheRunBeganDoesNotRefuse`,
the gate case `TestCLI_RollbackReleaseGate/G2_a_later_run_that_failed_during_its_action_refuses`, and
`TestRollbackJob_NamesALaterJobsKindAndWhatFailedThere`.

**Still open (owner design call).** A later run killed mid-task before its seal that wrote no journal entry for the
device is never counted.

## 552. govulncheck was killed for memory at the gate three times, and the memory was a new advisory making it trace a vulnerable call (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-20 and 21, `make pr-check` on 27a440a1: every leg had passed once, then three reruns died at
`ci-remote`'s govulncheck, killed in its memory cgroup at 3100M, 3300M and 4G (4.16 GB resident), where the first run
of the same commit had passed under 3100M the day before. It read as a machine short of memory, and the next steps
weighed were a larger cap or a push without the receipt.

**Root cause.** The commit had not changed; the advisory database had. GO-2026-6809 (`crypto/x509` trusting
intermediate certificates since found compromised) landed against go1.26.9, the toolchain line, fixed in go1.26.10,
and govulncheck traced a call to it: `pkg/pgclient`'s connector, through pq, to `x509.Certificate.Verify`. govulncheck
builds a call graph of the whole module only when a vulnerable symbol may be reached, so the advisory is what took its
peak from under 3.1 GB to over 4 GB here (7.0 GB resident on a Mac). A scan killed for memory prints nothing, so the
jump was the only sign of the finding. A second trap turned up on the way: the Mac's own go was go1.27.2, newer than
the toolchain line, so a scan there without `GOTOOLCHAIN` judged go1.27.2's standard library (fixed in go1.27.3)
rather than the one this module builds with.

**Fix.** `toolchain go1.26.10`, and both builder images pinned to the 1.26.10 digest (7b8ccafc); the scan then finds
nothing, in 8 s on the Mac. `main` still builds with go1.26.9 until this merges. pr-check now runs govulncheck on the
Mac when one is ready (`maccheck -phase vuln`, c6efa2de), between the Mac's prepare and test phases, naming `GOOS`,
`GOARCH` and `GOTOOLCHAIN` for this machine so its answer is the one a scan here gives, and here otherwise. Proven on
the real Mac through Pleiades in both directions: 7b8ccafc passes, and 27a440a1 scanned as go1.26.9 fails on
GO-2026-6809 with exit 1.

**Lesson.** When a check's resource use jumps between runs of the same commit, ask what it reads that the commit does
not fix (a live database, a newer tool) before raising its limits. A scanner killed for memory has said nothing, not
"clean".

## 553. The Controller's result consumer shipped without its dead-letter grant (a repeat of 258) (fixed)

**Symptom.** Phase 103a, Finding A, read from source in 2026-09 and proven on 2026-10-21: under mesh identity the
Controller could not publish `pleiades.dlq.pleiades.jobs.results.<job>`. On a real operator-mode broker the publish
was refused as a deadline, not a permissions error. `event.HandleDeliveryFailure` returns before `msg.Term` when the
dead-letter publish fails, so a result the Controller failed to record five times (a database outage of about a
minute) was neither dead-lettered nor terminated: the broker stopped delivering it and the job stayed running.

**Root cause.** `ControllerGrant` listed the dead-letter subjects of two of the three subjects the Controller consumes
through `Bus.Subscribe` (`job.requested` and the journal), by hand, in another package from the subscriptions. 258's
fix extended the real-broker gate for the check traffic it was about, and its lesson said to do so for every new
subject, which is a rule a person must remember. The result consumer was not new; nobody had looked.

**Fix.** The grant names the result dead-letter subject, and
`TestControllerGrantDeadLettersEveryConsumedSubject` (`internal/meshid`) derives the requirement from the code: it
finds every `Subscribe(ctx, topology.X(), handler)` in shipped source and requires the dead-letter grant for each,
failing on a subject its table does not know. It, the enumerated grant test and the real-broker release gate each
failed before the grant line.

**Lesson.** A permission that must accompany a call is checked against the calls, not against a second list of them.

## 554. Dead letters copied the whole message, so every dead-lettered dispatch put its secrets on the stream twice (fixed)

**Symptom.** Phase 103a, Finding B: `DeadLetterEnvelope.Payload` was the raw message. A dispatch carries `Secrets`,
`Fields`, `ExtraVars`, `Injected` and its registry and database passwords, and `job.requested` carries prompted
credential inputs, so each dead letter held a second copy of them on the same stream for the same retention.

**Root cause.** The envelope was designed for diagnosis by an operator, and copying the message was the easy way to
give one everything. Nothing asked what the message held.

**Fix.** The envelope keeps an allowlist: subject, masked reason, time, delivery count, and the Event's id, type,
correlation id, idempotency key and actor, decoded into those fields alone so the payload is never held. A consumer
learns a dead dispatch's job and device from its idempotency key through `topology.ParseDispatchIdentity`. Proven by a
sentinel planted in every secret-bearing field of a real dispatch dead-lettered through real NATS
(`TestAgent_FailedExecutionEventuallyDeadLetters`) and in an event's data (`TestNatsBusSubscribe_*`,
`TestDeadLetter_*`). The changelog gives the purge command for dead letters written before.

**Lesson.** A record that copies a message inherits every secret the message will ever carry; name what it keeps.

## 555. A run longer than the ack wait was delivered again while it ran, and the copies spent its delivery budget (fixed)

**Symptom.** Phase 103a, read from source in 2026-09 and seen in 496's log on 2026-10-21: no code called
`msg.InProgress()`, so every dispatch running past the consumer's 30 s ack wait was delivered again. The copy met the
run's own device lease and was NAKed as contention, burning deliveries; a long run that then failed found its retries
and dead letter already spent.

**Root cause.** The ack wait does two jobs, bounding a hung handler and noticing a dead Runner quickly, and a long but
healthy run looks like neither unless it says so. The lease heartbeat proved liveness to the lock store, never to the
broker.

**Fix.** `topology.DispatchAckWait` (still 30 s) is exported, and `handleMessage` reports the message in progress every
third of it from receipt until just before it acks, naks or terminates it (`agent_progress.go`). Proven by
`TestBusyDeviceReleaseGate_ARunLongerThanTheAckWaitIsDeliveredOnce`: a 75 s run under the real ack wait, delivered once
with no redelivery, one result. Mutation checks, 2026-10-21: with the progress reports removed that test fails on a
redelivery, and with a busy device never reported `TestBusyDeviceReleaseGate_TheSecondJobEndsBusyNamingTheFirst` times
out waiting for a result.

**Lesson.** A delivery deadline needs a heartbeat to the thing that enforces it, not only to whatever else the worker
holds.

## 556. A template's machine credential reached every device in the fan-out, API-only ones included, because the exemption was a list of types (fixed)

**Symptom.** Phase 117b's S1, reasoned 2026-09-28 and measured 2026-10-21 by
`TestMachineCredentialNeverReachesAnHTTPAPIDevice` on the unfixed tree: a template bound to the switches' machine
credential, launched against an inventory holding a `generic_http` device, dispatched that device with the switches'
username and password as its secrets, in place of the device's own stored credential. `http.request` sends them as
basic or bearer authentication to whatever answers at the device's base URL, so a device record an attacker can write
receives the switches' login. A Catalyst Center or an AWS account in the same inventory had its own credential
displaced the same way.

**Root cause.** `ApplyInjection` gave the machine credential to every device unless its type was registered through
`record.RegisterOwnCredentialType`. That list was an opt-in exemption: Part XVIII 119c added the Kubernetes cluster,
and later phases the AI provider and the Cloudflare account, but `generic_http`, `generic_grpc`, Catalyst Center and
the AWS account were never added, and a new API device type would not be either. The question being asked ("is this
type exempt?") was not the question that matters ("can this device be logged into?").

**Fix.** `record.TakesMachineCredential` is an allowlist derived from the device: the machine credential reaches a
device only when it has a login capability (SSH, WinRM, Telnet, a serial or console line, NETCONF, a network CLI),
and never a type registered as using its own credential. It asks `HasCapability`, not the declared list: a vendor
type unions a record's own capabilities into its declared set, so a Catalyst Center record declaring
`SSHTransportCapable` lists it, but the type implements no SSH accessor and is still refused
(`TestTakesMachineCredential_ADeclarationAloneOpensNothing`). The first cut of this fix read the declared list and
would have let an inventory writer reopen the leak; it was caught before the push, rereading the PR's own claim. A device reached only through an API falls back to its
own stored credential. The registration stays as an extra refusal. AWX's semantics change, and the changelog says so
twice (`machine-credential-logins-only.security.md`, `.breaking.md`). Tests: the fan-out test above (fails on the
unfixed tree, naming both fields), `TestTakesMachineCredential` (a table across device kinds).

**Lesson.** When a secret goes everywhere unless excluded, every new kind of recipient is a leak until someone
remembers it. Derive who may receive it from what the recipient is, so a new kind is refused by default.

## 557. validate and a Controller's admission checked no Collection method's required capabilities, only the engine did (a repeat of 151) (fixed)

**Symptom.** Phase 117b, re-measured 2026-10-21: `pleiades validate` passed a runbook calling a method that requires
`SystemdCapable` against a Cisco switch, and a Controller dispatched a WinRM-only Windows server for an SSH-only
method; each was refused only by the engine, on the Runner, once the run reached the task.

**Root cause.** 151 recorded that nothing read `Manifest.RequiredCapabilities`. Its later fix put the check in the
engine alone (`checkMethodCapabilities`), while `validate.CapabilityRule` and the Controller's admission
(`engine.CapabilityAdmits` over `runbook.Runbook.Required`) kept reading `engine.ActionCapability`, a table of the six
legacy transport actions (`ssh_exec`, `ios_backup`, `serial_exec`, `serialtcp_exec`, `telnet_exec`, `winrm_exec`).
Phase 75 added transports to validate and the engine, again not to admission. Each fix closed the place it was found
and no other.

**Fix.** One function, `collection.CheckCapabilities`, beside `CheckTransports`. `CapabilityRule` calls it for every
Collection method (and refuses a device-less call of a method requiring a capability); the engine calls it directly;
and admission (`dispatch.methodsAdmit`) calls both checks for every method the runbook names that the Controller has
registered (`runbook.Runbook.Methods`), leaving an external method to the Runner's preflight. The generic `pkg.*` and
`svc.*` dispatchers, which had hand-written copies of the loop, call it for the concrete method they pick. A task with a
`when:` of its own (`engine.DAG.Conditional`) is left out of the plan-time and admission checks, transports included,
because the engine evaluates the condition before it checks a device: holding it to its method there refused a runbook
choosing `pkg.apt.install` or `pkg.dnf.install` by OS family on every host, the shape of 249. Tests:
`TestCapabilityRule_RefusesADeviceWithoutAMethodsCapability` and its siblings, `TestWorker_SkipsADeviceAMethodCannotRunOn`,
`TestWorker_SkipsADeviceAMethodCannotReach`, `TestCheckCapabilities`.

**Lesson.** A check that exists in three places is three fixes; put it in one function and make every place that
decides call it, then a test per place proves each still does.

## 558. The reaper's leadership test gave the leader a fixed 60 ms, and a slow machine spent it on the first query (fixed)

**Symptom.** `make pr-check` on the 117b part 1 branch, 2026-10-21: the FreeBSD leg's strict repeat pass failed
`TestReaper_Run_RepublishesOnlyWhileLeader` once in three runs ("failed to list stale fanning_out jobs: context
deadline exceeded", then "published 0 events while leader"). The same pass's first run and every other machine passed.
The branch does not touch the reaper.

**Root cause.** The test ran the reaper as leader under `context.WithTimeout(ctx, 60*time.Millisecond)` and then
required an event. On the 4 GB FreeBSD VM the first stale-job query outlived the whole window, its context expired
mid-query, and nothing was published. The test bounded elapsed time where it meant to wait for an outcome.

**Fix.** The leader runs until the capturing bus has an event, or 30 s pass, and is then cancelled and waited for. A
broken leadership gate still fails, after 30 s rather than 60 ms. The non-leader half keeps its short window, since
running briefly can only make it pass for the wrong reason, never fail for one.

**Lesson.** A test that waits for something to happen waits for it, with a generous deadline; a short window proves
only how fast the machine was that day.

## 559. The capability check reached validate with no census of what already validates, and two cmd/pleiades gates failed in CI (a repeat of 550) (fixed)

**Symptom.** Pull request #84's `containers (1)` shard, 2026-10-21: `TestExamples_EveryRunbookBuildsAndValidates`
failed on `examples/scan_lab`'s `release.yaml` (`scan.*` requires `ContainerEngineCapable`, which `release-box` has
only once onboarding finds its engine), and `TestMigratePlaybookReleaseGate` failed validating its converted playbook
(`pkg.apt.install` requires `AptCapable`, and the gate's `web` was a bare `linux_server`). Both failed again alone.
`make pr-check` had passed, and the pull request said no existing fixture needed a capability added.

**Root cause.** 557's fix made `validate` hold every Collection method to its capabilities. Both runbooks could never
have run as written (the engine refuses the same calls), so the rule was right and the fixtures were wrong. But
nothing that would show it ran before the push: pr-check tests the packages a branch changes (`tools/prscope`), and
the examples and the migrate gate live in `cmd/pleiades`, which the branch did not change. The claim about fixtures
covered only the container-free importers that were run. 550's lesson (a new plan-time check's first run over
everything that exists is a census) was written as a sentence, not as a step, so it did not happen.

**Fix.** The migrate gate adds `web` with `--classify linux_server,debian_family,ubuntu`, which declares `AptCapable`
as an apt host does. `scan_lab` joins the examples validated after onboarding, and
`TestCLI_ScanCheckWritesNothingAndTheRunDoesTheWork` now validates the shipped `release.yaml` against the device it
onboarded. Both gates and the examples test pass.

**Lesson.** A branch that makes `validate` stricter runs `cmd/pleiades`'s examples and gates, and
`TestEveryDocumentedExampleValidates`, before the push, whatever pr-check's scope says, because those are where every
existing runbook is validated. A claim about "every existing fixture" names the packages it ran.

**Follow-up, 2026-10-22 (`chore/prscope-census`).** The lesson above is now a selection rule, not a step to remember.
`tools/prscope` adds the census to pr-check's scope whenever a branch changes a non-test file under
`internal/validate`, `internal/engine`, `pkg/collection`, `pkg/capability`, `internal/catalog`,
`internal/inventory/devices` or `examples/` (`tools/prscope/census.go`), and prints why on standard error. The census
is every package that validates or runs existing runbooks through `validate`: `cmd/pleiades`, `cmd/runner` (its gates
go through the Runner's validation), `internal/adapters/native` and `internal/forge/playbook` (its converted twin).
`tests/e2e` is left to CI, at about fourteen minutes alone. A rename counts by its old path as well as its new one
(`git diff --no-renames`), and paths are read NUL-separated, since the review found that a file moved out of a trigger,
and a path git quotes, both went unseen. The catalog
and device entries are there because a manifest's required capabilities, transports or parameters, and a device type's
declared capabilities, shift the same fixtures; a manifest shares its files with its method's body, so no narrower path
separates them. `examples/` is there because no package sits above an example, so changing one selected nothing at
all. `TestEveryDocumentedExampleValidates` is in `internal/archtest`, which pr-check always runs.

## 560. A check of container.prune listed no stopped container while inspect said it had exited (open; seen again on 2026-10-30, a repeat of 560)

**Symptom.** Pull request #84's run 39697697589, attempt 1, `containers (5)`, 2026-10-22:
`TestPrune_RemovesWhatItsCheckListed` (`internal/catalog/container/read_test.go`) failed with "a check of prune =
{Changed:false}, <nil>; state "exited"". It failed in the shard's package run and again in testgate's package-alone
coverage re-measure, passed when re-run alone, and passed on attempt 2 of the failed jobs. The branch did not touch
`internal/catalog/container`. Five local package runs under `-race -tags integration` passed.

**What is known.** The test runs two labelled nginx containers, stops one with `container.stop` (`timeout: 1`), then
checks `container.prune` with `what: containers` and the label. The check lists through the Engine API's
`ContainerList` with `All` and the filters `label=<label>` and `status=created,exited,dead`
(`internal/catalog/container/prune.go`, `candidates`), and found nothing. The test's own `state` helper, which
inspects the container, read "exited" in the same assertion. So the list and the inspect disagreed about one
container within a fraction of a second of its stop. That it failed in the package-alone re-measure too means it is
not only the other packages in the shard running at the same time; the same runner and daemon served both.

**Root cause.** Unproven. One theory: the daemon answers a list from a replica view of its containers that is updated
after `stop` returns, while inspect reads the container itself. It has not been reproduced, and no earlier entry
covers this class; the nearest is 408, where a container read as ready before Docker forwarded its port.

**Fix.** None yet. Reproduce first: loop the test, or a stop-then-list probe against the same daemon, until the list
misses a container inspect calls exited, and only then decide whether `container.prune` should wait for its listing
to agree, or the test should.

**Lesson.** Pending the cause. A method that decides by a listing reads a view that can lag the object it describes;
whether that is true of this daemon is the open question.

**Second sighting, 2026-10-30 (a repeat of 560).** The nightly run 41058796153 (schedule, `main` at `7e40c5e1`, job
124072978969, strict, 1h25m): `make test-full` failed on exactly one test, `internal/catalog/container`
`TestPrune_RemovesWhatItsCheckListed`, `read_test.go:222`, with the first sighting's words: "a check of prune =
{Changed:false}, <nil>; state "exited"" (0.26s). Two sightings in eight days (PR #84's run 39697697589 on 2026-10-22,
then this one). The two pull requests merged just before it (#92, #93) did not touch the package, but the code
between the sightings is not the same code: `internal/catalog/container` and `pkg/containerengine` changed on
2026-10-28 (b617af7f, 718a6eae, 0e4c5767, the first of which edited `read_test.go`). So "the same defect" rests on the
two failures' identical words, not on identical code. The run showed nothing else failing but skips. The nightly job
does not re-run a failure alone, so no isolation result exists for this sighting.

**What was tried, and what was not proven.** On this WSL host, 300 consecutive runs of the test
(`go test -race -tags integration -run 'TestPrune_RemovesWhatItsCheckListed$' -count=300`, Docker 29.8.0, 310 s) all
passed. So the list lagging inspect did not reproduce here, and the cause stays unproven: it could be a lagging list,
a list that never held the container, or a daemon or runner condition this host does not have. No fix was made,
because a fix without the cause would be a guess (it would change `container.prune` or the test on the strength of one
theory). Contention was not claimed either: nothing in either sighting shows it.

**What changed.** `internal/catalog/container/harness_test.go` gained `harness.listed`, and the failing assertion in
`read_test.go` now prints the engine's list as prune asks it (the label and the statuses created, exited, dead), the
list with the label only, inspect's state, and both lists again one second later, with the time since the check began.
The next sighting therefore shows whether the status filter hid a container the label alone finds, and whether a list
a second later holds the container the check's list did not. It does not show what the check itself saw: the
diagnostic reads through the harness's own client, after the check returned. The read happens only on a failure, so a
passing run costs nothing.

The first version of the diagnostic was wrong: it built the label-only query by chaining onto the filters it had just
used, and `client.Filters.Add` changes the receiver, so both queries carried the status filter and the "label only"
line could never differ. The branch review found it (a check that cannot discriminate). It is built from a clone
now, and a probe with a running container, which the status filter must hide, printed `as prune asks []` and
`label only [pleiades-test-... running]`, proving the two queries differ.

**Status.** Still open. Decide the fix, in `container.prune` or in the test, only from that output. See
LESSONS_LEARNED 357 for why the test was instrumented rather than fixed or re-run until green.

**Resolved 2026-11-06 (fixed on `fix/open-patterns-batch2`, `5d468d73`, with `501f7196` from review).** **Cause,
measured:** a Docker Engine bug, moby issue 50133, fixed in Docker Engine 28.3.0 (moby pull request 50136). The engine
answers a stop while its exit handler still holds the container's lock and has not yet written the new state to the
copy a list reads, so a list made at once can still say "running", while inspect, which takes that lock, reads the new
state.
CI's daemon is 28.0.4; this machine runs 29.8.0, which has the fix, so the 300 local runs above could never fail.
Reproduced with the real test binary inside `docker:28.0.4-dind`: 36 of 400 prune runs failed with the CI words.
Inside `docker:28.3.0-dind`: 0 of 300.

**Fix.** `settle` (`internal/catalog/container/lifecycle.go`) runs one inspect, which takes the container's lock, after
`container.start`, `container.stop` and `container.restart`, so each returns only once the engine's own list shows the
change. Test: `TestStop_TheListShowsTheStopWhenTheMethodReturns`; on 28.0.4 with `main`'s code, 200 of 200 stops were
still listed as running when the method returned. Review found that a failed settle read dropped the change's undo
(955), and that stopping an auto-remove container recorded an undo that could never run (956). A second model's
research (r560) was part of the search.

**Why it stayed open so long.** Nobody compared the engine CI runs with the one here (LESSONS 406, CI_LESSONS 29).

**Likely sibling, not changed.** `Session.RunToExit` (`pkg/containerengine/runtoexit.go`) and `Session.RunOnce`
(`pkg/containerengine/runonce.go`) wait on `WaitConditionNotRunning`. No caller lists right after, but on an engine
before 28.3.0 a later task's list could still see the old state.

## 561. pleiades validate checks the registers a template reads but not the ones a when: condition reads, so a misspelled register fails at run time (a sibling of 515) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-22, mutation-testing `pleiades doc --create-skill`'s teaching runbook: changing its condition from
`result.kernel.rc == 0` to `result.kernal.rc == 0`, a register no task writes, still passed `pleiades validate` with no
finding and no warning. Only the run failed, at that task: "CEL evaluation failed: no such key: kernal".

**Root cause.** 515's fix held a parameter template's reads to the registers some task writes (TemplateRule). Conditions
are read through `engine.ConditionReads` by two rules only: CheckModeRule (does a real task read a checked one) and
HandlersRule's `unguardedReads` (`internal/validate/handlers.go`), which flags a register a rescue or always may not
have written. Neither asks whether any task registers the name at all, so the plain typo goes through. It is the same
check 515 added for templates, missing at its sibling seam.

**Fix.** None yet. Planned: one rule over `engine.ConditionReads` (a dynamic read skipped) that refuses a condition
naming a register no task in the runbook registers, built with 117b part 2's single "names an expression reads"
function so templates and conditions share it. It changes `internal/validate`, so the census runs.

**Resolved 2026-10-22, on `feat/segmenter-117b` (`e2bf8a2a`, `c187fbb5`).** `internal/validate/condition_rule.go`'s
`ConditionRule` (rule name `condition`) refuses a `when`, `when_or` or `when_cel` that names a register no task in the
runbook registers, or one only the task itself registers. A dynamic read is skipped. So is a name the condition tests
with `has()` or `"name" in stat|nodes|result` (`engine.ConditionTestsPresence`), as HandlersRule already does, because
the only writer may be a task a tag selection left out (tagged `never`), and such a condition is written for the
register's absence. Tests: `TestConditionRule`, `TestConditionRule_AWriterTagSelectionLeftOut`,
`TestConditionRule_RunsInValidate`. Changelog: `changelog/validate-condition-registers.fixed.md`.

What the plan above said and what was built differ, and the difference matters: the single shared read function was
built (`engine.TaskReads`, `internal/engine/register_reads.go`), but validate's rules still each read their own seam
(TemplateRule templates, ConditionRule conditions, SecretMaskRule `secret_mask`). Only the segmenter calls `TaskReads`.
Entry 574 is what that left room for. Entry 572 is a gap in `TaskReads`' own first draft.

**Lesson.** When a check is added for one way of reading a value, the other ways of reading the same value are the
sibling sweep (LESSONS 281); templates and conditions both read registers.

## 562. A subcommand's --help exits 1, and one that takes a name prints no flags until a name comes first (fixed in 129d)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-22, a fresh agent working only from `pleiades doc --create-skill`'s SKILL.md: every
`pleiades <command> --help` printed its flags and then `pleiades: flag: help requested`, exiting 1, which an agent that
checks exit codes reads as a failure. `pleiades add-host --help` and `-h` printed no flags at all, only "usage: pleiades
add-host <name> ...: missing positional argument"; the flags appeared only with a placeholder name first
(`add-host x --help`), which adds nothing. The same holds for the other commands parsed through `splitPositional`
(`add-credential`, `trust-host`, `set-host`).

**Root cause.** Each subcommand parses with `flag.ContinueOnError` and returns `flag.ErrHelp` as an ordinary error,
which main prints and exits 1 on. Commands with a positional name split it off before the flag set sees `--help`, so a
missing name is refused first. Not yet traced further; both are read from the run, not from a fix.

**Fix.** None yet. The skill tells an agent both facts in the meantime. Wanted: `--help` exits 0 everywhere, and a
command that takes a name answers `--help` without one.

**Lesson.** A tool an agent learns from its own help needs that help to succeed, and to be reachable without
already knowing the command's arguments.

**Seen again (2026-10-25).** Blind CVD run 3 met it on four commands, and the cause is now traced; see 648.

**Fixed (2026-10-26, `2d9cd379`), with 648.** `--help`, `-h`, `-help` and `--h` exit 0 on every command: `main`
(`cmd/pleiades/main.go`) reads a command's `flag.ErrHelp`, a missing positional or a usage error as an answer when help
was asked (`asksHelp`), and prints the usage line without "missing positional argument". So `add-host --help` without
a name prints its usage line, which names its flags, and exits 0. `TestEveryCommandsHelpExitsZero` runs both forms on
every command in the table and on `journal list` and `journal show`, and checks that a command missing its argument
without asking still fails. It checks exit codes only, not the text printed.

## 563. Four methods recorded their undo only after reads that can fail, and a failed task's undo never reaches the journal (a repeat of 452 and 487) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-22, the review of `feat/doc-create-skill`: `pkg.apt.install` (its read of the installed set and
its dpkg re-query), `pkg.apt.remove` (its `recordDependencies` step and its re-query), `identity.user.create` (its
re-read of the account) and `identity.user.remove` each called `sdk.RecordInverse` only after reads that follow the
change. A connection dropped after `apt-get` or `useradd` had succeeded made one of those reads fail, the method
returned before it recorded anything, and a change that did happen was left with no undo. `main` has this order in
all four methods; the branch did not introduce it.

**Root cause.** 452's class. Each method treated "the change worked" and "the change is described" as one step, and
put reads that can fail between the two.

**Fix.** Two steps, the second found while writing this entry. First, each method records its undo right after the
changing command succeeds (`recordInstallUndo` in `internal/catalog/pkg/apt/install.go`, `remove.go`,
`internal/catalog/identity/user/create.go`, `remove.go`). That alone was not enough: each method still returned the
later read's error, and the engine leaves a failed method's undo out before anything is journaled (`failedStats` in
`internal/engine/collection_action.go`, "a failed task is journaled with none"; 507 and LESSONS 294 keep that rule),
so through a real run the journal still held no undo. Second, 452's other half: once the change has completed, a read
that fails is a warning and the method returns success, so the engine journals the undo with it. `pkg.apt.install`
records "installed X, but could not read its version back", `pkg.apt.remove` "removed X, but could not read dpkg
back", `identity.user.create` "changed X, but could not read the account back"; `recordInstallUndo` returns its own
warning (dependencies unreadable or past 128) for one combined record, and `recordDependencies` likewise, since
`sdk.RecordWarnings` replaces rather than appends. Tests drop the connection right after each change and require a
changed task that succeeds with its undo and the warning: `TestInstall_AReadThatFailsAfterTheInstallKeepsItsUndo`,
`TestInstall_RequeryConnectionFailure`, `TestRemove_RequeryConnectionFailure`,
`TestCreate_AReadThatFailsAfterUseraddKeepsItsUndo` (a new and a converged account); a warning that cannot be
recorded still fails the task. Since the method now succeeds, the engine's ordinary success path journals the undo;
no test injects the fault on a real device through the journal.

**Why 452's and 487's fixes did not prevent it.** 452 fixed `container.docker.run`, and 487 fixed
`build.digests.refresh`; each fix was made inside its own method, and no sweep looked for other methods that record an
undo after a read. 452's fix also had a second half that was not carried here: a failed read back after a completed
change became a warning, not a failure, because its lesson already said that whatever a method records is dropped
with its failure. The new tests read the undo below the engine, at the one boundary that drops it, so they pass either
way (RULE 0).

**Lesson.** An undo is proven where a rollback reads it, the journal (529's lesson). A test that reads it from the
method's context skips the step that throws it away.

## 564. A check of an account naming a group the device lacks predicted the change with a warning, so the check passed in full where the run fails (a repeat of 385) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-22, during this branch's agent dry runs: a check of `identity.user.create` or `modify` naming a
primary group the device did not have refused, which stopped an agent's check. To unblock it, the check was changed,
before any commit, to predict the change with a warning. That let a whole check exit 0 with full coverage while the
real run fails at that task, unless an earlier task creates the group.

**Root cause.** LESSONS 255: a check reads the device as it is now, and for state an earlier task may change it
answers "could not check". 385 fixed `virt.vbox.vm.delete` and the lesson states the rule. It did not hold because
the change was made to get an agent through, and a warning beside a prediction read as an honest middle ground. The
rule's wording speaks of a predicted failure, not a predicted success with a warning, and nothing tests every check
against "predicts through missing state".

**Fix.** `predictChange` in `internal/catalog/identity/user/user.go` returns `collection.CannotCheck` naming the
group, telling a missing group (`errNoSuchGroup`) from a `getent` that failed; a real run still refuses a group that is
missing when it gets there (`TestUserChecks_AGroupNotYetMadeCannotBeChecked`). An agent then
accepts the task by name with `--allow-unchecked identity.user.create`, proven in the sixth dry run.

**Lesson.** A check that cannot know says so; the convenience a person or an agent needs is accepting that one gap by
name, which already exists (LESSONS 307).

## 565. pkg.apt.install's undo could name more dependencies than the journal keeps, which would leave the run's whole undo incomplete (a repeat of 529) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Review, 2026-10-22: `pkg.apt.install`'s new undo names the packages an install pulled in, with no bound.
The journal refuses a list longer than 128 values (`engine.maxRecordedItems`), so an install that pulled in more
would have left that undo, and with it the run's undo, incomplete.

**Root cause.** 529's class: an undo built from values the journal cannot keep. 529's fix changed one method's lists
to comma-separated strings and its test held that one method; this branch let the journal keep a list for a
parameter the undo method declares a list, with a length limit the new list's producer was never tied to.

**Fix.** Over 128, the undo names the package alone and a warning says `apt-get autoremove` takes the rest
(`maxUndoDependencies` in `internal/catalog/pkg/apt/install.go`).
`TestInstall_AnUndoNamesNoMoreDependenciesThanTheJournalHolds` checks 128 and 129 against the journal's own
`engine.RecordableTexts`, so the two limits cannot drift apart.

**Lesson.** A list an undo carries is bounded by what the journal keeps, and the test asks the journal, not a copy of
its number.

## 566. seal.key was created empty and then written, so a concurrent first use could read an empty key and a crash left one that refuses forever (a repeat of 46) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Review, 2026-10-22: `credential.SealKey` created `.pleiades/seal.key` with `O_EXCL` and then wrote the
key. A second first use at the same moment got `ErrExist`, read the file, and could find it empty. A crash between
the create and the write left an empty `seal.key`, which every later call refuses as "not a seal key" and never
replaces.
