**Root cause.** 46's exact class (LESSONS 47): `O_EXCL` makes a file's existence atomic, not its content. 46's fix,
a temporary file linked into place, was made in `internal/crypto`'s key resolution. `internal/credential/seal_key.go`
was new code that wrote its own first-use create instead of following it. LESSONS 119 and 124 (end on a read; make
the result atomic and let callers race) say the same.

**Fix.** The key is written whole to a synced temporary file beside it and `os.Link`ed into place, which never
replaces a file; a caller that loses reads the winner's key. `TestSealKey_ConcurrentFirstUsesAgreeOnOneKey` runs
eight first uses at once under `-race`: one makes the key, all get it, and no temporary file is left.

**Lesson.** Creating a key file once is a solved problem in this repository; new code that makes one starts from
that solution, and its first test is concurrent first use.

## 567. New internal/credential tests assumed POSIX file modes, directory mode bits and unprivileged symbolic links, in a package the Windows leg runs (a repeat of 544) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Review, 2026-10-22: `TestSealKey_IsMadeOnceAndKeptEncrypted` required mode 0600,
`TestSealKey_RefusesWhatItCannotUse` relied on a 0500 directory refusing writes, and
`TestSealKey_NeverWritesThroughALink` made a symbolic link, none guarded, in `internal/credential`, a container-free
package that `make pr-check`'s Windows leg runs.

**Root cause.** 505's, 510's and 544's class. Each of those fixed the tests the Windows or FreeBSD leg had already
found. New tests are written on Linux, nothing at write time flags an unguarded mode check, and the Windows leg runs
a package only when a branch changes it, after the tests exist. 544's lesson predicted exactly this.

**Fix.** Each check is guarded with `runtime.GOOS`: the mode checks skip on Windows, the unwritable directory also
skips as root, and the link test skips on Windows when making a link needs a privilege. The branch's
pr-check Windows leg (`9687e4e3`) then failed three existing tests the package had never run there: two mode checks in
`master_key_test.go`, now guarded the same way, and `TestFileStore_LookupReadErrorWhenPleiadesDirIsAFile`, which was a
real difference: Windows reports a path through a regular file as not found, so a `.pleiades` that is a file read as
"no credential stored". `readCredentialsDocument` now looks at the parent before believing a missing file, so both
platforms report "is not a directory".

**Lesson.** A test that asserts a file mode or makes a link is written with its Windows guard from the start, in
any container-free package.

## 568. run's and adhoc's hand-written usage lines had lost --allow-unchecked and --fail-on-rescue (a repeat of 145) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-22: `pleiades rollback`'s usage line was found missing flags it parses and was fixed earlier on
this branch. Later, `run`'s and `adhoc`'s usage lines turned out to lack `--allow-unchecked` and `--fail-on-rescue`,
both of which they parse. An agent learning the CLI from its usage text would not know either flag exists.

**Root cause.** A usage line written by hand is a second copy of the flag set, with no test comparing the two: 145's
class and LESSONS 134's rule. 145's fix was a test for catalog documentation only, and the rule stayed a sentence, so
CLI usage strings were never swept. On this branch, the rollback fix covered one command and not its siblings
(LESSONS 281).

**Fix.** All three lines are built by `usageLine(command, fs)` (`cmd/pleiades/rollback.go`) from the `FlagSet` each
command parses. `TestRunAndAdhocUsage_NameTheFlagsTheyParse` and `TestRollbackUsage_NamesEveryFlagItParses` hold
them to it. Other subcommands still write their usage by hand (`seal-key` and `seal` in `cmd/pleiades/seal.go`, for
two).

**Lesson.** A usage line is generated from the flags it describes, or tested against them, from the day it is
written.

## 569. remotefile.Stat passed a path to stat and readlink with no end of options, and file.stat takes the whole path from a task (a repeat of 148 and 450) (fixed)

**Symptom.** Review, 2026-10-22: `pkg/remotefile.Stat` quoted its path and passed it to `stat` and `readlink` as an
operand with nothing ending their options, so a path such as `-L` or `--format=%n` would be read as an option. The new
`file.stat` takes that whole path from a task parameter.

**Root cause.** Quoting stops the shell, not option parsing (LESSONS 137). 148 fixed one `cd`; 450 fixed the docker
methods and said the sweep must search by what code does, not by a shell string's shape. That sweep did not reach
`pkg/remotefile`, and adding a method that hands it a caller's whole path is what exposed it.

**Fix.** `operand` in `pkg/remotefile/remotefile.go` passes a path that starts with a dash as `./path`, the same
file, rather than adding `--`, since BSD's and GNU's `stat` and `readlink` differ on it (494).
`TestOperand_ADashNeverReachesStatAsAnOption`.

**Lesson.** A new method that takes a caller's value whole is the moment to check each command the value reaches for
option parsing, in the shared package as well as the method.

## 570. The account undo judged whatever home passwd named at undo time, so a home moved since could be deleted in place of the one made (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Review, 2026-10-22, of this branch's new undo for `identity.user.create`, which removes the home the
account was made with while it still holds only what `useradd` copied from the skeleton directory. It read the home
from passwd when the undo ran. After a later `identity.user.modify` with `home:` pointing at a new, empty directory,
the undo would have judged that directory unchanged and deleted it, and left the home it made.

**Root cause.** The undo identified its target by what the device says at undo time, not by what the change made. It
is the class 2f7c2a4c guarded for VMs and containers (an undo pinned to a `uuid` or `id`), and near LESSONS 147
(build an undo from the value captured when deciding, not from a later read).

**Fix.** `identity.user.create`'s undo records the home it made as `created_home`, and `identity.user.remove` keeps a
home whose path differs from it, with a warning (`TestRemove_AHomeMovedSinceIsKept`).

**Lesson.** An undo that deletes names what it made, recorded at the change, and refuses anything else under the
same name or path.

## 571. Four comments, help texts and skill sentences claimed more than the code does, one of them a sealed file's refusal of surrounding text (a repeat of 228) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Review, 2026-10-22: a comment called `find -mindepth` POSIX, which it is not; `sealed.Parse`'s comment
said it refuses data around the sealed block, but `pem.Decode` skipped leading text, so text before the block was
accepted; `add-credential`'s `--passphrase` flag text did not mention the sealed file it applies to; and a skill
sentence said `file.copy` writes files 0600, when only a file it creates gets that mode.

**Root cause.** 228's class: a comment or help text describes what was meant, and nothing re-reads it against the
code. The `sealed.Parse` one is the shape 228 called worst, a security claim naming the function that should enforce
it.

**Fix.** Each text now says what is true, and `sealed.Parse` refuses text before the block as well as after it
(`TestParse_RefusesWhatThisVersionDoesNotWrite`, rows "data before the block" and "a broken block before it").

**Lesson.** A comment that claims a refusal is checked by a test of that refusal; if there is none, write it or cut
the claim.

## 572. engine.TaskReads' first draft left out a task's rollback: steps, which rollback_on_failure runs and renders inside the forward run (a repeat of 561) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Review by the fp-reviewer agent, 2026-10-22, before any push of `feat/segmenter-117b`. The first draft of
`engine.TaskReads` (`internal/engine/register_reads.go`, `1410e15e`) said in its doc comment that "a rollback: list is
left out: it never runs in the forward run", and a test pinned that. It is false. A block's `rollback_on_failure`
runs a task's authored `rollback:` steps inside the forward run, before the rescue, and prepares each one through
`run.prepare` (`internal/engine/rollback_on_failure.go`, `runUndoStep`), which renders its params against `nodes` and
`result`. Had it shipped, the segmenter (`internal/segment`) would not have carried a register an undo step reads
into that step's segment, so on the Walk tier the undo's render would fail with an undefined-variable error at the one
moment the undo is needed.

**Root cause.** The list of places a task reads a register was written from the forward walk (a condition, the
params' templates, `secret_mask`), not from the code that prepares a task. `run.prepare` has three callers
(`runNode`, `runGuarded`, `runUndoStep`), and the third was not on the list. The premise is also older than the code:
until `88e5ba65` (2026-10-20) an authored `rollback:` list ran only in a later `pleiades rollback`, so "never in the
forward run" was once true, the stale-claim shape of 539 and 547.

**Why 561's fix did not prevent it.** 561 is the same class: a register read missed by a check of register reads. Its
lesson named the sibling sweep and its two known members, templates and conditions. This branch built the shared read
function 561 planned, and the sweep for it again listed the ways of reading from memory of the forward run, so a
third reader (an undo step) was missed in the very function meant to end the class.

**Fix.** `8fe2cdd0`: `TaskReads` recurses into `task.Rollback`, and its doc comment now names `runUndoStep` as the
reason. `TestSplit_CarriesWhatAnUndoStepReads` covers it; a mutation that skips the recursion fails it.

**Lesson.** To answer "what does a task read or do", list every caller of the function that prepares a task
(`go_symbol_references` on `run.prepare`), not the steps of the forward walk. LESSONS 309.

## 573. The first segmenter accepted two plans one device's dispatch cannot keep, and refused a third it could (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Review by the fp-reviewer agent, 2026-10-22, before any push. The first draft of `internal/segment`
(`9d2bdb57`), which splits a runbook into the segments the Walk tier will dispatch one device at a time, had three
defects:
- It accepted a "unit" block (`engine.DAG.Units`: a block holding a task with its own target) with `rescue`, `always`
  or `rollback_on_failure` on several devices. On the Crawl tier a failure on one device fails such a block on all of
  them (its frames are keyed `unit:<block>`), but one device's dispatch cannot learn of another device's failure.
- It accepted `lock_acquisition: all_at_plan_time` on several devices. That strategy promises all locks or none, and
  the promise cannot hold when each device's dispatch locks only its own.
- It refused a guarded block whose first child is a parallel group that comes after a task on another target. The
  group's structural fan-out node landed in the earlier segment and was counted toward the block's span, so the block
  looked split when it was not.

**Root cause.** The split rule was written from what a runbook says (targets, blocks, registers) rather than from the
engine behaviors that tie one device's run to another's. Crawl runs every device in one process, so those ties are
free there and nothing in a single-process test shows them. For (c), the span check counted every node in a block,
structural ones included, when only nodes that run on a device decide where a block lies.

**Fix.** `1433bac6`: (a) and (b) are refused with messages that say why; (c) structural nodes are not counted toward a
block's span. Tests: `TestSplit_RefusesWhatOneDevicesDispatchCannotKeep`, `TestSplit_AParallelGroupOpensAGuardedBlock`;
each fix's mutation fails its test. `FuzzSplit` now also asserts that an accepted plan keeps every guarded block (one
with rescue, always or rollback) inside one segment.

No earlier entry is this class. The nearest are 539 and 542, which built the cross-device behavior of blocks (a block
reaching other devices runs as one unit; `always:` is a promise to every device) that the split had to keep.

**Lesson.** When work moves from one process to one process per device, list every engine behavior that couples
devices before writing the split rule, and refuse or keep each one. LESSONS 309.

## 574. validate holds a rollback: step to three of the rules a task meets, not TemplateRule, so a misspelled register in an undo step passes (a repeat of 561) (fixed)

**Symptom.** Review by the fp-reviewer agent, 2026-10-22, reasoned from the code and not reproduced. `validate`'s
`RollbackRule` (`internal/validate/rollback_rule.go`) runs only CollectionRule, ParamsRule and RequiredParamsRule over
a task's `rollback:` steps. TemplateRule never sees a step's templates. So a misspelled register in an undo step's
params passes `pleiades validate`, and fails only when `rollback_on_failure`, or a later `pleiades rollback`, renders
it. That is the moment a typo in an undo costs the most.

**Root cause.** The same class as 561: a register read checked at one seam (a task's params, by TemplateRule) and not
at another (an undo step's params). `RollbackRule`'s doc comment says a step "can never pass something a task would
not", which claims more than its three rules do (the shape of 228).

**Why 561's fix did not prevent it.** 561 was fixed by adding a rule for conditions over the runbook's own tasks.
Validate's rules still each read their own seam rather than the shared `engine.TaskReads`, which does count undo
steps (572), so the rules that walk the runbook's tasks never reach a step.

**Fix.** None yet; not fixed on this branch. Planned: hold each step to TemplateRule with the runbook's registers. It
changes `internal/validate`, so the census runs.

**Lesson.** A comment saying one rule holds X to "exactly what" another thing is held to is a list of rules to check
against the full list, not a summary to trust.

**Update, 2026-10-23 (`01cdbb70`, on feat/lab-importers, not yet on `main`).** `TemplateRule` now walks each task's
`rollback:` steps as well as its nodes (`paramTasks`, `internal/validate/param_tasks.go`), so its register check
reaches a step. `TestTemplateRule_AProjectPathReadsOnlyVars` proves the rule reaches a step: a step's project path read
from a result is refused under `tasks[1].rollback[0]`. No test yet writes a misspelled register in a step, which is
this entry's symptom, so it stays open until one does.

**Closed, 2026-10-23.** `TestTemplateRule_AMisspelledRegisterInARollbackStepIsFound`
(`internal/validate/rollback_template_test.go`) writes this entry's symptom: a step reading `result.chnage` where the
runbook registers `change` is refused under `tasks[1].rollback[0]`, naming the misspelling, and the correct spelling
passes.

## 575. Docker Desktop carried a net lab node's SSH port over whichever network's name sorted first, so taking a link down cut the test's own session (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-22, building Phase 127b's net lab (`internal/testsupport/netlab.go`). About half of all lab starts
reached a node's published SSH port over one of its link networks, not over the management network. When a test then
took that link down (as the route and failover tests do), the test's own SSH session hung: a channel open was never
answered. While the links were `--internal` networks, the lab failed to start instead, with "port 22/tcp sent no SSH
greeting", because the link address refused the connection. That start failure had been unexplained until then.
A second trap on the same networks: on a link that is not internal, the subnet's first address is Docker's gateway,
and a test that gave a node 10.212.0.17 failed; its addresses moved to .18 and .19, and `NetLabLink.Ends` now says
never to use a subnet's first address (`891014f1`).

**Root cause.** Docker Desktop forwards a published port through the container's network whose name sorts first. It
ignores the endpoint's `gw-priority` and the container's `HostConfig.NetworkMode`. testcontainers' `network.New` names
every network with a random UUID, so which network carried SSH was a coin toss on each start. Proven both ways with
one container on two networks: named `aa-link` and `zz-mgmt`, the port went over the link; swapped, over management.
Measured on Docker Desktop on this machine only; a native Linux daemon (the CI runners) was not checked.

No earlier entry has this cause. 186 is the nearest kin (a Docker network behavior that depends on how the daemon is
installed). 470 and 471 (a published port refusing every connection while the server listened) stay open: this cause
needs a container on two or more networks, and whether it explains either of them, whose fixtures are not net labs,
was not checked.

**Fix.** `c4621535`: `netLabNetwork` names the networks so the management network sorts first. Every net lab test
since then reaches its nodes over management, and `TestCLI_NetworkChangeIsGatedAppliedAndUndone` takes a link down
out of band and still drives the routers through it (passed 2026-10-22, 92.8 s).

**Lesson.** When a container sits on several networks, which one a published port uses is the daemon's choice and is
not what the API's priority fields say. Pin it by the rule the daemon actually follows, and test by taking every other
network down. On a non-internal network, never give a node the subnet's first address.

## 576. Docker's --internal networks dropped OSPF's multicast hellos, so no adjacency formed and wait.routes timed out (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-22, the first net lab with OSPF between FRR routers. No adjacency ever formed on a link, and
`wait.routes` timed out waiting for the routes OSPF should have learned.

**Root cause.** On a Docker network created with `--internal`, the bridge drops a packet whose destination is outside
the network's subnet. OSPF hellos go to the multicast address 224.0.0.5, which is outside every link subnet, so not
one crossed.

**Fix.** `81e2ebfc`: net lab links are no longer internal networks. Proven by the routers forming OSPF and eBGP
sessions in `TestMethods_OnRealRouters`, the `wait.routes` live tests and `TestCLI_NetworkChangeIsGatedAppliedAndUndone`.
The cost is 575's second trap: on a normal network the subnet's first address belongs to Docker's gateway.

No earlier entry is this class.

**Lesson.** An isolation setting is a filter on traffic, and a routing protocol's control traffic is often multicast
or link-local. Before wiring a lab of routers, check that the network passes the protocol's own packets, not only
unicast to a neighbor's address.

## 577. Secret masking split words at spaces and tabs only, and its keyword list missed RADIUS and TACACS server keys, FHRP, RIP and NHRP authentication, and snmp-server host communities (a repeat of 458) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Two findings in `pkg/netcfg`'s `Mask`, new on this branch (`03294512`), which masks configuration secrets
before a result, a model or Batfish sees them.
- `FuzzMask` (`8a03adc1`) found that `password\vzebra` came back unmasked. Mask split a line into words at spaces and
  tabs only. Any reader that splits at every Unicode space (Go's `strings.Fields`, among others) reads `zebra` as the
  password's own word. The input is kept as the regression seed `pkg/netcfg/testdata/fuzz/FuzzMask/0efe06de78653693`.
- The branch review (2026-10-22) found real configuration lines that kept their secret: the leading `key 7 x` inside a
  `radius server` or `tacacs server` block, `standby`, `vrrp`, `glbp`, `ip rip` and `ip nhrp` authentication, and an
  `snmp-server host` line's community string.

**Root cause.** Mask is a denylist: it masks the word after each secret word it knows. A denylist fails open, so any
form it does not list (a word boundary it does not split at, a keyword, a block where `key` holds a secret) passes
through unmasked. The keyword list came from the forms FRR and Cisco write that its author had in mind, not from each
vendor's configuration reference.

**Why 458's fix did not prevent it.** 458 found a secret check that asked where a parser files a password, not where
the receiving side accepts one (LESSONS 277). That lesson was written about URLs, and nothing carried it to a new
package masking a new kind of text. The `\v` case is the same mistake: Mask asked where its own splitter puts a word
boundary, not where a reader of its output does.

**Fix.** `8a03adc1`: Mask splits at every Unicode space. `26dca552`: Mask knows a key's block (a key chain's `key 1`
names a key and is kept; a RADIUS or TACACS server's `key 7 x` holds one and is masked), standby, vrrp, glbp, rip and
nhrp authentication, and an snmp-server host's community. `TestMask_ByVendor` holds real lines per vendor to the mask,
and lines with no secret to staying unchanged; `FuzzMask` checks that masking keeps the line count, is idempotent, and
leaves no word after `password` unmasked.

**Still open, by design.** Mask is still a denylist. A secret form that is not in the table still passes unmasked.

**Lesson.** A mask that names what to hide fails open. Write its tests from each vendor's list of secret-bearing
commands, fuzz it with a reader as broad as any consumer's, and state beside it that an unlisted form passes.

## 578. A new output path skipped the masking beside it: net.frr.command's show output, vtysh and frr-reload errors, and the Controller's grant properties (a repeat of 522) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** The branch review, 2026-10-22, before any push:
- `net.frr.command` returned `show running-config` unmasked in its `stdout` stat, while `net.frr.facts` masked the same
  text. `show running-config` is a show command, so `net.frr.command` accepts it.
- `vtysh` errors named the refused command, and `frr-reload` errors echoed configuration lines, both unmasked. A
  configuration line can hold a secret.
- The Controller's grant route (`POST /inventory/devices/{name}/capabilities`, `internal/api/devices_grants.go`)
  accepted a secret-named grant property. A grant rides every dispatch to its device, so the value would travel the
  JetStream stream on every job. The code's comment said the loader refuses such a property; the Controller loads no
  program, so nothing did.

**Root cause.** Masking was done by each output path, not where the device's text is read. `net.frr.facts` called
`netcfg.Mask` on its output; `net.frr.command`, written beside it, did not. The errors were a third path. The grant
route relied on a check in another binary, and its comment claimed more than the code did (the shape of 228).

**Why 522's fix did not prevent it.** 522's lesson was "mask a test's text where the program reads it, not where each
view shows it". It was applied to `tools/testgate`. Nothing carried it to the FRR package, where each method masks its
own output, so a new method had to remember. The fix below is still per path.

**Fix.** `26dca552`: `net.frr.command` masks `stdout` and every string inside `data`; `vtysh` errors and `firstLine`
mask and bound the device's text; the grant route refuses a secret-named property (`redact.SecretName`). `6e4943fa`:
a failed reload names frr-reload's own error lines, masked. Tests: `TestGrantRoutes_RefuseWhatTheyCannotRecord`'s
"a secret-named property" case and `TestReloadError`. `testCommand` in `internal/catalog/net/frr/frr_live_test.go` sets an OSPF key on a real router and requires
`net.frr.command show running-config` to return it masked (added after this entry was first written).

**Lesson.** When a package masks device text, mask it once where the text comes in from the device, and give every
new method a test that reads a secret back through it. A check that lives in another binary protects only that
binary's path.

## 579. A check of net.frr.config passed a change the account could not make, and a failed reload left the router in neither configuration (a sibling of 564) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the clean-slate routing lab (its G1 to G3) and the branch review (F8), 2026-10-22.
- An account in `frrvty` can read the configuration and run `frr-reload --test`, which needs no write access, so a
  check of `net.frr.config` predicted the change and passed. The real reload needs `/var/run/frr` writable, so the
  real run failed.
- `frr-reload` deletes lines before it adds them. A reload that could not write its files left the router in neither
  the old nor the new configuration, and the method's error showed only frr-reload's first INFO line, not the error.
  The undo failed the same way.
- With `save: true`, whether `frr.conf` was writable was asked only after the reload, so a refused save left the
  router changed and the task failed.

**Root cause.** The check asked a dry-run tool whether the change was well formed, and that tool needs fewer rights
than the change itself. Nothing asked whether this account could make the change. The writability of `frr.conf` was
checked in the wrong order.

**Related, not a repeat.** 564 is the same symptom (a check passed in full where the run fails) with another cause: it
predicted through state an earlier task could change. Here the state was fixed; the check asked a narrower question.
The tests' own images had hidden it: they granted the test account access to `/var/run/frr` that the docs never told
a user to grant (LESSONS 311).

**Fix.** `6e4943fa`: `net.frr.config` checks that `/var/run/frr` is writable before anything is sent, in a check as in
a real run, and a failed reload names frr-reload's own error lines, masked. `26dca552`: whether `frr.conf` can be
written (`canSave`) is asked before the reload, in both modes. Tests: `testConfig` in
`internal/catalog/net/frr/frr_live_test.go` removes the group's write access to `/var/run/frr` and requires the check
and the run to refuse with the router unchanged; `TestReloadError`. The same test makes `frr.conf` read-only and
requires a check and a run with `save` to refuse before the reload, the router unchanged.

**Lesson.** A check must ask every question the real change will ask, including "may this account do it". When the
check uses a dry-run mode, list what the real mode needs that the dry run does not, and ask those directly.

## 580. A masked configuration could be applied, and expect_sha256 matched it (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** The branch review, 2026-10-22, reasoned from the code. `net.frr.facts`' `running_config` is masked: every
secret becomes a `pleiades-masked-` placeholder. Fed to `net.frr.config` as a candidate, it would set every key to its
placeholder and drop every authenticated OSPF and BGP session. `expect_sha256` would not stop it, because
`net.batfish.check` hashed the same masked text it was given, so the digests matched.

**Root cause.** The digest proves the bytes applied are the bytes checked. It says nothing about whether those bytes
are a configuration or a masked copy of one, and nothing else asked.

**Fix.** `26dca552`: `net.frr.config` refuses a candidate that contains the mask prefix (`netcfg.MaskPrefix`) before
anything is sent, unless it is restoring a backup. `testConfig` requires a candidate holding the prefix to be refused.

No earlier entry is this class.

**Lesson.** A redacted copy of data must never be accepted where the real data is: when a method masks what it reads,
the method that writes the same kind of data refuses the mask's marker.

## 581. ovs-vsctl exits 1 both for "no port named" and for every fatal error, so a failed read was taken as absence (a repeat of 451) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** The branch review, 2026-10-22. `net.ovs.port` read any exit 1 from `ovs-vsctl port-to-br` as "no such
port". `ovs-vsctl` exits 1 for that and also for every other fatal error, such as a database it cannot reach or a
permission refused. So `state: absent` succeeded on a switch whose database could not be read, and the code's own
comment said the opposite of what ovs-vsctl does.

**Root cause.** LESSONS 138's second half: "I could not look" collapsed into "it is not there".

**Why 451's fix did not prevent it.** 451 found the same thing in `docker inspect` and fixed it in the container
package. The rule is a habit each new reader of a command's exit status has to remember, and nothing checks a new one.
This reader was written from an assumption about the tool's exit codes, not from the tool.

**Fix.** `26dca552`: an absence only when the exit is 1 and the output holds ovs-vsctl's own words, "no port named";
anything else is an error with the device's text bounded and quoted. `TestBridgeAndPort_OnARealSwitch` makes the
database socket unreadable and requires `state: absent` to fail rather than report the port absent.

**Lesson.** Before reading an exit code as an answer, make the command fail for another reason and see what it
returns. Most tools use one code for many failures.

## 582. Open vSwitch undos were recorded as exact when they could not put back what the change removed (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** The branch review, 2026-10-22.
- `net.ovs.port` removing a port recorded an exact undo that added it back with its tag only. The interface's `type`
  and `options` and the port's `trunks` and `vlan_mode` were lost.
- `net.ovs.bridge` removing a bridge lost its `fail_mode`, `controller`, `protocols` and `other_config` the same way.
- Moving a port to another bridge is a delete and an add, so the forward change itself dropped those settings, and
  the undo could not restore them.

**Root cause.** Each undo was built from the fields the method sets (bridge, name, tag), not from everything the
change destroys. LESSONS 147 says to build an inverse from the value about to be overwritten; here the overwritten
value was larger than what the method's parameters name.

**Fix.** `26dca552`: a removal's undo is marked partial and names what it cannot put back when the port or bridge
carried more than the defaults; a move of a port that carries more than a tag is refused. The method's declaration
now allows a partial undo (`MayBePartial`). `TestBridgeAndPort_OnARealSwitch` sets trunks on a real port, requires the
move to be refused with the port left where it was, and requires the removal's undo to be partial and to name trunks.

No earlier entry is this class.

**Lesson.** An undo is exact only when it restores everything the change destroyed. List what the object carries, not
what the method sets, and mark the undo partial when it cannot put something back.

## 583. The grant routes' scope tests ran with a fake admitter and an admin identity, so the routes' own scope was never exercised (a repeat of LESSONS 180) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** The branch review, 2026-10-22. The tests of the grant and revoke routes (`internal/api/devices_grants_test.go`)
mounted them behind an authentication that admits everyone and a fake admitter. Through that test router a caller
without `inventory:assert` got 200. Every scope assertion in the file was about constants, not about the routes.

**Root cause.** The test router was built for the handler's behavior and then reused for authorization. With the real
scope rule absent, and an admin identity bypassing every scope check anyway, nothing could fail.

**Why LESSONS 180 did not prevent it.** 180 says to test an authorization gate with an identity that can only pass
through the mechanism under test. It was written about the settings page and is a rule to remember, not a check. The
grant routes were tested by a helper that never installed the mechanism at all.

**Fix.** `26dca552`: `TestGrantRoutes_AnInventoryWriterIsRefused` mounts the routes behind the real token
authentication (`api.AuthMiddleware`) and `auth.NewTokenScopeRule`, and requires a caller holding `inventory:write`
and `inventory:onboard` but not `inventory:assert` to get 403 on both routes with nothing written. Its positive half
uses an admin, which proves nothing about the gate by itself (180's point); it stands because
`TestGrantRoutes_ScopeIsAdminsAlone` shows only admin carries `inventory:assert`, and the refusal carries the weight.

**Lesson.** A route's authorization test runs through the real authentication and admission chain the Controller
mounts, never through a test router that admits everyone.

## 584. The documented accept_unrecognized example split at an unquoted comma in a YAML flow mapping, and validate passed it (a repeat of 548) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the network release gate (`891014f1`). The documented example for `net.batfish.check`'s
`accept_unrecognized`, in `internal/forge/catalogdata` and `docs/16-network-verification.md`, wrote an entry as
`{text: ..., reason: a, b}`. In a YAML flow mapping an unquoted comma ends the value, so the entry had three keys
(`text`, `reason: a`, and `b`), not a reason holding a comma.

**Root cause.** YAML's flow syntax, and an example nobody had run. `pleiades validate` passed it, because a method's
structured parameters (a list of mappings) are not checked entry by entry at plan time.

**Why 548's fix did not prevent it.** 515 put every documented example through `pleiades validate`, and 548's lesson
says passing validate shows an example is well formed, not that it runs. Validate cannot see inside a structured
parameter, so this example was well formed to it. Only running it through the binary found it.

**Fix.** `891014f1`: the example quotes its reason, in both places.

**Still open.** Validate still does not check a structured parameter's entries, so the same mistake in a user's
runbook passes validate. This is not listed among Phase 127b's follow-ups.

**Lesson.** In a documented YAML example, quote any string that may hold a comma, colon or bracket, and run the
example through the binary.

## 585. Batfish parses Cisco GLBP, IP SLA, SLA tracking and BFD without a warning and does not model them, so a gate that refused only unrecognised lines would pass them (a sibling of 252 and 539) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-22, measured against the pinned Batfish while building `net.batfish.check`. The gate's first form
(`68c54499`) failed closed on any line Batfish reported unrecognised, unless accepted by name. On Cisco IOS, Batfish
parses GLBP, IP SLA, SLA-tracked static routes and BFD with no parse warning, and does not model them: it elects no
GLBP forwarder (a GLBP virtual address is answered by nobody), installs an SLA-tracked route as if the probe always
answered, and models BFD not at all. HSRP with interface tracking it does model, failover included. On FRR, `ip ospf
authentication-key`, `no bgp ebgp-requires-policy` and `vrrp` are reported unrecognised, so they were already
refused. A gate failing closed only on unrecognised lines would have passed every configuration in the first group.
A Batfish convert error did not refuse the gate either.

**Root cause.** A parser recognising a line was taken as the model acting on it. The parse warnings measure the
grammar, not the model.

**A sibling of 252 and 539.** Both were a keyword this project's own parser accepted and its executor ignored (a
runbook's `check_mode`, a block's `always:`). This is the same class in a third party's model. Their lessons were
about our own parser and did not lead anyone to ask it of Batfish.

**Fix.** `264491d5`: a measured list of features Batfish parses and does not model
(`internal/catalog/net/batfish/coverage.go`). A configuration using one is refused like an unrecognised line until the
task accepts the feature by name with a reason, and the result lists it as not modelled. `26dca552`: BFD is caught
anywhere on a line (`neighbor ... fall-over bfd`), and a convert error refuses the gate unless accepted. Tests:
`TestUnmodelledIn`, and `internal/catalog/net/batfish/cisco_live_test.go` against the real Batfish.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 310.

## 586. import-containerlab --trust-first-connect wrote an ephemeral lab's host keys into the user's own known_hosts (a repeat of 442) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-22. The clean-slate lab agent ran `pleiades import-containerlab --trust-first-connect` as the docs
described. It wrote the lab's host keys into the user's own `~/.ssh/known_hosts`: twelve lines for
`[127.0.0.1]:2201`, `:2202`, `:2203` and `:2211` (lines 28 to 39). The agent could not remove them; the owner has to
remove them by hand. A lab makes new host keys on every deploy at the same addresses, so on the next deploy those
entries refuse the new lab as a changed host key, and they teach the user to clear such warnings for addresses that
other services may use later.

**Root cause.** Trust on first connect wrote to the default known_hosts file, which is the user's own. The command is
meant for throwaway labs, whose keys belong in a file of the lab's own.

**Why 442's fix did not prevent it.** 442 found a test writing a fixture's key into the developer's real known_hosts,
and fixed it in the tests: each test points `PLEIADES_KNOWN_HOSTS` at a file of its own. The product's own
first-connect path was left writing to the default, and this new command reached it through a documented use, run by
a user rather than a test.

**Fix.** `6e4943fa`: `--trust-first-connect` refuses unless `PLEIADES_KNOWN_HOSTS` names a file, and the error says
why and how. `TestImportContainerlab_WritesEachNodeAndRefusesOtherLabs`' "trust with no lab known_hosts" case.

**Lesson.** A command that trusts keys it has never seen writes them only to a file the user named for that purpose,
never to the user's own known_hosts by default.


## 587. Net lab nodes still reached SSH over a link 2 starts in 10, after the networks were named so management sorted first (a repeat of 575) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, the fourth `make pr-check` on feat/network-verification-127, re-measuring `cmd/pleiades` alone:
`TestCLI_NetworkChangeIsGatedAppliedAndUndone` failed at its third run, the one taking r3's link to r1 down out of band.
Every SSH handshake to r3 then failed ("use of closed network connection", three attempts over 34 seconds), so
`net.frr.config` never reached r3 and the report showed no undo. The gate had passed in the full pass of the same run,
and passed again alone.

**Root cause.** Docker Desktop's choice of network for a published port is not name order. Measured on this machine
with one container on a management network and a link, management sorting first: 2 of 10 starts forwarded over the
link. 575's rule came from one two-network experiment, swapped once each way, which a coin toss weighted this way
passes as often as not.

**Why 575's fix did not hold.** It pinned the rule it inferred, not the behaviour: no test took every other network
down across many starts, which its own lesson asked for.

**Fix.** `3203fbf3`: `StartNetLab` starts each node on the management network alone and connects its links with
`docker network connect` once it runs. Measured: 20 of 20 starts with one late link, and 20 of 20 with two late links
both taken down, kept SSH on management; the gate then passed three times in a row (191.8 s) and every net lab package
passed.

**Lesson.** A rule about another program's choice, inferred from one A/B, is a guess. Measure it across enough starts
for a minority outcome to show, and prefer a setup that leaves the program no choice to make.

## 588. PredictPut refused, on FreeBSD, a group the file Put writes takes from its directory without a chgrp (a repeat of 521) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, the fourth `make pr-check`'s bsd leg: `TestPredictPut_AgreesWithPutWhenItWrites`, "a mode
change": `PredictPut = put .../Dockerfile: this login (pleiades) may not give a file the group wheel, so nothing was
written`. The file was in a directory whose group is wheel, which the login is not in.

**Root cause.** `Put` writes the new file beside the target, and on FreeBSD a new file takes its directory's group, so
it already has wheel and no chgrp is sent. `PredictPut` asked only whether the login is in the target group.

**Why 521's fix did not hold.** 521 taught `PredictWrite` that a new file's group is the directory's on FreeBSD and the
account's on Linux, in that function's own doc comment. `PredictPut`, new on this branch, wrote its own group check from
the login's groups without reading it. Its test, meanwhile, only called `PredictPut` and never `Put`, so "agrees with
Put" was never compared on any system.

**Fix.** `3203fbf3`: `whoAmI` also reads `uname -s` and the login's primary group, and `identity.newFileGroup` gives the
group a new file starts with: the directory's outside Linux, the directory's under a setgid directory on Linux, else
the login's. A target group equal to it is not a refusal. The test now runs `Put` on a fixture of its own for each
case, and `TestNewFileGroup_FollowsEachKernelsRule` covers each rule. `pkg/remotefile` passed on bsd-check
(`tools/bsdcheck`, 1m18s).

**Lesson.** A prediction that names what it agrees with has to run that thing in its test, on every system it claims.

## 589. A test left doctest's capability registered, so a later onboard ran its probe, and the re-run alone called it contention (a repeat of 188) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, the fourth `make pr-check`: `TestOnboard_AProgramsProbeGrantsItsCapability` failed with a
second grant in its report, `doctest.widget`, whose probe failed. Re-run alone it passed, and testgate reported it as a
test that "lost a race".

**Root cause.** `TestDoc_RendersAProgramsCapability` registered `doctest.widget`, with a probe, into the process-wide
capability vocabulary and never restored it. Onboarding runs every registered capability's probe, so every later test
in the binary saw it. Running the two tests together failed every time; neither alone did.

**Why 188's fix did not hold.** 188's guard is `make test-repeat`, which repeats each test in a container-free package.
`cmd/pleiades` is a container package, and this leak crossed from one test to another, which repeating either alone
cannot show. The tolerant re-run then ran the failing test alone, without the test that leaked, and passed it.

**Fix.** `3203fbf3`: the doc test restores the vocabulary with `t.Cleanup(capability.SnapshotForTest())`. Proven by
running both tests together, failing before and passing after. No other test function in the module registers a data
capability without a snapshot.

**Lesson.** A failure that passes alone has passed without the tests that ran before it. Before calling it contention,
run it with the tests that preceded it.

## 590. An empty standard input's end could reach sshd before the exec request, so "cat > file" waited forever (a regression from 149's fix) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, the sixth `make pr-check` on feat/network-verification-127: `internal/catalog/net/frr` hit
the 30 minute package timeout in the full pass and again re-measured alone. Under `-race` the package hung in
`net.frr.config`'s backup about half the time and never without it. The goroutine dump showed `writePrivate` waiting
in `remoteexec.Conn.run`; on the router, `cat` had been running for 42 seconds and the `.saved` backup of an empty
`frr.conf` was 0 bytes.

**Root cause.** `Conn.run` started the goroutine copying standard input before `session.Run` sent the exec request.
With nothing to copy, the goroutine closed the pipe at once, so the channel's end of input could reach OpenSSH's sshd
before the exec request, and sshd never delivered it to the command it then started. `cat` waited forever. The race
detector's slower scheduling made the close win often enough to see. Any `RunWithStdin` with empty input could hang
the same way; a non-empty one sent its data first, which sshd buffers.

**Why 149's fix did not prevent it.** 149 took the copy away from `x/crypto/ssh` so a remote that stops reading is not
a failure, and started its goroutine before `Run`. No test sent empty input to a real sshd, and 149's own lesson says
the in-process server never develops sshd's timing.

**Fix.** `pkg/remoteexec`: the copy starts after `session.Start` returns, then `session.Wait`. Proven by
`TestSSHContainer_AnEmptyStdinEndsTheCommandsInput` (internal/transport/ssh, real OpenSSH): forty empty inputs to
`cat > file` over one connection, under `-race`; before the fix run 7 of 40 hung until its 10 second deadline, after
it all forty pass. `internal/catalog/net/frr` then passed five times in a row under `-race`, and `pkg/remoteexec`
three times.

**Follow-up.** A command killed by a cancelled context's SIGTERM came back as exit 143, not as the cancellation:
`run` reports `ctx.Err()` only when `Wait` returns something other than an exit status.

**Lesson.** A fix that moves work onto a goroutine moves its ordering too. Say what must have happened before the
goroutine starts, and test the empty case against the real server.

## 591. A Batfish live test required "domainname localdomain", which FRR writes only where the Docker host gives a search domain (a repeat of 426) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, PR #88's `containers (5)` (run 39932132697, job 120342742453):
`TestCheck_RealRoutersAgainstRealBatfish` failed `check_live_test.go:142` (`not_modelled` named no `domainname`) and
`:165` (the refusal of an unaccepted line did not name `domainname localdomain`), and failed again re-run alone. Its
other assertions held. A local `make pr-check` at the same commit had passed it.

**Root cause.** FRR copies the container's DNS search domain into its running configuration as `domainname`. Docker
Desktop on this machine gives the container `localdomain`; the runners' Docker Engine gives none, so the routers there
had no such line, and the test asserted one.

**Why 426's lesson did not prevent it.** 426 named a fixture's login stack as part of its environment; the same holds
for its resolver, and nothing tied a test's expected device output to what the host contributes to it.

**Fix.** The test requires the lines the routers' own configuration always holds (`ip ospf authentication-key` in
`not_modelled`, `no bgp ebgp-requires-policy` in the refusal). The accept entries for `domainname localdomain` stay in
the test, the network gate and the routing lab, since accepting a line a configuration lacks changes nothing (the
gate passed in CI with it). docs/16 and the routing lab's README say when FRR writes the line.

**Lesson.** A live test asserts what the device's own configuration put there, never a line the container host adds.

## 592. telnet_exec demanded a stored credential its transport never sent, so a console with no login was unreachable (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, proving `pleiades import-gns3` on feat/lab-importers: a GNS3 VPCS node imported as a
`console_device` failed `telnet_exec` with "no credential stored for device pc1", though VPCS asks for no login.

**Root cause.** The engine's transport executor looked up a credential for every binding before dispatch, and the
telnet, raw passthrough and serial transports then ignored it: none of those protocols has a login of its own, and
`pkg/telnetexec` answered no login prompt either. The requirement guarded nothing and blocked every console without
one.

**Fix.** `TransportBinding.CredentialOptional` on the three bindings: a stored credential is used, a missing one is
not an error, and any other lookup failure still is (`TestTransportActionExecutor_ACredentialIsOptionalWhereTheProtocolHasNoLogin`).
The Telnet session now answers a device's login prompts with that credential (593's branch).

**Lesson.** A requirement a code path checks and then never uses is a refusal with no reason; trace each input to
where it is read before demanding it.

## 593. The IOS dialect waited for a privileged "#" prompt, so an account landing in user mode hung every net.ios method until its byte bound (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, on the DevNet CML sandbox's IOL XE routers over Telnet: the login landed at `R1>`, and
`netcli.IOS`'s exec prompt `(?m)^[\w.\-]+#\s*$` never matched it, so `netcli.Open` would have read until its bound.

**Root cause.** Every net.ios method had been proven against one device, the Catalyst 8000 Always-On sandbox, whose
account is privilege 15 and lands at `#`. Nothing modelled user mode or `enable`, and no credential could carry an
enable secret, so an ordinary operator account could not be used at all, over SSH or Telnet.

**Fix.** The IOS exec prompt accepts `>` and `#`; a Dialect names its `Unprivileged` prompt and its `Enable` command;
`netcli.Open` enters enable with `Options.EnableSecret` from the credential's new `EnablePassword`
(`add-credential --enable-password[-stdin]`, `wire.SecretEnablePassword`); `Config` in user mode refuses naming the
fix; a wrong secret is refused without being named. Proven by `TestTelnet_*` in `pkg/netcli` and on the sandbox by
`TestCLI_ImportCMLReachesIOSOverTelnet`.

**Lesson.** A device method proven with an administrator's account has been proven for administrators. Prove it with
the account a lab or an operator actually gets.

## 594. A Telnet login answered by a delayed refusal was taken as accepted, because the session read 500 ms of quiet as the answer (a sibling of 149) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, the first run against a real telnetd (BusyBox's, behind its `/bin/login`): a wrong password
opened a session with no error. Every scripted test had passed.

**Root cause.** After answering the password prompt the session read until the device was quiet for 500 ms. BusyBox's
login waits about three seconds before "Login incorrect", so the read ended on silence, saw no refusal and no prompt,
and returned a session. The scripted servers answered at once; IOS does too, which is why the sandbox never showed it.

**Fix.** `Session.answer` reads after a login answer until the device has said something besides blank lines, up to
`Options.LoginTimeout` (default 20 s), then until quiet (`TestSession_AgainstARealTelnetd`).

**Lesson.** As 149 found for SSH: a scripted server never develops a real one's timing. Run a login against a real
login program before trusting its refusals.

## 595. trust-host reported a refused connection as a host that presented no host key (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, `pleiades trust-host R1 --first-connect` against the CML sandbox's router said "10.10.20.171
presented no host key", which sent the investigation to SSH algorithms. The router runs no SSH server; port 22 refused
the connection.

**Root cause.** `hosttrust.Scan` dropped every attempt's error and reported only that no key came back.

**Fix.** The last attempt's error is kept; a dial failure says the host "could not be reached over SSH", anything else
"presented no host key" with its cause (`TestScan`).

**Lesson.** An error that summarises several attempts keeps the last cause; a summary without one names the wrong layer.

## 596. The generic CLI prompt pattern allowed only whitespace after the prompt, so a shell's terminal query hid it (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, `netcli.FromPrompt("lab$")` over a real telnetd never matched its first prompt: BusyBox's ash
printed `lab$ ` followed by `ESC[6n`, a cursor position query.

**Root cause.** The pattern was `^<prompt>\s*$`; a terminal control sequence after the prompt is not whitespace.

**Fix.** The generic pattern also allows CSI control sequences after the prompt (`TestSession_AgainstARealTelnetd`).

**Lesson.** A terminal session carries the terminal's own traffic; a pattern for where output ends allows it.

## 597. A tag change was recorded as a revision and never written to hosts.yaml, because the file repository's Save wrote properties only (a repeat of 261 and 274) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, on feat/lab-importers, while adding `--tag` and `--untag` to `pleiades set-host`: a tag change
moved the host's version and recorded a revision under `tags` in the sidecar, and `hosts.yaml` still held the old
tags. The command reported success. Nothing could change a host's tags from the CLI before, so nothing had shown it.

**Root cause.** `fileRepository.Save` (`internal/inventory/file_repository_save.go`) wrote the version, state, history
and reserved properties to the sidecar, and wrote back to `hosts.yaml` only `hosts[hostIdx].Properties`. Tags live in
`hosts.yaml` beside the properties, and Save never set them.

**Fix.** Save also writes `hosts[hostIdx].Tags = tagsToStrings(item.Tags())`.
`TestSetHost_TagsAndUntagsAndRecordsIt` (`cmd/pleiades/sethost_test.go`) tags and untags through `runSetHost`, reads
the host back through the repository and reads `hosts.yaml` itself with `inv.ReadHosts`, and checks that the `tags`
key disappears when the last tag is removed.

**Why 261 and 274 did not prevent it.** 261's fix added `record.Base.ChangeTags`, which bumps the version and records
the revision, and proved it through the API handler against the real ent repository. The Crawl tier's file repository
is a second store, and no path put a tag change through it until now. 274's lesson says to treat every place a type's
fields are enumerated as a place that must change; `Save`'s list of what goes back to `hosts.yaml` was such a place,
and nobody looked at it when `ChangeTags` was added, because the lesson depends on someone remembering it.

**Lesson.** A change method on a record (`ChangeTags`, `ChangeState`, `AddInfo`) is proven once per repository, by
reading back the store's own file or table, not the record in memory.

## 598. An unknown flag before set-host's name took the name as its value, so the command said the name was missing (a repeat of 50) (fixed before push in set-host; open in the other commands)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, found when the owner had an agent change a Cisco router through pleiades: a call like
`pleiades set-host --label r1` (a flag set-host does not define, placed before the name) failed with "missing
positional argument", which sent the agent looking for a missing name instead of a wrong flag. The agent's own calls
used `--tag`, which set-host did not define until this branch added it (597 is what adding it exposed).

**Root cause.** `splitPositional` (`cmd/pleiades/addhost.go`) assumes every `-` token it does not know as boolean takes
the next token as its value. An undefined flag took the host name, so no positional was left, and set-host checked the
positional count before the flag set ever saw the flag.

**Fix.** set-host splits with `splitPositionals` and calls `fs.Parse` before it checks how many positionals it got, so
the flag set reports "flag provided but not defined: -label" (`TestSetHost_AnUnknownFlagIsNamed`, with the flag both
before and after the name). Still open: `add-host` and the other commands that split with `splitPositional` check the
positional first and would report the same wrong thing.

**Why 50 did not prevent it.** 50's fix kept the premise and exempted the boolean flags each caller names. An unknown
flag is one no caller can name, so the premise still fails for it. Only the flag set knows what a flag takes. 562
(open) has the same ordering at its root: a missing name is refused before the flag set sees `--help`.

**Lesson.** Let the flag set parse before any count of positionals is checked; a splitter that guesses which tokens
are values will guess wrong for the flag nobody defined, which is the one a user most needs named.

**Resolved 2026-11-09 (fixed in the other commands on `fix/cli-flag-splitting`, `71614896`, with `18c3bf1f`).** The
splitter is replaced by `parseArgs`, `parseOneArg` and `parseCheckedArgs` (`cmd/pleiades/args.go`), which every command
that used the splitter now calls. Each parses the flags before any positional is counted, so an unknown flag before a positional
is reported as `flag provided but not defined`, not as a missing positional argument. A help request is the one
exception, and is answered as before (1062). Test, shown red on the old code: `TestEveryCommandSplitsItsOwnBoolFlags`
(`cmd/pleiades/args_test.go`), which gives every splitting command `-vxf` before its positionals and expects the flag
error.

## 599. net.ios.command reported a read-only show command as changed, so a second run could not prove it changed nothing (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, found when the owner had an agent change a Cisco router through pleiades: the agent's proof
that a second run changed nothing failed on `net.ios.command` with `show version`, which reported changed every time.

**Root cause.** `net.ios.command` returned `Changed: true` for every command that ran without error, as
`net.cli.command` and `exec.command` do, because a command's effect cannot be inspected. A show command is the one case
whose effect is known.

**Fix.** `iosShow` (`internal/catalog/net/ios/command.go`) reports unchanged for a line whose first word is `show` or
an IOS abbreviation of it (at least two letters), unless one of its pipes is `redirect`, `append` or `tee` (or an
abbreviation), which write a file. `TestIOSShow_OnlyAShowThatWritesNoFile` covers the abbreviations and the pipes; on
the DevNet CML sandbox router, `TestCLI_ImportCMLReachesIOSOverTelnet` asserts `show ip interface brief` returns status
`ok`. The method's documentation says so.

**Lesson.** "Cannot be inspected, so changed" is right for a command in general and wrong for the commands a device
documents as reads; an agent proving idempotence runs reads, so name them.

## 600. The insecure_telnet advice said to set it "on the task", and an agent wrote it as a task key the builder refused (a repeat of 270 and 488) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, found when the owner had an agent change a Cisco router through pleiades: following the
refusal "set insecure_telnet: true on the task to accept that", the agent wrote `insecure_telnet: true` beside the
task's `name:`, and the runbook builder refused it as an unknown task key.

**Root cause.** `insecure_telnet` is a method parameter (`sdk.ParamInsecureTelnet`, read from the method's params by
`sdk.OpenShell`). "On the task" reads as a task key to anyone who knows tasks have keys of their own. The same wording
was in `pkg/sdk/shell.go`'s refusal, `docs/16-network-verification.md`, the skill (`cmd/pleiades/doc_skill.go`), the
next-step lines `import-cml` and `import-gns3` print, and the `telnet-login` changelog fragment.

**Fix.** Each now says to pass it among the method's parameters, beside its other parameters, not as a task key; docs/16
shows `net.ios.facts: {insecure_telnet: true}`.

**Why 270 and 488 did not prevent it.** 270 says to follow an instruction once before shipping it, and 488 says a
refusal naming a parameter needs a test that sets it through the whole path. The CML gate does set `insecure_telnet`
among the parameters and passes, so the parameter was right. What no test can check is where a reader puts it: the
author placed it correctly because the author knew. An agent reading only the message is what found it, as LESSONS 311
found for docs.

**Lesson.** Advice that names a key says where it goes in the runbook's own terms (a method parameter, a task key, a
runbook key); "on the task" is not one of them.

## 601. The GNS3 fixture found console ports free and then let Docker bind them, and another test took one in between (a sibling of 123) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, under `make pr-check`: starting the GNS3 container failed with "address already in use" on a
console port.

**Root cause.** `freeConsoleRange` (`internal/testsupport/gns3.go`) finds free ports by listening on them and closing
the listeners; Docker binds them a moment later. A closed listener reserves nothing, so a test running beside it could
take one first. 123 met the other half of the same fact: a released port is neither unused nor reserved.

**Fix.** `StartGNS3` retries with a fresh range, up to `gns3StartAttempts` (5), and only when the error says "address
already in use"; any other failure stops at once, now with the container's last 30 log lines.

**Lesson.** A port found free is a guess until it is bound. When the binder is another process, retry on the bind
error rather than trusting the guess.

## 602. The GNS3 2.2.61 container's API did not answer within two minutes once, with the machine idle, and answers in about 5 s every other time (open)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, once, outside `make pr-check` (load average about 2): the fixture's wait for `/v2/version` on
the 2.2.61 container timed out after two minutes. Run by hand, the same container answered in about 5 s, and the next
five runs passed in 4 to 5 s.

**Root cause.** Not known. No log of the failed container was kept. It has the outward shape of 470, 471 and 481 (a
fixture's server never answering within the wait), but those were seen under load, and nothing ties this one to them.

**Fix.** Diagnosis only: a failed start now prints the container's last 30 log lines (601's change), so the next
occurrence shows what the server was doing.

**Lesson.** When a failure cannot be reproduced, the fix is to make the next one explain itself, and the record says
the cause is unknown.

## 603. net.ios.config's first fallback recorded its undo lines as a Go []string, which the method's own reader refuses (a sibling of 529 and 534) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, on feat/lab-importers, before push: the first draft of `net.ios.config`'s fallback (a device
that cannot keep a checkpoint) recorded an undo whose `lines` were a Go `[]string`. `sdk.StringSlice`, which reads
`lines`, accepts only `[]any`, the shape YAML and JSON decode a list into, so replaying that undo would have failed
with "lines must be a list of strings". The test of the no-checkpoint path (now
`TestConfig_WithoutACheckpointTheUndoLinesAreShownNotRecorded`) caught it.

**Root cause.** A method built a value for its own later use in the Go type it had at hand, not in the shape a task's
params arrive in. Params only ever reach a method after decoding, so a value that skipped decoding met a reader that
had never seen its type.

**Fix.** Overtaken by 604: the fallback records no undo at all. It reports the masked lines under `undo_lines` for the
task's `rollback:` list, and the test now requires that no undo is recorded.

**Why 529 and 534 did not prevent it.** 529 found an undo whose values the journal cannot keep, and its guard
(`TestFirewallRule_UndoIsJournalable`) holds that one method's undo. 534 found a value of the wrong type reaching a
method's reader and fixed it for rendered and literal params. Neither reaches a new method that builds its own undo
params in Go.

**Lesson.** A value a method writes for a later task to read is written in the shape that task's params will have
after decoding (`[]any`, `map[string]any`, `float64` or `int`), and a test replays it through the method's own reader.

## 604. Withholding net.ios.config's fallback undo made validate refuse rollback_on_failure on every net.ios.config task, and the docs said the in-run undo would replay the withheld lines (a repeat of 228 and 571) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, on feat/lab-importers, before push. A draft declared an `sdk.InverseSpec` for the fallback undo
with its lines under `Withhold`, since they are configuration read off the device. Two things followed. `pleiades
validate` refused `rollback_on_failure` over every `net.ios.config` task, because it refuses that key over a task whose
undo is not exact. And the method's description and the docs said a block's `rollback_on_failure` would replay the
withheld lines inside the run. It would not: the engine's in-run undo (`internal/engine/rollback_on_failure.go`)
replays only an undo the journal holds exactly.

**Root cause.** The text described what the author meant the fallback to do, not what the engine does with a withheld
parameter. No test ran `rollback_on_failure` over the fallback, so nothing held the claim to the code. Declaring the
spec also changed what validate allows for every call of the method, the checkpoint calls included.

**Fix.** The fallback records no undo and reports its lines, masked, under `undo_lines`, with a warning to copy them
into the task's `rollback:` list. `net.ios.replace` (checkpoint and expect paths, and the Telnet opt-in, nothing else)
is the method's only declared undo. The description, docs/16 and the changelog say so. The CML gate
(`TestCLI_ImportCMLReachesIOSOverTelnet`) runs a `rollback_on_failure` block on the sandbox router and proves the
change undone through the checkpoint.

**Why 228 and 571 did not prevent them.** Both found text claiming more than the code does, and 571's lesson says a
claim of behavior is checked by a test of that behavior or cut. The claim here was written in the same draft as the
code, before the gate that tests it existed, and nothing makes the test come first.

**Lesson.** Before a doc or description says what `rollback_on_failure` or `pleiades rollback` does with a method's
undo, run it, and check what declaring an `InverseSpec` does to validate for every call of the method.

## 605. A container_host with no host declared SSH and a network address, so validate passed wait.port on it and the run asked for a credential (a sibling of 316 and 345) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-22, routing lab gap G6 (`examples/routing_lab/GAPS.md`): a `container_host` with no `host`, which
is the machine pleiades runs on reached through its own engine socket, passed `pleiades validate` for
`pleiades.builtin.wait.port`, an SSH method. The run then failed asking for a credential that no SSH login could use.

**Root cause.** `container.NewHost` (`internal/inventory/devices/container/host.go`) put `SSHTransport` and
`NetworkAddressable` in every host's baseline, whether or not the record named a host. The existing test asserted the
claim on a bare record with no host ("expected the vendor baseline to include SSHTransportCapable"), so the test
pinned the defect, the tell 273 describes.

**Fix.** Both capabilities are declared only when the record's `host` property is set (`b53d4db2`).
`TestNewHost_BaselineCapabilities` requires both on a host with an address and neither on one without. Waiting for a
service on this machine is `http.wait`'s job now.

**Why 345 and 316 did not prevent it.** 345 removed one capability edge a device could not serve and 316 taught the
generated reference to show a conditional capability. Neither checks that a type's static baseline holds for every
record the type accepts.

**Lesson.** A capability a type declares for every record must hold for every record the type accepts. When it
depends on a property, declare it from that property, and test the record without it.

## 606. IOS scrolled a command longer than 80 columns sideways in its echo, so the echo was not stripped and stayed in the output (a sibling of 596) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, on the DevNet CML sandbox's IOS XE 17.15 IOL router: the new checkpoint commands (`copy
running-config unix:...`, `show archive config differences unix:... system:running-config`) are longer than 80
columns. IOS echoed each one scrolled sideways, with a `$` where it cut the line, and the session's output kept that
garbled echo.

**Root cause.** `stripEcho` in `pkg/netcli` removes an echo only when it matches the line sent. The IOS dialect set
`terminal length 0` and left the terminal width at its default, so any long command, the checkpoint's or a user's,
came back changed.

**Fix.** `Dialect.DisableWrapping`: IOS's dialect sends `terminal width 512` after `terminal length 0`
(`TestOpen_DisablesPagingAndWrappingWhenDialectNamesThem`). The CML gate runs the long checkpoint commands on the
sandbox router.

**Why 596 did not prevent it.** 596 fixed the prompt pattern for the terminal's own traffic after a prompt. The echo is
a second place a terminal rewrites what the session expects, and nothing had sent a command that long.

**Lesson.** A terminal session sets every terminal property that changes what it reads (paging and width), and a
test sends a command longer than the default width.

## 607. http.wait's not-ready test closed a listener and reused its port, and the released-port guard refused it (a repeat of 123, 177, 183 and 478) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, on feat/lab-importers, before push: `internal/archtest`'s `TestNoReleasedPortIsUsedAsAnAddress`
refused the first draft of `TestWait_AServiceThatIsNotReadyYet`, which closed a listener and then used its address for
a service that "starts later".

**Root cause.** The construction 123 named: a released port is anyone's, so another test can take it before the
service starts, and the wait then measures the wrong server. 601 met the same fact in the GNS3 fixture on the same
branch.

**Fix.** The test holds its port the whole time: `droppingListener` accepts and closes every connection until the
service is "ready", then serves it, so the wait sees dropped connections first and an answer later.

**Why 478's fix did not prevent it.** It did its job: 478 added the guard, and the guard caught this before push. The
construction is still the first one a test author reaches for.

**Lesson.** To imitate a service that is not ready yet, hold its port and drop connections; never release it.

## 608. VarsRule refused a task with its own when:, which the run may skip (a repeat of 557) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, on feat/lab-importers, before push: the new validate rule `VarsRule` (routing lab gap G11)
refused a task whose params read a `vars.<name>` no `--extra-vars` supplied, even when the task had a `when:` of its
own that would skip it.

**Root cause.** 557 settled that a task with its own `when:` (`engine.DAG.Conditional`) is left out of the plan-time
checks, because the engine decides the condition first. That decision lives in each rule (`TransportRule`,
`CapabilityRule`), and a new rule starts without it.

**Fix.** `VarsRule` leaves a conditional task to the run, as `TransportRule` does (`TestVarsRule`). The
`validate-extra-vars` changelog fragment says so.

**Why 557 did not prevent it.** 557's fix is a check in each existing rule, not a property of the rule framework, so
every new rule has to remember it.

**Lesson.** A new validate rule starts by asking what the existing rules skip (conditional tasks, device-less calls,
`rollback:` steps), and copies each answer or says why not.

## 609. net.ios.config, net.cli.config and net.netconf.config applied lines holding a masked placeholder, and net.ios.config's new undo_lines would hand an author such lines (a repeat of 580) (fixed)

**Symptom.** Found by an agent's review, 2026-10-23, on feat/lab-importers: `net.ios.config`'s fallback reports its
undo lines masked under `undo_lines`, and the docs tell an author to paste them into a `rollback:` list. Pasted
unchanged, each `pleiades-masked-` placeholder would have been applied, setting each secret on the device to the
placeholder. `net.ios.config` did not refuse such a line. Neither did `net.cli.config` or `net.netconf.config` on
`main`.

**Root cause.** 580's class: a masked copy of data accepted where the real data is.

**Fix.** `netcfg.RefuseMasked` (`pkg/netcfg/refuse.go`, `TestRefuseMasked`) is the one refusal, now called by
`net.frr.config`, `net.cli.config`, `net.netconf.config` and `net.ios.config` before the device is reached
(`TestConfig_RefusesAMaskedSecret` in `internal/catalog/net/ios`, `TestConfig_RefusesAMaskedSecretBeforeTheDevice` in
`internal/catalog/net/cli`).

**Why 580 did not prevent it.** 580's fix was in `net.frr.config` alone. Its lesson says the method that writes the same
kind of data refuses the mask's marker, but nothing lists those methods, and this branch added a masked output that
feeds one of them.

**Lesson.** When a method starts emitting masked configuration, every method that applies configuration of that kind
calls the one shared refusal; a new configuration writer calls it from its first draft.

## 610. pkg/iosparse's ShowInterfaces keeps genieparser's failure on an "Encapsulation X, medium is Y" line (open)

**Symptom.** Found 2026-10-23 while porting genieparser's `ShowInterfaces` (`pkg/iosparse`, `67a70f8e`). Not met on the
CML sandbox's IOL router.

**Root cause.** genieparser's own parser reads the medium from the wrong match on an "Encapsulation X, medium is Y"
line and raises `KeyError`. The port keeps genieparser's behavior so its fixtures hold the port to upstream, and
returns a `*ParserError` where genieparser raises. `pkg/iosparse/doc.go` lists this among the port's known
differences.

**Fix.** None yet. A fix would make the port differ from genieparser on that line and would need a fixture of its own.

**Lesson.** A port held to upstream fixtures inherits upstream's defects. Name each one where users read about the
port, and fix it as a deliberate, tested difference.

**Fixed (2026-11-06, `f129e543`, branch `fix/open-patterns-fable`).** `ShowInterfaces` now reads the medium from the
match that holds it (`m1` in `encapsulation`), so an "Encapsulation X, medium is Y" line gives the interface its medium
rather than a `*ParserError`. It is the deliberate, tested difference this entry's lesson asks for: genieparser still
has the defect at 26.7, and `pkg/iosparse/doc.go`'s list of known differences now says so.
`TestShowInterfaces_MediumLine` takes two real genieparser fixtures and swaps one Encapsulation line for its medium
form ("Encapsulation ARPA, medium is broadcast", and a dot1q VLAN line with "medium is p2p" in a three-interface
output). Each failed with the KeyError before the fix and now yields the fixture's result plus the medium. The refusal
case that pinned the KeyError is gone. Caveat: the medium lines come from genieparser's own source comments; no device
capture with one exists here. The fix began as a second model's proposal, and its test was rebuilt on the fixtures
(LESSONS 403).

## 611. pkg/iosparse's ShowVlan joins wrapped lines quadratically on pathological output, bounded only by netcli's read limit (a sibling of 48) (open)

**Symptom.** Found 2026-10-23 while porting genieparser's `ShowVlan` (`pkg/iosparse/show_vlan.go`). No real device's
output has shown it.

**Root cause.** The port joins a wrapped line onto the text before it the way genieparser does, which costs time
quadratic in the number of continuation lines. The only bound on that input is `pkg/netcli`'s limit on how much a read
takes from the device.

**Fix.** None yet.

**Lesson.** As 48 found, a loop that rebuilds its accumulated text on every step needs either a builder or a bound on
its input, and a read limit sized for transport is not a bound sized for a parser.

**Fixed (2026-11-06, `dd7e7905`, branch `fix/open-patterns-fable`).** `ShowVlan` keeps the joined text in a
`strings.Builder`, reseeded from the previous line unless the builder already holds it, so a run of continuation lines
costs time linear in its length. The output is unchanged: every fixture and the fuzz seed corpus pass, and a
throwaway differential test over 300,000 seeded random inputs built from `ShowVlan`'s line shapes found no difference.
`TestShowVlan_WrappedRunIsLinear` counts bytes allocated, not time, for 1,024 and 4,096 copies of a real wrapped status
line, after checking that no pattern handles that line. Before the fix the larger run cost about 15 times the smaller
(about 10 under `-race`); now it costs about 3.8 times (3.3 under `-race`), and the test holds it to at most 6.
`TestShowVlan_WrappedNamesInARow` guards the reseed. The fix began as a second model's proposal, whose 2x/3x bound
passed on the old code under `-race`, so its test could not have failed in that mode. The test was rebuilt with a 4x
step in input and a bound of 6, set from the costs measured in both modes (LESSONS 403).

## 612. net.ios.config's checkpoint files stay on the device until the change is undone, and nothing prunes them (fixed in 129a)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-23, by design of `9ab84fe4`: each `net.ios.config` run that changes the configuration leaves two
files on the device's default writable file system (the checkpoint before and the configuration after), named
`pleiades-...`. `net.ios.replace` deletes both when it runs. A change that is never undone keeps its files.

**Root cause.** The checkpoint is the undo, and the undo may be run at any later time, so the method cannot know when
the files are no longer needed.

**Fix.** None yet. `docs/16-network-verification.md` ("Undoing an IOS change") tells users the files stay until the
undo runs, and how to delete them by hand with `net.ios.command` once the undo is no longer wanted.

**Lesson.** An undo that keeps state on a device owes a way to list and prune that state, or a limit on how much of it
builds up.

**Fixed (2026-10-25, Phase 129a):** `net.ios.checkpoints` lists the checkpoints `net.ios.config` left (only files `mintedCheckpoint` matches) and, with `prune` and `keep` or `older_than`, deletes the older ones. Age is measured by the device's own clock (`show clock`), so a router whose clock was never set is measured against itself. Proven by `TestCheckpoints_ListsAndPrunesOnlyMintedFiles`, `TestCheckpoints_AgeIsTheDevicesOwn` and `TestCheckpoints_AFailedDeleteSaysWhatWent`, and listed and pruned live on the CML sandbox. Pruning a change's checkpoint makes that change's `net.ios.replace` undo refuse, which the method's reversibility note says.

## 613. net.ios.replace deleted whatever file checkpoint or expect named after a replace, so checkpoint: nvram:startup-config would have erased the saved configuration (a repeat of 570) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's whole-branch review, 2026-10-23, on feat/lab-importers, before push.
After a successful `configure replace`, `net.ios.replace` ran `delete /force` on the files its `checkpoint` and
`expect` parameters named, to clean up the two files `net.ios.config` leaves. It deleted whatever they named. A call
written `checkpoint: nvram:startup-config` would have replaced from the saved configuration and then erased it, and a
journal entry could name any `flash:` file for the undo to delete.

**Root cause.** The cleanup trusted the call to name only files the method made. The parameters are a caller's
values, and the undo is replayed from the journal, so they can name the operator's own files. The reviewer also cited
450 and 497: a caller's value reaching a destructive device command unchecked.

**Fix.** `01cdbb70`: only names that `newCheckpointNames` mints (`pleiades-<12 hex>.cfg` and
`pleiades-<12 hex>-after.cfg`) are deleted (`mintedCheckpoint`, `internal/catalog/net/ios/checkpoint.go`). A replace
from any other file replaces from it and leaves it there. `TestReplace_NeverDeletesAFileItDidNotMake`.

**Why 570's fix did not prevent it.** 570 fixed one method, `identity.user.create`'s undo, and its lesson ("an undo that
deletes names what it made, recorded at the change, and refuses anything else") is a rule an author has to remember.
Nothing checks a new undo against it, and `net.ios.replace` was written a day later on this branch without it.

**Lesson.** Before a method deletes anything on a device, ask what happens if its argument names the operator's own
file. Delete only names the method itself made, in a shape it can recognize.

## 614. validate accepted reversible: and rollback_on_failure over net.ios.config calls that record no undo (checkpoint: false), so the in-run undo would stop halfway (a repeat of 156) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's whole-branch review, 2026-10-23, on feat/lab-importers, before push.
