`internal/engine/journal_entry.go` set `entry.Become` from `BecomeFor(task)`. So the record followed what was asked,
never what happened, and nothing could notice the gap.

**Fix.** Commits `2680ad5a` and `04d1f0bd`. `sdk.BecomeApplied` (`pkg/sdk/connect.go`) is set only after the
`WithBecome` probe (`sudo -n true`) succeeds on a connection the task opened, and `engine.recordBecome`
(`internal/engine/become.go`) writes `StatBecome` only when it is set; a task that finished without it is warned about
as having run as the login. `engine.ranAs` reads that stat and is the one source for the journal's `Become`, a block's
in-run undo (`asAccountOf`) and so a later `pleiades rollback`. `sdk.RefuseBecome` refuses before contact in
`sdk.OpenShell` and in svc's dispatch to a method with no SSH transport. `Manifest.NoBecomeReason` set to
`sdk.NoBecomeCLISession` on the CLI-session methods lets `validate`'s `BecomeRule` refuse them at plan time.
`refuseEngineActionBecome` refuses `become` on an engine action in both `Execute` and `Check`. Tests:
`TestCollectionActionExecutor_BecomeIsRecordedOnlyWhenAConnectionRanAsIt` and
`TestCollectionActionExecutor_BecomeWarnsOnlyAfterWorkThatFinished` (`internal/engine/become_applied_test.go`, a real
in-process SSH server with a stand-in `sudo`), `TestBecomeRule_RefusesTheRealCLISessionMethods`,
`TestOpenShell_RefusesBecomeBeforeReachingTheDevice`, `TestDispatch_BecomeIsRefusedForAMethodSpeakingWinRM`, and the
release gate `TestCLI_BecomeRunsATaskAndItsUndoAsRoot` (`cmd/pleiades/become_release_gate_test.go`, commit `efcaf1a8`):
a real Debian sshd, logged in as a `deploy` account with passwordless sudo, where the task writes a file under `/root`
that the login alone cannot, the journal records root, and the undo removes the file.

**Why 748's fix did not hold.** 748's fix closed one route, an external Collection's method, by refusing `become` there
at plan time and at run time. It left the engine writing the stat from the request, so every other route that did not
apply `become` still produced a record saying it had. LESSONS 358 (privilege fails closed) and LESSONS 363 (check the
rule along every route) were applied route by route, as each was found, instead of at the one point every route
passes: the carrier that actually runs the command, and the record of whether it did.

**Lesson.** A stat or a journal field that says how a command ran is set by the code that ran it, after it ran, not by
the engine from the task's settings. Then a route nobody listed records the truth instead of the request.

## 758. A failed change that kept its undo dropped its become stat, so once the journal read the account from the stats a root change was undone as the login (a repeat of 749) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review of this branch before push (2026-11-01). A task that ran as root,
changed something, then failed and kept its undo through the failure (`MayKeepOnFailure`) was journaled with no
account. A block's `rollback_on_failure` and a later `pleiades rollback` then ran its undo as the login. For
`net.frr.config` the undo would be refused outright, leaving a router half-applied.

**Root cause.** Introduced by this branch. 757's fix made `ranAs` read the account from the stats the executor records,
and wired it into every reader: the journal, the in-run undo and so the replayed rollback. One writer of those stats
was missed. The kept-undo branch of `runOne` in `internal/engine/executor.go` builds a fresh `journalStats` map for a
failed task, copying only the inverse and the diff, so `StatBecome` never reached it. Before 757's fix the journal read
the task's request and did not need the stat, so nothing showed the gap.

**Fix.** Commit `830b0086`: the kept-undo branch carries `StatBecome` into `journalStats` beside the inverse and the
diff. `TestKeptUndo_AFailedChangeIsUndoneAsTheAccountItRanAs` (`internal/engine/rollback_kept_test.go`) fails without
the fix. In the same area, commit `04d1f0bd`: a task's `rollback:` steps refuse `become` keys of their own, since a step
ran elevated inside the run but would run as the login in a later rollback, and `RollbackRule` now holds an elevated
task's steps to `BecomeRule`; and `asAccountOf` clears a step's keys when the change ran as the login, so a change made
as the login is never undone as root. Tests: `TestRollbackRule_HoldsAnElevatedTasksStepsToBecome`, and the "ran as the
login" case added to `internal/engine/rollback_on_failure_test.go`.

**Why 749's fix did not hold.** 749 found two paths that run an undo disagreeing on its account, and fixed it by making
the in-run undo follow the change's account. This branch moved where that account comes from, from the task to the
stats, and so made every place that writes the stats part of the contract. The writers were not listed. Only the
readers were, and the one map built on a failure path dropped the field.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 366.

## 759. Under become, gate.run reported a refused TCP precondition as a SKIP, and db.pg.* and net.netconf.config passed validate only to fail after the sudo probe (a repeat in kind of 557) (fixed before push; one gap open)

**Symptom.** On this branch, after 757's fix (2026-11-01). Under `become`, a `gate.run` check with a TCP precondition
was reported `SKIP`, with the reason "needs tcp host:port: remoteexec: become does not apply to a forwarded TCP
connection". A refusal read as an unmet precondition, so the check never ran and the result looked like a closed port.
Separately, every `db.pg.*` method and `net.netconf.config` passed `validate` with `become`, then failed at run time
only after the `sudo -n true` probe had run on the device.

**Root cause.** Plan time and run time checked different things. At run time the elevated connection refuses
`DialTCP`, `DialUnix` and `Subsystem`, since they send no command `sudo` could wrap. At plan time `BecomeRule` reads a
declaration, `Manifest.NoBecomeReason`, and the six `db.pg` methods (each reaches PostgreSQL through a forward the SSH
login opens) and `net.netconf.config` (an SSH subsystem) did not carry one. `gate.run` saw the dial's refusal as any
other failure to reach the port, which its precondition logic maps to a skip.

**Fix.** Commit `e0956a12`. `NoBecomeReason` on the six `db.pg` methods (`noBecomeForward` in
`internal/catalog/db/pg/pg.go`) and on `net.netconf.config`, published in `docs/reference/schemas/module-catalog.json`
as `noBecomeReason`. `gate.run`'s TCP precondition (`internal/catalog/gate/preconditions.go`) calls `sdk.RefuseBecome`
before any connect and returns a `FAIL` naming `become`. `TestRun_ATCPPreconditionUnderBecomeFailsAndDoesNotSkip`
fails without the fix, showing the `SKIP`, and checks that the guarded command never ran.

**Why 557's fix did not reach this.** 557 put the capability check in one function that plan time, admission and run
time all call. `become` has no such shared check. Its plan-time rule reads a hand-set declaration and its run-time
refusal sits in the connection, so a method that forwards or opens a subsystem passes the first and fails the second
unless someone remembers to declare it. 605 has the same shape (validate passed what the run then refused).

**Open.** `container.*` depends on the device's carrier and is not refused at plan time. A forwarded engine socket is
refused at run time, after the sudo probe; `dial-stdio` runs elevated; a TLS or local carrier runs as the login with a
warning (757's `recordBecome`).

**Lesson.** A plan-time refusal that reads a declaration needs the run-time refusal it mirrors to be checked against
it. Until one function decides both, list every method that reaches the refused calls (`DialTCP`, `DialUnix`,
`Subsystem`) and declare each.

## 760. The collection coverage ratchet walked only the ledgers that exist, so deleting or renaming one took its floor out, and a ledger with no floor was only logged (a repeat of 403 and 397) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review of branch `feat/c0-roadmap-and-coverage-ledger` before push
(2026-11-01). `internal/archtest`'s `TestCoverageLedgers` compared each ledger under `coverage/collections` with its
floor in `coverage-floor-collections.json`. Deleting a ledger, or renaming its directory, took it out of the loop, and
its floor was never read again: the ratchet passed with nothing under it. A ledger with no floor was written to the
test log with `t.Logf` and passed.

**Root cause.** The loop ran over ledgers, never over floors. That is 403's shape (a floor with nothing measured
behind it is never visited), in a second ratchet file read by a different checker.

**Fix.** Commit `37147b76`. `coverageledger.FloorFile.Orphans` (`internal/coverageledger/report.go`) returns each
floored collection with no ledger, and `TestCoverageLedgers` fails on each one and on a ledger with no floor
(`internal/archtest/coverage_ledger_test.go`). Test: `TestFloors_AFloorWithNoLedgerIsAnOrphan`
(`internal/coverageledger/report_test.go`). The floor file's own comment now says both fail.

**Why 403's fix did not reach this.** 403's fix is `unmeasured` in `tools/coverage-check/measured.go`, and it guards
only `coverage-floor.json`'s package floors. The collection ratchet is new code with its own file and its own checker,
and it was written in the shape 397 and 403 had already fixed once: walk what was measured, compare it with its floor,
stop. A rule held in one tool's code does not travel to the next ratchet someone writes.

**Lesson.** As 403's: a ratchet checks both directions, every measurement against its floor and every floor against a
measurement. Write the second loop in the same change as the first, in every ratchet.

## 761. The coverage ledger confined one read of four, so contract.json, map.yaml and a proof's test directory could be read through a committed symbolic link outside the repository (a repeat of 260 and 321) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent before push (2026-11-01), through its vuln-corpus `search_patterns` and
`list_findings` calls for class C4; the plain sweep did not report it. Earlier on the same branch, commit `b52e0ab8`
had made `coverageledger.Ledger.ReadSource` read the vendored contract through `os.OpenRoot` on the ledger's
directory. The other reads of the same ledger did not: `Load` read `contract.json` and `map.yaml` with `os.ReadFile`,
and a proof's test directory, checked only by `filepath.IsLocal` on its text, was globbed for `*_test.go` and passed to
`go list` on the real filesystem. A ledger is data a pull request may change and CI reads, so a committed symbolic
link in place of either file or of the test directory read a path outside the repository on whatever machine ran the
check.

**Root cause.** The confinement rule was applied to the read it was found on, not to the data source. `b52e0ab8`
fixed `ReadSource` because the sweep named it; `Load` and the proof check were siblings reading the same ledger
(LESSONS 244), and the test directory, a path derived from `Proof.Test`, was treated as checked because its text was
local. A lexical check says what a name looks like, not where the filesystem resolves it (LESSONS 229).

**Fix.** Commit `37147b76`. `Load` opens the ledger's directory with `os.OpenRoot` and reads both files through it
(`internal/coverageledger/ledger.go`). `insideRoot` in `internal/archtest/coverage_ledger_test.go` resolves the
repository root and the proof's directory with `filepath.EvalSymlinks` and requires the second inside the first
before the glob and `go list` run. Tests: `TestLoad_ReadsNeitherFileThroughALinkOut` (a link out in place of each
file is refused) and `insideRoot`'s negative control in `TestCoverageLedgerChecks_CanFail` (a directory that links out
is reported outside). Recorded in vuln-corpus as `C4_auto-roboto_2026-11-01`, beside `C4_auto-roboto_2026-10-31`
for `ReadSource`.

**Why 260's and 321's fix did not reach this.** Each fixed one read by opening it through `os.Root`, the right fix for
that read. Nothing makes the next reader of a new data source use it: no shared helper reads committed repository
data, and no check finds an `os.ReadFile` or a glob on a path taken from that data. This branch repeated the class
twice, the second time on the day after fixing the first, in the same package.

**A gap found while recording this, then fixed before push.** `insideRoot` confined the directory, not the files in
it: `testFuncExists` globbed `*_test.go` there and parsed each with `go/parser`, so a `*_test.go` that is itself a
symbolic link out would have been read. `testFuncExists` now skips a test file that is a symbolic link (`os.Lstat`),
proven by `TestCoverageLedgerChecks_CanFail`, whose linked `elsewhere_test.go` is not counted. Residual, not
measured: `go list -deps` in such a directory may still read a linked file's package clause and imports.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 367.

## 762. Untrusted ledger data panicked the archtest and the docs generator, and a proof naming a function go test never runs was accepted (a repeat in kind of 317) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent before push (2026-11-01). A proof's `test` with no dot made
`coverageledger.SplitTest` slice `ref[:-1]` and panic, in `TestCoverageLedgers` and in `tools/gendocs`, which
rendered a ledger without calling `Ledger.Problems` first. The reference pattern also accepted a name like `Testfoo`,
which `go test` never runs, since a test name cannot go on after `Test` with a lower-case letter.

**Root cause.** 317's kind: input someone else writes was handed to code that assumed its shape. `SplitTest` used
`strings.LastIndex` without checking that it found a dot, and the pattern said `Test[A-Za-z0-9_]*` rather than go
test's own rule. `Problems` held the shape check, and gendocs never called it.

**Fix.** Commit `37147b76`. `SplitTest` returns `ok` and refuses a reference that does not match the pattern or whose
directory is not local (`internal/coverageledger/mapping.go`); the pattern is `Test([A-Z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)?`; and
gendocs refuses a ledger with any `Problems` (`tools/gendocs/coverage.go`). Test: `TestSplitTest`
(`internal/coverageledger/ledger_test.go`), whose bad references include `TestFoo` with no directory, `a.`, `.`,
`a.Testfoo` and three that leave the module.

**Why 317's fix did not reach this.** 317's fix hardened one package's filename guard. The class it showed (code that
parses outside input assumes a shape and fails hard when the shape is wrong) has no shared check; each new parser has
to refuse its own bad input.

**Lesson.** A function that splits or parses a reference reports whether it could, and every caller that renders or
reads the data runs the validator's check first, not only the validator.

## 763. The OpenAPI reader skipped what it could not count, matched keys in any case and kept the last of repeated keys, each of which would raise a collection's coverage (a repeat of 325) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent before push (2026-11-01). `coverageledger.ExtractOpenAPI`, which lists a
contract's operations, skipped a path item written as a `$ref`, a method in upper case and any key it did not know,
dropped a Swagger 2 `basePath`, and returned zero operations without an error. Its decode through `encoding/json`
matched `"Paths"` as `paths` and kept only the last of two repeated keys. Each one makes the operation list shorter or
other than the contract's, and a shorter list reads as higher mapped and live percentages.

**Root cause.** Two. The reader treated what it could not count as nothing to count, the hole LESSONS 104 names (a
measurement is confidently silent where its model is wrong). And it trusted `encoding/json`'s forgiving defaults for a
document whose every key matters, which is 325's root cause.

**Fix.** Commit `37147b76` (`internal/coverageledger/openapi.go`). Keys are matched exactly. `refuseRepeatedKeys`
reads the document token by token and refuses a repeated key anywhere. An unknown path-item key, a `$ref`, a near-miss
top-level key (such as `Paths`), a `basePath` that is not text and a document with no operations are refused, and a
`basePath` is joined to every path. Tests: `TestExtractOpenAPI_RefusesWhatItCannotCount` and `TestExtractOpenAPI`
(`internal/coverageledger/report_test.go`).

**Why 325's fix did not reach this.** 325's fix, `parseJSONKeyTree` in `internal/engine/json_strict.go`, is the
engine's own reader for JSON runbooks. It is not a shared strict decoder, so a new package reading JSON starts again
from `encoding/json`'s defaults.

**Lesson.** A reader that feeds a measurement refuses what it cannot count. Skipping it changes the number, and the
number is the only thing anyone reads.

## 764. A declared method could count an operation as mapped, and its proof skipped the reach check (the class of LESSONS 15) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent before push (2026-11-01). A ledger could map an operation to a method whose
status is declared but not implemented, and the operation counted as mapped. Since a declared method has no `Invoke`,
`checkProofTests` skipped its reach check, so its proof was held to nothing more than a test existing.

**Root cause.** The ledger checks asked only whether a named method is registered. A declared method is registered
and implements nothing, the distinction LESSONS 15 says a linter must know.

**Fix.** Commit `37147b76`. `checkLedgerNames` in `internal/archtest/coverage_ledger_test.go` fails a ledger that names
a method whose `Manifest.Status` is not `collection.StatusImplemented`.

**Lesson.** A count of what is covered counts only what is implemented. Every check that asks "is this method known"
also asks "does it run".

## 765. The coverage ledger's first records said more than the code and upstream support: the changelog, the floor file's rule, the published schema's field names and the vendored contract's copyright and version (a repeat of 571 and 228) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent before push (2026-11-01). Five statements, each read as settled:

1. The changelog fragment said every operation was mapped to a method or excluded with a reason. Fifty-four were
   neither (42 in `virt.clab` alone).
2. `coverage-floor-collections.json` said lowering a floor needs a written reason, and nothing compared a floor with
   its earlier value.
3. `docs/reference/schemas/collection-coverage.json`, published as `schemaVersion` 1, carried each proof's fields as
   Go's names (`Status`, `Test`), while every other field is lower case.
4. The vendored containerlab API contract carried no `LICENSE`, though it is Apache-2.0, and its `NOTICE` said
   "Copyright the containerlab authors". Upstream's `LICENSE` names no copyright holder.
5. The vendored contract's version was stated and unverified: nothing tied it to the server the live tests run.

**Root cause.** 228's class: a record states what was meant, and nothing re-reads it against the code or the source.
The license text is LESSONS 318's rule not applied: carry the upstream license verbatim, and the notice as upstream
gives it.

**Fix.** Commit `37147b76`. The fragment says each operation is shown as mapped, excluded or not implemented
(`changelog/collection-coverage-ledger.added.md`). The floor comment says a lowering is caught in review of the file's
diff. `coverageledger.Proof` carries `json:"status"` and `json:"test,omitempty"`. `coverage/collections/virt.clab/source/LICENSE`
is upstream's, copied unchanged from the pinned commit, and the `NOTICE` says upstream's license names no holder. The
image `internal/testsupport.ClabAPIImage` pins was read for its labels (revision
`a70e099b481bb2be7c873cbad506bb40e234c43f`, version `v0.9.0`), its comment names both, and `checkPinnedRevisions` in
`internal/archtest/coverage_ledger_test.go` fails when the `NOTICE`'s upstream commit is not named beside the image.

**Why 571's fix did not reach this.** 571's fix corrected four texts and set a rule (a claimed refusal is checked by a
test of that refusal). New records on a new feature are written fresh, and a review is still the only thing that reads
them against the code.

**Lesson.** As 571's. A record that states a version or a copyright is checked against the source it names, and
where a test can hold the two together, one does.

## 766. Two "live" proofs rested on a refusal and on a log line, and node.start, which the live test runs, was declared fixture (a repeat of 467 and 491) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent before push (2026-11-01). `virt.clab`'s `map.yaml` declared
`virt.clab.capture.packetflix` live through `TestLive_ARealLabEndToEnd`, which reaches only the server's refusal
("Edgeshark is not running"); a capture link the method returns was never proven. `virt.clab.edgeshark.status` was
declared live through the same test, which only wrote its result to the log with `t.Logf`. `virt.clab.node.start`
was declared fixture, though the live test runs it as the undo of a stop.

**Root cause.** 467's class: a test counted as proof of what it touched, not of what it asserted. A refusal and a log
line both pass whatever the method does. LESSONS 158 says the same of presence checks.

**Fix.** Commit `37147b76`. `packetflix` is `status: none`, with a comment saying why. The live test asserts
`edgeshark.status` reports `running: false`, and that a stop's recorded undo is `virt.clab.node.start`, which then
brings the node back to running; `node.start` is declared live. The live test was run against the real server after
the change and passed. The mapped and live percentages are unchanged (one live proof removed, one added).

**Why 467's and 491's fix did not reach this.** Both fixed one gate's assertions. A ledger that declares proof per
method makes every assertion in a shared live test a claim, and a declaration is checked by `internal/archtest` only
for the test existing and reaching the method, never for what it asserts.

**Lesson.** A test named as a method's proof asserts that method's answer. A refusal or a logged value is not one.

## 767. An fp-reviewer launched seconds after its definition gained the triad tools ran with the new instructions and the old tool list, and reported the triad unavailable (open: cause unknown; the agent now checks its tools first)

**Symptom.** On 2026-11-01, commit `c111f52d` gave the fp-reviewer agent the security triad's MCP tools by editing
`.claude/agents/fp-reviewer.md`. An instance launched seconds after the edit had the new instructions (its transcript
holds the new triad section) but only the gopls tools, and it reported that no triad tool was available. A probe
launched minutes later had all 17.

**Root cause.** Unknown. The evidence fits a stale copy of the definition's tool list being used for a launch made
soon after an edit, while the instructions were read fresh. Not reproduced.

**Fix.** Commit `a0c282e6`. The definition tells the agent to call `mcp__vuln-corpus__status` before anything else,
and to say so in its first line and stop when that or any triad tool it lists is missing. After editing an agent's
definition, relaunch it and check its first line before relying on its review.

**Lesson.** A review agent proves the tools its review depends on before it reviews, and says so first. A review that
silently lacks a tool reads like one that had it.

## 768. validate refused pleiades.builtin.fail, assert and set_fact, which the engine runs, because the Collection rules kept their own list of dotted builtins (a repeat in kind of 661's doc_topics list and LESSONS 273) (fixed)

**Symptom.** Found 2026-10-31 on `feat/c1-language` while adding the timed pause and its dotted spelling
`pleiades.builtin.pause`. `pleiades validate` refused `pleiades.builtin.fail`, `pleiades.builtin.assert` and
`pleiades.builtin.set_fact` as collection names nothing registered, though the engine runs all three. The dotted fail
and assert came with Phases 88 and 89 (`dad90e5b`) and the dotted set_fact with Phase 87 (`26ec87d8`), both on
2026-10-27, so v0.3.0 shipped with the refusal.

**Root cause.** `internal/validate`'s Collection rules (`CollectionRule`, `ParamsRule`, `ParamTypeRule`,
`ParamChoiceRule`, the required-params and rollback rules) skipped engine actions through their own hand-kept map,
`dottedBuiltinExemptions`, which named only `pleiades.builtin.set_metadata`. Each new dotted engine action needed a
line there, and nothing failed when it was missing.

**Fix.** `09a9cd2a`. The map is gone; the rules ask `engine.IsBuiltinAction`, which reads the engine's own table of
the actions it runs (`engineActionStatKeys`, `internal/engine/journal_entry.go`). `TestValidate_AcceptsEveryDottedBuiltin`
validates the dotted fail, assert, set_fact and set_metadata, and `TestValidate_AcceptsATimedPause` both spellings of
pause. The user-facing note is in `changelog/timed-pause.added.md`.

**Why 661's sibling fix and LESSONS 273 did not prevent it.** 661's review found a hand list in `doc_topics.go` and
held that one list to the engine's table; it did not look for other lists of engine names. LESSONS 273 says a hand
list read by a guard is that guard's defect, and this list predated it.

**Lesson.** A list of the engine's own names outside the engine is a second source; read the engine's table instead,
and test the spellings a user writes.

## 769. A flaky start-order assertion was committed because the test step was piped through `| tail` inside an `&&` chain (a repeat of LESSONS 100 and 192) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-10-31, commit `e0eff519` (async and poll) held `TestAsync_ABackgroundTaskRunsWhileTheRunGoesOn`
asserting the marks `long+,quick+,quick-,long-`. Which of the background task and the next task starts first is the
scheduler's choice, so the assertion failed on some runs. The test step before the commit ran in an `&&` chain with its
output piped through `| tail`, and the chain went on to the commit.

**Root cause.** A pipeline's status is its last command's. `tail` succeeded, so the chain read success. The assertion
itself named an order nothing promises.

**Fix.** The commit was amended 43 seconds later (`2c128590`, now `632c7552`), before any push: the assertion accepts
either start order and holds what the design promises, that the quick task started and finished while the long one ran.

**Why LESSONS 100 and 192 did not prevent it.** Both were written about reading a gate's verdict, and both say to
capture the status of the command that matters in its own statement. The habit was not applied to a quick test step in
a chain, where a hidden failure becomes a commit rather than a wrong report.

**Lesson.** As 100 and 192: never pipe a command whose status decides the next step. And an assertion on two
concurrent starts names only the order the design guarantees.

## 770. A background job's goroutine read the task's result while startJob went on writing it (a repeat in kind of 64) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found while writing `632c7552` (async and poll), before it was committed. `startJob`
(`internal/engine/async.go`) handed `result` to the job's goroutine and then went on writing `result` (its stats, its
background mark, a failure when the job id could not be registered), so two goroutines touched one value at once.

**Root cause.** 64's class: what a goroutine reads was not final when the goroutine started.

**Fix.** In the same commit: the job starts from its own copy (`start := result`), taken before the `go` statement,
with a comment saying why.

**Why 64's fix did not reach this.** 64 moved one handler's header writes above its handoff, and its lesson is worded
for an `http.ResponseWriter`. Nothing checks what a caller does to a value after `go func`.

**Lesson.** Whatever a goroutine reads is final, or copied, before the `go` statement; after it, the caller writes only
its own copy.

## 771. --limit first narrowed every target, so a task naming a device outside the hosts would lose it under a limit (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** While building `pleiades run --limit` (`dc47e646`), the first version filtered every target the run
resolved, not only the runbook's hosts. A task that names a device outside the hosts (a lab server, a Batfish service)
would lose that device under a limit. Ansible's `--limit` leaves `delegate_to` alone, and `serial:`, built the same
day, divides only the hosts.

**Root cause.** The limit was applied to the resolver as a whole, which answers for every target, rather than to the
set of hosts.

**Fix.** In the same commit: `limitResolver` (`cmd/pleiades/run_limit.go`) narrows only the devices among the runbook's
hosts and passes every other target through. `TestLimit_NarrowsWhatARunReaches` runs a task naming `lab` under
`--limit w1` and requires `lab@lab,a@w1`.

**Lesson.** A filter on which devices run applies to the hosts, the same set `serial:` divides. A device a task names
itself is the author's choice, and a filter that wraps the whole resolver changes it without a word.

## 772. serial: batches followed the devices' generated IDs, not their names, so a rollout ran s3 and s4 first (a sibling of 411) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** `TestCLI_SerialRunsTwoDevicesAtATime` (four real Debian devices, `serial: 2`, `fe89f92f`) found the CLI's
batches in the order s3, s4, s1, s2.

**Root cause.** `engine.Batches` keeps its input order, as Ansible keeps the play's host order. The CLI's resolver
returns devices in the order of their generated IDs, which says nothing about their names. 411's class: an order a user
reads, taken from IDs that carry none.

**Fix.** `fe89f92f`: `engine.BatchDevices` sorts a run's devices by name before batching (`TestBatchDevices_OrdersByName`
feeds it out of order), and the CLI uses it. The Controller numbers a job's queued devices by name once
(`AssignBatches`, `6e8ba355`). The guide and `docs/reference/task-keys.md` say batches are in name order.

**Lesson.** When a feature's order is visible to a user, choose it on purpose and test it with input in another
order; a store's order is its IDs'.

## 773. The Runner serial gate made its failure marker as root in sticky /tmp, so the task's login could not remove it and no task failed (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** `TestSerialReleaseGate_TwoAtATimeAndAFailedBatchStops` (`cmd/runner/serial_release_gate_test.go`,
`3155e238`) fails a task by having it remove a marker: when `rm /tmp/fail-<tag>` succeeds, the task exits 1. As first
written, the gate made the marker through the container's exec, which runs as root. `/tmp` is sticky, so the login the
tasks run as could not remove a root-owned file there, `rm` failed, the task took its success branch, and no batch
failed.

**Root cause.** The fixture was made by a different account than the one the task runs as, in a directory where the
sticky bit lets only a file's owner remove it.

**Fix.** In the same commit: the gate creates the marker and gives it to the gate's SSH login (`chown` to
`releaseGateSSHUser`), with a comment saying why. The gate measures `S S E` on the device and the second batch skipped.

**Lesson.** A fixture a task acts on is made as, or given to, the account the task runs as. A container's exec is root.

## 774. A task timeout never ended an SSH command whose child held its output, on Debian's sshd, and the task reported success (a sibling of 506, the class of 740) (fixed)

**Symptom.** Found 2026-10-31 by the async gate on a real Debian sshd (`cmd/pleiades/async_release_gate_test.go`):
under `timeout: 3`, `sleep 60 & wait` ran its whole minute and the task reported success. The task timeout of
2026-10-18 (`11493533`) had promised that a timeout stops the command on the device.

**Root cause.** At a timeout `pkg/remoteexec` sends the command SIGTERM over SSH, closes the session, and then waited
on `session.Wait`. OpenSSH's sshd answers a client's close only once the command's output ends, and the backgrounded
child held it; on Debian's sshd the signal did not reach the command either. Wait returned when the sleep ended, with
the command's own exit status. The 2026-10-18 change was proven by `TestConn_RunSignalsTheCommandWhenCancelled`,
against an in-process SSH server that ends the session when it receives a signal request, which a real sshd does not
promise.

**Fix.** `fe9c4d62`: `waitOrAbandon` (`pkg/remoteexec/conn.go`) waits for the command, or, once the context ends, for at
most `abandonGrace` (two seconds) more, and then returns the context's error; the connection is tainted, so the
abandoned Wait ends when it closes. The gate's first run, `timeout-gate`, requires the task to fail within 60 seconds
of a 120-second sleep (first written as 20 against 30, too close to tell apart; see 788).
The command itself may still run on such a device, as `changelog/ssh-timeout-ends-the-task.fixed.md` says; an
`async:` task stops it.

**Why 506's fix did not reach this.** 506 made the Runner's child handle its signal so the method's context ends. This
is the next link, the SSH side, and it was proven only against a stand-in server that obeyed the request (740's class:
a stub built from assumed shapes).

**Lesson.** A stop is proven against the real server it must stop, with a command shaped like real work, one that
starts a child. A stand-in that obeys the request proves the request was sent, not that anything stopped.

## 775. An async task ran attached in the Runner's child, because the detach mark was a context value no process boundary carries, and the Runner gate first passed without it (a repeat of 748 and LESSONS 363) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** `fe9c4d62` made an async task's SSH commands run detached on the device, marked by
`remoteexec.WithDetach`, a context value. On a Runner a method runs in a per-task or session child, and an external
Collection's method in its own program. Each builds a fresh context from the `wire.ChildRequest` it receives, and the
request did not say the call was async, so the child ran the command attached. The Runner gate,
`TestAsyncReleaseGate_DetachedOnARunner`, as first written checked that the task failed at its limit, that the sleep it
started was stopped and that no job directory was left. It passed without the mark: this image's sshd delivers the
signal, so the attached command died to it at the limit, the same outcome a detached stop gives.

**Root cause.** LESSONS 363's class: a mechanism applied along the in-process route only. A context value does not
cross a process boundary, and nothing fails when it is missing, since a missing mark reads as false. The gate checked
outcomes both paths produce.

**Fix.** `d5e80674`. `wire.ChildRequest.Detach` carries the mark. The per-task parent (`ipc_parent.go`), the session
(`ipc_session.go`) and the external proxy (`internal/loader/proxy_unix.go`) set it from `remoteexec.Detached(ctx)`,
and `pkg/external.InvokeRequestFor` marks the child's context (`TestInvokeRequest_AnAsyncCallRunsDetachedInTheChild`).
The gate now watches the device for the job's directory while the task runs, which only a detached run makes, and
fails when none appears.

**Why 748's fix and LESSONS 363 did not prevent it.** 363 (2026-10-31, in the tree when this branch was cut) says to
list every route a method can take before adding a mechanism that changes how a call runs. It was written about
`become`, and the async change did not write its list; its in-process tests and the Crawl gate passed.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 368 and 369.

## 776. The test binaries' child entry ran on a bare context.Background(), so SIGTERM killed it before any stop ran: 506's fix lived only in the real Runner's main (a repeat of 506 and 693) (fixed)

**Symptom.** Found 2026-11-01 while writing the Runner async gate. A Runner ends a task's child with SIGTERM at its
limit. The real Runner's child runs its method on a context that SIGTERM ends (506's fix, `cmd/runner/child.go`),
so the method stops its work on the device before the child exits. The test binaries that stand in for that child
(`cmd/runner`'s `TestMain` in `ssh_mesh_release_gate_test.go` and `tests/e2e`'s in `harness_test.go`) called
`native.RunChildFor(context.Background(), ...)`. There SIGTERM killed the child at once and no stop ran, so every gate
since 2026-10-18 ran a child unlike the real one.

**Root cause.** 506's fix was a function in `cmd/runner`'s `main` package, which no test binary can call, so each
`TestMain` kept its own line. 693's class: a harness that wires a production object by hand and leaves out what the
composition root passes.

**Fix.** `d5e80674`. `native.ChildContext` (`internal/adapters/native/child_context.go`) is the one function the
Runner's `main` and both test mains call, and `cmd/runner/child.go` is gone. `TestChildContext_EndsOnSIGTERM`.

**Why 506 and 693 did not prevent it.** 506 fixed the half of a graceful stop that handles the signal, in one binary,
and its test checked the function, not that every entry point used it. 693's lesson (LESSONS 351) asks to compare a
harness's constructor with the composition root's, and a `TestMain` that routes to the child was not seen as one.

**Lesson.** A production entry point's setup lives in a package a test can call, and the test's stand-in calls it. A
copied line is a second program.

## 777. A detached job's stop did not run when the limit landed inside a poll, nor when the child's connection had already closed (a sibling of 506) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found while proving async on a Runner (`d5e80674`). Two paths left a detached job running past its async
limit. (1) When the limit landed while a poll's command was in flight, that command failed with the context's error,
and the loop treated the failure as a dropped connection: it reconnected or reported the job as possibly still
running, and did not stop it. (2) A Runner's child is told to stop by the same signal that closes its connections, so
the stop ran its commands on a connection already gone and stopped nothing.

**Root cause.** The stop was written for the path the first tests took: the limit between polls, on a live connection.
The other exits were not walked, as the Failure-Mode Walk asks.

**Fix.** `d5e80674`. In `runDetached` every poll command that fails after the context ended goes to the stop. When its
own connection fails, `stopDetached` redials as the same account (`become` kept) and runs the stop there; TERM is
given three seconds before KILL, inside a 20-second bound. `TestDetached_TheStopReconnectsWhenItsConnectionIsGone`
closes the connection first and requires the job's child gone and its directory removed;
`TestDetached_ALostConnectionThatCannotBeRedialedIsNamed`; the Runner gate checks the started sleep is gone. No test
written in `d5e80674` lands the limit inside a poll on purpose, so path (1) rests on the code and the gate.

**Lesson.** As 506's: a stop has a sender and a handler, and here the handler has every exit of the loop it ends. Walk
each one, and the state of the connection at each.

## 778. remoteexec.run read a command's output buffers while x/crypto/ssh's copiers could still write them, once waitOrAbandon had abandoned the command (a repeat of 197, made by 774's fix) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review of `feat/c1-language`, 2026-11-01. 774's fix (`fe9c4d62`) lets
`run` (`pkg/remoteexec/conn.go`) return two seconds after its context ends without waiting for the command. `run` then
built its `Result` from the stdout and stderr buffers before deciding the outcome. On an abandoned command
x/crypto/ssh's goroutines that copy the streams into those buffers are still running, so the read raced them. Under
`-race` the old code reports a data race at `conn.go:248`.

**Root cause.** 197's class: only the wait that joins the copiers makes the buffers safe to read, and an abandoned
command has no such wait. The async release gate missed it twice over: its timed-out command wrote nothing, and the
gate's binaries are not built with `-race`.

**Fix.** `2e91d59d`. The buffers are read only on the two paths where `Wait` returned (exit 0, or an exit status); an
abandoned command returns the context's error and no output. `TestRun_ACommandWhoseServerNeverAnswersIsAbandoned`
(`pkg/remoteexec/abandon_test.go`) puts a TCP proxy between client and server that stops forwarding the server's side,
which is how Debian's sshd behaves here, inside a package test the race detector watches. It fails on the old code.

**Why 197's fix did not reach this.** 197 fixed one `cmd.Process.Wait()` in a test and swept the module for that call.
This is the same rule (read what a goroutine writes only after joining it) at a different API, where giving up on the
wait is the feature.

**Lesson.** A call that may return without waiting owns nothing its helpers still write. LESSONS 370 for why no gate saw it.

## 779. A detached command ran unlike the same command attached: the start script's umask leaked into it, it ran under sh rather than the login shell, and a login banner broke the job-directory parse (the class of 749) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. Under `async:` (`pkg/remoteexec/detach.go`,
`detachStart`): (a) the script's `umask 077`, meant for the job's own files, applied to the user's command, so the files
and directories it made were 0600 and 0700 where a plain run made them by the account's umask; (b) the command ran
under `sh -c`, where a plain run's command goes to the login shell sshd gives it; (c) the job directory was taken from
all of stdout, so a login shell's startup output before it broke the parse, and the pattern `jobDir` let a newline
through.

**Root cause.** 749's class: two paths that run one thing, and the second written without holding it to the first. The
detached path was tested for detaching, not for running the command as an attached run would.

**Fix.** `54c0cff4`. The script saves the caller's umask and the job restores it; the job runs under the account's login
shell, or `sh` under `become` as a plain elevated run does (`jobShell`); the directory is the last line of output
(`lastLine`), and `jobDir` refuses a newline. It also refuses MSYS and Cygwin, where a command written for cmd.exe would
run under sh, and runs the command where it stands instead. `TestDetached_TheJobKeepsTheCallersUmaskAndShell`,
`TestDetached_ALoginBannerBeforeTheDirectoryIsSkipped`.

**Lesson.** A second way to run a command is tested against the first for everything the command can see: its
umask, its shell, its input, its output.

## 780. A detached command was an argument of the job's process for its whole life, visible in any process listing on the device (a repeat in kind of 455 and 719) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. `detachStart` received the user's command as `"$1"`
and passed it on to `sh -c`, so the command, and any secret written into it, sat in the argv of a long-running process
that every account on the device can list.

**Root cause.** 455's class: a value that may hold a secret placed on a command line. A plain run sends the command
in the SSH exec request, which no other account sees; the detached path turned it into an argument.

**Fix.** `54c0cff4`. The command travels on the start script's stdin into a 0600 file in the job's private directory,
and the job runs that file. `TestDetached_TheCommandIsNeverAnArgument`.

**Why 455 and 719 did not prevent it.** Both fixed what a method reports; this was the transport's own construction of
a process on the device, a place no earlier fix looked.

**Lesson.** Whatever may carry a secret travels on stdin or in a private file, never in a process's arguments, on the
device as on this machine.

## 781. Under become with a sudo that keeps the login's HOME, the job base sat in a directory the login owns, so the login could steer root's polls and kills (a repeat in kind of 761 and LESSONS 367) (fixed before push; the attack was reasoned, not reproduced)

**Symptom.** Raised as suspected by the records-keeper agent on 2026-11-01, from reading `detachStart`. The job base was
`$HOME/.pleiades-async-<uid>`. Under `become`, where sudo keeps the login's `HOME`, root made that base inside a
directory the login owns, and then polled and stopped the job through paths in it as root (`cat .../out`,
`kill -TERM -$(cat .../pid)`). A process running as the login could swap the job directory for its own between the
start and the first poll: an `out` linked to `/etc/shadow` would be read by root into the task's output, and a `pid`
file could name any process group for root's kill. Nobody reproduced this.

**Root cause.** 761's class (LESSONS 367): a path built from a location another account controls, and trusted. The base
was chosen by account id so that become would get its own, without checking who owns `HOME` or the base.

**Fix.** `54c0cff4`. The script uses the base only when `$HOME` and the base belong to the account running the job and
the base is not a link, and makes it 0700; otherwise it exits 70 and the command runs where it stands.
`TestDetached_AHomeTheAccountDoesNotOwnRunsTheCommandWhereItStands`, `TestDetached_ALinkedBaseIsRefused`.

**A test that could not fail.** `TestDetached_ALinkedBaseIsRefused` first passed against the old script: it checked for
the job's directory after the run, and a finished job removes its own directory, so the old script and the new one
looked the same. It now tells attached from detached by the command's stdin (a pipe when attached, `/dev/null` when
detached) and fails on the old script. That is LESSONS 368, written the same day, met again in a unit test.

**Lesson.** As LESSONS 367: under elevation, a path the elevated side reads or acts on is owned by the elevated account
from its root down, and checked before each use, not only named.

## 782. A detached command's 20-second stop sat inside a 5-second kill, and an external Collection's program had no SIGTERM handling at all, so the stop never reached the device (a repeat of 776 at a sibling site, and of LESSONS 225) (fixed)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. At an async limit the Runner sends its collection child
SIGTERM and kills it `childWaitDelay` (5 s) later; the loader does the same to an external program after its kill
grace. The detached stop (777's fix) can take up to 20 s, since it may redial first, so the kill could land before the
stop reached the device. And `pkg/external.Main` ran its method on `context.Background()` with no signal handling, so
SIGTERM killed an external program at once and its detached job ran past the limit.

**Root cause.** LESSONS 225's class: an inner budget inside an outer deadline, which fires first. And 776's: 776 gave
the Runner's own child a SIGTERM-ending context and left the external SDK's entry point, the third stand-in for the
same child, as it was. By reading the code, not by a run, the same held before this branch for a plain timeout in an
external program: SIGTERM killed it before its method's context ended, so no SSH signal was sent (506's shape).

**Fix.** `7a95bfa4`. `remoteexec.DetachStopBudget` names the stop's time. The Runner's per-task and session children
are given `killDelay` (`childWaitDelay` plus the budget when the call is detached), and the loader's `newCommand` adds
the budget to `WaitDelay` under a detached context. `external.Main` runs the method under `signal.NotifyContext` for
SIGTERM. `TestProgram_SIGTERMEndsTheMethodsContext` (`pkg/external/sigterm_test.go`; the old code ends "signal:
terminated"), `internal/adapters/native/kill_delay_test.go`, `internal/loader/detach_delay_test.go`.

**Why 776's fix and LESSONS 225 did not prevent it.** 776 was framed as "the test mains differ from the Runner", so the
search for stand-ins stopped at test binaries. LESSONS 225 was not consulted when the stop's budget was chosen.

**Lesson.** A stop's budget is checked against every kill that can end the process running it, and every entry point
that runs a child method handles SIGTERM the same way.

## 783. A background job ran on context.WithoutCancel, so a cancelled run waited out the job's whole async limit, and a failed job-id record reported a failed start while the job ran (the class of 777; its comment said the opposite) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01, in `startJob` (`internal/engine/async.go`). (1) The
job ran under `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`. Nothing in the engine ends a level's context, so this dropped only the run's
own cancel: a cancelled run's job ran on, and `drainJobs` held the run open for the job's async limit, which may be a
day. The comment beside it said the job was "bounded by ... the run's own context". (2) The job id was recorded in the
register after the job's goroutine started, so a failed record failed the task while its job ran on, uncollectable.

**Root cause.** Both are exits not walked: the run's cancel, and a failure after the act had begun. The comment
described the intent, and no test cancelled a run with a job in flight.

**Fix.** `736a4d79`. The job runs under the run's own context, with a comment saying why that is the only cancel it
sees. The job id is recorded before the job starts, and a failed record releases the lease the job would have held.
`TestAsync_CancellingTheRunStopsABackgroundJob` (60 s on the old code).

**Lesson.** A goroutine that outlives its caller takes the cancel of whatever must be able to stop it, and is started
only after everything that can fail its start has succeeded.

## 784. A handler with its own target, a handler whose call needs no device, a handler locking all devices at plan time, and a background task inside a rollback_on_failure block were all accepted and then skipped, failed or left un-undone on every run (a repeat of 252 and 324) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. A handler runs on the devices whose tasks notified it.
One with a `target:` of its own, or whose call acts on no device, never found a notification and skipped on every run.
One with `lock_acquisition: all_at_plan_time` failed on every run that notified it, since a handler runs on each device
alone. A `poll: 0` task inside a block with `rollback_on_failure` passed validation, though the block's undo cannot undo
a job still running and the job would change the device after it.

**Root cause.** 252's class: a combination the parser accepts and the run cannot honor, refused nowhere.

**Fix.** `736a4d79`. `validateHandlers` refuses the three handler shapes by name (`ErrHandlerLockAll` for the lock), and
the async check refuses a background task in a self-undoing block (its rescue and always run after the undo, so they
are held only to an enclosing block's). Cases in `TestNotify_RefuseWhatCannotMeanWhatItSays` and
`TestAsync_RefusesWhatCannotMeanWhatItSays`.

**Why 252 and 324 did not prevent it.** Their fixes refused the keys they found. A new feature brings new combinations,
and each needs its own list of what it cannot honor.

**Lesson.** When a feature is added, list every existing key it can be combined with and either honor it or refuse it.

## 785. A limit made only of separators parsed to the zero Limit, which admits every device (a sibling of 723) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. `engine.ParseLimit(",")`, and `",,:"`, dropped the
empty patterns and returned no error and the zero `Limit`, which admits every device. A limit written as `$HOSTS,`
with `HOSTS` empty would have run on every host.

**Root cause.** 723's class: an empty parse read as "everything". The zero value of `Limit` means "no limit", which is
right for no flag and wrong for a flag with nothing in it.

**Fix.** `736a4d79`. Text that leaves no pattern is refused, naming why. `TestLimit_RefusesWhatItCannotRead` covers
`","` and `",,:"`.

**Lesson.** A filter someone wrote never widens to everything: when its parse leaves nothing, refuse it.

## 786. A Controller serial job with forks ran unbatched after one failed batch assignment, and a definition gone before its batches left the job running for ever (the class of 79) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. `serialGate` (`internal/dispatch/serial.go`) repaired a
serial job's missing batches only when `forks` was 0. With forks set, one failed `AssignBatches` left the pump running
every device unbatched, forks at a time, with no stop on a failed batch. With forks 0, a definition that could no
longer be read left the queued devices queued, and the job stayed running.

**Root cause.** 79's class: a state with no way out. The repair was written for the path the first tests took.

**Fix.** `e67f2baf`. The gate reads the definition whenever queued devices carry no batch, whatever the forks, and a
definition that went away fails the queued devices with its reason, so the job completes.
`TestSerial_AFailedAssignmentIsRepairedWhateverTheForks`, `TestSerial_ADefinitionGoneBeforeItsBatchesFailsTheQueuedDevices`.

**Lesson.** A repair path runs on every configuration that can need it, and every state a job can enter has an exit.

## 787. The CLI cut serial: percentages from every resolved host and the Controller from the admitted ones, and a serial: runbook with no hosts ran nothing, device-less tasks included (a repeat in kind of 749) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. A percentage gave different batches on the two tiers
when some hosts' lifecycle did not admit a run, because the CLI counted them and the Controller, which queues only
admitted devices, did not. And on the CLI a `serial:` runbook whose hosts matched nothing made no batches, so even its
device-less tasks never ran.

**Root cause.** 749's class: one behavior built twice, on two tiers, from different inputs.

**Fix.** `5406e60e`. `planSerial` (`cmd/pleiades/run_serial.go`) cuts batches from the hosts the lifecycle admits in the
run's mode; a host it does not admit joins the first batch, where the engine skips it once, naming why. With no hosts
there is no plan and the run goes ahead unbatched. `TestSerial_APercentageCountsTheAdmittedHostsAsTheControllerDoes`,
`TestSerial_NoHostsIsNoPlan`.

**Why 749's fix did not prevent it.** 749 aligned one undo's account across two paths; the shared `engine.BatchDevices`
gave both tiers one batching function, but not one input.

**Lesson.** Where two tiers share a function, they also share what they feed it; test each tier with an input where the
two could differ.

## 788. The async release gates ordered two tasks by racing a fixed sleep, and bounded a timeout at 20 seconds against a 30-second sleep (a repeat of 211 and 769) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. In both async gates the background job wrote its line
after `sleep 3`, betting that the later task had written first. A job that ran only after the later task would have
passed too, and a later task slower than three seconds would have failed it. The CLI gate's timeout case required a
failure within 20 s of a 30-second sleep, a margin a slow machine can eat.

**Root cause.** 211's class: a fixed sleep standing for an order, and 769's: an order nothing promised.

**Fix.** `60e5e147`. The job waits for the later task's line before writing its own, so the order can only happen if
the two ran at once; the timeout bound is 60 s against a 120-second sleep.

**Why 211 and 769 did not prevent it.** 769 was fixed in a unit test the day before; the gates written the same evening
were not read for the same shape.

**Lesson.** As 211's: a test waits for the event it orders by, never for a time.

## 789. Text that the branch's own changes made false: the stop's SIGKILL time, the list of Ansible keywords a runbook lacks, the converter's notes, a merged doc comment, and comments naming a removed list (a repeat of 571 and 765) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01, all on `feat/c1-language`. The guide said a detached
job's SIGKILL came "up to ten seconds" after SIGTERM, where the code waits three. `ansibleTaskKeywords` still listed
`async` and `poll` as keywords a runbook lacks. The playbook converter's notes said notify, handlers, async and serial
have no native equivalent. `IsBuiltinAction`'s doc comment had run into `engineActionStatKeys`', leaving the table
without one. Two comments named the exemption list 768 removed. Nothing held `engineActionStatKeys` equal to the
executor's switch in `action.go`, which is what 768's fix reads.

**Root cause.** 571's class: text that states what was true, with nothing that reads it against the code.

**Fix.** `a5956a15` and `56a42de4`: each text corrected; the converter's notes say it does not carry those keys yet and
how to write them by hand. `internal/engine/builtin_table_test.go` holds `engineActionStatKeys` and the executor's
switch equal both ways.

**Why 571 and 765 did not prevent it.** Their rule is a review; this was found by one.

**Lesson.** When a change makes a sentence false, the change corrects it: search the docs and comments for the names it
changes before committing.

## 790. Two tests in container packages still held behavior the branch had changed (an Ansible gate's argv expecting the dropped --limit, and the runbook guide's async example naming a tag its gate's inventory lacks), and pr-check, which leaves container packages to Actions, passed (a repeat in kind of 756) (fixed before the pull request)

**Symptom.** `make branch-containers` at `77303189` on `feat/c1-language`, 2026-11-01, run 41341971748: shard 5 failed
`cmd/runner`'s `TestAnsibleReleaseGate_LaunchFieldsReachRealInvocation`, whose wanted argv still held `--limit sw1`,
which `d8c59440` stopped passing to ansible-playbook on purpose (the Controller applies the limit before it dispatches).
Shard 1 failed `cmd/pleiades`'s `TestCLI_WritingRunbooksPageExamplesValidate`: the guide's async example, added in
`fe9c4d62`, used `hosts: search`, and the gate validates every example against an inventory with only the `web` tag, so
validate warned. A local `make pr-check` had passed at the same commit.

**Root cause.** 756's class: pr-check leaves container packages to Actions by default, and both tests live in container
packages (`cmd/runner`, `cmd/pleiades`). The commits that changed the behavior ran the gates they wrote, not the older
tests in the same packages that read the same behavior.

**Fix.** The Ansible gate's wanted argv drops `--limit`, keeps the launch's `limit` field in the payload, and its comment
says why no limit reaches ansible-playbook; the guide's example runs on `hosts: web`. Both pass locally against real
containers.

**Why 756 did not prevent it.** 756 kept `internal/archtest` in pr-check; it did not make pr-check run a changed
container package's other tests, and `make branch-containers` exists for exactly this. It caught both before a pull
request, as designed.

**Lesson.** A change to a behavior other tests read (a breaking flag, a documented example) runs the whole package those
tests live in before the push, container package or not: `go test -run . ./cmd/runner` is minutes, a CI round is an hour.

## 791. Two detach tests dropped the connection when the job directory appeared, which the start script makes before it answers; reading the command from stdin widened that window, and fast-macos cut the start instead of a poll (a repeat of 211 and 788) (fixed in the pull request)

**Symptom.** PR #99's advisory `fast-macos` job, 2026-11-01: `pkg/remoteexec`'s `TestDetached_OutlivesADroppedConnection`
failed with "remote command exited without exit status or exit signal". It passed on Linux, in pr-check and in every
other job.

**Root cause.** The test (and `TestDetached_ALostConnectionThatCannotBeRedialedIsNamed`) dropped the server's
connections as soon as a job directory existed. The start script makes that directory before it starts the job and
before it answers, so a drop there cuts the start command itself, a different case from a dropped poll. `54c0cff4` added
a read of the command from stdin between the two, which widened the window enough for a macOS runner to land in it.

**Fix.** `866436fd`: both tests wait for the server to log the job's first poll (`cat .../rc`), which comes only after
the start has answered, before dropping.

**Why 211 and 788 did not prevent it.** 788 fixed the same shape in the release gates the same day; these two older
tests waited for a mark that comes before the event they meant, and nothing read them for it when the script changed.

**Lesson.** As 211's: wait for the event itself. When a change moves what happens between two marks, re-read every
test that waits on the first one.

## 792. Generated files were written through a symlink at their name, and forge's "refuse to overwrite" was a check then a write

**Symptom.** Found by reading during a vuln-corpus sweep triage on 2026-11-01, then measured. `writeGeneratedFile`
(`cmd/pleiades/forge_scaffold_io.go`, every `forge new-*` subcommand) checked the target with `os.Stat` and then wrote
it with `os.WriteFile`. A dangling symlink at a generated file's name passed the check (Stat follows the link and finds
nothing) and the write created the link's target, wherever it pointed; a symlinked directory on the way carried the
write outside `--dir`; and a file created between the check and the write was silently overwritten.
`writeImportable` (`cmd/pleiades/import_awx_credential_types.go`, `import awx-credential-types --out`) wrote each
`<namespace>.json` with `os.WriteFile`, which writes through a symlink planted at that name. Reaching either needs
someone else able to write into the output directory the operator chose, so the severity is low.

**Root cause.** Two separate calls for one decision ("create this file, and only this file"), and path-based writes
that follow links. Same family as 260 and 321 (a read through a symlinked path), on the write side.

**Fix.** On the branch `fix/generated-file-writes-no-symlink-follow`: `writeGeneratedFile` opens an `os.Root` on the
output directory, creates directories through it, and creates the file with `O_EXCL`, so "does not exist yet" and
"create it" are one step that refuses an existing file or symlink and cannot leave the directory.
`firstExistingFile` uses `Lstat`, so `--skip-existing` counts a dangling link as present. `writeImportable` writes
through a new `replaceInRoot` (`cmd/pleiades/replace_in_root.go`): a fresh `O_EXCL` temporary file inside the root,
synced, renamed over the name; a rename replaces a link instead of following it. Tests, each failing on the old
code: `TestWriteGeneratedFile_DoesNotWriteThroughASymlinkAtTheName`,
`TestWriteGeneratedFile_DoesNotFollowASymlinkedDirectory`, `TestFirstExistingFile_CountsASymlinkAsExisting`,
`TestImportReplacesALinkAtADocumentsNameInsteadOfWritingThroughIt`; `TestReplaceInRoot_ReplacesALinkAndKeepsItsTarget`
covers the helper.

**Lesson.** Writing a file you mean to create is one call, not a check and a write: `O_EXCL` for "new only", a
temporary file renamed into place for "replace", and an `os.Root` on the directory so no link along the path counts.

**Class.** C4 (path traversal and confinement escape), CWE-59 and CWE-367
**Portable.** yes: any generator, exporter or installer that checks a path and then writes it, or writes a fixed name into a directory someone else can write
**Detector.** `os.Stat`/`os.Lstat` on a path followed by `os.WriteFile`/`os.Create` on the same path; `os.WriteFile` into a caller-chosen directory; plant a dangling symlink at the output name and run the command

## 793. A lease's fencing token was about to order the jobs on a shared lease, whose holders overlap, so a job that joined first could change a device after a later one began and still read as earlier (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by reasoning through Phase 40a's edge-case list on 2026-11-01, on `feat/c2a-rollback-ordering`,
before push. The phase orders Walk jobs on a device by the fencing token of the device lease
each Runner held: the job with the higher token is later. A shared device (`wire.DispatchPayload.SharedDevice`, a
Kubernetes cluster) takes `lock.ModeShared`, and each holder that joins gets a new, higher token (the conformance
subtest `FencingTokensOrderAcquisitions` holds both managers to that). Job A joins, job B joins, both run at once, and A
changes the cluster after B began. With tokens stamped, a rollback of B finds A's token lower, reads A as earlier, and
undoes B beneath a change A made after it.

**Root cause.** An order of acquisitions is an order of changes only when one holder ends before the next begins. The
phase's edge-case list named shared leases only as "(a check journals nothing)", but a dispatch on a shared device
journals like any other, through the Runner's journal publisher.

**Fix.** `5b49013d`: the Runner puts the token on the run's context only for an exclusive lease
(`internal/runner/agent_exec.go`, `lock.FencingToken(lease)` and `!payload.SharedDevice`), so a shared-lease job's rows
carry no `lease_revision` and the planner orders that pair by the journals' clock times (`laterOn`'s `byClock` in
`internal/rollback/order.go`, named in `Plan.OrderedByClock`). Tests: `TestAgent_ExecuteWithLease_ASharedLeaseHandsTheRunNoFencingToken`
and, for the exclusive case, `TestAgent_ExecuteWithLease_HandsTheLeasesFencingTokenToTheRun`.

**Lesson.** A fencing token says who acquired first. It says who changed last only where holding is exclusive; where
holders overlap, record no token and say the order came from the clock.

## 794. The rollback planner found an undo step's latest attempt by FinishedAt, a second clock comparison Phase 40a's text did not name (a repeat in kind of 551) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found while building Phase 40a, 2026-11-01. `fullyUndone` (`internal/rollback/history.go`) decides whether
a later run is undone, so no longer blocks a rollback, from the latest attempt at each of that run's undo steps, and it
picked the latest with `e.FinishedAt.After(prev.at)`. Two rollbacks of the same later run, written under a clock set
back or by two Runners that disagree, could be read in the wrong order: an earlier attempt that succeeded under a fast
clock would hide a later one that failed, the later run would read as undone, and the target's rollback would run
beneath it.

**Root cause.** The clock comparisons the phase set out to replace were the ones 551's update found by reading
`laterRunProblems` and `EntStore.onDevicesSince`. Nobody searched the package for every time comparison a "later"
decision reaches.

**Fix.** `abd1be84`: `entryAfter` (`internal/rollback/order.go`) orders two entries by attempt and sequence within one
run, by lease revision between two Walk jobs on one device, by start tick between two Crawl runs, and by `FinishedAt`
only when an entry carries neither. `fullyUndone` keeps the entry, not its time. Test:
`TestOrder_TheLatestUndoAttemptIsFoundWithoutAClock`, both ways round, with each attempt's clock set against its tick.

**Why 551 did not prevent it.** 551's update listed the two comparisons that could explain its symptom, and the phase
copied that list. A list read from two functions is not a search of the package.

**Lesson.** When a fix takes a clock out of a decision, search everything the decision calls for `After`, `Before`,
`Sub` and `Compare` on a time before writing the phase, not only the comparison the symptom pointed at.

## 795. The NATS lease's revision moves on every KeepAlive, so the "NATS KV revision" the phase named as the fencing token was not the acquisition's; a separate fence field holds it (a repeat in kind of LESSONS 82) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found while building Phase 40a, 2026-11-01, reading `internal/lock/nats.go`. The phase item said a lease
exposes "the revision of its acquisition ... (the NATS KV revision)". `natsLease.revision` is the key's current
revision: `KeepAlive` republishes the key with compare-and-set and stores the new revision there, and the lease needs
that value for its next compare-and-set and for its release. Read after any renewal, it names the renewal, not the
acquisition, so a long job that renewed often could carry a higher number than a job that began after it. The Runner
reads the token once, before the run starts, so that path would have read the acquisition's value by timing alone; any
other reader would not.

**Root cause.** The phase text named the value by the word the design used, and the field with that name holds a
different value, one that must keep moving for the lease to work.

**Fix.** `4250e101`: `natsLease.fence` is set from the acquiring write's sequence (a create, or a shared holder's
join) and never changed; `FencingToken` returns it. The in-process manager returns its holder counter. The conformance
subtest `FencingTokensOrderAcquisitions`, run for both managers by `runManagerConformance`
(`internal/lock/conformance_fencing_test.go`), fails if a KeepAlive moves the token, if a lease taken after a release
holds a token no larger than the first, or if a later shared joiner's is no larger.

**Why LESSONS 82 did not prevent it.** LESSONS 82 is about naming a field for the value it really holds. A phase item
is written before the code is read, and nothing holds the field it names to that meaning; reading the code before using
the field caught it here.

**Lesson.** Before a field stands for a value in a design, read every write to it. A field the code must keep moving
cannot also name a moment that is over.

## 796. The run counter's failure paths went in untested, and internal/journal measured 91.3% against its 94.1% floor (a repeat of 731 and 744) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-01, on `feat/c2a-rollback-ordering`: measuring `internal/journal` against `coverage-floor.json`
after `internal/journal/clock.go` was written, before any gate ran, gave 91.3% against a floor of 94.1%.

**Root cause.** `clock.go` adds failure branches (the project directory, the counter's own lock, the rebuild's reads,
the write and the rename) that the first tests did not drive, and `writeClock` had three separate branches for a
temporary file's write, sync and close that no portable test can make fail.

**Fix.** In `b49f5b3f`: `TestTickClockFailsLoudly` (a project directory that is a file, a lock held past the wait, a
journal directory that is a file, a counter that is a directory, a read-only `.pleiades`) and
`TestTickClockPassesOverWhatItCannotRead` (the rebuild passing over an empty journal, a line that is not JSON, a seal
that is not JSON or is oversized, and a subdirectory). `writeClock` now joins its write, sync and close errors with
`errors.Join` into one branch, which also reports every failure among the three rather than the first.

**Why 731 and 744 did not prevent it.** They did their part: 744's rule, to measure each touched package against its
floor before committing, is what found this before the gate. Neither reaches the step before, writing a new file's
failure paths together with their tests.

**Lesson.** As 744's. A new file with many failure branches gets its failure tests in the same sitting, and branches no
portable test can reach are folded into one only where the fold reports at least as much as before.

## 797. A run killed before its seal recorded no end tick and counted as later than every run after it, forever, and the refusal said it "was stopped, or is still running", which cannot be true while a rollback holds the run lock (a repeat in kind of 652 and 551) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review of `feat/c2a-rollback-ordering`, 2026-11-01. Phase 40a's planner
counts a Crawl run with a start tick and no end tick as possibly later than the run being undone, and
`--despite-run` accepts it. A run's end tick is written only by its seal, and `cmd/pleiades` installs no signal
handler, so a run killed by a signal or lost with its machine never gets one. Nothing ever bounded it: every
rollback of any older run on the same devices would be refused over it for the life of the project, and the only way
on was `--despite-run`. The refusal added that the run "was stopped, or is still running", but a rollback takes the
run lock exclusive (`journal.LockRuns`) and every run holds it shared, so no run can still be running while the
refusal is printed.

**Root cause.** The phase's edge case ("a run killed before its end tick counts as possibly later, accepted by
`--despite-run`") said what to do with the run and not for how long. "Possibly later" with no bound is "later than
everything after it". The reason text was written from the case's name, not from the locks in force when it prints.

**Fix.** `6590317e` and `43613be4`. Run markers (`internal/journal/clock_live.go`): while a run lives it holds a lock
on `.pleiades/clock.d/<start tick>.live`, taken on a temporary file before the file is renamed into place, so no run
can find the marker unlocked while its owner lives. Each run, as it begins, marks every earlier marker nobody holds as
`<tick>.ended`, holding its own start tick; `ReadRun` takes that as the dead run's end tick. A sealed run removes its
own marker. Where a lock cannot tell a live process from a dead one (`activeLocks` false), no run is marked ended,
the safe direction. The refusal now says "no run began after it stopped to record that it was gone". Tests:
`TestRunMarkers_ADeadRunIsBoundedByTheNextRun`, `TestRunMarkers_ALiveRunIsNotMarkedEnded`,
`TestRunMarkers_FailAndPassOverLoudly`, and the reason in `TestOrder_ARunThatNeverRecordedItsEndCountsAsLater`.

**Why 652 and 551 did not prevent it.** 652's lesson is that a refusal offering an override must say which case it
is, or users learn to pass the override. This refusal named a case that could not be true, and with no bound it
would have taught exactly that habit. 551's update recorded the "never recorded one" rule as a fact, and the edge-case
test was ticked against the phase's wording, which never asked what ends it.

**Lesson.** A state that makes a record "possibly later" needs an event that ends it. And a reason printed under a
lock is checked against what that lock rules out.

## 798. A job that kept running after its Runner lost the exclusive lease kept stamping the old, lower token, so it read as earlier than the job that took the device (a repeat in kind of 793 and 80) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. A non-interruptible dispatch whose heartbeat
`KeepAlive` fails logs "lost device lease heartbeat but task is not interruptible, continuing to completion" and runs on (FAILURE_PATTERNS 320 describes the heartbeat).
Its lease may lapse and another job take the device with a higher token, while the first job keeps changing the
device under its old token. Its rows then read as earlier than the second job's, and `OnDevicesSince` left them out
when selecting by revision, so a rollback of the second job could run beneath changes the first made after it.

**Root cause.** The token was read once, as the run began, and stamped on every entry after. A fencing token only
orders work while the lease is held; 793 found the same assumption for holders that overlap by design, and this is
holders that overlap by failure.

**Fix.** `43613be4`: `lock.Fence` carries the token and its epoch, the heartbeat calls `Lose` before anything else
when a renewal fails (a later renewal never restores it), and the journal publisher reads it on every `Record`, so
entries after the loss carry no token. The planner treats a job whose rows on a device mix a revision with none as
ordered by clock (`highestRevision`, `internal/rollback/order.go`). Tests: the lost case in
`TestJournalPublisherStampsTheLeaseRevision`, the lost-lease job in `TestOrder_RevisionsFromAnotherEpochOrderByClock`,
`TestFence_CarriesATokenUntilLost`.

**Why 793 and 80 did not prevent it.** 80's fix and LESSONS 83 put the token on writes so a holder that lost its claim
is refused. Here nothing refuses: the token only labels the work for a later reader, so a stale label is silent. 793
asked whether two holders can overlap and answered for shared leases only, and LESSONS 372, written from it, says
"exclusive holding" where it needed "exclusive holding that is still held". This entry breaks LESSONS 372 as written;
see its update and LESSONS 373.

**Lesson.** A token that labels work is good only for work done while its lease was held: read it at each record, and
drop it once the lease is lost.

## 799. Fencing tokens were compared across lives of the lock bucket, whose stream sequence counts from one again when it is re-created, while the Controller's database keeps the old rows (a repeat in kind of 154) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. A NATS lease's token is the JetStream sequence of the
lock bucket's stream. When that stream is re-created (lost NATS data, a deleted bucket, a reinstall; a destroyed
stream is re-created by whichever process arrives first, as 195 records), the sequence restarts, and the Controller's
journal rows keep the old numbers. A job from before the reset with a high revision would read as later than a new job
with a low one, and a new job's rows would not be selected as later than an old target's.

**Root cause.** A number from a sequence was compared as if the sequence had one life. Nothing journaled which life a
token came from.

**Fix.** `43613be4`: `lock.Fenced` gains `FencingEpoch`. The NATS manager's is `"nats:"` plus the bucket stream's
creation time, read at each acquisition through a fresh `js.Stream` handle's `CachedInfo` (800); the in-process
manager's is `"process:"` plus a random id. It is journaled as `lease_epoch` (folded into the same unmerged migrations,
sqlite 0041 and postgres 0038), and revisions compare only within one epoch, in the planner and in
`EntStore.OnDevicesSince`. A lease whose epoch cannot be read carries no token. Tests:
`TestFencingEpoch_TwoInProcessManagersNeverShareOne`, the epoch check in the conformance subtest
`FencingTokensOrderAcquisitions`, `TestOrder_RevisionsFromAnotherEpochOrderByClock`.

**Why 154 did not prevent it.** 154's lesson is about a zero value with two meanings; the class is a number whose
meaning depends on context it does not carry. Nothing ties that rule to a counter that can restart, and 795's fix
read the stream sequence as "only grows" without asking for how long.

**Lesson.** A number from a sequence orders only within that sequence's life. Carry the life with the number, and
compare two numbers only when their lives match.

## 800. Reading the lock bucket's epoch with kv.Status raced with the shared KV handle's Get between concurrent acquisitions (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found while building 799's fix, 2026-11-01, under `-race`: reading the bucket stream's creation time
through `kv.Status` on the manager's shared KV handle raced with that handle's `Get` in another acquisition.

**Root cause.** A defect in the NATS client library, settled by reading its source. In nats.go v1.54.0 (the version
this module pins), `kv.Status` calls the KV handle's `stream.Info`, which stores the answer in the stream's cached
`s.info` pointer with no lock (`jetstream/stream.go:498`), and `kv.Get` reaches `stream.getMsg`, which reads
