`s.info.Config.AllowDirect` with no lock (`:577`). The library documents no limit on concurrent use of a KV handle;
only some consumer methods say they cannot be used concurrently. v1.55.0 makes the field an `atomic.Pointer`
(`stream.go:173`), which is the upstream fix.

**Fix.** `43613be4`: `natsLockManager.epoch` (`internal/lock/nats.go`) reads through a stream handle of its own
(`js.Stream`, then its `CachedInfo`, one round trip per acquisition); its doc comment records why. That avoids the
race whatever the version. The owner chose to bump nats.go to v1.55.0 in its own pull request after this one, which
removes it at the source: on `chore/nats-go-1.55`, a probe running `kv.Status` and `kv.Get` at once on one handle
against a real NATS server raced under `-race` on v1.54.0 and ran clean on v1.55.0 (measured, 2026-11-02).

**Lesson.** A shared client handle is safe for the calls already made on it concurrently, not for every method it
has; a new call on one runs under `-race` with the old ones before it ships.

## 801. A target journaled before the run counter was ordered by clock against a ticked run, though every ticked run came after every unticked one (a repeat in kind of 794 and LESSONS 371) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. `laterOn` fell back to clock times whenever either
run lacked a tick. When the target is the unticked one and the other run carries a tick, the order is already known:
the counter did not exist when the target ran. A clock stepped back would still have hidden the later run.

**Root cause.** The phase text said "falls back to wall-clock times only for journals written before this phase",
and the code read that as "for any pair with one such journal". The direction of the pair decides whether an order is
known.

**Fix.** `43613be4`: a target with no tick counts every ticked run as later. The reverse pair (a ticked target, an
unticked other) stays on the clock, since an older binary can still write an unticked run after a ticked one. Test:
`TestOrder_ARunWithATickIsLaterThanATargetFromBeforeTheCounter`, with the ticked run's clock a day back.

**Why 794 and LESSONS 371 did not prevent it.** Both are about clock comparisons that replaced a logical order. This
one was the fallback the phase asked for, so a search for time comparisons found it and passed it as intended.

**Lesson.** A fallback to the clock is checked case by case: before using it, ask whether the facts already in hand
settle the order in that direction.

## 802. The run counter's rebuild read journals and seals with none of the strict reader's checks, and the counter's and the run lock's files were opened following links (a repeat of 395, 163 and 761) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01; security-relevant, low. The rebuild in
`internal/journal/clock.go` opened each journal with `os.Open` and each seal with `os.ReadFile`: no symlink, owner or
size checks. A seal linked to `/dev/zero` would hang every `BeginRun`, and a very large one could exhaust memory.
`clock.lock` and `run.lock` were opened without `O_NOFOLLOW`. Reaching any of it needs write access to the project's
`.pleiades/journal`.

**Root cause.** The rebuild is a second reader of the files the strict reader already reads through `openPrivate`, and
it was written with plain opens because it "only needs a floor".

**Fix.** `6590317e`: every read in the rebuild goes through `openPrivate` (`readPrivate`, `readNumber`), bounded by the
strict reader's own limits; both lock files open with `noFollow`. Tests: `TestTickClockReadsOnlyWhatTheStrictReaderWould`,
`TestLocksRefuseALink`.

**Why 395, 163 and 761 did not prevent it.** 395 and 163 bound a read where it was found; 761 confined the other reads
of one source, and LESSONS 367 says a confinement rule found on one read binds every read of that source. The rebuild
was a new reader in the same package as the confined one, and nobody held it to that rule while writing it.

**Lesson.** As LESSONS 367: a new reader of files a strict reader already guards uses the same open, even when it only
wants one number from them.

**Class.** C4 (path traversal and confinement escape) and resource exhaustion, CWE-59 and CWE-400
**Portable.** yes: any rebuild, index or cache that reads files a validating reader also reads
**Detector.** `os.Open`/`os.ReadFile` in a package that has its own guarded open; plant a link to `/dev/zero` at a file the code scans

## 803. A recorded tick of the largest uint64 made the next tick wrap to zero, the value that means "no tick", and stopped the counter silently (a repeat in kind of 154) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. `TickClock` returned `max(current, recorded) + 1`. A
journal, seal or marker holding `math.MaxUint64` (only by hand) made that zero, and zero is what a run from before the
counter carries, so every later run would have read as unticked.

**Root cause.** 154's class: an arithmetic edge produced the one value the design reserves as a sentinel.

**Fix.** `6590317e`: `ErrClockExhausted` when the floor is already the largest value. Test:
`TestTickClockRefusesTheLargestTick`.

**Why 154 did not prevent it.** 154's rule is about choosing a sentinel; it does not ask what arithmetic can produce
one.

**Lesson.** Where zero is a sentinel, every addition that can wrap is checked against it.

## 804. Every tick rescanned every journal while holding the counter's lock, so a large project made other runs wait, and a seal that timed out at the 10-second wait would have left a run with no end tick (fixed before push; suspected, not measured)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. `TickClock` took the counter's lock and then read the
first line of every journal and every seal to find the highest recorded tick. The lock is waited on for at most
`clockLockWait` (10 s). A seal that could not take it in time would fail its end tick, leaving 797's unbounded case.
Not measured on a real project.

**Root cause.** The scan only answers what the counter does not already hold (a deleted or restored counter's past),
but it ran in the critical section with the counter itself.

**Fix.** `6590317e`: `highestRecordedTick` runs before the lock. That is safe because any tick taken meanwhile is in
the counter, which is read under the lock.

**Lesson.** Keep in a critical section only what needs the lock's guarantee; read the rest before it, and write down
why the gap is safe.

## 805. pleiades run's end-of-run warning that another run changed a device while this one worked still decided its window by wall clock (the class of 551, in a warning) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's review, 2026-11-01. `journal.ChangesDuring`
(`internal/journal/active.go`), called from `cmd/pleiades/run_concurrent.go` with the run's start time and
`time.Now()`, keeps entries whose `FinishedAt` falls inside that window. A clock stepped during or between runs can
drop a concurrent change from the warning or add an old one.

**Root cause.** Phase 40a replaced clock order in the rollback planner only. This warning is not a rollback safety
decision, but LESSONS 371 covers it.

**Fix.** The owner chose to fix it in the same pull request. `ChangesDuring` takes the run's own start tick
(`journal.FileStore.BeginRun`, handed through `concurrency.startTick`): when both runs carry a tick, the other run
counts when it overlapped this one (it never recorded its end, or ended after this run began, the run markers
bounding a dead one), and every change it made to the shared devices is reported, its message saying it overlapped
this one "by the project's run counter", since the counter says the runs overlapped, not when on that span the change
came. The clock window stays for a pair either of which carries no tick. Test:
`TestChangesDuring_TheCounterDecidesWhenBothRunsCarryIt`, a run overlapping under a clock stepped back a day found and
an earlier run whose clock reads inside the window passed over, with the clock-only control showing the opposite.
`TestCLI_ASecondRunOnTheSameDevicesIsNoticed` still passes against a real device.

**Lesson.** As LESSONS 371. A rule found for one decision gets a search for every other decision of the same shape.

## 806. internal/journal fell under its 94.1% floor again, at 93.0%, with the run marker code (a repeat of 796) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-01, the same day as 796: after the review's fixes added `internal/journal/clock_live.go`,
measuring `internal/journal` before the gate gave 93.0% against its 94.1% floor.

**Root cause.** The same as 796's: new failure branches without their tests, and branches no test could reach.

**Fix.** In `6590317e`: real failure-path tests (`TestRunMarkers_FailAndPassOverLoudly` among them), an unreachable
branch removed, and three read branches that duplicated one another folded into `readPrivate` and `readNumber`. Final
94.21%.

**Why 796 did not prevent it.** 796's lesson, failure tests in the same sitting, was hours old, and the review's fixes
were written as fixes, not as a new file. The pre-gate measurement 744 asks for caught it again.

**Lesson.** As 796's. A review fix that adds a file is new code, and its failure paths get tests before it is
measured.

## 807. The first predicted-state ledger keyed a path as the runbook wrote it, so a symbolic link, a merged /usr, a bind mount or a case-folding filesystem gave one place two keys (a repeat in kind of 313, and of LESSONS 229 and 367) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's first review of Phase 46a, 2026-11-02. The first design (`68c25da5`) kept,
per device, the paths a check predicted removed or made, keyed by the path as written. A later task that named the same
place another way (through a symbolic link, `/bin` against `/usr/bin` on a merged-/usr system, a bind mount, or another
case on a case-folding filesystem) missed the record, or met a record that did not describe where its real run would
land. The ledger vouched for paths the real run meets differently.

**Root cause.** LESSONS 229's class: a lexical path names a spelling, not a place on the device. A ledger of predicted
state is a map from place to state, and it took the place from text.

**Fix.** `71242adb` keys each prediction where the device resolves it: `remotefile.Locate` reads the physical path and
each existing directory's `dev:ino` in one `sh` command, and one directory identity met under two paths drops the
predictions. `d57b0f73` records a path only where it resolves as written (a link along it records unknown, since where
the link leads in the real run depends on earlier tasks) and also dropped on names a case-folding filesystem could
join. Since `4a1ccaf8` the ledger records removals only (808), so a second spelling of a path can only miss a record,
which reads the device as it is. Tests: `TestLocate` (compared with `syscall.Stat`),
`TestLedger_ADirectoryUnderTwoPathsDropsTheLedger`, `TestCheckRemove_APathThroughALinkDropsThePredictions`, and
`TestCLI_RollbackReleaseGate`'s G8 ("a check sees a path made through a link").

**Why 313, 229 and 367 did not prevent it.** Each was written about confinement: whether a path stays inside a root.
The ledger confines nothing, so nobody read those rules as applying to it. But a key says "this is the same file",
which is the same question about the filesystem asked another way.

**Lesson.** A map keyed by path claims identity, and is held to LESSONS 229: key it by what the device says the place
is, and treat a second spelling as a reason to stop trusting the map, not as a new key.

## 808. The predicted-state ledger held claims that later tasks could make false, and three reviews of two designs kept finding more: each hole a "this is gone or empty" undone by something made (fixed before push, by recording removals only)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's three reviews of Phase 46a, 2026-11-02, besides 807's keys. Pass 1 (on
`68c25da5`): a method without `PredictsPaths` reporting "no change" was trusted, though its answer was read against the
device as it is; real tasks between `check_mode` tasks in a mixed run changed the device the ledger described; a task
skipped by its condition was not accounted for. Pass 2 (on `71242adb`): a later path was located against links an
earlier task made or removed; predictions restarted after a drop; a "present" record was wider than the path it named;
sibling tasks overlapped on an ancestor directory. Pass 3 (on `d57b0f73`, whose "fresh" state recorded paths made where
nothing was): directories `mkdir -p` makes went unrecorded; a copy into a removed directory was treated as making it;
and devices sharing a filesystem each kept a ledger that the other's tasks could falsify. Each let a later task's check
answer differently from its real run, which includes passing where the run fails (the outcome 564 and 739 record).

**Root cause.** The ledger made two kinds of claim, that a path is gone and that a path is present, and admitted tasks
whose effects it could not see in full. A claim that a path is gone, or a directory empty, is made false by anything
that creates a path, and a path can be created by many routes the ledger never saw: a parent made by `mkdir -p`, a copy,
a link, a real task in a mixed run, another device's task on a shared filesystem. Each fix closed the routes its review
named and kept the design, so the next review found another route.

**Fix.** `4a1ccaf8`: record removals only. `file.remove` is the one method declaring
`collection.Manifest.PredictsPaths`, and the first task in the run that is anything else, on any device (another
method whatever it reported, a skip, a failed or unchecked task, a deviceless task, a `parallel:` marker, a recorded
unknown, an external program's records, the bound), drops every device's predictions for the rest of the run. A drop
lasts for the run (`d57b0f73`), and only a run that is a check throughout keeps a ledger (`71242adb`). Tests:
`TestLedger_AnythingButARecordedRemovalDropsEveryDeviceForGood`, `TestLedger_SiblingsRemovingInEitherOrderAgree`,
`TestLedger_PastItsBoundIsDropped`, `TestCheckPredictions_AnUndeclaredMethodDropsTheDevice`,
`TestCheckPredictions_ARealRunCheckingSomeTasksKeepsNone`, `TestCheckPredictions_AParallelGroupDropsThem`,
`TestMethodsThatMakePathsDoNotPredict`, and `TestCLI_RollbackReleaseGate`'s G9, which runs each review's runbooks and
asserts that a check never passes what the real run fails; mutation checks showed each rule is needed.

**Why the earlier fixes did not hold.** `71242adb` and `d57b0f73` each fixed what their review named and kept recording
paths made. A design that admits claims something made can falsify has to see every way a thing is made, and no list of
routes was ever complete. LESSONS 374 and 375.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 374 (what a cache of predicted state may hold) and 375 (narrow the scope before the third
patch).

## 809. A check's directory listing ran through the account's login shell, so a POSIX script met zsh, fish or csh (a sibling of 779) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's first review of Phase 46a, 2026-11-02. The directory listing
`file.remove`'s check reads, to see whether every entry is predicted gone, was sent as a command for the account's login
shell. A login shell of zsh, fish or csh parses a POSIX script differently, or refuses it.

**Root cause.** sshd hands the command string to the account's login shell. A script written for POSIX `sh` is POSIX
only when `sh` runs it.

**Fix.** `71242adb`: the listing runs under `sh -c`. `Locate` and `Removable` (`pkg/remotefile/locate.go`) do the same,
and each script is one line, because the login shell still parses the quoted command before `sh` runs it and csh refuses
a newline inside quotes (the comment on `locateScript`).

**Why 779 did not prevent it.** 779 is the other half: a user's command goes to the login shell, as an attached run
sends it. It said nothing about the platform's own scripts.

**Lesson.** Decide for each remote command whose language it is. A user's command goes to the login shell; the
platform's own script goes to `sh -c`, on one line.

## 810. The predicted_paths stat reached register: and reports (a sibling of 507) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent's second review of Phase 46a, 2026-11-02. The stat a check records its
predictions in (`sdk.StatPredictedPaths`) stayed on the node's result, so it reached a task's `register:` and every
report, where it is engine bookkeeping rather than a result.

**Root cause.** The record rode the ordinary stats map, and nothing took it off once the engine had read it.

**Fix.** `d57b0f73`: the engine takes the stat off the result when it reads it, and a real run that records it fails
the task. Test: `TestCheckPredictions_ReachALaterTaskOnEachDevice` asserts the stat is not on the result;
`TestCheckPredictions_ARealRunHasNoneAndMayRecordNone` holds the real run.

**Why 507 did not prevent it.** 507 is about the same shape (what an outcome may carry, enforced where every outcome
passes) for the undo stat. A new engine-only stat was added without asking that question.

**Lesson.** A stat the engine reads for itself is taken off the result where it is read, in the same change that adds
it.

## 811. A removal the real run cannot make (a parent the login may not write) was carried into a later task's check, which then passed where main's failed (a repeat in kind of 564 and 739) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the claim-refuter agent, 2026-11-02, on `4a1ccaf8`. A `file.remove` of a file in a directory the
login could not write was predicted, and recorded as gone. A later `file.remove` of a directory holding it read that
prediction, found the directory empty, and its check passed. The real run fails at the first removal with EACCES. On
main the same check failed too, but at the later task, refused as "not empty": it agreed with the real run by
coincidence.

**Root cause.** A prediction rests on the real run making the removal its check predicted. `file.remove`'s check does
not ask whether the directory holding the path allows the removal, and the ledger took every predicted removal as one
the real run makes. (Read in the code on this branch, not changed by it: `file.remove`'s own check of that one removal
still predicts success where the parent refuses, as on main. Only carrying it forward is fixed.)

**Fix.** `a32ad8f6`: `file.remove` records a removal only when `remotefile.Removable` says the device allows it
(`test -w` and `-x` on the parent; under a sticky bit, root or the owner of the parent or the entry, by POSIX
`find -user`) and it is not a recursive directory removal, whose subdirectories could refuse partway. A directory found
empty only through predictions, in a parent that refuses its removal, is `CannotCheck`. A task with `ignore_errors`
drops the ledger, since its author expects its real run may fail. The first version of `Removable` had no sticky rule,
and G7 failed, because `/tmp` is sticky; the sticky rule was added before the commit. Tests:
`TestCheckRemove_RecordsOnlyARemovalTheRealRunCanMake`, `TestCheckRemove_AnUnansweredRemovalQuestionRecordsUnknown`,
`TestRemovable`, and `TestCLI_RollbackReleaseGate`'s G7 and G9.

**Residual, by the owner's decision (2026-11-02).** What refuses a removal only when it is tried (an immutable flag, a
busy mount point, a delete-deny ACL on macOS or ZFS, an ACL under BusyBox) is not visible to a check, so such a refusal
carries into a later task's answer: the same refusal a check of that one removal cannot see. It is documented in
`docs/02-get-started.md` and `docs/11-extending-pleiades.md`. LESSONS 376.

**Why 564 and 739 did not prevent it.** Both say a check must not pass where the run fails, and 739 says a check asks
the write's own prediction rather than a stand-in. The ledger made one check's answer the input of another, and the
first check's blind spot (no question about the parent) had been harmless until a later check leaned on it.

**Lesson.** When one check's answer feeds another, the first check's blind spots become the second's. Before leaning on
a prediction, ask what its check does not look at.

## 812. BusyBox's test -w says writable to root on a read-only mount, because it reads the mode bits itself where dash, bash and FreeBSD's sh ask access(2); the project's own sshd test image runs BusyBox (a repeat in kind of 248 and 375) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Measured by the claim-refuter agent's second pass, 2026-11-02, on `a32ad8f6`. `remotefile.Removable` asked
`test -w` and `test -x` of the parent directory, on the understanding that `test` answers through access(2), which
counts the mode bits, an ACL, a read-only mount and root. BusyBox's `test` reads the mode bits itself: for root it says
writable to anything, and for any login it does not see a read-only mount. So `Removable` said yes to a removal the
real run cannot make, and 811's fix did not hold on BusyBox. The project's own sshd test image is Alpine, whose `sh` is
BusyBox.

**Root cause.** "`test -w` is access(2)" is true of dash, bash and FreeBSD's sh, and was assumed of every `sh`.

**Fix.** `bd024a25`: `removableScript` finds BusyBox (`readlink /proc/$$/exe`, or `sh --help` naming it). Under BusyBox,
root is answered no, and another login is answered yes only when the mount holding the directory (the longest mount
point above it in `/proc/self/mountinfo`) is listed `rw`. An ACL it still cannot see, which is part of 811's residual.
Test: `TestRemovableScript_RefusesWhatItCannotVouchFor` (BusyBox, mountinfo, root in a user namespace). `pkg/remotefile`
passed on the FreeBSD lab VM (bsd-check) at `bd024a25`.

**Why 248 and 375 did not prevent it.** 248 found GNU and BusyBox `chmod` reading one argument differently, and 375 a
BSD fallback never run on BSD. Each lesson named its own tool. Nothing asks, of a shell builtin a decision rests on,
which shells the project meets and whether each answers the same.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 377: a shell test a safety answer rests on is measured on every shell the project meets, starting
with its own test images.

## 813. A Go test's os.FileMode(0o1777) was never sticky: Go's sticky bit is os.ModeSticky, and the octal 01000 bit maps to nothing (a sibling of 375) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, writing `Removable`'s tests (`pkg/remotefile/locate_test.go`). A fixture made its directory with
`os.FileMode(0o1777)`, expecting the sticky bit. The directory was made `0777`, so the sticky case tested a plain
directory.

**Root cause.** `os.FileMode` keeps the permission bits in its low nine bits and the special bits as its own flags
(`os.ModeSticky`, `os.ModeSetuid`, `os.ModeSetgid`). The octal 01000 bit is not one of them, and the conversion to a
system mode drops it.

**Fix.** The fixture uses `0o777 | os.ModeSticky` (`TestRemovable`, `TestRemovableScript_RefusesWhatItCannotVouchFor`).

**Lesson.** In Go, write a special mode bit as its `os.Mode*` flag, never as an octal digit, and have a fixture assert
the bit it needs before the test relies on it.

## 814. Locate's script ran set -- before reading $2, so a directory never listed its own identity (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02. `remotefile.Locate` should print the `dev:ino` of the path itself when it is a directory. It
never did. `TestLocate`, which compares each identity with `syscall.Stat`, caught it.

**Root cause.** `locateScript` cleared the positional parameters with `set --`, to build the list of directories, before
it read `$2`, the path's last name. `$2` was then empty, so the "is this path a directory" test never held.

**Fix.** In `d57b0f73`: the script copies `$1` and `$2` into variables first (`d=$1; name=$2`) and only then runs
`set --`.

**Lesson.** In a shell script that reuses `"$@"` as a list, copy every argument into a named variable on the first line.

## 815. filepath.Join cleaned away the `..` a test meant to pass (a sibling of 813) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, `TestLocate`. The test meant to hand `Locate` a path holding `..`, which it must refuse, and
built it with `filepath.Join`. `Join` cleans its result, so the `..` was gone before `Locate` saw it.

**Root cause.** The fixture used a helper that normalizes, for an input whose point is that it is not normal.

**Fix.** The test builds the path by concatenation (`root + "/a/../b"`).

**Lesson.** As 813's: a fixture whose point is an unusual input is built without a helper that could normalize it, and
the test checks the input it built.

## 816. Two internal/engine test fixtures stood for something other than what they modeled: parallel branches on one device, and directory identities numbered by path length (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, writing Phase 46a's engine tests. A test of a `parallel:` group put both branches on one device,
where they contended for the device lock. A fixture numbered each directory's identity by the length of its path, so
two directories whose paths were the same length shared one, which the ledger reads as one directory under two paths.
What each failure looked like when it was hit was not recorded.

**Root cause.** Each fixture modeled the case loosely: one device cannot run two branches at once, and an identity has
to be unique to stand for one.

**Fix.** `TestCheckPredictions_AParallelGroupDropsThem` puts its branches on different devices. `dirsOf`
(`internal/engine/predicted_internal_test.go`) numbers each directory by a hash of its path.

**Lesson.** A fixture that stands for a device or a filesystem keeps the property the code relies on: one device is
locked by one task at a time, and an identity is unique.

## 817. README's check-mode count stayed at "235 of the 257" while CLAUDE.md's was updated, and CLAUDE.md's own module count still said 210 beside its new 257; pr-check would not have run tools/gendocs, which reads the changed catalog but was not itself changed (a repeat of 678; 631's class) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass on `1a342c7e` (Phase 46b, C2c). Nine methods gained a check, so 244 of the
257 implemented methods check. CLAUDE.md's check-mode line was edited to say so; README.md still said "235 of the 257
can predict". `tools/gendocs`' `TestStatusCounts_MatchTheRegistry` holds README's counts to the registry, so CI would
have failed. The same review found CLAUDE.md's module catalog line still saying "212 registered FQCNs; 210 implemented"
beside its own edited check line naming 257.

**Root cause.** The counts are written by hand in more than one file and more than one sentence. The edit updated the
file in view, not the one a test reads. `make pr-check` runs the packages a branch changes, plus the census
(`tools/prscope/census.go`), whose packages are `cmd/pleiades`, `cmd/runner`, `internal/adapters/native` and
`internal/forge/playbook`. `tools/gendocs` imports `internal/catalog` but was not changed, so it is a reverse dependent,
which prscope does not select (631). The local gate would not have run the test that catches this.

**Fix.** `e7caa208`: README says "244 of the 257"; CLAUDE.md's module line says "259 registered FQCNs; 257
implemented, 2 declared-not-implemented (2026-11-02)".

**Why 678 did not prevent it.** 678's lesson is to run `go test ./tools/gendocs/ ./internal/archtest/` before the commit
that adds a method. This branch added no method. It changed which methods support check mode, which moves a counted
number just as surely, and the rule was read as being about new methods. 631's gap (no reverse dependents in prscope)
is still open, so nothing mechanical ran the test either.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 380: a count stated by hand in two files is updated in both in the same edit, starting with the one
a test reads, and any change to a counted property (check support, status), not only a new method, runs
`tools/gendocs`' tests before the commit.

## 818. exec.winrm.shell's first creates/removes guard used PowerShell's Test-Path, which answers False with exit 0 for a path it cannot read, so a removes guard would have skipped the task's work (a repeat of 147 and 451; LESSONS 138) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass on `1a342c7e`. The guard added to `exec.winrm.shell` (Ansible `win_shell`'s
`creates` and `removes`) decided existence with `Test-Path`. Measured on the lab's win-check VM through pleiades:
`Test-Path` returned `False` for `\\localhost\pleiades-no-such-share\stamp`, where
`[System.IO.File]::GetAttributes` threw an `IOException`. So a path the guard could not read counted as absent: a
`removes` guard would skip the task and report no change, and a `creates` guard would run the script again. Recorded
in the vuln-corpus as C9_auto-roboto_2026-11-02.

**Root cause.** `Test-Path` returns a boolean and folds "I could not look" into "it is not there". Nobody measured its
answer for an unreadable path before building the guard on it.

**Fix.** `e7caa208`: `guardScript` (`internal/catalog/exec/winrm/shell.go`) decides as Ansible's `Test-AnsiblePath`
does. `GetAttributes` answering means present; `FileNotFoundException` or `DirectoryNotFoundException` means absent;
anything else (access denied, a share that does not answer) fails the task. `guardAnswer` accepts only exit 0 with
`skip` or `run` and fails on anything else. Tests: `TestGuard_AGuardThatCannotBeReadFails`,
`TestGuard_AnswerIsReadStrictly`, and `TestWinRMGate_ShellGuards` on win-check, which fails when the guard reads
through `Test-Path` (its missing-share step) and when the guard never skips.

**Why 147 and 451 did not prevent it.** 147 fixed the POSIX guard in `exec.command` with a distinct exit status for "could
not look", and 451 fixed one docker predicate. LESSONS 138 states the rule. Each fix lives in its own code, and this
guard was written fresh in another shell, whose usual existence primitive quietly answers two ways where three are
needed. LESSONS 377, written the same day, says to measure a shell builtin a safety answer rests on, but it listed the
POSIX shells and the edges root, read-only mount and ACL, not PowerShell and not "cannot look at all".

**Lesson.** LESSONS 379: an existence guard decides only on a definite answer, and the primitive it uses is measured on
the real target for a path it cannot read before anything is built on it.

## 819. Several new virt.clab checks predicted a change the server refuses: a redeploy of a lab that is not deployed, host tools by a login that is not a superuser, veth endpoints not in x:y form, and veth and vxlan checks that never logged in (a repeat in kind of 811 and 564) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass on `1a342c7e`. The branch's rule was that a method whose effect is known in
kind is checked by reading what the run reads and predicting the change. Several checks predicted without reading
what the server checks first. `virt.clab.lab.redeploy`'s check predicted a redeploy of a lab that is not deployed,
which the server's contract answers with 404. `veth.create`, `vxlan.create` and `node.disable_tx_offload` predicted a
change for any login, while the contract keeps those calls for superusers. `veth.create` accepted endpoints not in
`x:y` form. The `veth.create` and `vxlan.create` checks returned before logging in at all, so a refused login also
passed the check.

**Root cause.** "Always changes" was read as "a check needs nothing but the parameters". The refusals that decide
whether a run gets anywhere are the server's: whether the object exists, whether the login may call, and whether each
identifier has the shape the server takes. None of them is device state, so none was in view of a rule written about
predicting the change.

**Fix.** `e7caa208`: the redeploy check reads the lab (`s.inspect`) and refuses one not deployed, as save and restart
already did. `session.superuser` reads `GET /api/v1/users/{username}` and refuses a login whose `isSuperuser` is
false; a bearer token names no user, so its check answers `CannotCheck`. `veth.create` holds both endpoints to `x:y`
in the run and the check. Tests: `TestChecks_RefuseWhatTheServerWouldRefuse` (stub server),
`TestChecks_PredictWhatAlwaysChangesAndSendOnlyReads`, and `TestLive_ARealLabEndToEnd` against a real containerlab
server, where the superuser read works for the live login and a redeploy check of a missing lab is refused.

**Why 811 and 564 did not prevent it.** Both say a check must not pass where the run fails. 564 was about missing device
state (a group), and 811 about a removal the parent forbids; both were about what the device holds. Here the refusal
was the server's own rule about who may call and what exists, and the methods had no device state to read, so the
rule looked satisfied.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 378: a check of a method that always changes still reads, and refuses, everything the server would
refuse before acting.

## 820. TestGuards_RefusedBeforeAnythingDials could not fail: it asserted only that the error mentioned "creates", which the dial error after a missing refusal also did (a repeat of 467) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass on `1a342c7e`. The test meant to prove that a bad `creates` or `removes` is
refused before anything dials. It asserted only that the error contained "creates". With the refusal removed, the
method dialed, failed, and returned an error that named the guard too, so the test still passed.

**Root cause.** The assertion matched a word the failure path shares with the success path. It never showed the
refusal happened, or that nothing dialed.

**Fix.** `e7caa208`: the test asserts the refusal's own words, points the device at a refusing port
(`internal/testsupport/refusing.Port`), and asserts the stats are empty. It was mutation-checked: removing the refusal
fails it.

**Why 467 did not prevent it.** 467's lesson is that a test of a mode that must not act asserts the answer as well as the
absence of action. This test did assert an answer, but one loose enough that the wrong path gave it too. LESSONS 338
(prove a hazard with a control that must fail without the fix) was not applied when the test was written.

**Lesson.** An assertion on an error matches words only the intended refusal can produce, and the test is run once with
the refusal removed to see it fail.

## 821. windowsAbsolute accepted the device-namespace forms \\?\ and \\.\ and a UNC server named "..", so a guard path no one had measured reached the device (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass on `1a342c7e`, from argus `expand_seeds`. `windowsAbsolute`
(`internal/catalog/exec/winrm/shell.go`), which holds `creates` and `removes` to an absolute Windows path, accepted
`\\?\...`, `\\.\...` and `\\..\...`. How the guard's `GetAttributes` reads those forms was never measured, and a guard
read as absent fails open for `removes`.

**Root cause.** The check accepted any text after `\\` with a server and a share, so it took the device-namespace
prefixes and a dot-named server as a UNC path.

**Fix.** `e7caa208`: `windowsAbsolute` refuses a NUL, the `\\?\` and `\\.\` forms, and a server named empty, `.`, `..` or
`?`. The parameter docs say the device forms are refused. Test: `TestWindowsAbsolute`, a direct table test.

**Lesson.** A path check that guards an existence test admits only the forms someone has measured, and is tested
directly with the prefixes the platform treats specially.

## 822. exec.winrm.shell's timeout was documented as bounding the whole operation, while a guarded run made two operations, each given the full timeout (LESSONS 182's class) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass on `1a342c7e`. The `timeout` parameter says it "bounds the whole
operation". With a guard, the method ran the guard's PowerShell and then the script, and each `winrmexec.Execute` got
the whole timeout, so a task could take twice what it promised.

**Root cause.** Adding a second remote call under one parameter did not revisit what the parameter promised.

**Fix.** `e7caa208`: the guard and the script share one deadline. The script gets what the guard left, and a guard that
used it all fails the task with that reason.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 182: a timeout is a promise about the whole operation. When a method gains a second call, its
timeout is split, not repeated.

## 823. An empty creates was refused at run time but admitted by CheckCall, so validation and the run disagreed on one call (the sibling-guard class, LESSONS 244) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass on `1a342c7e`. `exec.winrm.shell` refused `creates: ""` when it ran, while
its `CheckCall`, which validation uses to refuse `check_mode` on an unguarded call, treated the empty value one way and
the run another.

**Root cause.** Two readers of one parameter (the run's `guardParams` and the check's `unguardedCheck`) each decided what
empty means.

**Fix.** `e7caa208`: empty is unset in both, as `exec.command` reads it, so a template that renders no guard runs
unguarded and is named unchecked.

**Lesson.** Where a parameter is read in two places, both read empty the same way, and the way the sibling method
already reads it.

## 824. The Windows guard gate used a fixed folder on the shared lab host (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass on `1a342c7e`. `TestWinRMGate_ShellGuards`
(`cmd/pleiades/winrm_shell_guard_release_gate_test.go`) worked in one fixed folder on the win-check VM, which other
runs and other gates share.

**Root cause.** The folder name was a constant, so two runs, or a run after one that stopped early, would meet each
other's files and could pass or fail on them.

**Fix.** `e7caa208`: the gate makes a folder per run.

**Lesson.** A gate on a shared lab host works in a folder named for its own run, never a fixed one.

## 825. A new test closed a listener and then used its port, and the released-port guard refused it (a repeat of 607, 123 and 478) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, while writing this branch's tests: `internal/archtest`'s `TestNoReleasedPortIsUsedAsAnAddress`
refused a test that closed a listener and then used its address as one nothing answers.

**Root cause.** 123's construction: a released port is anyone's, so another test can take it before it is used.

**Fix.** The test uses `internal/testsupport/refusing.Port`.

**Why 607 did not prevent it.** As in 607, the guard (478's) did its job and caught it before any commit. The construction
is still the first one a test author reaches for.

**Lesson.** For an address nothing answers, use `refusing.Port`; never release a port.

## 826. A gate's PowerShell setup failed on a missing path although it used Remove-Item -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue, and exec.winrm.shell reported exit 1 (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, building `TestWinRMGate_ShellGuards` on win-check. A setup step removed a path that might not
exist with `Remove-Item -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`. On a missing path the task failed with exit 1.

**Root cause.** `SilentlyContinue` hides the error record but the cmdlet still fails. When it is the last cmdlet,
`exec.winrm.shell` reports a failed cmdlet as exit 1, as its `exit_code` documentation says.

**Fix.** The gate's setup and cleanup remove a path only when `Test-Path -LiteralPath` finds it (`if (Test-Path ...) {
Remove-Item ... }`), so no failed cmdlet ends the script (`cmd/pleiades/winrm_shell_guard_release_gate_test.go`).

**Lesson.** In a script `exec.winrm.shell` runs, `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` silences the message, not the failure.
Test for the path first, or end on a command that succeeds.

## 827. On win-check, the Administrator login still read a file's attributes after icacls denied it Full Control on the file and its folder, so an ACL deny could not make an unreadable path for the gate (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, building `TestWinRMGate_ShellGuards`. To show the guard fails on a path it cannot read, the gate
first denied the login Full Control with `icacls` on a file and its folder. The Administrator login (high integrity)
still read the file's attributes, so the step did not produce the case it was for.

**Root cause.** Not measured. An ACL deny for that login did not stop `GetAttributes` on this host; why was not
established.

**Fix.** The gate uses a share that does not exist (`\\localhost\pleiades-no-such-share\stamp`), for which
`GetAttributes` throws and `Test-Path` answers False (818).

**Lesson.** A fixture meant to be unreadable is checked to be unreadable, by the same call the code makes, before a
test relies on it. On Windows, an ACL deny is not a reliable way to do that for an administrator login; a missing
share is.

## 828. A live clab test's command with single quotes (cut -d' ') broke through virt.clab.node.exec's wrapper (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, writing `TestLive_ARealLabEndToEnd`, which checks that no node's first process starts again. A
shell command reading the start time with `cut -d' '` failed when run through `virt.clab.node.exec`.

**Root cause.** The single quotes did not survive the wrapper the command passes through on its way to the node. How the
wrapper quotes was not traced for this record.

**Fix.** The test reads `/proc/1/stat` through the node and parses it in Go.

**Lesson.** A test that needs a value from a node fetches the raw text and parses it in Go, rather than building a
quoted shell pipeline through a wrapper whose quoting it does not control.

## 829. The Runner's executor knew no secrets, so a fact holding a dispatched credential would have been stored in the Controller's database and served to inventory:read (a repeat of 394 and 578) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass over C2d (Phase 41), before any push. `facts.Prepare` refuses a fact whose
value holds one of the run's secrets, and the engine fed it the run's known-secret set. The Crawl CLI fills that set
(`engine.WithKnownSecrets`). The Runner's executor (`internal/adapters/native/adapter.go`) was built without the
option, so on the Walk tier the list was empty. A method that emitted a fact holding the dispatched credential (an API
echoing its token, say) would have had the value published on the job's facts subject, stored as plaintext in the
Controller's `facts` table, and served by `GET /inventory/devices/{name}/facts` to anyone holding `inventory:read`.

**Root cause.** The Runner masks with the dispatch's secrets in its adapter, after the executor returns (394 says so:
"The Walk tier was not affected: its adapter masks with the dispatch's own secrets"). Nothing before this branch needed
the executor's own set on that tier. The fact guard was the first consumer of the set to run inside the executor on
both tiers, and an empty list fails open without a sound. `WithKnownSecrets` is a functional option, the shape LESSONS
154 says every caller but its author forgets.

**Why 394 and 578 did not prevent it.** 394's lesson is that every path that hands a secret to code also hands it to the
masking set; 578's is to mask where text comes in, not per output path. Both were applied to output masking. The new
path here was storage, and it read an existing list that was checked on one tier only. Neither lesson says to check
that each composition root fills a list a new guard starts to read.

**Fix.** `5763c04f`: the Runner passes `engine.WithKnownSecrets(dispatchSecrets(payload))`, which holds the device
credential's secret values and every injected value the dispatch masks. `facts.Guard` gains two checks that need no
list: `redact.SecretName` on the key and `redact.SecretShaped` on the value. The engine applies them on both tiers, and
the Controller applies them again when it verifies a Runner's batch (`facts.Verify`, in
`internal/facts/entstore/subscriber.go`). Tests: `TestDispatchSecrets_HoldsTheCredentialAndWhatWasInjected`
(`internal/adapters/native`); `TestFacts_NothingIsStoredFromACheckAFailureOrASecret` (`internal/engine`, including a
secret caught by name and by shape with no secret known); `TestPrepare_StoresOnlyWhatMayBeStored` and
`TestVerify_RechecksWhatARunnerPublished` (`internal/facts`). Recorded in the vuln corpus as class C7 (CWE-312),
severity MEDIUM. `TestExecute_PublishesNoFactHoldingTheDispatchsSecret` (`internal/adapters/native`) drives the real
`Adapter.Execute` with a task that reports its own password under an ordinary name, and fails if `adapter.go` stops
passing the option (mutation-checked: the batch then carries the password). Residual: the name and shape checks are a
strip list, not a proof. A secret the run
does not know, in a shape `internal/redact` does not recognize, is still stored.

**Lesson.** When a new guard reads a list that an existing option fills, check every composition root that builds the
object for that option, and give the guard a check that needs no list (LESSONS 381).

## 830. The CLI's fact file store read, compared and appended with no lock between processes, and wrote its side file through one fixed temporary name, so two runs at once lost facts (a repeat of 135, 528 and 566) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass over C2d's first file store (`internal/facts/file.go`, `5e8f3c06`). Each
device's history is an append-only JSON Lines file, `.pleiades/facts/<device id>.jsonl`. A write read it, compared each
new value with the current one, and appended what changed. The last-seen times sat in a side file,
`<device id>.seen.json`, written through one fixed temporary name and renamed. Runs of the CLI take the project's run
lock shared, so two runs may write one device at once. Two writers over one directory
(`TestFileStore_ConcurrentWritersTakeTurns`, two stores writing 50 facts each) kept 80 to 84 of the 100 facts without a
lock. A crash in the middle of an append would leave a last line that is not whole JSON.

**Root cause.** A read-compare-write on a shared file with nothing ordering the writers. A writer that read before
another's append compared against a stale history and wrote its side file over the other's, and two writers sharing
one temporary name wrote into each other's temporary file.

**Why 135, 528 and 566 did not prevent it.** 135's lesson is that "two processes cannot lose one another's work" must
hold for every file a design writes. 528 noted that two `pleiades` processes on one project are kept apart only by
`.pleiades/run.lock`, and runs take that lock shared, so it orders nothing between them. 566's lesson is that new code
making a file starts from the repository's existing solution. The file store was new code, written from the
single-process case. 135's own fix (one file per writer, named by content) does not fit a history that must be one
ordered file per device, and nothing pointed the author at the lock it needed instead.

**Fix.** `5763c04f`: each device's write holds a lock of its own, `<device id>.lock`, taken with `flock(2)` on Unix and
`LockFileEx` on Windows (`internal/facts/lock_unix.go`, `lock_windows.go`; other platforms take none, as
`lock_other.go` says), across the read, the compare and both writes. Readers ignore a last line with no newline, and
the next writer cuts it off before it appends. The side file is written to a temporary file created with `O_EXCL` under
a random name, then renamed. Every file is opened through an `os.Root` on the directory. Tests:
`TestFileStore_ConcurrentWritersTakeTurns` (all 100 facts, each with its last-seen time), which failed with the lock
removed, and `TestFileStore_AnUnfinishedLineIsIgnoredAndCutOff`. The lock repeats the `flock` and `LockFileEx` calls of
`internal/journal`'s run lock (`runlock_unix.go`, `runlock_windows.go`) rather than sharing them.

**Lesson.** A store that reads, compares and writes a shared file takes one lock across all three. Its first test is
two writers at once, run once with the lock removed to show it fails. An append-only file also decides, before
anything reads it, what a torn last line means.

## 831. A late observation replaced a newer current value in both fact stores, which compared with the newest row rather than with the value as of the observation's own time (a repeat in kind of LESSONS 371) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass over C2d. Both stores (the CLI's file store and the Controller's
`internal/facts/entstore`) decided whether a value had changed by comparing it with the device's newest row for that
key, and kept one last-seen time per key. Take value A observed at 10:00 and confirmed at 15:00, then a batch that
arrives late (a JetStream redelivery, or a Runner whose clock is behind) holding value B observed at 11:00. B was
written as a new row and read as the current value, though A was confirmed after it, and the key's one last-seen time
could move for the wrong value.

**Root cause.** The stores assumed observations arrive in the order they were made. A row's place in the store said when
it was written, not when its value was observed.

**Why LESSONS 371 did not prevent it.** 371 says a decision about which of two events came later reads an order the
system keeps, never arrival or a clock. It was written for rollback's "a later run on the same device". The fact stores
were written as an append of what changed, which did not read as an ordering decision until a late batch was
considered.

**Fix.** `5763c04f`: each store compares an observation with the last value observed at or before the observation's
own time (`valueAt` in `internal/facts/file.go`; `CreatedAtLTE(at)` in `internal/facts/entstore/store.go`). Each keeps
a last-seen time per value (key and hash), and the current value is the one with the latest last-seen time. Tests:
`TestFileStore_ALateObservationDoesNotReplaceANewerOne` and `TestStore_ALateBatchDoesNotReplaceANewerValue`, which
also stores the late batch twice and finds one row. Residuals: the order is still the observation time, a clock
reading from the machine that ran the task (the CLI's host, or each Runner), not a number the system orders as 371
asks. Facts gate no change, so that is recorded here rather than fixed. Two Controller replicas storing the same new
value at the same moment can each write a row; Phase 41's notes document it.

**Lesson.** A store that keeps a history and a current value decides "current" by when each value was observed, never
by when it arrived, and its tests include a batch that arrives late and one that arrives twice.

## 832. A large integer came back rounded from the Controller's fact table, because ent's JSON column decodes a map's numbers as float64 (a repeat of 706) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass over C2d. `internal/facts/entstore` first stored a fact's value inside the
`payload` JSON column as a map. Read back, 9007199254740993 (2^53 + 1) came back changed, so the API would have served a
value the device never reported.

**Root cause.** ent decodes a `field.JSON` of type `map[string]interface{}` with `encoding/json`, which makes every
number a `float64`. A whole number past 2^53 loses its low digits.

**Why 706 did not prevent it.** 706's fix decodes with `UseNumber` where open maps cross the Runner's child pipe and the
dispatch (`pkg/wire`), and its lesson names a process boundary. A database column is a boundary too, but its decode
lives in ent's generated code, where no `UseNumber` can be passed, and nothing carried 706 there.

**Fix.** `5763c04f`: the payload holds the value's canonical JSON as text (`{"json": "<text>"}`), which `entstore`
decodes with `UseNumber`. The Controller also decodes a Runner's batch with `UseNumber` before it checks the hashes
(`internal/facts/entstore/subscriber.go`). Test: `TestSubscriber_ABigIntegerCrossesTheWireWhole` (2^53 + 1 through the
subscriber and the store, read back whole).

**Lesson.** A value read back through an ORM's JSON column is decoded by code you do not control. When its numbers must
survive, store it as text and decode it yourself.

## 833. The fact table's new key and last_seen_at columns were first NOT NULL with no default, a contracting migration the compatibility check refused (a repeat of 389) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, building C2d. Adding `key` and `last_seen_at` to the existing `facts` table generated migrations
that `internal/ent/migrate`'s compatibility check (`compat.go`) classed as contracting: an old Controller, which writes
neither column, could not insert into a table where they are NOT NULL with no default.

**Root cause.** ent makes a new field NOT NULL with no SQL default unless told otherwise. On an existing table that
breaks a rolling upgrade.

**Why 389 did not prevent it.** 389's lesson ("design schema changes as expand-only first") was not applied when the
fields were written. As in 389, the classifier caught it before the branch was pushed.

**Fix.** `key` has the SQL default `''` with `NotEmpty()`, so every write still refuses an empty key, and
`last_seen_at` is `Optional()` (nullable; a reader falls back to `created_at`). Both dialects' migrations were
regenerated in place: `internal/ent/migrate/migrations/sqlite/0042_fact_key_last_seen.sql` and
`internal/ent/migrate/migrations/postgres/0039_fact_key_last_seen.sql`.

**Lesson.** A column added to an existing table is nullable or has a default from its first line; `NotEmpty()` keeps
the write rule where the SQL cannot.

## 834. A Bash heredoc decoded a JSON-style escape for U+202E into a real RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE inside a Go fuzz seed (a repeat of 256) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, writing `FuzzPrepare` (`internal/facts/facts_fuzz_test.go`). One seed was meant to hold JSON
escape text for NUL, ESC and U+202E inside a Go raw string. Written through a Bash heredoc, the U+202E escape arrived
in the file as the character itself, and `internal/archtest`'s `TestNoInvisibleControlCharactersInGoSource` failed.

**Root cause.** 256's: the agent's shell tool decodes a backslash, "u" and four hex digits in its input before it runs
the command.

**Why 256 did not prevent it.** 256's check (the archtest) held and caught it before any commit. Its other half,
LESSONS 202 (write byte escapes or build the characters in code, then check the bytes that landed), is a habit, and a
JSON escape is the natural way to write such a seed.

**Fix.** The seed was rewritten so the file holds the six-character escape text, built in code (`chr()`, or a
`\xNN` byte escape) so no escape passed through the tool.

**Lesson.** Text holding a backslash-u escape is built by code, never typed into a heredoc or a tool argument. The
archtest is the backstop, not the method.

## 835. A new architecture test, first written as "the engine must not reach internal/ent", failed on the engine's existing transitive dependency rather than on anything this phase added (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, building C2d. The first version of the rule that the engine reaches facts only through its
port refused any path from `internal/engine` to `internal/ent`. It failed at once: the engine already reaches
`internal/ent` transitively (`go list -deps ./internal/engine` lists `internal/inventory`, `internal/credential` and
`internal/transport/hopchain` beside it), from before this phase.

**Root cause.** The rule was written about what the phase must not add, but measured against the whole dependency
graph, which already held the edge.

**Fix.** The rule is narrowed to what this phase adds: the engine may import `internal/facts` (the shared rules, which
import no store) and must reach no package under `internal/facts/`, where the stores live
(`TestEngineReachesFactsOnlyThroughItsPort`, `internal/archtest/facts_port_test.go`). Its comment says it leaves direct
imports of persistence to `TestEngineNeverImportsPersistence`, and it fails if the engine stops reaching
`internal/facts` at all, so it cannot pass while examining nothing.

**Lesson.** Run a new architecture rule against main before relying on it, and scope it to the edge the phase adds. A
rule that fails on main's existing graph is either a finding about main or written too wide.

## 836. A field a later task's secret_mask marks secret was stored as a fact, because the earlier task's facts were stored at its level barrier before the mask had run (a repeat of 829) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, found by the owner's question about `secret_mask`. A task registers a result and emits facts;
a later task's `secret_mask:` names a field of that register. The field's value was stored as a fact: in
`.pleiades/facts` on the Crawl tier, and in the Controller's fact table, served at `GET /inventory/devices/{name}/facts`,
on the Walk tier. On `main` since PR #105 (`5987ba53`); unreleased, since it came after v0.3.0.

**Root cause.** `secret_mask` runs as its own later task and reaches back to an earlier register. Its value joins the
run's secrets only when that later task runs. The engine stores the earlier task's facts at that task's level barrier
(`internal/engine/facts.go`), which comes first, so the value was not yet in the secrets the fact guard reads.

**Why 829 did not prevent it.** 829's fix gave the Runner's executor the dispatch's secrets and added name and shape
checks that need no list. Each reads what is known at the moment the facts are stored, and a secret the runbook marks
later is not known then. The gap was seen and left open: the handoff for PR #105 listed "a value masked only at report
time (`secret_mask`) is not in the fact guard's known-secret list" as an owner question, so it merged as a question
rather than as a refusal.

**Fix.** `45193c98`: `maskedLater(dag)` collects each field any `secret_mask` in the runbook names for a register, and
the engine refuses to store those fields from the task that writes the register. `5212a405`: `maskedLater` reads the
full graph (`dag.full`), not the tag selection, so `--tags` cannot drop the masking task and keep the value (the shape
of 540, a tag selection losing something the runbook declares). Tests: `TestFacts_AFieldALaterSecretMaskMarksIsNeverStored`
and `TestFacts_ASecretMaskATagSelectionDropsStillKeepsTheFieldOut` (`internal/engine/facts_test.go`), both
mutation-checked. Changelog: `facts-secret-mask.security.md`. Related: vuln-corpus finding `C7_auto-roboto_2026-11-02`.

**Residuals.** The refusal is by register and field name, not by value, so the same value emitted under another key
and field is not caught. `run.publish` status messages are masked only with the secrets known when each is sent
(pre-existing, best effort).

**Lesson.** A guard that reads "what is secret so far" misses every secret the runbook marks later. When a declaration
anywhere in a runbook can make a value secret, read it from the whole runbook, never from the tag selection, before
storing anything it covers.

## 837. The Controller's check of a Runner's facts against each method's declaration was dead code in the shipped binary, which links no Collection, so collection.Lookup found nothing (a repeat of 52 and 578; in kind of 110, 180 and 693) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass over Phase 41b, before push. `internal/facts/entstore`'s Subscriber held
each batch a Runner published to the facts the method declares (`189be213`), finding the method through
`collection.Lookup`. `cmd/controller` links no Collection: under `internal/catalog`, `go list -deps ./cmd/controller`
lists only `internal/catalog/fragment`. So in the shipped Controller every lookup missed and no batch was held to a
declaration. Every test passed: the subscriber's test registered an in-process fixture method, and the Walk release
gate ran inside `cmd/runner`'s test binary, which links the catalog.

**Root cause.** The check reached the declarations through the process's registry, which only a binary that imports
the catalog fills. Each test ran in a binary that had filled it; the one binary the check runs in had not.

**Why 52, 578, 110, 180 and 693 did not prevent it.** 52 (LESSONS 56) is a registry left empty in the binary that
matters while each package's own test finds itself; its fix was an aggregator the CLI and the Runner import, and nothing
asks which binaries link it when a new reader of `collection.Lookup` appears in Controller code. 578's grant route
relied on a check in another binary ("the Controller loads no program"); its fix was the route's own check, not a rule
about where a check runs. 110, 180 and 693 are the same gap through constructor options: the test wires what the
shipped root does not. Each lesson names its own mechanism, and this was a fourth.

**Fix.** `5212a405`: `entstore.CatalogIndex(wellknown.ModuleCatalog)` builds the declarations from the generated module
catalog the Controller embeds, and `cmd/controller/main.go` passes it with `entstore.WithDeclarations`. A batch is held
by its keys, whatever method it names. Test: `TestSubscriber_HoldsBatchesToTheEmbeddedCatalog`
(`internal/facts/entstore/store_test.go`), against the real embedded catalog.

**Lesson.** A check that runs in one binary is tested with what that binary links. Before Controller code reads an
`init()`-filled registry, run `go list -deps ./cmd/controller` and look for it; when it is absent, build the data from
something the binary embeds (LESSONS 382).

## 838. On PostgreSQL every fact chain would have failed verification, because the chain hashed the observation time to the nanosecond and timestamptz keeps microseconds (a repeat of 371 and 92; in kind of 832) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass over Phase 41b, before push. The per-device fact chain (`462786a6`)
hashed each observation's time at full precision. PostgreSQL's `timestamptz` keeps microseconds: measured, it stored
`.123456789` as `.123457`, rounding rather than truncating. A row read back from PostgreSQL hashes a different time from
the one written, so verification would fail on any real time. Every store test ran on SQLite, which keeps nanoseconds,
with whole-second fixture times, so nothing saw it.

**Root cause.** The hash was taken before the store changed the value. A fixture time with no fraction is a value no
precision changes, so the tests could not tell.

**Why 371 and 92 did not prevent it.** Both lessons say a property that holds on the test dialect needs a run on the
production one, and LESSONS 250's second half says the same. They were applied to SQL statements and to refusals.
`internal/facts/entstore` had no PostgreSQL test at all and was not a container package. 832 had just shown a database
round trip changing a value (a JSON number), and its fix covered the payload column only; the time was the next value
through the same boundary.

**Fix.** `5212a405`: `facts.StoredTime` (`internal/facts/provenance.go`) truncates to the microsecond in both stores,
before storing and before hashing. `TestStore_ConformanceOnPostgres` (`internal/facts/entstore/postgres_test.go`) runs
the shared conformance suite (`internal/facts/factstest`) on real PostgreSQL through the versioned migrations, and it
fails without the fix. `internal/facts/entstore` is now in the Makefile's `DOCKER_DEPENDENT_PACKAGES`.

**Lesson.** A value hashed into a durable record is normalized to the coarsest precision any supported store keeps,
before it is hashed, and its fixtures hold values that normalization changes (LESSONS 383).

## 839. Equal run-order tokens never fell back to the clock, so within one Walk dispatch a second uptime gathered after a reboot was dropped as late, and a late batch of the same job could become current over a newer one (a repeat in kind of 831) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass over Phase 41b, before push. `facts.Later` returned `a.Token > b.Token`.
All batches of one Walk dispatch share the lease's fencing token, so two observations from one job compared as "not
later" either way. A second uptime gathered after a reboot in the same job was dropped as late, and a batch of that job
arriving late could become current over a newer one.

**Root cause.** The comparison read "equal tokens" as an answer ("not later") when it means the token cannot say.

**Why 831 did not prevent it.** 831 moved "current" from arrival to the observation's own time. Phase 41b then moved
the order to a run-order token, as LESSONS 371 asks, and dropped the clock everywhere, including where the token holds
no order. 793 and LESSONS 373 name that fallback (order by the clock where the token cannot, and say so), but for
rollback; nothing carried it to the fact order.

**Fix.** `5212a405`: tokens decide only when they differ; equal ones are ordered by the clock, and the history marks
them `ordered_by_clock`. Test: the conformance case "within one run, the clock orders its observations"
(`internal/facts/factstest/conformance.go`), mutation-checked.

**Lesson.** An order token decides only when two differ. An equal pair goes to the next source of order, and the record
says which source decided.

## 840. The Crawl CLI ordered stored facts by each run's start tick, though CLI runs overlap, so a run that started earlier and observed later was ordered first (a repeat of 793 and LESSONS 372) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, the fp-reviewer pass over Phase 41b, before push. The CLI ordered the facts a run stored by
the journal tick the run took when it started. CLI runs can overlap, since the run lock is shared. A run that started
first and observed a value after a later-started run was ordered before it, so its newer value read as older.

**Root cause.** A start tick is an order of starts. Where runs overlap, it says who began first, not who observed last.

**Why 793 and LESSONS 372 did not prevent it.** Both say exactly this: an order of acquisitions is an order of changes
only under exclusive holding. They were written about the Walk lease's fencing token, and the CLI's run tick did not
read as an acquisition order, though the shared run lock makes it one.

**Fix.** The reviewer's suggested fix, a tick per store write, was rejected: facts are stored at the level barrier,
which can be well after the observation. `5212a405`: the engine asks a recorder that implements `engine.FactOrderer`
for an order when a fact-emitting task finishes. The CLI's `facts.RunOrdered` takes `journal.NextTick`, which takes the
counter alone under its lock (`BeginRun` has already floored it at every recorded tick, so no task rescans the
journal). Tests: `TestNextTickContinuesTheCounterAndInterleavesWithRuns` (`internal/journal/clock_test.go`),
`TestFacts_AnOrderingRecorderOrdersEachObservationWhenItsTaskFinishes` (`internal/engine/facts_test.go`) and
`TestRunOrdered_TakesATickForEachObservation` (`internal/facts/file_failures_test.go`).

**Lesson.** An order is taken when the thing it orders happens: at the observation, not at the run's start (who began
first) and not at the write (which can come later).

## 841. The shipped Controller's device admission and rollback route read a method registry it never fills, so admission checked nothing and every recorded undo was refused, in v0.3.0 too (a repeat of 837, and so of 52 and 578) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, found after Phase 41b merged (PR #106, `a29afac9`). `cmd/controller` links no Collection:
under `internal/catalog`, `go list -deps ./cmd/controller` shows only `internal/catalog/fragment`, and nothing it links
calls `collection.Register` outside tests. Two Controller paths still read that registry:

- `dispatch.methodsAdmit` (`internal/dispatch/worker_devices.go`) skips a method `collection.Lookup` does not find. In
  the shipped Controller it found none, so Phase 117b part 1's capability and transport admission (the fix for 557)
  checked nothing. The Runner's preflight and the engine still refused such a device, later, on the Runner.
- `internal/rollback`'s `declaredUndo` refused every recorded undo on `POST /jobs/{id}/rollback` as "not a built-in
  method this build runs". `changesNothing` read the same registry, so a failed read-only task became an unknown gap.

Proven in the Controller's own test binary on 2026-11-03 with a throwaway test: `collection.Lookup("file.permissions")`
returned false, and `rollback.Verify` of a recorded `file.permissions` undo refused it. The `v0.3.0` tag has the same
lookups in `internal/rollback/verify.go` and `internal/dispatch/worker_devices.go` and the same imports, so Walk-tier
rollback of a recorded undo never worked in a released Controller. The Runner side re-verifies with its full registry,
which is why the Runner was never the problem.

**Why no test caught it.** Every test ran in a binary that had filled the registry. `internal/dispatch`'s admission
tests register synthetic descriptors. `internal/api/dispatcher_rollback_test.go` blank-imports `internal/catalog`.
`cmd/runner`'s rollback release gate builds the Dispatcher inside `cmd/runner`'s test binary, which links the catalog.
No test ran either path in a binary that links what `cmd/controller` links.

**Root cause.** The same as 837's: Controller code reached method declarations through an `init()`-filled registry
that only a binary importing the catalog fills. Here two more readers did it, and they predate 837.

**Why 837, 52 and 578 did not prevent it.** 837 was found the day before, in the same shape, and its fix
(`entstore.CatalogIndex` over `wellknown.ModuleCatalog`) fixed the one consumer in view: the facts Subscriber. Nobody
then listed every other `collection.Lookup` the Controller links, so the fix closed an instance and not the class. The
records keeper's note on 837 named `methodsAdmit` as the same class, and the previous handoff carried it as "found, not
fixed". LESSONS 382, written for 837, says to run `go list -deps ./cmd/controller` before Controller code reads a
registry; it speaks of new code and does not ask for a sweep of the old. 52 (LESSONS 56) and 578 did not prevent it for
the reasons 837 gives: each fixed its own mechanism. LESSONS 155 and 157 already say to enumerate every surface that
can carry a class before calling it closed; they were not applied when 837 closed.

**Fix.** `8d8bdd6b` on `fix/controller-catalog` (not merged when written). `pkg/collection` gains `InstallCatalog`,
`BuiltinManifest` and `ManifestOf` (`pkg/collection/catalog.go`): the registry first, then the module catalog that a
binary registering no Collection installs once. `cmd/controller` installs `wellknown.ModuleCatalog` at start
(`cmd/controller/builtin_catalog.go`, called from `main.go`). Admission (`internal/dispatch/worker_devices.go`),
rollback's declarations (`internal/rollback/verify.go`, `steps.go`) and `engine.ListParam`
(`internal/engine/journal_entry.go`) read through them. Tests:
`TestWorker_AdmitsFromTheInstalledCatalogInABinaryWithNoRegistry`
(`internal/dispatch/worker_method_admission_test.go`, mutation-checked);
`TestInstallBuiltinCatalog_TheControllerTrustsABuiltInsRecordedUndo` (`cmd/controller/builtin_catalog_test.go`, in
the Controller's own test binary, which links no Collection either); and `TestTheControllerReadsNoRegistryItDoesNotFill`
(`internal/archtest/controller_registry_test.go`, mutation-checked), which refuses a new `collection.Lookup` in any
package the Controller links unless it is listed with why it never runs there. Changelog:
`changelog/controller-builtin-catalog.fixed.md`.

**Lesson.** When a class is found once, sweep every consumer of the same assumption before closing it, and make the
sweep a test so the next consumer is refused too. This is LESSONS 155 and 157 again, applied to LESSONS 382's case; no
new lesson was written. The archtest is the sweep made permanent.

## 842. On macOS a device's facts lock open (os.Root OpenFile with O_CREATE) failed with "no such file or directory" while another store created the same lock file: macOS openat(2) relative to a directory fd reports ENOENT under concurrent create (cause reproduced 2026-11-03; mitigated by a bounded retry)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-02, GitHub Actions run 41522289001 on `feat/c2d-persisted-facts` at `497a2cc7`, leg `fast-macos`,
strict. `internal/facts`'s `TestFileStore_ConcurrentWritersTakeTurns` failed with `facts_test.go:321: facts: openat
dev.lock: no such file or directory`: two stores were creating the same device's lock file at once, and one open with
`O_CREATE`, through an `os.Root` on a directory that still existed, was refused as if the file's directory were
missing. The other store created the file at once. It has not been seen on Linux, FreeBSD or Windows.

**Root cause (reproduced 2026-11-03, on the lab Mac once it was back).** On macOS 27.0.1 (darwin/arm64, APFS),
`openat(2)` with `O_CREAT`, relative to a directory file descriptor, sometimes returns ENOENT while another thread
creates the same name; the same call given an absolute path (`AT_FDCWD`) never does, and `O_NOFOLLOW` makes no
difference. Go's `os.Root` opens through a directory fd, so it inherits it. Measured with a throwaway program, 16
goroutines creating one file at once, 400 rounds (6,400 opens each): `openat` from a dirfd 1,244 ENOENT (1,304 with
`O_NOFOLLOW`), `os.Root.OpenFile` 1,454, `openat` from `AT_FDCWD` with an absolute path 0, plain `os.OpenFile` 0. The
facts stress tests, run 300 times each there (`go test -count=300 -run 'TestFileStore_(ConcurrentWritersTakeTurns|ManyStoresCreateOneDevicesFilesAtOnce)$'`),
passed 600 of 600; 271 of the 300 stress runs needed 1 to 5 retries (29 needed none). GitHub's hosted macOS runners
showed 0 retries in #106's run, so they do not reach the contention. Kernel or file system behaviour, not this code
and not Go's; whether to report it to Apple or the Go project is the owner's decision, and nothing was reported.

**Fix: the mitigation is the fix.** `724a9d09` (in PR #105): `openLock` (`internal/facts/file.go`) tries the open again, at most
`lockOpenAttempts` (20) times, only on "not exist" and only while the directory is still at its path, and counts each
retry in `lockOpenRetries`. The same commit added `TestFileStore_ManyStoresCreateOneDevicesFilesAtOnce` (eight stores
creating forty devices' files at once), which logs the count. PR #106 made the count visible in CI: testgate prints
the notes a passing test logs as `note: ` lines (`4f329cc6`, `tools/internal/flakegate/notes.go`). In PR #106's run
41562963070 the fast-macos and repeat passes reported 0 retries, on darwin/arm64 and on linux/amd64. Zero retries means
the race did not recur in that run; it does not show the cause is gone. `os.Root` stays, for what it is there for
(a link planted in the store cannot lead a write outside it), so the retry is the answer: the worst case seen was 5
retries against a bound of 20.

**Handled as 448 was.** 448 (`pkg/tftpxfer` on macOS) is a different failure with the same constraints: intermittent,
on a platform nobody could log in to, cause unknown. LESSONS 269 (make the fixture say why) applies here as it did
there.

**Lesson.** An intermittent failure on a platform you cannot reach is mitigated narrowly (bounded, only on the exact
error, only while the precondition still holds) and made measurable in CI, and its cause stays "unproven" in the
record until a run reproduces it. This one closed only when the machine came back and a minimal program separated the
kernel's behaviour from the code's: the reproduction, not the CI count, named the cause.

## 843. container.image.save's check predicted a digest the real save missed now and then, because classic Docker stamps the archive's blobs/sha256/ directory with the time of the save and lists several images in any order, and CI tolerated it three times as contention (a repeat in kind of 589) (fixed)

**Symptom.** `internal/catalog/container/image`'s `TestSaveAndLoad_OneArchiveByItsDigest` failed on GitHub's
`containers` shards three times in ten days, each on a branch that did not touch it (2026-10-24 run 40047970897 on
`feat/lab-importers`, 2026-11-01 run 41315681516 on `fix/become-honored-or-refused`, 2026-11-03 run 41576491763 on
`fix/controller-catalog`): `save returned sha256:d1eb..., the check predicted sha256:d776...`. Each time it passed when
run again alone, so the tolerant rule recorded it as contention and the pull request merged. It never failed on this
machine.

**Root cause.** Classic Docker (28.5.2, overlay2; what the hosted Ubuntu runners use) writes the archive's
`blobs/sha256/` directory entry with the time of the save, at second resolution; every file in the archive, and the
index and manifests, are the same. So two saves of one image in different seconds differ, and the method's check
(which hashes one save) and its real run (which writes another) agree only when both fall in the same second. Proven
in a `docker:28-dind` engine: two saves back to back matched 10 of 10, two saves 1.1 s apart differed 10 of 10, and
`tar -tv` of the pair differs in that one line. Docker Desktop here uses the containerd image store, whose save is
byte-stable (30 saves of one image, and a freshly imported image saved twice 20 times, all matched), which is why it
never failed here. The same stamp also made "saving again is no change" false across a second boundary, so a
recorded archive's digest could churn between runs.

**A second difference, found in review (2026-11-03).** With more than one image, classic Docker 28 also writes
`manifest.json`'s and `index.json`'s lists in a different order from save to save (measured in `docker:28-dind`: three
images saved twenty times gave three orders of each), which no time normalization reaches, since the bytes are in the
files' contents. Every test had saved one image.

**Why 589 did not prevent it.** 589's lesson was that a failure the re-run alone calls contention can still be a
defect. The ledger (`tools/failures`) had this test three times; nobody read the ledger across pull requests until the
third, when `record-actions` printed a new entry on a green run.

**Fix.** `normalize.go` (`normalizedArchive`): `container.image.save` re-writes the engine's archive as it streams,
entry by entry, with every entry's times at the Unix epoch, its extended records reduced to the xattrs (an allowlist),
the root `manifest.json`'s and `index.json`'s lists sorted by each entry's compact JSON, and every blob unchanged,
before both the check's hash and the real store, so the same images give the same archive and digest on every engine.
`TestSave_SeveralImagesGiveOneArchive` and the epoch-time assertion in `TestSaveAndLoad_OneArchiveByItsDigest` hold the
wiring on a real engine; they can fail only on an engine that writes other times or orders (the classic one CI runs),
since this machine's containerd-store engine already writes epoch times.
`TestNormalizedArchive_TheSameImagesGiveTheSameBytes` (USTAR, PAX and GNU archives a second apart; mutation-checked),
`TestNormalizedArchive_ABrokenArchiveFailsTheRead`. Proven on real classic-engine output: two saves 1.1 s apart differ
raw and match normalized, and the classic engine loads a normalized archive. The method's documentation says the
archive's entries carry 1970-01-01.

**Lesson.** A check that predicts a digest of what an outside system produces holds only as far as that system is
byte-stable, which differs by engine and version; normalize what it produces before hashing it. And a test the
ledger shows tolerated more than once, on unrelated branches, is a defect until proven otherwise: read the ledger's
repeats, not only the run in front of you.
