## 844. systemctl's options after its verb were read as unit names under POSIXLY_CORRECT, so facts.gather's services probe listed nothing in the SSH harness (the class of 494 and 420; caught by 494's harness setting) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, Phase 41c-1 on `feat/facts-41c-1`, writing the services subset. Run through the SSH test
harness (`remoteexectest`), `systemctl list-unit-files --type=service ...` printed no unit, so the services probe gave
no `service.*` fact.

**Root cause.** systemctl parses its arguments with getopt_long, which honors `POSIXLY_CORRECT`: under it, parsing
stops at the first word that is not an option. The verb `list-unit-files` is that word, so every option after it was
read as a unit name to match. The harness sets `POSIXLY_CORRECT=1` on purpose (494's fix), so a Linux test sees the
parse a BSD userland uses. On a real device the variable is usually unset, so the command would have worked there, and
failed on any device whose environment sets it.

**Why 494 did not prevent it, and why that is fine.** 494's fix is the harness setting, and it worked as designed: it
caught this before the commit. 494's lesson (a platform difference a Linux machine can be made to show is a harness
setting) is what found it.

**Fix.** `f8234fc1`: every systemctl option goes before the verb (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_services.go`).
Proven by `TestGather_PackagesAndServicesMatchThisMachine`, which compares the services subset with this machine's own
systemctl under the harness.

**Lesson.** Put a command's options before its first operand or verb, always. A non-permuting parser (BSD's, or GNU's
under `POSIXLY_CORRECT`) reads anything after it as an operand. No new lesson: this is 494's, applied.

## 845. facts.gather's probes went to the account's login shell, so under csh, tcsh or fish a multi-statement probe failed to parse and the task succeeded with no package or service facts (a repeat of 809, and of 779's class) (fixed before push here; the same class in about 20 other send sites is open, for the next pull request)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, found in review of `feat/facts-41c-1`. Phase 41c-1's package and service probes are POSIX
scripts with several statements (`command -v dpkg-query >/dev/null && ...`, loops on FreeBSD and macOS). They were sent
as the SSH command string, which sshd hands to the account's login shell. Under csh, tcsh or fish they fail to parse.
The SSH path reads no exit status for a probe, so the task succeeded and stored no `package.*` or `service.*` fact.
With the fix removed, a tcsh login gathered 0 packages, and the task succeeded.

**Root cause.** 809's: a script written for POSIX `sh` is POSIX only when `sh` runs it, and sshd runs the command
string through the login shell. The probes before 41c-1 were single commands (`uname -s`, reading `/etc/os-release`)
that every shell parses the same way, so the defect stayed hidden until 41c-1 added scripts.

**Why 809 did not prevent it.** 809's fix wrapped one check's listing, and `remotefile.Locate` and `Removable`, in
`sh -c`. Its lesson (the platform's own script goes to `sh -c`, on one line) is a habit: no rule and no test holds a
new probe to it. And no test could have seen it: the in-process SSH harness runs every command through `/bin/sh`
whatever the account's shell, so it cannot show a login shell's grammar. That is LESSONS 174's blindness: the fixture
neutralizes the one condition (a non-POSIX login) that the defect needs.

**Fix.** `ab881c13`: every SSH probe runs as `remoteexec.QuoteCommand([]string{"sh", "-c", probe})`
(`internal/catalog/facts/gather_transport.go`), each probe one line, since csh refuses a newline inside quotes. The
platform is read from the last line of `uname -s`'s output, since a login that prints a banner prints it first
(`lastLine`, `TestLastLine_SkipsALoginBanner`). Proven by `TestCLI_FactsReleaseGate`, which switches the container
login's shell to tcsh, then fish, and reads each gather's own report (`adhoc --json` stats) for the package count.

**Open: the class elsewhere.** A product-wide audit on 2026-11-03 found the same class in about 20 other places that
send a platform script to a login shell. The owner decided (2026-11-03) that every SSH command runs under `sh`, raw
ones too, in its own pull request, next. Its test switch (`PLEIADES_TEST_LOGIN_SHELL`) is saved in `git stash`
("shell-agnostic: PLEIADES_TEST_LOGIN_SHELL switch"). Until it lands, this class is open outside `facts.gather`.

**Lesson.** A rule about how to send a command that only a habit enforces does not hold. Put the rule in the one
function that sends commands, and give the harness a switch that runs commands under another login shell, so a test
can see it. LESSONS 386 records the form proven under five shells.

**Resolved, 2026-11-03.** The open class is fixed by 858 (`4a7db76d` on `fix/shell-agnostic-ssh`): every command
a connection sends is encoded for `sh` in `pkg/remoteexec`, raw only where `inventory.ExecIsPOSIX` says the device
has no POSIX shell, and every sshd-backed suite 858 names passes with `PLEIADES_TEST_LOGIN_SHELL` set to fish,
tcsh and zsh. Two more of the class, the release gates' own helpers (862), were found by that run.

## 846. The macOS packages probe ran Homebrew's brew, a script under a prefix another account may own, as the gather login, possibly root (a repeat in kind of 781, and of vuln-corpus finding C4_auto-roboto_2026-11-01) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, found in review of `feat/facts-41c-1`. The macOS packages probe ran
`/opt/homebrew/bin/brew` or `/usr/local/bin/brew` to list formulae and casks. `brew` is a shell script, and Homebrew's
prefix belongs to whichever account installed it. A gather that logs in as root, or as any account other than that
owner, ran another account's code with its own rights.

**Root cause.** The probe trusted a program by its path. A path under a directory another account controls runs
whatever that account last put there (CWE-426, untrusted search path; CWE-250, running with more rights than needed).
Reasoned, not exploited: it needs the attacker to own the Homebrew prefix and the gather to run as another account.

**Why 781 and C4 did not prevent it.** 781 (a job base in a directory the login owns, under become) and vuln-corpus
finding C4_auto-roboto_2026-11-01 (the detached job's HOME, fixed with `[ -O "$HOME" ]`) are the same idea: do not act
with one account's rights on a path another account controls. Each was fixed where it was found. Neither became a
check that a new probe passes through, and a read-only gather did not look like a place where code runs.

**Fix.** `ab881c13`: the probe runs `brew` only when the login owns it and is not root:
`[ -x "$b" ] && [ -O "$b" ] && [ "$(id -u)" != 0 ]` (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_bsd_items.go`). Otherwise it
lists only pkgutil's receipts. Proven on the lab Mac (macOS 27.0.1) by
`TestCLI_FactsGatherOnMacOSMatchesItsOwnTools`, whose Homebrew count still matches.

**Lesson.** A probe that runs a program, not only one that writes, runs it with the login's rights: check who owns
the program before running it, and never run another account's program as root. No new lesson; this is LESSONS 367's
rule (a confinement rule binds every read of the same source) applied to running a program.

## 847. dpkg's package probe kept only the "ii" state, dropping held and partly installed packages, and its test computed the expectation with the same filter, so it could not fail (a repeat of 54) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, found in review of `feat/facts-41c-1`. The dpkg probe kept a line only when its status was
`ii`. A held package (`hi`) and any installed state other than "installed" (unpacked, half-configured, triggers
awaited or pending) gave no fact, so drift could not see them. `TestGather_PackagesAndServicesMatchThisMachine`
passed, because it counted this machine's packages with the same `^ii` filter.

**Root cause.** The code assumed the desired-action letter and the state letter were both `i` for every installed
package. The test was written from the code, not from dpkg, so it shared the assumption.

**Why 54 did not prevent it.** 54 is a test whose fixture only exercises what the code already reads; its lesson
(LESSONS 58) asks whether a test's fixture can tell the feature from its absence. Here the expectation was derived
with the code's own filter, the same shape, and nobody asked dpkg what "installed" means.

**Fix.** `ab881c13`: a package is installed when its status letter is one of `iUFWt` (`dpkgInstalled`,
`internal/catalog/facts/gather_packages.go`). The machine test counts dpkg's own `${db:Status-Status}` words
(installed, unpacked, half-configured, triggers-awaited, triggers-pending) rather than the code's filter, and the parser
fixture in `TestPackageParsers_ReadEachDatabasesOwnOutput` has `hi`, `iU`, `iH` and `pn` lines.

**Lesson.** A test's expectation comes from the tool's own answer, not from the code's reading of it. When both use
the same filter, the test checks nothing.

## 848. The playbook converter passed Ansible's gather_subset through unchanged though the two meanings differ, so ['!facter', '!ohai'] converted cleanly and failed on every host (a repeat of 334) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, found in review of `feat/facts-41c-1`. `setup`'s `gather_subset` was copied to
`facts.gather`'s. The words mean different things. Ansible's `all` never includes packages or services (those are
`package_facts` and `service_facts`), while `facts.gather`'s `all` does. Ansible's `facter`, `ohai`, `network` and
`virtual` have no `facts.gather` subset and were refused at run time, so the common `gather_subset: ['!facter',
'!ohai']` converted with no note and then failed on every host.

**Root cause.** 334's: a table mapping another program's interface was written from the names, not from that
program's own description of them. Equal words were taken as equal meanings.

**Why 334 did not prevent it.** 334's fix and test (`TestEntries_ArgsMatchAnsibleCore`) check argument names and
values against `ansible-doc`. A subset list's meaning (what `all` covers, what a removal alone starts from) is not an
argument name, so nothing compared it.

**Fix.** `bcce2fe0`: `setupSubset` (`internal/forge/playbook/adjust.go`) computes what Ansible would gather (removals
win whatever their order; a list of removals alone starts from `all`) and passes `[min]` or `[min, hardware]`,
leaving out each added name with no counterpart under a `module.semantics` note. In `facts.gather` itself a list of
removals alone now starts from `min` and `hardware`, so a task lists packages only by naming them or `all`. Tests:
the `setup` cases in `internal/forge/playbook/modules_test.go` (removals only, removal wins, nothing left, network).

**Lesson.** Map a value's meaning, not its spelling: for each value the other program accepts, write down what it
does there and test the conversion on that outcome (LESSONS 234).

## 849. Package facts from two databases on one host overwrote each other, because names were told apart within one probe only, and the test proving it called a combination Gather never makes (a repeat of 54 and 571) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, found in review of `feat/facts-41c-1`. A host with two package databases (dpkg and rpm on
one host; Homebrew and pkgutil on a Mac) can list one name in both. Each probe told its own repeated names apart
(`:arch`, then `@source`), but the two probes' facts were joined afterwards, so the second `package.bash` replaced the
first. The test that seemed to prove the naming fed both outputs to one probe's naming, which Gather never does.

**Root cause.** The naming state lived in each probe's parse, not where Gather emits facts for the whole run.

**Why 54 and 571 did not prevent it.** 54's lesson is that a fixture must reach the code path the feature uses; 571's
is that a comment or test must not claim more than the code does. This test's call order was not Gather's, so it
proved a path the product never takes, and its name claimed the product's behavior.

**Fix.** `ab881c13`: Gather tells keys apart across every probe of the run (`gatherNames`,
`internal/catalog/facts/gather.go`): `:arch`, then `@source`, then `#n`. The test helper `distinctAll` emits facts the
way Gather does, and `TestPackageParsers_ReadEachDatabasesOwnOutput` checks that dpkg's and rpm's `bash` give
`package.bash` and `package.bash:x86_64`.

**Lesson.** A test of a property that holds across a run calls the code the way the run does. A helper that builds
the case another way tests the helper.

## 850. Adding one container test to internal/catalog/facts moved the whole package to the container tier, so none of its tests ran on the non-Linux container-free legs (a sibling of 631 and 756) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, review of `feat/facts-41c-1`. `8c0ca796` added a test that runs the rpm probe in a Rocky
Linux container, and `90f47225` one that runs OpenRC in an Alpine container. `tools/internal/flakegate`'s
`TestEveryContainerPackageIsListed` then required `internal/catalog/facts` in `DOCKER_DEPENDENT_PACKAGES`. A
container package runs only in the containers tier, on Linux, so the package's parser and gather tests stopped running
on the macOS, FreeBSD and Windows container-free legs, which are the platforms 41c-1 added.

**Root cause.** The tier is decided per package. One container test moves every test in its package.

**Why 631 and 756 did not prevent it.** 631 (pr-check selects changed packages, not dependents) and 756 (the
container opt-out dropped `internal/archtest`) are other ways a test leaves the run it belongs in. Neither says that a
new container test changes where its siblings run, and the guard that moved the package is correct; it reports the
move but does not say what it costs.

**Fix.** `4787bbb6`: the rpm and OpenRC tests moved to `internal/catalog/facts/live`, which reaches the probes
through an exported view (`facts.Probes`, `internal/catalog/facts/probes_export.go`; `TestProbes_AreTheProbesGatherRuns`
holds it equal to what Gather runs). The `Makefile`'s container list and `tools/testgate/durations.json` name the new
package; `internal/catalog/facts` is container-free again. Each command in a container now has a deadline.

**Lesson.** Before adding a container test to a package, ask what else the package's tests prove and where they must
run. Put the container test in its own package when the others belong on every platform.

## 851. A literal U+200B (zero-width space) sat in a Go test string, and internal/archtest's invisible-character check passed it (a repeat of 256 and 834) (fixed before push; the archtest gap is open)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, review of `feat/facts-41c-1`. A case in `TestItemKey_EncodesWhatAKeyCannotHoldExactly`
(`internal/catalog/facts/gather_subsets_internal_test.go`) held a real zero-width space in its source, invisible in
an editor and a diff. `internal/archtest`'s `TestNoInvisibleControlCharactersInGoSource` passed.

**Root cause.** Two. The character reached the file as itself, as in 256 and 834. And the archtest asks
`termsafe.Unsafe`, which does not count zero-width characters as unsafe, so the backstop that caught 834 missed this
one.

**Why 256 and 834 did not prevent it.** Their fix is the archtest plus a habit (LESSONS 202: build such characters in
code). The habit was not followed, and the archtest covers the characters a terminal acts on, not every invisible one.

**Fix.** `ab881c13`: the character is built in code, `string(rune(0x200b))`. **Not fixed:** the archtest still
passes a zero-width character in Go source. Widening it (or `termsafe.Unsafe`) is open.

**Resolution of the archtest gap (2026-11-04, branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`).** `f041ed28` widens the archtest, not
`termsafe.Unsafe`: it also refuses Unicode's Cf, Zl, Zp, Variation_Selector and Other_Default_Ignorable_Code_Point,
with a negative control over a tree of its own. It found raw U+2028 and U+2029 in two test files. See 905.

**Lesson.** A backstop's list is part of what it proves: an invisible-character check that does not name zero-width
characters lets them through. Build such characters in code, and treat the archtest as the backstop it is.

## 852. A test container with sleep as PID 1 never reaped children, so a daemon OpenRC started from docker exec became a zombie that start-stop-daemon would not stop (a repeat of 343) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, writing `90f47225`'s OpenRC test on `feat/facts-41c-1`. The test booted OpenRC in an Alpine
container, started `crond`, stopped it, and read the services subset. After the stop the gather still saw `crond`
running.

**Root cause.** 343's: the container's PID 1 was `sleep`, which never reaps. A daemon OpenRC started through `docker
exec` was orphaned to PID 1, and once it exited it stayed a zombie. start-stop-daemon found the process still there
and refused to stop it.

**Why 343 did not prevent it.** 343 fixed the two containers in view (the benchmark's runner and the Ansible
adapter's), and its lesson says any container that runs a process tree needs an init. No harness default or check
applies it, so a new test container started the old way.

**Fix.** The test container starts with `HostConfig.Init` (docker `--init`), now in
`internal/catalog/facts/live/live_test.go` (`90f47225`, moved by `4787bbb6`). `TestGatherServices_ReadsARealOpenRC`
holds the stopped state.

**Lesson.** 343's, again; LESSONS 385 states it for a test that starts a daemon.

## 853. Past MaxFactsPerObservation (8192) an observation was stored as none of it while the task succeeded (a repeat in kind of 265) (fixed before push; a Runner's publish failing mid-split is open)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, review of `feat/facts-41c-1`. Phase 41 refuses an observation of more than 8,192 keys as a
whole. A host with that many packages and services gave a `facts.gather` that succeeded and stored nothing, with only
a log line saying why.

**Root cause.** The bound was checked where facts are stored, after the method returned success. The method did not
know the bound, so it could not fail the task.

**Why 265 did not prevent it.** 265 is one bad record failing a whole sync; this is one bound making a whole
observation vanish while reporting success. Both turn a per-record outcome into a whole-run outcome at another stage,
and 265's lesson (check every stage that touches a record) was applied to its own plugin contract only.

**Fix.** `ab881c13`: `facts.gather` counts its facts and fails past `collection.MaxFactsPerObservation`, with an error
naming `gather_subset` and `filter` as the way to gather less (`TestGather_MoreFactsThanOneTaskMayRecordFailsTheTask`).
`collection.MaxFactsPerObservation` (`pkg/collection/facts.go`) mirrors `internal/facts`' bound, since a Collection may
not import `internal/`; `internal/engine`'s `TestFactCaps_AgreeAcrossTheBoundary` holds the two equal.

**Open.** A Runner splits an observation into batches under 512 KiB. When a publish fails partway, the batches already
sent are stored and the rest are not, so the stored observation is partial.

**Lesson.** A bound that drops data is enforced where the task can still fail, and said in the task's result.

## 854. The secret-name exemption for item families applied to every Prefix declaration, so a future field-named family (env.DB_PASSWORD) would have been stored (the class of LESSONS 337 and FAILURE_PATTERNS 655) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, review of `feat/facts-41c-1`. `f648b8ec` let a key inside a declared family pass the
secret-name guard on its prefix only, since a package called `password-store` is a name, not a field. The exemption
applied to any `Prefix` declaration. A later family whose suffix is a field name, such as environment variables
(`env.DB_PASSWORD`), would have skipped the guard and been stored.

**Root cause.** The exemption was inferred from the declaration's shape (a prefix) instead of being declared. A prefix
family can hold item names or field names, and only the method knows which.

**Why 337 and 655 did not prevent it.** Both say a guard is an allowlist of what each value is, never an inference.
This exemption was new code that inferred.

**Fix.** `ab881c13`: `collection.FactSpec.ItemNames` (`pkg/collection/facts.go`) is an explicit opt-in, validated:
it needs `Prefix` and a prefix ending in a dot (`TestValidateFacts_RefusesEachMalformedDeclaration`). Only such a
family's suffix skips the name guard; the value is still held to every secret check.
`TestPrepare_AFamilyMembersNameIsDataNotAFieldName` (`internal/facts/kind_test.go`) shows `package.password-store`
kept and `env.db_password` refused.

**Lesson.** An exemption from a secret guard is declared by name, never inferred from a shape that other uses share.

## 855. The Crawl file store's Record scanned the whole history once per fact, quadratic for thousands of packages against a growing history (the class of 490 and 611) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, review of `feat/facts-41c-1`. Phase 41c-1 makes a host's observation thousands of keys.
The file store's `Record` read the device's whole history once per key to find that key's latest value, so one gather
cost the number of keys times the length of the history, and grew with every gather.

**Root cause.** The store was written for eight keys per observation, where a scan per key was cheap.

**Why 490 and 611 did not prevent it.** Both are a per-item pass over a whole input (a line count per reference, a
join per wrapped line). Their fixes were local; nothing asks a structure's existing loops to be re-checked when its
input grows by orders of magnitude.

**Fix.** `e9be6fd2`: `Record` indexes the history's lines by key once per call and reads each key's lines from the
index (`internal/facts/file_store.go`). **Not changed:** `sdk.NoteFactKey`'s linear check for a repeated key, bounded
by the 8,192 cap.

**Lesson.** When a phase multiplies a structure's input, re-read each loop over it for work done once per item over
the whole.

## 856. A file named gather_windows.go built only on Windows (a repeat of 374) (fixed before commit)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, writing `724a2010` on `feat/facts-41c-1`. gopls reported no package metadata for the new
`internal/catalog/facts/gather_windows.go`, and its code was not built on Linux.

**Root cause.** 374's: Go reads a file name ending `_windows.go` as a build constraint.

**Why 374 did not prevent it.** 374's lesson is a naming habit with no check behind it. gopls caught it before the
commit, as `go_diagnostics` after each edit is meant to.

**Fix.** Renamed to `gather_win.go` before the commit.

**Lesson.** 374's. A file about one OS takes the OS name anywhere but last.

## 857. A "this machine" test filtered on package.bash, which a Mac does not have, and failed only on the macOS runner (a repeat of 54) (fixed on the pull request)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, pull request #109, `fast-macos (2)`: `TestGather_PackagesAndServicesMatchThisMachine`
failed with "a filter naming package.bash kept 0 facts", alone on its re-run too. The SSH harness gathers the runner's
own packages; on macOS those are Homebrew's and pkgutil's, and none is called bash.

**Root cause.** The test chose its example package by what a Debian or Alpine machine has, not by what the machine it
ran on had listed. Moving the package's container tests out (850) put it back on the macOS legs, the first runs that
could see this.

**Why 54 did not prevent it.** 54's lesson is that a test's expectation must come from the system, not from the
author's picture of it. The reviewer of `feat/facts-41c-1` named this exact assumption as a test note; the dpkg version
check beside it was guarded, and this line was missed.

**Fix.** The test filters on a package key this machine's own gather listed, one holding no pattern character, and
skips the filter step where the machine lists no package (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_test.go`).

**Lesson.** A test that runs on "this machine" picks every example from what this machine reported.

## 858. Every command pkg/remoteexec sent over SSH went to the account's login shell, so under a fish or tcsh login the file methods, check mode, rollback, detach, scp, onboarding and the other platform scripts broke, some reporting success having done nothing (a repeat of 845, and of 809 and 779) (fixed; a fish host onboarded before the fix stays raw until onboarded again, open)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, branch `fix/shell-agnostic-ssh`. sshd hands an exec request's command string to the account's
login shell, and every command the platform builds is POSIX shell. Under fish and tcsh logins these broke:
`pkg/remotefile` (`Stat`, `Checksum`, `Read`, `Write`, `DirectoryEmpty`, `whoAmI`, `writeBeside`), the detached
job's start and stop, scp (its multi-line script under tcsh), the onboarding probes, `gate.run`, `db.pg` dump and
restore, `wait.port`, `net.frr.config`, `build.digests.refresh`, `pkg.apt.*` (tcsh, on `VAR=x cmd`), `identity.user`
and `net.linux.bridge` (tcsh, multi-line), and `exec.command` and `exec.shell` (tcsh on a multi-line command; fish
on a backslash pair or a backslash-quote inside single quotes). A baseline run of `cmd/pleiades` with its sshd
fixtures logging in to fish failed 11 tests: check mode, external Collection checks, rollback, the journal, the
concurrent-run notice, `migrate-playbook` and tags.

**Root cause.** 845's and 809's: a script written for POSIX `sh` is POSIX only when `sh` runs it. Each send site
chose its own way to reach `sh`, or none, and no test could see the difference: the in-process SSH harness runs every
command through `/bin/sh` whatever the account's shell (LESSONS 174).

**Why 845 did not prevent it.** 845 fixed `facts.gather`'s probes alone and recorded about 20 other send sites as
open, for this pull request. Its lesson (put the rule in the one function that sends commands, and give the harness a
login-shell switch) is what this branch builds. 809 and 779 each fixed one or two scripts by wrapping them in
`sh -c`, a habit with no rule behind it, and the login shell still parsed the quoted argument before `sh` ran it.

**Fix.** `4a7db76d`. `Conn.run` and `Conn.Start`, the only two places a connection sends a command, encode it with
`pkg/remoteexec/shline` after become wraps it (the encoder LESSONS 386 describes; `shline`'s package comment holds the
exact line as committed). `Conn.Raw()` sends a command as written, and is chosen only by `inventory.ExecIsPOSIX`
(false for `NetworkCLICapable`, or for onboarding's discovered `shell` fact `not posix`) in `sdk.Connect`, in the
`ssh_exec` transport (`transport.Target.LoginShell`, set by `engine.SSHTarget`) and, after 860, in `net.ssh.ping`. A
detached job runs under `sh` as a plain command does. Owner decision 2026-11-03: raw `ssh_exec` commands run under
`sh` too, as Ansible's shell module runs its command. Proof: `TestEveryLoginShellHandsShTheSameCommand`
(`internal/transport/ssh`, real sshd) runs one POSIX script through the real `ssh_exec` transport under ash, bash,
zsh, tcsh and fish logins and holds every answer byte-identical, with the same script sent raw failing under fish as
its control. `PLEIADES_TEST_LOGIN_SHELL` (`testsupport.EnvLoginShell`, `testsupport.UseLoginShell`) gives every sshd
container a test starts that login shell; `cmd/pleiades`, `cmd/runner`, `internal/transport/ssh`,
`internal/catalog/file`, `pkg/scpxfer`, `pkg/sftpxfer`, `pkg/containerengine` and `internal/adapters/native` pass
under fish, tcsh and zsh. On the lab, the Mac (its login is zsh) passes `TestCLI_FactsGatherOnMacOSMatchesItsOwnTools`,
and bsd-check (FreeBSD 15.1) with its account switched to tcsh, then restored to sh, passes
`TestCLI_FreeBSDFileChecksMatchTheirRealRuns` and the FreeBSD facts gate. `internal/archtest`'s
`TestOnlyRemoteexecOpensAnSSHSession`, with its negative control `TestSessionOpensFindsBothWays`, refuses an SSH
session opened outside `pkg/remoteexec`.

**Open.** A `generic_ssh` host whose account logs in to fish and was onboarded before this change was recorded
`not posix` by the old raw probe, so its commands stay raw until it is onboarded again; the discovery carries no probe
version to tell an old record from a new one, so the changelog fragment tells the user to run `pleiades onboard`
again. The Ansible gate's container is not switched, since Ansible chooses its own shell.
`TestEveryLoginShellHandsShTheSameCommand` installs the shells from the Alpine mirror at test time, bounded by a
three-minute deadline, not pinned in an image.

**Resolution of the open half (2026-11-04, branch `fix/ssh-sweep-2026-11-04`).** The stale record was worse than
"stays raw": fish does not treat `QuoteArg`'s quoting as a boundary, so a quoted value could run as code. `01e5c792`
gives the new meaning a new value, `no posix sh`, and reads the old `not posix` as unrecorded, so such a host gets the
`sh` wrapper without being onboarded again. See 893 for the cost (a no-`sh` device onboarded before #110 must be
onboarded again, and an older Runner reads the new value as POSIX).

**Lesson.** 845's, now built: one encoder in the one place commands are sent, an archtest that keeps every session
there, and a harness switch that runs the whole suite under another login shell (LESSONS 388).

## 859. sh-encoding a command dropped a NUL byte that sshd used to refuse, so /srv/app/.<NUL>./etc passed a Go ".." check and reached the device as /srv/app/../etc (CWE-158; a repeat in kind of 438, and of 317's NUL class) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, found by the fp-reviewer agent's review of `fix/shell-agnostic-ssh` before push. Before
`4a7db76d`, a command holding a NUL byte was refused by sshd. The new encoding writes a NUL as `\0000`, and `printf
%b` inside command substitution drops it (measured on dash, `bash --posix` and busybox ash), so the bytes on either
side of it were joined. A path such as `/srv/app/.<NUL>./etc` holds no `..` segment to a Go check, and would have
reached the device as `/srv/app/../etc`: path traversal through a null byte (CWE-158).

**Root cause.** The old channel's refusal was a property of sshd, not of any code in the platform, so nothing in the
platform knew it was relying on it. The encoding replaced the channel and its refusal went with it.

**Why 438 and 317 did not prevent it.** 438's lesson is that a guard decides on exactly the bytes the far side will
read. The path guards still decided on the bytes the platform meant to send; the change was below them, in how those
bytes became the bytes `sh` reads, and no one re-asked what that step could drop. 317 (and 371) are a NUL reaching a
format that treats it specially; each fixed its own boundary, and nothing lists the bytes a transport used to refuse.

**Fix.** `09acef1e`: `Conn.wire` refuses a command holding a NUL before anything is sent
(`TestConn_RefusesANULAndHoldsTheArgumentLimitExactly`); `TestFor_EveryByteReachesShAsItself` sends every byte from
1 to 255 through this machine's `sh` and holds each to itself. Submitted to vuln-corpus as `C13_auto-roboto_2026-11-03`
(pending review).

**Lesson.** When a new encoding replaces a channel that refused a byte, refuse that byte explicitly (LESSONS 387).

## 860. net.ssh.ping dialed through Runner.Run and skipped the device rule, so a Windows OpenSSH or network-CLI device got the sh-encoded line (a sibling of 757 and 823; LESSONS 244 and 363) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, review of `fix/shell-agnostic-ssh` before push. `4a7db76d` sent a command raw to a device
`inventory.ExecIsPOSIX` says is not POSIX, in `sdk.Connect` and the `ssh_exec` transport. `net.ssh.ping` opens its
connection through `Runner.Run`, not `sdk.Connect`, so it never asked, and sent its echo encoded for `sh` to a network
CLI or a Windows OpenSSH server, where no `/bin/sh` exists.

**Root cause.** The device rule was applied where `sdk.Connect` and the `ssh_exec` transport build a connection, not along every
route that opens one, and `net.ssh.ping` (which never pools) opens its own.

**Why 757, 823 and LESSONS 244 and 363 did not prevent it.** Each says a rule for a mechanism is checked along every
route a method can take to a device. The branch listed send sites, the places that build a command, and
not the routes that open a connection, so the third route was found by review rather than by the list.

**Fix.** `09acef1e`: `net.ssh.ping` follows `sdk.Connect`'s rule through `inventory.ExecIsPOSIX`
(`internal/catalog/net/ssh/ping.go`), proven by `TestPing_SendsANetworkCLITheEchoAsWritten`. A redialed detach stop
keeps a raw view raw.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 363's: list the routes to a device, not only the send sites that looked unsafe.

## 861. The 128 KiB line limit admitted 131072 bytes, which Linux refuses because the closing NUL counts, and Start checked it after opening a session, so a refused command tainted a pooled connection (LESSONS 121's boundary class; a repeat in kind of 105) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, review of `fix/shell-agnostic-ssh` before push. sshd passes the whole command line to the
login shell as one argument, and Linux refuses an argument of 128 KiB or more with its closing NUL counted
(`MAX_ARG_STRLEN`). `4a7db76d` refused a line over 131072 bytes, so a line of exactly 131072 passed the check and
failed on the device. `Conn.Start` checked the length only after opening a session, so a refused command tainted a
pooled connection for a command it never sent.

**Root cause.** The bound was written from the documented size, not measured at its edge. The check in `Start` sat
after the step it should have guarded, as 105's guard ran after the deletions it guarded.

**Why LESSONS 121 and 105 did not prevent it.** 121 says to prove a length limit at the last length that works and the
first that does not; `4a7db76d`'s test (`TestConn_RefusesALineOverOneArgumentBeforeSendingIt`) checked lines well over the limit
(a quarter of `MaxBytes` in quotes, each encoded to five bytes), never the edge. 105's lesson is about ordering a guard before
the writes; nothing ties it to a session a pool will mark tainted.

**Fix.** `09acef1e`: the limit is `>= shline.MaxBytes`, and `Conn.wire` runs before `openStream` in both `run` and
`Start`. `TestConn_RefusesANULAndHoldsTheArgumentLimitExactly` runs 131071 bytes and refuses 131072.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 121's: prove a limit at both sides of its edge; and refuse before taking anything a refusal
would leave marked.

## 862. The release gates' own verification helpers dialed their own SSH client and sent POSIX checks raw to the login shell, so they failed under fish, zsh and tcsh logins (a sibling of 858) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, the first `PLEIADES_TEST_LOGIN_SHELL` runs of `fix/shell-agnostic-ssh`.
`cmd/pleiades`'s `verifyOverSSH` and `cmd/runner`'s `readOverSSH` read a device's state "independently" of the
product, over an SSH client of their own, to check what a run did. They sent their POSIX checks as written: under
fish an `if` exited 127, under zsh an unmatched glob exited 124, and tcsh read
`2>/dev/null` as an argument.

**Root cause.** A helper that talks to a device is a send site, and these were outside `pkg/remoteexec`, so 858's
encoder did not reach them and the static audit of send sites, written against product code, did not list them.

**Fix.** `142d53bb`: both helpers send through `shline.For` (`cmd/pleiades/ssh_release_gate_test.go`,
`cmd/runner/external_collection_release_gate_test.go`). Found only by running the suites under fish, tcsh and zsh.

**Lesson.** A test helper that reads a device over its own client sends the way the product does (LESSONS 389).

## 863. testsupport.UseLoginShell counted installer warnings as accounts and could not install fish on Rocky (a sibling of 779's banner parse) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, switching the Debian and Rocky fixtures with `PLEIADES_TEST_LOGIN_SHELL`.
`testsupport.UseLoginShell` read each switched account's shell from the installer's whole output, so apt's debconf
notes, written even when quiet, were counted as accounts and the switch was judged to have failed. On Rocky, `dnf`
could not install fish, which only EPEL carries.

**Root cause.** The helper parsed every line of a command whose output it did not control, as 779's detached start
parsed all of stdout after a login banner.

**Fix.** `aeff581b` (`internal/testsupport/sshd.go`): each account's shell is printed on a marked line
(`shell:<path>`, read back from `getent passwd`), and only marked lines are read; `dnf` falls back to installing
`epel-release` first. The Debian devices, Rocky, the Docker and Podman engine hosts and every other switched fixture
pass under fish, tcsh and zsh.

**Lesson.** 779's: read a remote command's answer from a line it marked, never from all of its output.

## 864. A new test file used a helper from a file built only off Windows, so the package's tests did not compile for Windows (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-03, `make pr-check` on `fix/shell-agnostic-ssh`: the `pr-check-vet` step failed under `GOOS=windows` with `pkg/remoteexec/script_test.go: undefined: detachedServer`. Linux and macOS built and passed.

**Root cause.** `detachedServer` lives in `pkg/remoteexec/detach_test.go`, which carries `//go:build !windows` (its harness runs `/bin/sh`). The new `script_test.go` called it with no constraint of its own, so it built on Windows against a helper that did not.

**Why nothing caught it sooner.** Every local run was on Linux, and gopls reports the host's build only. The cross-OS vet step in pr-check is what exists to catch this, and did.

**Fix.** `script_test.go` carries the same `//go:build !windows` and says why.

**Lesson.** A test file that calls a helper inherits the helper's build constraint: check the helper's file header, or run `GOOS=windows go vet` on the package, before the gate.

## 865. internal/redact imported pkg/remoteexec/shline, breaking its standard-library-only rule, because only the new archtest had been run (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, `make pr-check` on `fix/shell-agnostic-ssh`: `internal/archtest`'s `TestRedactPackageDependsOnNothingButTheStandardLibrary` failed, `internal/redact` depending on `pkg/remoteexec/shline` (added in 09acef1e to mask a secret's encoded form).

**Root cause.** `internal/redact` is held to the standard library alone, so every process can mask without pulling in the module. The masker fix imported the encoder for one function. Locally only the branch's new archtest was run (`-run TestOnlyRemoteexecOpensAnSSHSession`), never the whole package, so the existing rule was not consulted.

**Fix.** `internal/redact/masker.go` keeps its own copy of the encoding (`shEncoded`), and `TestMasking_EncodedSecretsMatchShline` holds it equal to `shline.Encode` over every byte from 1 to 255.

**Lesson.** After adding an import to a package, run all of `internal/archtest`, not the one test the change adds; a layering rule elsewhere may already forbid it.

## 866. facts.gather's Windows files probe used Get-Item -Force, which throws ItemNotFoundException for C:\pagefile.sys, a file that exists, so a present file read as absent (a repeat of 818; LESSONS 379) (fixed before commit)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, building Phase 41c-2's `files` subset, measured on win-check (Windows Server 2025) through
pleiades. The first Windows probe read each path with `Get-Item -Force` and called a path absent on
`ItemNotFoundException`. For `C:\pagefile.sys`, which exists, `Get-Item -Force` throws that same exception, so the
probe could not tell a file that is absent from one it cannot reach, and a present file would have been stored as
`absent`.

**Root cause.** PowerShell's provider layer folds errors: it answers "not found" for a file it cannot open as well as
for one that is not there. The probe read that layer's answer as the system's.

**Why 818 and LESSONS 379 did not prevent it.** 818 fixed `exec.winrm.shell`'s guard to decide as Ansible's
`Test-AnsiblePath` does (`GetAttributes`, with only `FileNotFoundException` or `DirectoryNotFoundException` as absent),
and LESSONS 379 says an existence guard decides absent only when the platform says not found. The facts probe was
written fresh in another package, and `Get-Item` did say "not found", so it met 379's wording. 379 did not say that
the "not found" must come from the system itself and not from a layer above it.

**Fix.** `e84c0dc3` (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_win_items.go`): the probe reads `[IO.File]::GetAttributes`, and a
path is absent only when the innermost exception is `FileNotFoundException` or `DirectoryNotFoundException`; anything
else is `unreadable`. `TestCLI_FactsGatherOnWindowsMatchesItsOwnTools` gathers `C:\pagefile.sys` on win-check and
requires it present (with no digest), and `C:\nonexistent\x` absent.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 391: "absent" is a claim only the system's own not-found answer may make; decide from the innermost
error type, never from a layer that folds errors.

## 867. The files path check accepted //server/share, /\server\share, //?/UNC/..., //./pipe/... and //./PhysicalDrive0, which Windows reads as network or device paths, because the facts copy of windowsAbsolute was weaker than exec.winrm.shell's (a repeat of 821; LESSONS 244) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-41c-2` before push. Reasoned, not measured. `gatherFilePaths` accepted
any path starting with `/` as a POSIX path. Windows reads `/` as `\`, so `//server/share`, `/\server\share`,
`//?/UNC/...`, `//./pipe/...` and `//./PhysicalDrive0` would have reached a Windows device as a UNC path or a device
namespace path: a read of another machine through this one, or of a pipe or a raw disk. A device name such as `CON`,
`NUL` or `COM1` in any directory was also accepted.

**Root cause.** The facts package kept its own path check. It held Windows paths to a drive letter, but checked the
POSIX form only for a leading `/`, and so never asked what a Windows device does with a POSIX-looking path.

**Why 821 and LESSONS 244 did not prevent it.** 821 fixed `exec.winrm.shell`'s `windowsAbsolute`, refusing `\\?\`,
`\\.\` and odd server names. LESSONS 244 says that when one of two sibling paths carries a guard, check the other, and
move the guard into one helper both call. The facts check is a sibling that was written without reading 821's, and
the guard was not shared. The two still are not: `internal/catalog/facts/gather_files.go` and
`internal/catalog/exec/winrm/shell.go` each keep a `windowsAbsolute`, with different rules on purpose (the facts one
refuses every UNC path), and no test holds them together.

**Fix.** `ae4c5657`: a path starting with two separators of either kind is refused, a Windows device name (`CON`,
`PRN`, `AUX`, `NUL`, `CONIN$`, `CONOUT$`, `COM0` to `COM9`, `LPT0` to `LPT9`, the superscript digits too) is refused,
and once the device names its platform each path is held to that platform's own absolute form (`gatherFilesFor`).
Tests: `TestGatherFilePaths_RefusesWhatCannotBeReadSafely`, `TestGatherFilesFor_HoldsEachPathToTheDevicesOwnForm`,
`TestGather_RefusesAPathWrittenForTheOtherKindOfSystem`.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 244's: when a second check of the same kind of input is written, start from the first one's
refusals, and ask what the far side does with each form the check admits.

## 868. A stored, unkeyed SHA-256 and size of a task-named file would be readable by anyone with inventory:read, an offline guessing oracle for a small secret file (a repeat in kind of 829) (fixed before push; the keyed design is open)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-41c-2` before push. Security. The `files` subset stored a SHA-256 and a
size for every regular file the login could read. Facts are served to `inventory:read`, which a viewer holds. For a
small secret file (a password file, a key, a PIN), the digest lets anyone who can read the facts confirm guesses
offline, and the size narrows the guesses. Reasoned, not measured against an attacker.

**Root cause.** The roadmap item asked for "a digest and metadata" of each path. The design treated a digest as safe
because it is not the content, and did not ask who reads it or how small the input can be.

**Why 829 did not prevent it.** 829 kept a secret value out of the fact store by the run's known secrets, a secret key
name and a secret shape. A digest is none of those: the harm is derived from it, not carried in it, so no strip list
can catch it.

**Fix.** `ae4c5657`, by the owner's decision of 2026-11-04 to withhold now. A regular file is hashed only when it is
world-readable: on POSIX, its mode allows others to read and every directory above it allows others to search,
computed on the device in `sh` arithmetic; on Windows, its ACL allows read to Everyone, Authenticated Users or
BUILTIN\Users with no matching deny (`Get-Acl`). Any other file has no `sha256` and no `size`, carries
`digest: withheld`, and is never hashed on the device. Tests: `TestGather_FilesReportDigestsAndNeverCallUnreadableAbsent`
(a 0640 file, and a 0644 file inside a 0700 directory, both withheld), `TestCLI_FactsReleaseGate` (`/tmp/mine`, mode
0600, withheld), `TestCLI_FactsGatherOnFreeBSDMatchesItsOwnTools` (`/etc/master.passwd` withheld) and
`TestCLI_FactsGatherOnWindowsMatchesItsOwnTools` (`C:\pagefile.sys`, no digest).

**Open.** The owner's keyed hybrid is the next pull request: a plain digest for a world-readable file, an HMAC at the
store boundary for a restricted one, and the stats stripped in the engine (LESSONS 390: a fact is also a stat).

**Lesson.** A derived value (a digest, a size, a count) of a secret can be as sensitive as the secret when the input
is small; decide who reads the store before storing one.

## 869. /proc/net/udp lists an unbound UDP socket as 0.0.0.0:0 in state 07, which the Linux ports parser reported as a listener on port 0 (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, found by `FuzzGatherParsers` with seeds taken from the API model's output plus a new
invariant that a port is from 1 to 65535. The Linux parser read state `07` in `/proc/net/udp` as a bound UDP socket,
and an unbound one has local port 0 in that state, so it became `port.udp:0.0.0.0:0`. The kept failing input
(`internal/catalog/facts/testdata/fuzz/FuzzGatherParsers/c370165e73df7491`) is a TCP-table row in state `0A` with
local port 0, which the parser also passed.

**Root cause.** The parser checked the state column and not the port, and no test fed it a socket that is not bound.

**Fix.** `ae4c5657` (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_ports.go`): a row with local port 0 is no listener, whatever its
state. `FuzzGatherParsers` keeps the port-range invariant and the regression input.

**Lesson.** A fuzz target holds the parser to the output's own invariants (a port is 1 to 65535), not only to "does
not panic"; that is what found this.

## 870. FreeBSD sockstat prints one line per (process, descriptor), so a listener held by N workers became port...:80, port...:80#2, #3, churning with the worker count (a repeat of 849) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-41c-2` before push. A web server with several workers sharing one
listening socket printed one `sockstat -46lq` line per worker, and the parser made each a fact, told apart by `#n`. The
number of facts moved as workers came and went, so drift would have shown a listener appear and vanish with no change
to what was listening.

**Root cause.** The parser took sockstat's lines as sockets. A line is a (process, descriptor) pair, and one socket
has as many as there are processes holding it.

**Why 849 did not prevent it.** 849 made names distinct across every probe of a run with `:arch`, `@source` and `#n`.
That suffix keeps two items apart; it does not decide whether two lines are two items, and here they were one.

**Fix.** `ae4c5657` (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_bsd_more.go`): one fact per socket, its process named by the lowest
pid. `TestParseSockstat_ReadsFreeBSDsListeners`.

**Lesson.** Before naming items apart, decide what one item is; a suffix that keeps a key unique also hides a
duplicate that should have been merged.

## 871. macOS netstat -anv cuts an IPv6 address to its column width, so a listener's address was stored truncated (a sibling in kind of 606) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, measured on the lab Mac (macOS 27.0.1). `netstat -anv` printed a local IPv6 address cut to its
column, as `2601:84:ca01:103.56230`, so the key held an address the host does not have.

**Root cause.** The probe read a tool's display output, whose columns have a fixed width, and nothing checked that a
value fit its column. 606's class: a terminal or display width rewrote what the reader expected.

**Fix.** `ae4c5657`: the probe runs `netstat -anvl`, which prints the address whole (measured on the lab Mac), and
names a process only from a `name:pid` field. `TestParseDarwinNetstat_ReadsTheProcessBetweenFixedColumns`.

**Lesson.** A parser of a tool's column output checks the value it takes against the form it must have, and the probe
asks the tool for its unabridged form.

## 872. Linux /proc/net byte order was guessed from uname -m, which cannot tell little-endian from big-endian MIPS (a repeat of LESSONS 343) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-41c-2` before push. Reasoned. `/proc/net/tcp` prints addresses in the
host's byte order. The probe chose the order from `uname -m`, and `mips` names both orders, so on one of them every
address would have been read backwards.

**Root cause.** The machine name stood in for the property the parser needed.

**Why LESSONS 343 did not prevent it.** 343 says detect a capability by asking for it, never by a proxy. It was
written about test helpers and check scripts, and nothing applied it to a probe's own guess at the device.

**Fix.** `ae4c5657` (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_ports.go`): the probe asks the device,
`printf '\001\000' | od -An -tx2`, which prints `0001` on a little-endian host and `0100` on a big-endian one (measured
on Alpine, Debian, Rocky and macOS); `uname -m` is only the fallback. `TestParseLinuxPorts_ReadsTheKernelsTablesInItsByteOrder`.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 343's: ask the device for the property, here its byte order, rather than infer it from a name.

## 873. The Windows files, ports and users scripts failed the whole task on a host lacking Get-LocalUser or the TCP/IP cmdlets, and [IO.File]::GetAccessControl does not exist in PowerShell 7, while their comments said every script read what any host has (a repeat of 789) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-41c-2` before push, found by a second model given the code; reasoned,
not measured. The scripts ran under `$ErrorActionPreference='Stop'`, so a host without `Get-LocalUser` or without the
`Get-NetTCPConnection` and `Get-NetUDPEndpoint` cmdlets failed the whole gather, not one subset. The files script read
ACLs through `[IO.File]::GetAccessControl`, which PowerShell 7 does not have, so under it the owner was lost and, once
868's rule was in, every file read as not world-readable and was withheld. Comments claimed every script read only
what any host has.

**Root cause.** The scripts were written against the lab's Windows Server and its Windows PowerShell, and the comments
stated a rule nothing checked.

**Why 789 did not prevent it.** 789's lesson is that a change corrects the sentence it makes false; its rule is a review,
and here the comments were false from the first commit, written as an intention.

**Fix.** `ae4c5657` (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_win_items.go`): each cmdlet a host may lack is guarded by
`Get-Command`, ACLs are read through `Get-Acl` (PowerShell 5.1 and 7), and the network cmdlets tolerate only an
`ObjectNotFound` error. The comments say what the scripts now do. Proven on win-check by
`TestCLI_FactsGatherOnWindowsMatchesItsOwnTools`.

**Lesson.** A script that claims to run on any host is written against the oldest and the newest interpreter it can
meet, and each optional command is guarded where it is called.

## 874. Windows [IO.File]::OpenRead asks FileShare.Read, so a file open for writing elsewhere read unreadable until the writer closed it, drift on an unchanged file (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-41c-2` before push. Reasoned. The files script hashed with
`[IO.File]::OpenRead`, which opens with `FileShare.Read`. A file another process holds open for writing (a log) refuses
that, so it read as `unreadable`, then as present once the writer closed it: drift with no change to the file.

**Root cause.** `OpenRead`'s sharing mode is the default for a reader that wants no one to write under it, not for an
observer.

**Fix.** `ae4c5657`: the script opens with `[IO.File]::Open(..., 'ReadWrite, Delete')` sharing, so a writer or a
deleter does not block the read.

**Lesson.** An observer opens a file with the widest sharing mode the platform allows, so the observation does not
depend on what else has the file open.

## 875. The Linux ports probe printed whole socket tables and every descriptor link, so a busy server would pass the 64 MiB output limit (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-41c-2` before push. Reasoned. The probe printed every row of
`/proc/net/tcp`, `tcp6`, `udp` and `udp6`, and `ls -l` of every process's descriptors, and parsed them in Go. On a busy
server with many connections and open files that output would pass the transport's 64 MiB limit, and the subset would
fail where it is most wanted.

**Root cause.** The probe moved the filtering to the platform side, so output grew with connections rather than with
listeners.

**Fix.** `ae4c5657` (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_ports.go`): the device keeps only rows in state `0A` or `07` and
only `socket:` links (`grep` on the device), so the output grows with listeners.

**Lesson.** A probe filters on the device to what it will keep, so its output is bounded by the answer, not by how
busy the device is.

## 876. An IPv6 zone index (Windows %4) in a port key moved when an adapter was added, renaming an unchanged listener (a sibling of 870) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-41c-2` before push. A listener on a link-local address carries a zone,
`%4` on Windows (the interface index). The key kept it, so adding an adapter that renumbered the interfaces renamed the
listener: one fact gone and another new, with nothing changed in what listened.

**Root cause.** 870's: a fact's key held a value that moves with something other than the item.

**Fix.** `ae4c5657` (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_ports.go`): the zone is cut from the address in the key and kept in
the value.

**Lesson.** A fact key holds only what names the item; anything that moves with the host's state goes in the value.

## 877. The new tests repeated old test-quality classes: lab gates compared UDP counts read at different moments and waited with a fixed sleep, password asserts could not fail, the fact key bound was copied with no equality test, a filter dropping every path gathered nothing silently, and a malformed stat line was accepted (a repeat of 788, 211 and 422; LESSONS 136 and 134) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-41c-2` before push.
- The lab gates compared the gather's count of ports with a count read at another moment, UDP included, and a UDP
  endpoint can open or close between the two reads; the release gate started a listener and slept one second.
- Asserts that a user fact carries no `password` key could not fail, because no parser ever wrote such a key.
- `gatherMaxFileKeyBytes` copied `internal/facts.MaxKeyBytes` with no test holding the two equal.
- A `filter` that dropped every named path gathered nothing and succeeded.
- A stat line with a non-numeric size, a negative id or a mode wider than 12 bits was accepted.

**Root cause.** Each is a class already recorded: a count taken twice and a fixed sleep (211, 422, 788), a test that
cannot fail against its defect (LESSONS 136), and a copied value with no comparing test (LESSONS 134).

**Why the earlier fixes did not hold.** Each lives as a lesson or in the test it fixed; the new gates were written
fresh and not read against them before review.

**Fix.** `ae4c5657`. The lab gates count TCP listeners only. The release gate waits for the listener in the kernel's own
table (`/proc/net/tcp`, port 7070 as `1B9E`), not a sleep. The password checks hold the probe text, which passes the
password field through `cut -d: -f1,3-` so it never leaves the device (`TestUserProbes_NeverCarryThePasswordField`).
The bound is `collection.MaxFactKeyBytes`, held equal to the store's by `TestFactCaps_AgreeAcrossTheBoundary`. A
filter that drops every named path is refused. `parseFileSection` refuses a stat line whose numbers do not parse in
range (`TestParseFileSection_ReadsEachStatAndTellsUnreadableFromAbsent`).

**Lesson.** Before review, read each new test against the test-quality titles in this file: a test written fresh
repeats the old classes unless someone looks.

## 878. A Runner counted the dispatched credential's username as a secret, so every fact naming the login was refused on the Walk tier (a repeat of 120; 394's identifier allowlist lived on the CLI only, and 829's fix carried the gap into the fact guard) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, found by the new Walk gate on `feat/facts-keyed-digest`
(`TestFactsReleaseGate_APrivateFilesDigestIsStoredOnlyKeyed`). On a Runner every fact that named the login was refused
as "its value holds a secret of this run": the login's own `user.<name>`, any file it owns, and with a root login
nearly every file fact. A short username was also scrubbed out of paths in the job's output. It shipped with PR #111
(41c-2), whose `users` and `files` subsets are the first facts to name the login.

**Root cause.** `childSecretValues` (`internal/adapters/native/ipc_parent.go`, since `9e7c455a`) counted every value of
the dispatched credential as secret through `redact.MapValues`: the username, a certificate's public half and a seeded
login's identifiers as well as the password and keys. The CLI's `credentialSecrets` leaves those identifiers out (394),
because a substring scrub of a short name such as `root` corrupts every path holding it. 829's fix
(`5763c04f`) fed the same list, through `dispatchSecrets`, to the executor's fact guard, so over-masking in output
became refusal of facts.

**Why 120, 394 and 829 did not prevent it.** 120 fixed the class for injected credential types (`wire.Injected.Mask`),
not for the device credential a native method is handed. 394 wrote the allowlist into the CLI path and said the Walk
tier "was not affected", which was true of the leak it fixed and said nothing of over-masking. 829 reused the Runner's
existing list without asking what it held. One rule lived in two copies with no test holding them equal.

**Fix.** `98005436`: `engine.CredentialSecrets` is exported and the Runner's `childSecretValues` calls it, so both
tiers count a credential the same way; the password and keys stay masked. `container_exec_walk_test.go` had encoded
the old masking of the username and was updated. Proven by the Walk gate above, which stores a file fact on a real
Runner. Residual: `internal/loader` and the legacy adapter still mask the username, which is stricter, so the tiers
still differ for external Collections; `pkg/netconf` keeps its own copy of the identifier allowlist.

**Lesson.** A rule about which values are secret is one function every tier calls. When a fix says another tier "was
not affected", check that the other tier does the same thing, not only that it leaks nothing.

## 879. The Runner invoker path returned before the digest rewrite, which a mapper's report said one call point covered on both tiers (a sibling of 860; LESSONS 244 and 363) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, while building `feat/facts-keyed-digest`. A raw digest (`sha256_raw`) a Runner's child handed
back was not sealed: the rewrite never ran on that path. `facts.Prepare`'s scrub dropped the raw value before it was
stored, so nothing leaked; the digest was lost instead of kept.

**Root cause.** The collection executor has two invoker paths. The Runner's child path returns early
(`internal/engine/collection_action.go`), before the line after `collector.Facts()` where the rewrite was first
placed. A go-mapper report had said that one point covered both tiers, and the code was written to that claim.

**Fix.** In `3e6bb38c`, `digestsOf` runs on each path, on failure as on success (`collection_action.go`, the child path
and the in-process path), and in `70d3032b` the executor scrubs every node's stats (`scrubResultDigests`). Proven by
`TestFactDigests_AChildsRawDigestIsHandledToo` and the other `TestFactDigests_*` tests in
`internal/engine/fact_digests_test.go`, which run a real Executor on both paths; removing the rewrite fails three of
them.

**Lesson.** See LESSONS 393: a map of where code runs is a hypothesis until each path it names has its own test.

## 880. A session script that copied a method's Doc into catalogdata cut the Go literal at the wrong closing brace, twice, leaving a file that did not compile (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04. Syncing `facts.gather`'s documentation into
`internal/forge/catalogdata/collections_gating.go` left the file unable to compile. It happened once on
`feat/facts-41c-2` and again on this branch.

**Root cause.** The script, kept outside the repository, found the end of the `Doc` literal by counting braces and
did not skip braces inside string literals. The documentation text holds braces, so it stopped early.

**Fix.** String-aware brace matching in the script. The build caught both cases before any commit, so no broken file
was committed.

**Lesson.** A script that edits Go source by position must read Go's own syntax (strings, runes, comments), or use
`go/parser`; counting a delimiter in text that may quote it fails on the first quoted one. When the same tool fails a
second time, record it rather than fixing it quietly again.

## 881. The Controller read PLEIADES_FACTS_DIGEST_KEY after it had bound its listener and migrated the database (a repeat of 297; LESSONS 216) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, fp-reviewer pass over `feat/facts-keyed-digest`. A malformed `PLEIADES_FACTS_DIGEST_KEY`
stopped the Controller only after it had bound its port and migrated its database.

**Root cause.** 297's class: a configuration value checked where it is used, not where it is read. The new key was
read beside the facts consumer it feeds, which `cmd/controller/main.go` builds late.

**Why 297 did not prevent it.** 297 moved one variable (`NATS_URL`); LESSONS 216 states the rule, and nothing checks a
new variable against it.

**Fix.** `70d3032b`: `loadFactDigestKeys` (`cmd/controller/fact_digest_keys.go`) runs before the Controller binds or
migrates. Proven by `TestFactDigestKeyReleaseGate_AMalformedKeyStopsTheControllerFirst`, which starts the real
binary with a malformed key and asserts exit 1, no database file and no listener.

**Lesson.** Every new environment variable a composition root reads is checked before the first side effect, with a
test that asserts what had not happened yet.

## 882. The chart's existingSecret path could not deliver the new digest key, so two combinations rendered a controller that would not start (a repeat in kind of 234) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-keyed-digest`. With `secrets.existingSecret` set, `secrets.factsDigestKey`
was never written anywhere the controller reads, and `secrets.existingSecretHasFactsDigestKey: true` without an
`existingSecret` made the deployment read a key from the chart's own Secret that it did not hold.

**Root cause.** 234's class: the chart's `existingSecret` branch is a second path for every secret, and the new value
was wired through one path only.

**Fix.** `70d3032b`: `helm/the-pleiades/templates/_validations.tpl` refuses `factsDigestKey` together with
`existingSecret`, and `existingSecretHasFactsDigestKey` without one, each with a message naming the setting to use.
`21e07e95` adds both to `tools/helm-lint`'s refusal profiles (`profiles.go`), each held to its message; disabling
one makes `make helm-lint` fail on exactly that case (negative control run 2026-11-04).

**Lesson.** A new chart secret is checked against each combination of `existingSecret` and its own flag, and each
refusal joins `tools/helm-lint`'s refusal profiles.

## 883. A digest the store could not keep was dropped without a word, in the engine and in the Controller (a sibling of 853) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-keyed-digest`. An executor told neither a keyer nor a sealer, and a
Controller without `PLEIADES_FACTS_DIGEST_KEY` or holding a sealed digest that would not open, dropped the digest and
reported success with nothing said, so an operator could not tell a private file with no digest from a missing
configuration.

**Root cause.** 853's class: a bound or a refusal applied by dropping data while the task succeeds.

**Fix.** `70d3032b`: every loss is said. On the CLI and a Runner the task carries a warning naming the fact, never the
value (`appendWarning`, `internal/engine/fact_digests.go`); the Controller logs a warning per batch by fact, logs its
key's identity at start (`loadFactDigestKeys`), and a Runner logs a seal key that will not parse
(`internal/adapters/native/fact_seal.go`). Proven by `TestFactDigests_AnExecutorToldNeitherDropsThem` and
`TestSubscriber_WithoutKeysStoresTheFactWithoutItsDigest`.

**Lesson.** A fail-closed drop is right; a silent one is not. Each drop names what it dropped where the operator reads.

## 884. The raw-digest scrub looked only at the top level of a fact, a typed in-process value skipped it, and the store trusted the sender to leave out a private file's plain digest (a repeat in kind of 696; LESSONS 350) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, the fp-reviewer pass and two independent diff reviews of `feat/facts-keyed-digest`. Three
gaps in one guard: `facts.ScrubDigests` dropped `sha256_raw` only at the top level of a fact's value, so one nested
deeper survived; a value an in-process method returned as a Go type rather than a `map[string]any` was not walked; and
the store kept a plain `sha256` or `size` of an object marked `world_readable: false` if a sender put one there.

**Root cause.** 696's class: a strip list applied to the top level only. The third gap assumed the producer is honest,
where the store must hold its own rule.

**Fix.** `70d3032b`: `facts.ScrubDigests` (run in `Prepare`) drops a raw digest at any depth and inside typed values,
drops a sealed one except at a sealing Runner's top level, and drops a plain `sha256` and `size` of any
`world_readable: false` object whoever sent it; the executor scrubs every node's stats (`scrubResultDigests`). Proven
by `TestScrubDigests_NoRawDigestAtAnyDepthAndNoPlainOneOfAPrivateFile`,
`TestFactDigests_ARawDigestDeeperInAValueIsDropped`, `TestFactDigests_NoExecutorsResultKeepsARawDigest` and
`TestSubscriber_NeverStoresARawDigest`.

**Lesson.** A guard over data walks the whole value in every shape it can arrive in, and a store holds its own
invariants rather than trusting what the sender left out.

## 885. A sealed digest bound its device and fact but not its job, so one could be replayed into a later job, and a NUL in a bound field was accepted (the NUL class of 317 and 859) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, an independent diff review of `feat/facts-keyed-digest`. A sealed digest captured from one
job's batch could be placed in a later job's batch for the same device and fact, so a changed private file would read
as unchanged. A NUL in the job, device or fact field could make two different bindings encode the same way.

**Root cause.** The binding named what the digest is of, not when it was taken. The binding fields were joined without
refusing the separator.

**Fix.** `70d3032b`: `facts.SealPlaintext` binds job, device and fact, the Controller checks all three against the
batch before keying, and a NUL in any bound field is refused. Proven by
`TestSealPlaintext_BindsTheDigestToItsJobFactAndDevice`, `TestFactSealing_SealsToTheDispatchKeyBoundToItsJob`, and the
Walk gate, whose device ID and name differ (888).

**Lesson.** A sealed value carries everything that makes it valid in one place and time; a binding of "what" without
"when" is replayable.

## 886. Text the branch made false still said a private file's digest is "withheld" (a repeat of 789) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-keyed-digest`. After a private file's digest became keyed, text from
41c-2 still said it is withheld: in `facts.gather`'s documentation and generated reference, a changelog fragment, the
Windows probe's comments and the production guide.

**Root cause.** 789's class: a behavior change not followed through every sentence that described the old behavior.

**Why 789 did not prevent it.** Its lesson is to search for the old words after a change; the search was not run before
review.

**Fix.** `70d3032b`: `changelog/facts-files-ports-users.added.md`, `internal/catalog/facts/gather.go`,
`gather_win_items.go`, `internal/forge/catalogdata/collections_gating.go` and the generated reference were corrected,
and the production guide's section "Digests of files only some may read" stands on its own.

**Lesson.** When a change replaces a word that names a behavior (here "withheld"), search the tree for it before review.

## 887. pleiades seal offered the fact-digest purpose, which only a Runner can use, so a hand-sealed value could only fail (a repeat in kind of 221) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-keyed-digest`. `pleiades seal --purpose fact-digest` sealed a value the
Controller would never accept, since a sealed digest must carry a job, device and fact binding the command cannot
supply.

**Root cause.** 221's class: an interface offered a choice the receiving side always refuses. The new purpose was added
to `internal/sealed` and the command accepted every purpose the package knows.

**Fix.** `70d3032b`: `cmd/pleiades/seal.go` refuses `--purpose fact-digest` and names the purpose to use instead
(`seal_test.go`, case "a runner's fact digest").

**Lesson.** A new value in a shared vocabulary is checked against each place that offers the vocabulary to a person.

## 888. The branch's tests repeated old test-quality classes: the Controller's digest wiring was untested, gates checked a digest's shape and not its value or a change, a purpose check could not fail, and the Walk gate used one string for device ID and name (a repeat of 467; LESSONS 235, 351 and 381) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, review of `feat/facts-keyed-digest`.
- `cmd/controller/main.go` wired the digest keys into the Worker and the facts consumer by hand, and no test held
  that wiring.
- The CLI and lab gates asserted that a private file's fact carried `hmac_sha256` and `hmac_key`, not that the value
  was the right HMAC or that a change gave a new one.
- A store test's purpose check passed for a reason other than the purpose: its device did not match, so the binding
  check refused first.
- The Walk gate used one string as the device's ID and its name, so a check on the wrong one could not be told apart.

**Root cause.** Classes already recorded: asserting what was left alone rather than what was produced (467), a test
that cannot fail against its defect (LESSONS 235), and a composition root's options with no test (LESSONS 351 and 381).

**Why the earlier fixes did not hold.** As in 877: each lives as a lesson, and new tests were not read against them
before review.

**Fix.** `70d3032b`. The wiring is one helper, `factDigestOptions`, which `main` and
`TestFactDigestOptions_KeyWhatARunnerSealedThroughTheConsumerMainBuilds` both use. `TestCLI_FactsReleaseGate` holds
the stored value to the project key's HMAC of the real content, stable over two gathers and new after a change; the
FreeBSD, macOS and Windows lab gates check the keyed shape and that a change shows, all passing 2026-11-04. The
purpose test's device now matches, so only the purpose can refuse it (negative-controlled). The Walk gate
(`TestFactsReleaseGate_APrivateFilesDigestIsStoredOnlyKeyed`) gives the device an ID and a name that differ, and
asserts the stored value equals the Controller's HMAC of the real digest and that no row holds the raw.

**Lesson.** Read new tests against the test-quality titles before review (877's lesson, repeated): a digest test
checks the value against an independent computation and checks that a change shows.

## 889. The engine's result scrub wrote into an action's stats map, which an executor may share across the devices it runs on at once (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** `make pr-check`'s fast pass, run under `-race`, failed `TestExecutor_DeviceFanOut` and
`TestWithin_ResolvesOnlyNamesInsideTheBound` in `internal/engine` with "race detected during execution of test"; the
first failed again when re-run alone. Every earlier run of the package on this branch passed, because they ran
without `-race`.

**Root cause.** `70d3032b` added `scrubResultDigests` (`internal/engine/fact_digests.go`), called on every node's
`actionResult.Stats` in `executor.go`, and it wrote each scrubbed value back into that map. An executor may return
one map to every device of a fan-out (a test executor returning a literal it built once, and nothing forbids a real
one), so each device's goroutine wrote into the same map. The scrub was added late, from review finding D3, and
only the digest tests were rerun, without `-race`.

**Fix.** `scrubResultDigests` builds and returns a new map and never writes to the one it was given. The two tests
pass three times under `-race`, and so does the whole package.

**Lesson.** A function the engine calls on an executor's result treats that result as shared and read-only: build a
new value rather than write into it. Rerun a package under `-race` after any change to code the executor calls per
device, however small.

## 890. TestJournalAdmitsOnlyDeclaredKeys planted "0644", a value the entry's random hex IDs can spell, so it failed main by chance with nothing leaked (a repeat of 236) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, main's post-merge run after PR #111 (merged as `f19fa172`), Actions run 41876826581, job
`fast`, on Linux: `internal/engine.TestJournalAdmitsOnlyDeclaredKeys` failed with `journal_entry_test.go:423: the
journal entry carries "0644"; no value a device, a credential store, a decrypted envelope, or an injector produced may
reach it`. Nothing had leaked. The test and its planted value date from `533d0b9d` (2026-09-12, Phase 40's run
journal) and had passed until then.

**Root cause.** `assertNoValueLeaked` (`internal/engine/journal_entry_test.go`) joins the entry's fields into one text
and does a substring search for each planted value. The planted stat value `"0644"` is all hex digits, and the entry
carries a random hex run ID and DAG version, so `0644` turns up in them by chance: a four-digit run is 1 in 65,536 at
each position, roughly a few in a thousand per run over the entry's random fields. The assertion of absence was over
text that holds random identifiers, and the planted value was possible in their alphabet.

**Why 236's fix did not hold.** 236 was the same class: a substring check for a value was refuted by text that spelled
the value without depending on it. Its fix changed the one fuzz property in `internal/setup` to a differential check,
and the rule became LESSONS 195 (prove independence, not absence) and, for the journal's own fuzz target, LESSONS 172
(an empty-input baseline as the control). Neither reached this example test, which was written on the same day as
LESSONS 172 with a plain substring search, and nothing checked what a planted value could collide with. A baseline
would not have helped here either, since a random ID is new on every run.

**Fix.** `43942bd8` (branch `fix/journal-test-planted-values`, not yet merged). The test plants
`"planted-mode-rw-r--r--"`, and `assertNoValueLeaked` now fails the test at once (`t.Fatalf`) for any planted value
made only of hex digits and dashes, before it searches. Negative control: putting `"0644"` back makes the test refuse
at once with `planted value "0644" could appear in a random hex ID`. `TestJournal*` passed three times.

**Lesson.** An assertion that a planted value is absent from text holding random identifiers plants a value those
identifiers' alphabet cannot spell, and the helper refuses one that could. CI_LESSONS 25.

## 891. pkg/remoteexec returned a cancelled SSH command as a completed one: partial output with no error, or exit 143, and a context already done still sent the command (a sibling of 774; a repeat in kind of 352, of 149's fix and of 859) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, from the Batch sweep of merged code (`.IGNORE/claude-api/out/sweep-2026-11-04/VERDICTS-ssh.md`),
then measured against the real OpenSSH sshd container on branch `fix/ssh-sweep-2026-11-04`:
- a cancelled `echo started; sleep 30` returned `Stdout` "started" with a nil error;
- a cancelled `RunWithStdin` returned `ExitCode` 143 with a nil error;
- a context already done still sent the command (the test's marker file was written).

The same commit found three more on the same path:
- a failed read of standard input was sent to the device as a clean end of input, so `cat > f` wrote a prefix of the
  file and reported 0;
- `RunWithStdin`'s deferred wait on its stdin copy could wait forever on a copy blocked on an SSH window the remote
  stopped granting;
- the detached (async) path never reached `Conn.wire`, so it skipped the NUL refusal.

**Root cause.** `waitOrAbandon` (`pkg/remoteexec/conn.go`) returned whatever status sshd reported after the
watcher's SIGTERM and session close, and `run` read it as an ordinary result: a nil error became success, an
`ExitError` became a finished command with that exit code. Nothing checked the context before `NewSession` or
`Start`, and neither takes a context. The stdin copy's error was dropped whole, a read error included. The NUL check
lived in `wire`, which the detached branch does not call.

**Why the earlier fixes did not hold.**
- 774 bounded the wait after a cancel (`abandonGrace`) but kept reporting the status that came back, so a status sshd
  sent after the signal still read as the command's own.
- 149's fix dropped the stdin copy's error on purpose, because a remote that stops reading has finished. That reason
  covers a write error only. A read error from the local source is a different event, and it was dropped with it.
- 352 bounded the handshake (`closeOnDone`), not the session open and exec start after it, which were left with no
  guard.
- 859 put the NUL refusal in `wire`, the one place it was believed every command passes; the detached branch is a
  second route that does not.

**Fix.** `a50bc048`. `cancelWatch` (`pkg/remoteexec/conn_watch.go`) starts before `NewSession`; when the context ends
it sends SIGTERM, closes the session, and after `abandonGrace` closes the connection chain, which ends a session open,
a Wait and a blocked stdin copy that a session close alone does not. A run the watch fired on returns the context's
