error and no `Result`. A done context sends nothing. `stdinSource` stops the command and fails the call on a read
error. `refuseNUL` runs before the detached branch. Tests, each failing on the old code:
`TestSSHContainer_ACancelledCommandIsNotACompletedOne`, `TestSSHContainer_ACancelledInputIsNotReportedAsCompleted`
and `TestSSHContainer_AContextAlreadyDoneRunsNothing` (`internal/transport/ssh/ssh_cancel_container_test.go`, real
sshd), and `pkg/remoteexec/conn_cancel_test.go` (`TestRun_AContextAlreadyDoneSendsNothing`,
`TestRunWithStdin_AFailedReadIsNotAnEndOfInput`, `TestRunWithStdin_ACopyTheRemoteStoppedGrantingIsBounded`,
`TestRun_ASilentConnectionCannotHoldASessionOpen`, `TestRun_ADetachedCommandHoldingANULIsRefused`). `72474f70` added
`TestRun_AContextEndingWhileTheSessionOpensIsACancellation` and `TestRun_AConnectionDroppedMidCommandIsAnErrorNotAStatus`.

**How it was nearly missed.** The first two tests of the cancel were written against the in-process SSH server and
passed on the old code. `x/crypto/ssh`'s server answers a channel CLOSE at once and drops any status sent after it,
so it never shows what OpenSSH shows. They were replaced by the real-sshd tests (LESSONS 396).

**Open.** `pkg/remoteexec/stream.go` (`Conn.Start`, `Process`, subsystems) has the same cancelled-as-completed shape
(fp-reviewer finding F4), carried to the next SSH pull request.

**Resolution of the open part (2026-11-05, branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`).** `bd9fc13b` gives the streamed path `run`'s
cancel watch, and `987603a2` makes its test count the exec requests sent after the context ended. See 896.

**Lesson.** After a cancel, the context's error is the answer, whatever the server sends next: a status that arrives
after the client asked the command to stop is not the command's result. When a guard lives in one function, list the
routes that skip it (here the detached branch), as LESSONS 363 says.

## 892. sdk.Connect, ConnectPort and ConnectFresh ignored the device's route, so a Collection method dialed a device behind a bastion directly, and so did net.ssh.ping (a sibling of 860; LESSONS 244 and 363) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, from the Batch sweep of merged code. A device with a `route` of SSH hops was reached
through the bastion by `ssh_exec`, but every Collection method built on `sdk.Connect`, `sdk.ConnectPort` or
`sdk.ConnectFresh`, and `net.ssh.ping`, dialed the device's own address. `TestCLI_ACollectionMethodReachesARoutedDeviceThroughItsBastion`
(`cmd/pleiades/route_collection_test.go`), with the target known only by its container name on the bastion's
Docker network, failed on the old code with `lookup ... no such host`.

**Root cause.** The engine already resolved the route and handed the method a dialer through it (`sdk.Router`'s
`RouteDial`); `sdk`'s connect never read it. `net.ssh.ping` opens its own connection and did not read it either.

**Why 860 and LESSONS 244 and 363 did not prevent it.** 860 found that `net.ssh.ping` took a different route from
`sdk.Connect` and missed the device rule, and fixed that one rule on that one route. The route of hops is a second
rule with the same two routes, and nobody asked of it the question 860 asked of the shell rule. LESSONS 363 says to
check a rule along every route to a device; it was applied per rule as each was found, not to the list of rules a
connection must follow.

**Fix.** `9ca3ef7c`: `remoteexec.Runner.ConnectVia` opens a connection through a given dialer, checking the target's
host key against known_hosts as a direct connection does, and `sdk`'s connect uses it for a routed device, unpooled
(the pool dials directly). `bd004d1e`: `net.ssh.ping` goes through the route too. Tests:
`TestCLI_ACollectionMethodReachesARoutedDeviceThroughItsBastion` (real binary, two sshd containers; an unknown target
key is refused through the route), `TestConnect_DialsARoutedDeviceThroughItsRoute` (`pkg/sdk`),
`TestPing_ARoutedDeviceIsPingedThroughItsRoute` (`internal/catalog/net/ssh`), and the `TestConnectVia_*` tests in
`pkg/remoteexec/connectvia_test.go`.

**Open.** Crawl tier only. A Runner, an external Collection and the onboarding SSH probe still dial the device's
address directly; `docs/11-extending-pleiades.md` and `changelog/ssh-cancel-route-legacy-shell.security.md` say so.

**Lesson.** For each way a connection is opened, list every rule a connection must follow (route, shell, host key,
pool key) and check each one, not only the rule that brought you there.

## 893. inventory.NotPOSIX kept the stored string "not posix" when #110 changed what it meant, so a fish or tcsh host onboarded before #110 had its commands sent raw to fish, where a quoted value is not a boundary (the open half of 858) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, from the Batch sweep of merged code. Before #110 (`4a7db76d`, FAILURE_PATTERNS 858),
onboarding recorded `shell: not posix` for a device whose login shell was not POSIX, such as fish or tcsh on a host
that has `/bin/sh`. #110 kept the same string but made it mean "this device has no POSIX sh", which sends commands raw.
So a fish host onboarded before #110 had every command sent raw to fish. `QuoteArg` is not an injection boundary in
fish, which reads a backslash inside single quotes, so a quoted value could end its quote and run as the login.

**Root cause.** A persisted value kept its spelling while its meaning changed, and a record carries no probe version,
so the reader could not tell an old record from a new one. 858 recorded the stale-record half as open and left it to
the user to onboard again (its changelog said so), which nothing enforced.

**Fix.** `01e5c792`. The new meaning has a new value, `no posix sh` (`pkg/inventory/execshell.go`), which the probe
records; the old value `not posix` is read as nothing recorded, so such a device gets the `sh` wrapper.
`TestExecIsPOSIX_OnlyANetworkCLIOrAProvedNonPOSIXShellIsNot` (`pkg/inventory/execshell_test.go`) holds both values.
`CLAUDE.md` names the new value.

**Consequences, stated in the changelog fragment.** A device with no `sh` (a Windows OpenSSH server, a router or
appliance added as `generic_ssh`) onboarded before #110 now fails at `/bin/sh` until it is onboarded again. A Runner
older than this release reads the new value as POSIX and fails the same way on such a device until it is upgraded.
Both fail closed: a command fails rather than runs where it should not.

**Lesson.** Never change the meaning of a persisted value in place. Give the new meaning a new value, and read the old
one by its old meaning or as unrecorded (LESSONS 397).

## 894. ConnectVia's first version claimed a routed target's breaker probe and the route's own dial claimed it again, so after one cooldown the circuit reopened on its own refusal and a routed device stayed refused for good (a repeat of 146 and 398) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, found by the fp-reviewer agent on `fix/ssh-sweep-2026-11-04` before the pull request.
`ConnectVia` as written in `9ca3ef7c` dialed through `dialChain` and `dialWithRetry`, which claim the target
address's half-open probe with `Allow`. The route's own dialer (`DialThroughHops`' `dialFinalLegWithRetry`, on the
same shared Runner and the same address key) claimed it again. After a cooldown, the outer claim took the probe, the
inner one saw it in flight and refused, and that refusal was recorded as a failure, which reopened the circuit. Every
cooldown repeated it, so a routed device that once had five failures was never dialed again.
`TestConnectVia_ARoutedTargetsCircuitRecovers` (`pkg/remoteexec/connectvia_test.go`) failed on `72474f70`.

**Root cause.** Two layers on one dial path each guarded the same address with the same breaker: 146's shape exactly,
reached through a new caller.

**Why 146 and 398 did not hold.** 146 split `Permitted` (look) from `Allow` (claim) so that only the code about to
dial claims. Here both layers were code about to dial, each through its own retry loop. 398 leased the probe so a
lost one is reissued after a cooldown; but this probe was not lost, it was held by the same call's outer layer, and the
inner refusal recorded a failure that reopened the circuit, so the lease never came into play.

**Fix.** `bd004d1e`: `ConnectVia` dials its one leg once, with no breaker or retry of its own, since the route's
dialer applies both to the same address. `TestConnectVia_ARoutedTargetsCircuitRecovers` passes.

**Lesson.** When a new path wraps an existing dialer, find which layer owns the breaker and retry for that address,
and give the outer layer neither. 146's lesson stands: a claim made twice on one path is a wedge.

## 895. A cancel's sever closed a routed target's client, whose Close waits on the tunnel's pumps, so a cancelled command through a stalled bastion had no bound (vuln-corpus C15; a repeat in kind of 352) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, found by the fp-reviewer agent on `fix/ssh-sweep-2026-11-04` before the pull request. On a
routed connection, 891's `cancelWatch` (as first written) severed the connection by closing the routed target's client.
`hopTunneledConn.Close` waits on the tunnel's pumps, which wait on the bastion, so with a bastion that stopped
answering a cancelled command never returned. `TestRun_ACancelledCommandThroughAStalledBastionIsBounded`
(`pkg/remoteexec/connectvia_test.go`) hung to the test timeout on `72474f70`.

**Root cause.** The sever's one job is to end the connection without waiting on the peer, and it called a Close that
waits on the peer.

**Why 352 did not hold.** 352 bounded the handshake through a bastion, where a tunneled connection has no deadline,
by closing on the context's end. The sever was new code on this branch, and it closed from the target inward, the end
whose Close waits, rather than from the first hop, whose close does not.

**Fix.** `bd004d1e`: `hopTunneledConn.sever` (`pkg/remoteexec/tunnel.go`, chosen by `severerFor` in `hop.go`)
closes the first hop's client first, without waiting on the pumps, then the rest of the chain. `TestRun_ACancelledCommandThroughAStalledBastionIsBounded` and
`TestRun_ACancelledCommandThroughAPlainRouteIsBounded` pass.

**Class.** C15 (unbounded wait on a peer; CWE-1088, CWE-400)

**Lesson.** A close used to end a wait must itself not wait on the peer. On a tunnel, cut from the outermost hop.

## 896. A started SSH command (Conn.Start, Process, a subsystem) ran on after its context ended and Wait reported exit 0 with a nil error (the open part of 891) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`, measured against OpenSSH 10.3 before the fix. A cancelled
`echo started; sleep 30` started through `Conn.Start` ran its full 30 s, and `Wait` reported 0 with a nil error. A
context already done still started the command. The old watchdog only closed the session, so on a silent connection
`Wait` was held forever.

**Root cause.** `pkg/remoteexec/stream.go` had its own watchdog, written before 891. 891 fixed `run`'s path
(`cancelWatch`) and left the streamed path as it was.

**Why 891 did not hold.** It did not reach this path, and said so: 891's entry carried `stream.go` as open
(fp-reviewer finding F4). This entry closes that part.

**Fix.** `bd9fc13b`: the stream uses `run`'s cancel watch. When the context ends it sends SIGTERM and closes the
session, closes the connection after the abandon grace, taints the lease, and `Wait` reports the context's error. A
done context starts nothing. Tests, each failing on the old code: `TestSSHContainer_AStartedCommandCancelledIsNotACompletedOne`
(`internal/transport/ssh/ssh_cancel_container_test.go`, real sshd), and in `pkg/remoteexec/stream_cancel_test.go`
`TestStart_AContextAlreadyDoneStartsNothing`, `TestStart_AContextEndingWhileTheSessionOpensIsACancellation` and
`TestProcess_ACancelledCommandOnASilentConnectionIsBounded`. `987603a2`: the second of those checked only the error;
it now counts the exec requests the server receives and requires none after the context ended. On `stream.go` from
before `bd9fc13b` it fails with "the server received 1 exec requests after the context ended".

**Lesson.** 891's: after a cancel, the context's error is the answer. A fix to one path of a shared shape is not done
until each path that has the shape uses the fixed code (LESSONS 244).

## 897. A command cut off for passing its output bound held the call until the command ended by itself (a sibling of 891) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`, measured against OpenSSH 10.3 before the fix. A `sleep 20` whose
output passed the call's bound held the call for the full 20 s after the cut.

**Root cause.** The output cap stopped reading but did nothing to the command. Only a cancel ended a command, and the
cap is not a cancel.

**Fix.** `bd9fc13b`: the cut ends the command as a cancellation does (SIGTERM, session close, connection closed after
the grace). `TestSSHContainer_ACommandCutForItsOutputIsEndedNotWaitedOn` (`internal/transport/ssh/ssh_cancel_container_test.go`,
real sshd). Its first version bounded the elapsed time from above; see 914.

**Lesson.** Every exit that stops reading a command's output must also end the command. A cap is one more exit, as
LESSONS 214 lists them.

## 898. A command sshd refused to start came back as "ssh: command <line> failed", the whole command in the error, where a secret in shell-encoded form escapes masking by value (a repeat in kind of 23) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. When sshd could not start the command (it could not fork for the
account), `golang.org/x/crypto/ssh` returned an error quoting the whole command line. A secret in that line carries
the shell's quoting (quotes, `$` escapes), so the by-value mask, which looks for the secret as stored, does not find
it. Measured against a second sshd run under `ulimit -u 1`, which refuses the exec for real.

**Root cause.** `Run` and `Start` returned the library's error as it came.

**Why 23 did not hold.** 23 taught that an error path can carry a secret and masked the transport error by value. That
works only when the secret appears as stored. Here it appears encoded, so masking cannot be the defense; the text must
not be there.

**Fix.** `bd9fc13b`: `Run` and `Start` return `ErrCommandRefused`, which names no command. Tests, failing on the old
code: `TestSSHContainer_ARefusedCommandIsNotInItsError` (`internal/transport/ssh/ssh_refused_exec_container_test.go`),
`TestRefusedExec_NamesNoCommand`, and `TestWithoutCommand_KeepsOtherErrors` (other errors are kept).

**Lesson.** Masking by value finds a secret only in the spelling it was stored in. An error that would quote a command
must name no command at all.

## 899. A detached command that reached the device cut short was started as the job, because cat took the prefix and an end of input (a repeat in kind of 891) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. Under `async:`, a command whose channel ended partway through the
send was written to the job file as its prefix and started.

**Root cause.** The start script read the command with `cat` until end of input, and a cut channel looks like an end
of input to `cat`.

**Why 891 did not hold.** 891 stopped a failed read of the local input from being sent as a clean end of input. That
is the client's side. On the device's side a cut channel still reads as a clean end, and nothing there could tell.

**Fix.** `49688a6e`: the start script takes the command's length as an argument and starts nothing on a mismatch.
`TestDetached_ACommandThatArrivesCutShortIsNeverStarted`.

**Lesson.** When the receiver cannot tell a cut stream from a whole one, send the length and check it there.

## 900. A login whose shell prints startup output (~/.ssh/rc) broke every poll of a detached job, which was abandoned as "may still be running" (a repeat of 779) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`, measured against the sshd container before the fix. With
`~/.ssh/rc` printing ahead of every command, the poll's 64-byte answer bound overflowed at the first poll, and the job
was given up as possibly still running.

**Root cause.** Each poll read all of standard output as the job's status.

**Why 779 did not hold.** 779 fixed the same banner for the start's answer (the job directory is the last line). The
poll is a second command on the same login with the same banner, and it was not given the same treatment (LESSONS
244).

**Fix.** `49688a6e`: the poll's answer is a marked last line under a 4 KiB bound (64 KiB since `a1243fae`, see 910),
and job files are read after a marker line, so the banner reaches neither the status nor the output.
`TestSSHContainer_ADetachedCommandSurvivesStartupOutput` (`internal/transport/ssh/ssh_detach_container_test.go`),
`TestPollRC_ReadsOnlyTheMarkedLine`, `TestAfterMarker_SkipsStartupOutput`, `TestReadJobFile_RefusesWhatItCannotRead`.

**Lesson.** Every command a feature sends on a login meets that login's startup output, not only the first. Mark the
answer of each.

## 901. On BusyBox ash with no setsid, a detached job had no process group, so the async limit stopped the wrapper and the command ran on (a repeat in kind of 504) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`, measured against the sshd container before the fix. The job's
marker appeared after the async limit had stopped it.

**Root cause.** Without `setsid`, the start script relied on `set -m` for a process group. A shell has no job control
without a terminal, so the job got no group and the group kill reached only the wrapper.

**Why 504 did not hold.** 504 found that dash's `set -m` gives no group without a terminal, in the OS checks' stop
scripts. That knowledge stayed in those scripts and their entry; the detach script's fallback was written apart from
it and tested where `setsid` exists.

**Fix.** `49688a6e`: where neither gives a group, the script refuses to detach and the command runs attached, under
the same limit. `TestSSHContainer_ADetachedCommandWithNoSetsidIsStillStopped`.

**Lesson.** A stop by process group first proves the group exists. Without job control, `set -m` proves nothing.

## 902. A detached start that failed after reaching the device, a start with no job directory in its answer, and a poll that could no longer be made each left the job running, unnamed and unstopped (a repeat in kind of 777 and 783) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. Each of these exits returned an error saying the job may be running,
and nothing stopped it, since the client did not know the job's directory.

**Root cause.** The device chose the job's name and told the client. When that answer was lost, the client had no
handle to stop the job by.

**Why 777 and 783 did not hold.** 777 made the stop run on the exits where the limit lands, and 783 fixed a failed
job-id record. Both stopped a job they could name. These exits had no name to stop by, and were left as reports.

**Fix.** `49688a6e`: the client chooses the job's name (`newJobName`, `jobByName`), so each of these exits stops the
job, and the error says whether the stop ran. `TestDetached_FailuresAreNamedAndNeverRunTwice` covers the start with
no job directory. The script and its parsing moved to `pkg/remoteexec/detach_script.go`.

**Lesson.** A handle that the far side assigns is lost with its answer. When a lost answer must still allow a stop,
choose the handle on the near side.

## 903. internal/redact's Masker.Attr masked only string values, so an error, a byte slice, a Stringer, a URL with a password or a struct reached both log handlers whole, and a secret-named group's leaves were not masked by name (a repeat in kind of 23) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. A log attribute whose value was not a string (an error quoting
device output, a `[]byte`, a `fmt.Stringer`, a `*url.URL` with a password, a named string type, a struct) reached the
text and JSON handlers with a registered secret in it. `slog.Group("password", ...)` or `WithGroup` did not mask the
group's leaves, whose own keys are ordinary words.

**Root cause.** `Attr` ran only `string` values through `Text`, and judged a key by its own name only.

**Why 23 did not hold.** 23's lesson was to mask every path a value can leave by, not only the common one. The common
one here was a string value; the other kinds were the uncommon paths, unexamined.

**Fix.** `eaafb354`: such a value is rendered as a handler prints it (`%+v`, and its JSON encoding) and replaced by the
masked text when masking changes it; a value with nothing secret keeps its shape. A secret-named group masks its
leaves by name, keeping an identifier (username, host, port and the like) shown. `TestAttr_ASecretInAValueThatIsNotAStringIsMasked`
and `TestAttr_ASecretNamedGroupMasksItsLeaves` run through the real handlers and failed on the old code;
`TestAttr_AValueWithNothingSecretKeepsItsShape`. Two gaps in this first fix are 904 and 912.

**Lesson.** A masker is held to every kind of value its callers pass, and a test of it runs each kind through the real
handler.

## 904. The first fix of 903 rendered a byte slice as its decimal bytes, the secret in another spelling, and a panicking MarshalJSON ended the logging goroutine (a repeat in kind of 455 and 898) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, the branch review of `eaafb354`. A `[]byte` or `json.RawMessage` holding a known secret was
replaced by its masked `%+v`, which for a byte slice is its decimal bytes: a substring check cannot see the secret
there, and anyone can read it back. A value whose `MarshalJSON` panicked panicked the logging goroutine, since
`ReplaceAttr` runs outside slog's recovery. An identifier key inside a secret-named group stayed shown for a struct,
which can hold anything.

**Root cause.** The rendering was chosen for its general case (`%+v`) without asking what it does to a byte slice, and
it called third-party code (`MarshalJSON`) in a place with no recovery.

**Why 455 and 898 did not hold.** Both found a secret in an encoded spelling (a base64 header, shell quoting) and fixed
that one site. Masking by value cannot see any encoding, and the new rendering made a new one.

**Fix.** `ec9b0a23`: a byte slice of any named type is rendered and replaced as its text; a panic in a marshaller is
recovered and that rendering skipped; an identifier under a secret-named group stays shown only for a string or a
scalar. The value test logs each value with two different secrets and requires the same line (LESSONS 195), which the
decimal form fails. `TestAttr_APanickingMarshallerDoesNotEndTheLogCall`,
`TestAttr_AStructUnderAnIdentifierKeyInASecretGroupIsMasked`; `BenchmarkAttrNonStringValue` measures the added cost
(about 390 ns for an error value).

**Lesson.** LESSONS 195: prove a message does not depend on the secret, not that the secret's spelling is absent.

## 905. internal/archtest's invisible-character check passed U+2028, U+2029, zero-width and other format characters, tag characters, variation selectors and the Hangul fillers, and two test files held raw U+2028 and U+2029 (the archtest gap of 851) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. `TestNoInvisibleControlCharactersInGoSource` asked
`termsafe.Unsafe`, which answers what a terminal acts on. Raw U+2028 and U+2029 (a line break to some viewers, so a
comment's tail can read as code) sat in string literals in `pkg/aitask/fuzz_test.go` and `pkg/iosparse/py_internal_test.go`.
The walk stopped on an editor's dangling lock link, an AppleDouble file or a file gone mid-walk.

**Root cause.** 851's: the check's list was a terminal's list, not the list of characters a reader cannot see.

**Fix.** `f041ed28`: the check also refuses Unicode's Cf, Zl, Zp, Variation_Selector and
Other_Default_Ignorable_Code_Point. The two literals are escapes now, with the same value. The walk is factored out
with a negative control over a tree of its own (`TestScanGoSource_FindsWhatItMustAndOnlyThat`) and passes over a
dangling link, an AppleDouble file and a vanished file. See 913 for that test's symlink case on Windows.

**Lesson.** 851's: a backstop's list is part of what it proves. Name the reader the check protects, then take that
reader's list.

## 906. Two detach tests read where a command ran with [ -p /dev/stdin ], which on FreeBSD is not a pipe without fdescfs, so they failed on bsd-check, on main as well as on the branch (a repeat of 505) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-04, bsd-check of branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. `TestDetached_AHomeTheAccountDoesNotOwnRunsTheCommandWhereItStands`
and `TestDetached_ALinkedBaseIsRefused` read every command as detached and failed. They fail on `main` there too.

**Root cause.** The tests used a Linux device file as their probe. FreeBSD has no `/dev/stdin` pipe without fdescfs
mounted.

**Why 505 did not hold.** 505 found tests assuming a Linux or macOS host and fixed those instances; nothing checks a
test's shell probe for portability. These tests reached `main`, so no FreeBSD run judged them before the merge.

**Fix.** `2dcb1f18`: the tests read `$0`, which ends in `/cmd` only for a job sh reads from its file, and
`TestDetached_WhereItRanTellsTheTwoApart` is the control that it reads both ways. CI_LESSONS 26.

**Lesson.** A test asks the shell what it knows, not a device file; and a probe that decides a test's verdict gets a
control that reads both answers.

## 907. The detached stop script signalled whatever its pid file held, so a red-first test that wrote pid 1 through remoteexectest's local-sh server ran kill -KILL -1 as the developer account and killed the user session twice (a repeat in kind of 689) (fixed)

**Symptom.** On branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`, the first version of `TestStopDetached_ReportsAStopOnlyWhenItSignalledAJob`
(`pkg/remoteexec/detach_script_test.go`) wrote a job's pid file holding `1` and called `conn.stopDetached` through
`remoteexectest`'s in-process SSH server. That server runs each command through this machine's own `/bin/sh`
(`pkg/remoteexec/remoteexectest/server.go`, `exec.Command("/bin/sh", "-c", command)`). The old stop script ran
`kill -TERM -"$p"` and `kill -KILL -"$p"`, that is `kill -KILL -1` as the developer account, which signals every
process the account may signal. The first time, the session died and it was read as "WSL crashed". The second time,
2026-11-05 at 08:56:03 to 08:56:05 EST, `journalctl` shows `user@1000.service` "Main process exited, code=killed,
status=9/KILL" two seconds after the capped `go test -race -run ...` started. Afterwards `~/.local/bin/capped` failed
with "Failed to connect to bus" until the owner ran `sudo systemctl start user@1000.service`.

**Root cause.** Two. In the product, the stop script trusted a value read from a file: a pid of 1 is a kill of every
process the account may signal, 0 its own group, and `01` or a value past 2^32 can reach the same through the shell's
parsing; a file under a base another account wrote could name any of them. In the test, a red-first test (written to
fail on the old code) sent the old code a destructive value through a harness that runs on this machine, so failing
meant doing the damage.

**Why 689 did not hold.** 689 (and 153) was a kill on this machine whose target nobody proved: `pgrep -f` matched the
agent's own shell. Its guard covers the agent's own `pkill` and `pgrep` commands. A kill run by product code inside a
test harness on the local shell is a path no guard looks at.

**Fix.** `6bef8e91`, `a1243fae`: `detachStop` (`pkg/remoteexec/detach_script.go`, beside `detachStart`) signals only a
pid that is digits with no leading zero, at most seven of them, and more than 1, and only after checking the base is a
directory the account owns, not a link, inside a HOME the account owns, as the start already requires. It signals
only the process group (see 909). A job with no such pid has its directory, which holds its command, removed, and the
stop reports that it stopped nothing. A Raw view's failed start sends no stop (`TestDetached_AFailedStartOnARawViewSendsNoStop`),
since its CLI would take the script for a command. The dangerous pids (0, 1, 01, -1, " 1", "1 2", +5, 12345678,
4294967297) are tried only by running the script locally with `kill` replaced by a logging shell function
(`TestDetachStop_NeverSignalsAPidAJobCannotHave`), behind a control that requires a real child's pid to reach the
function and the child to stay alive. The round trip through the server uses only values no kill acts on. On the old
script the new test fails every case, each kill logged and none sent.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 398 and 399. A script that acts on a value read from a file trusts it only as far as its shape and
its owner allow.

## 908. The detached stop reported "was stopped" for a job that had already finished, so an error could lead a reader to run the command a second time (a repeat of 789, 571 and 228; LESSONS 156) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-05, fp-reviewer on branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. The stop script exited 0 after its `rm` whenever the
pid was well formed, whether or not a job was running, and `49688a6e`'s errors said the job was stopped.

**Root cause.** The script's exit status said "the script finished", and the error read it as "a job was stopped".

**Why 789, 571 and 228 did not hold.** Each was text claiming more than the code does, fixed at its site. Here the
text was new and claimed what the exit status never said.

**Fix.** `a1243fae`: the script exits 2 (`detachStopEnded`) when the job's process group is gone, and `stopDetached`
returns a `stopOutcome` (stopped, had already finished, may be running) that every error carries.
`TestStopResult_NamesWhatTheStopFound`, `TestDetachStop_AJobWhoseGroupHadEndedIsNeverSignalledByPid`.

**Lesson.** An error that says what happened on a device takes that from a status that distinguishes the cases, never
from "the script ran".

## 909. After a detached job's group was gone, the stop sent TERM and KILL to its pid alone, which by then may be an unrelated process, as root under become (a repeat in kind of LESSONS 327; the family of 153 and 689) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-05, fp-reviewer on branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. The stop script on `main` ran
`kill -TERM -"$p" ... || kill -TERM "$p"`, and the same for KILL. When the group had ended, the fallback signalled the
pid alone, and a pid is reused.

**Root cause.** The fallback was for a job with no group (no `setsid`). Since 901, `detachStart` makes `$!` a group
leader or starts nothing, so the fallback could only ever reach a process that is not the job.

**Why LESSONS 327 did not hold.** 327 says a process is stopped by its group, not a pid. The fallback predates the
start's guarantee and was not revisited when the start changed.

**Fix.** `a1243fae`: only the group is ever signalled, and the grace loop probes the group (`kill -0 -"$p"`). Run
against the logging kill only: `TestDetachStop_AJobWhoseGroupHadEndedIsNeverSignalledByPid`, and the control's exact
kill list.

**Lesson.** When a guarantee changes upstream (every job has a group), remove the fallback written for its absence; a
fallback with no remaining case can only act on the wrong thing.

## 910. A failed detached start threw away the stop's result, and a 4 KiB answer bound let a chatty ~/.ssh/rc cut a stop short (a repeat in kind of 777 and 783; LESSONS 244) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-05, fp-reviewer on branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. When a start failed after reaching the device, its
error did not say what the stop found. The start, poll and stop answers were bounded at 4 KiB (the stop's 4096 bound
was on `main`), so enough startup output from `~/.ssh/rc` could fail the stop's own command.

**Root cause.** The start's error path called the stop and dropped its return; the bound was sized for the script's
own answer, not for a banner ahead of it (900's cause, at one more site).

**Why 777 and 783 did not hold.** Both made a stop run on an exit; neither made the exit report it. LESSONS 244 (a
guard on one of two sibling paths) applies to the bound: 900 fixed the poll's parse and the bound beside it stayed small.

**Fix.** `a1243fae`: a failed start's error carries the stop's outcome; the start, poll and stop answers are bounded at
64 KiB (`detachAnswerLimit`).

**Lesson.** A stop run on an error path reports what it found in that error. A bound on an answer that a login banner
precedes is sized for the banner too.

## 911. A finished detached job whose output passed its limit or could not be read left its directory, which holds the command, on the device (a repeat in kind of 452, 563, 638 and 728; LESSONS 214) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-05, fp-reviewer on branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. On `main`, `runDetached` returned the read error
before its `rm -rf`, so the job's directory (its command, which may hold a secret, and its output) stayed in the
account's home.

**Root cause.** The cleanup sat after reads that can fail, the shape of 452, 563, 638 and 728, where an undo was
recorded only after such reads.

**Why those did not hold.** Each fixed the order in its own methods. Nothing checks, for a cleanup in general, that
every early return passes it.

**Fix.** `a1243fae`: the directory is removed on those exits too. `TestDetached_OutputPastTheLimitLeavesNoJob`.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 214: list every early return against what it leaves behind. A cleanup belongs before the reads
that can fail, or on every exit after them.

## 912. Masker.Attr masked a map or struct value only by its text, so a "password" map key or a Password field whose bytes were never registered reached both log handlers whole (a repeat in kind of 696 and 884; LESSONS 350) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-05, fp-reviewer on branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. `{"password": ...}` in a map, or a `Password`
field in a struct, was printed in full by the text and JSON handlers when its value was not a registered secret,
though `Masker.Value` already masks such keys by name for stats. This was true on `main` and after 903's fix.

**Root cause.** 903 masked non-string values by registered text only; masking by key name lived in `Value`, which
`Attr` did not call.

**Why 696 and 884 did not hold.** Both looked only at the top level of a nested value and were fixed at their sites.
LESSONS 350 says one function, looking inside nested values, for every tier; `Value` was that function and `Attr` did
not use it.

**Fix.** `b34d029e`: a map, list or struct (not an error, not a byte slice) goes through `Value`, and the attribute
becomes the masked value, keeping its JSON shape, when that changes anything. A value that will not marshal is left to
the text renderings, so a panicking `MarshalJSON` still cannot end the logging goroutine.
`TestAttr_ASecretNamedKeyInsideAValueIsMasked` fails 12 times on the old code (six shapes, two handlers). `Attr`'s
comment now says rendering calls `Error`, `String` and `MarshalJSON`, whichever the handler uses.

**Open.** A `[]byte` field inside a struct that holds a registered secret is still printed as base64 (JSON) or as
decimal bytes (text), and missed.

**Resolution (2026-11-05).** Fixed by 918.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 350: two maskers of one value are one function.

## 913. TestScanGoSource_FindsWhatItMustAndOnlyThat failed rather than skipped where symbolic links cannot be made, such as Windows without the privilege (a repeat of 567 and 544) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-05, fp-reviewer on branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. 905's new test called `t.Fatal` when it could not
make its dangling link.

**Root cause.** It assumed unprivileged symbolic links, which the Windows leg does not have.

**Why 567 and 544 did not hold.** Their rule is CI_LESSONS 3, and `need.Require` exists for it; the new test was
written without either.

**Fix.** `3aa5337a`: the symlink case uses `need.Require`, as the other symlink tests do.

**Lesson.** CI_LESSONS 3.

## 914. TestSSHContainer_ACommandCutForItsOutputIsEndedNotWaitedOn bounded the call's elapsed time from above (a repeat of 479, 422 and 211) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-05, fp-reviewer on branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. 897's test required the call to end within 12 s, a
wall-clock upper bound that a stalled runner can miss with nothing wrong.

**Root cause.** The test measured time to prove "not waited on", where an outcome can prove it.

**Why 479, 422 and 211 did not hold.** Each removed a timing bound at its site; CI_LESSONS 6 and 19 are rules, not a
check.

**Fix.** `3aa5337a`: the command now outlives the call's 60 s deadline by far, and the test requires
`ErrOutputTooLarge` and not `DeadlineExceeded`, so a call that waits on the command fails without a timer. Passed
against the real sshd container in 1.2 s on 2026-11-05.

**Lesson.** Prove "did not wait" by an outcome that waiting would change (which error came back), not by a stopwatch.

## 915. TestDetached_TheStopReconnectsWhenItsConnectionIsGone passed with nothing checked when the job's child pid file never appeared (a repeat in kind of 436 and 440) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-05, fp-reviewer on branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. The test, on `main` since 777, checked the child
only when its pid file existed, so a job that never recorded its child passed.

**Root cause.** A missing precondition was read as nothing to check.

**Why 436 and 440 did not hold.** Each was a vacuous pass fixed at its site; CI_LESSONS 15 is a rule, not a check.

**Fix.** `a1243fae`: the test fails when the job never records its child.

**Lesson.** CI_LESSONS 15: a precondition a test relies on is asserted, never skipped over.

## 916. TestProcess_ErrorsNeverCarryTheCommandText's own command wrote the marker to standard error, which an error carries by design, so it failed on FreeBSD when that stderr arrived before the close (a repeat in kind of LESSONS 368) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-05, `bsdcheck` of `pkg/remoteexec` on branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b` at `44e72fe5`: the test failed in
one of three runs with `Write() error = "remoteexec: write to remote command on 127.0.0.1:...: EOF (server stderr:
\"cat: /srv/secret-looking-path: No such file or directory\\n\")"`. It passed in every Linux run.

**Root cause.** The test started `cat '/srv/secret-looking-path'` and asserted the marker never reaches the `Write`
error. The path does not exist, so `cat` itself printed the marker to standard error, and a stream's errors append the
server's stderr deliberately (`stream.stderrSuffix`). Whether that stderr was drained before `Close` depended on
timing, which FreeBSD's scheduler made come out the other way. The code was right; the fixture produced the very text
the test says must be absent.

**Why LESSONS 368 did not hold.** 368 is about a test watching for a mark another path can also leave; this is its
mirror (an absence a second path can break), and the test was on `main` from before 368 was written.

**Fix.** `pkg/remoteexec/process_test.go`: the marker is an argument to `:`, which ignores it, then `cat` runs, so the
command's own output can never hold it. 20 runs pass locally under `-race`; rerun on bsd-check.

**Lesson.** A test asserting a value is absent from an output must make sure no other legitimate channel into that
output (a remote program's stderr, a log line, an echo) can produce it.

## 917. The docker host fixture's unpinned apk add of openssh-server broke when Alpine's index moved past the pinned dind image's own openssh client packages (a repeat in kind of 465) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-05, `make branch-containers` run 42062491556 for `fix/ssh-sweep-b` at `da5be229`: shards 2 and 6
failed, every test that builds the docker host fixture (`internal/testsupport` `TestDockerHost_*`,
`internal/adapters/native` `TestContainerExec_RunnerChildReachesTheDevicesEngine`, eight `internal/inventory/onboard`
engine tests) with `apk add`: `openssh-client-common-10.3_p1-r1: breaks: openssh-client-default-10.3_p1-r2`. Each
failed again when re-run alone. Reproduced here with `docker build --no-cache`; unrelated to the branch's diff, so `main`
was broken the same way.

**Root cause.** `testdata/docker-sshd/Dockerfile` pins its base (`docker:29.9.0-dind`) but installs `openssh-server`
from Alpine's live index. The base ships OpenSSH's client packages at r1; the index moved to r2, whose server package
needs the r2 client packages, and `apk add` does not upgrade an installed package unless asked, so it could not
resolve. A warm local image cache hid it; CI builds the fixture fresh.

**Why 465 did not hold.** 465 made pr-check ask a registry whether each pinned image is served; it says nothing about
packages a Dockerfile installs from a moving index on top of a pinned image.

**Fix.** `apk add --no-cache --upgrade openssh-server openssh-client-common openssh-client-default`: the client
packages move with the server. The engine is not an apk package in that image, so Docker stays 29.9.0 (checked in the
rebuilt image). `TestDockerHost_*` pass against the cold-built fixture.

**Lesson.** A fixture that adds a package from a live index onto a pinned base that already carries part of that
package's family upgrades the family with it, or it breaks the day the index moves.

## 918. A registered secret held in a []byte inside a struct, a map entry or a list reached the logs and the stats as base64, since the value walk converts through encoding/json and Text saw only that spelling (a repeat in kind of 904) (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-05, 912's open note, on branch `fix/ssh-sweep-b`. `output{Host: "sw1", Stdout: []byte("stdout: "
+ secret)}` logged through either handler, `map[string]any{"stdout": []byte(...)}` and `[]any{..., []byte(...)}`
printed the secret as base64 (JSON) or decimal bytes (text); `Masker.Value` on a stat map holding such bytes returned
the base64 unmasked. `TestAttr_ASecretInAByteFieldIsMasked` and `TestValue_ASecretInBytesIsMaskedAsItsText` fail 9
times on the old code (four shapes under two handlers, and the stat).

**Root cause.** `Value` turns any shape it does not know (a struct, a nested `[]byte`) into what `encoding/json` writes,
and JSON writes a `[]byte` as standard base64. `Text` knows a secret's literal and shell-encoded spellings, not its
base64, so the walk compared nothing it could match. 904 fixed the same spelling problem only for a `[]byte` at the
top of an attribute.

**Why 904 did not hold.** It handled the top-level value's renderings; nested bytes go through `Value`'s JSON
conversion, a different path.

**Fix.** `Masker.maskString`: a string the walk masks is also checked, when it is standard base64 (alphabet scanned
first, so megabytes of command output are refused without allocating), as the bytes it spells; if those hold a secret
the string becomes them as masked text, otherwise it keeps its spelling. Both log handlers and every stat gain it, since
`Attr` walks structured values through `Value`.

**Lesson.** A masker that converts a value before matching must match every spelling the conversion can produce.

## 919. A facts batch whose job or device ID held a NUL failed every PostgreSQL query made with it, so the Controller handed it back for redelivery until its delivery budget ran out (a repeat of 208, through the dialect gap of 371) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by an API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (the facts verdicts, item 2); measured and fixed on
2026-11-05 on `fix/facts-sweep-security`. A facts batch whose device ID held a NUL failed its PostgreSQL query with
SQLSTATE 22021 ("invalid byte sequence for encoding UTF8: 0x00"). `entstore.Subscriber.Handle` returned the error, so
the bus redelivered the batch until its delivery budget ran out. Any Runner may publish on any job's facts subject, so
one Runner could do this to any job. `TestSubscriber_APoisonedBatchIsAcknowledgedOnPostgres`, on real PostgreSQL 15,
showed it on the old code: the device case returned the 22021 error, and the job case reached the admission check,
which in production queries with the IDs.

The reviewer's claim was different, and measurement refuted it. The verdict said a NUL or an out-of-range number
(`json.Number` "1e200000") in a fact's value would poison the batch. Both are stored fine: the store keeps the value's
canonical JSON as a string inside its JSON column (payload `{"json": "<text>"}`), so `jsonb` never sees `\u0000`.
Invalid UTF-8 cannot ride the wire at all, since `encoding/json` writes it as U+FFFD.

**Root cause.** `Handle` checked only that each ID was not empty. It acknowledged the permanent failures it knew by
name (a batch it cannot decode, nothing that passes, an unknown device, a job never dispatched) and returned every
other error for redelivery. A value the server refuses as data is just as permanent, but it came back as a plain store
error. SQLite keeps a NUL and simply matches no row, so the SQLite-backed tests could not see it.

**Why 208 and 371 did not hold.** 208 is this class: a consumer that splits "retry" from "give up" on the wrong axis
turns a permanent failure into a poison pill. Its fix was a sentinel (`journal.ErrUnstorable`) for the values the
journal's own store validates, in that one consumer. It left no shared way to tell a value the server refuses from a
server that is down, and the facts subscriber was new code with its own list of cases. 371's lesson (a property that
holds on the test dialect needs one run on the production dialect) was applied to sign-in; no test sent the facts
subscriber a malformed ID on PostgreSQL.

**Fix.** `9221ff2f` checked both IDs before any query and acknowledged SQLSTATE class 22, inside the facts
subscriber. The branch's review then found the same hole in the journal and result consumers (924), so the checks
moved into one package all three call, `internal/poison`: `CheckID` (not empty, valid UTF-8, no control characters,
and no length limit, since a device ID is the operator's and its column has none; the first version's 256-byte cap
could refuse a real one) and `Unstorable`, over `ent.DataExceptionCode` (`internal/ent/data_exception.go`, hand
written), which reports SQLSTATE class 22 anywhere in an error's chain. A refused batch is acknowledged and logged
with the check that failed, and a class 22 failure with its SQLSTATE only, never the server's message, which can
quote the value. Class 23 is left out on purpose: a unique violation is how two replicas racing
on one chain learn to retry. `TestSubscriber_ADataExceptionIsAcknowledgedAndOthersRedelivered` uses real server
errors: 22021, 22003 and 22012 are acknowledged; 23505 and a connection error are redelivered.

**Lesson.** Reproduce a reviewer's failure on the production dialect before fixing it. Here the path the reviewer
named was safe and a neighboring one (the IDs) was not. A consumer decides between acknowledging and redelivering by
whether the same bytes could ever succeed, and the server's own error class answers that better than a list of cases.

## 920. A fact whose value held a field named like a secret was stored, because Prepare held only the fact's own key to the secret-name rule (a repeat of 696, and in kind of 884) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 2); fixed on 2026-11-05.
`facts.Prepare` asked `SecretName` of the fact's key only (`nameOf(key)` in `facts.go`). An object fact such as
`{"db": {"password": "..."}}`, or a list of objects each with an `api_token` field, passed and was stored whole: in
the Crawl CLI's fact store, and again on the Controller, since `facts.Verify` calls `Prepare`. Only a known secret
value, or text shaped like a secret, would have been caught.

**Root cause.** A name rule applied at the top level only. It asked whether the fact is named for a secret, not
whether the fact carries a field that is.

**Why 696 and 884 did not hold.** 696 fixed this shape for device vars through `redact.CleanVars`, which the fact
guard does not call. 884 made the facts digest scrub walk every depth, but only for raw digest fields; the
secret-name check beside it stayed at the key. Both lessons say a guard over data walks the whole value, and neither
fix reached this check. The verdict also named 854; that entry is about which keys may skip the name rule, so it is a
neighbor of this one, not its class.

**Fix.** `5999dd16`: `secretField` (`internal/facts/nested.go`) walks every field name at any depth of the normalized
value with the same `SecretName` check. A fact with such a field is refused with a reason that names the field
(`%q`), never the value. Tests: `TestPrepare_ASecretNamedInsideAValueIsNotStored` and
`TestVerify_ASecretNamedInsideAPublishedValueIsDropped`, built from the production guard (`redact.SecretShaped`,
`redact.SecretName`). Checked: no built-in declared object fact (the `package.`, `service.`, `file.`, `port.`, `user.`
and `group.` families of `facts.gather`, and the `net.catalyst` and `net.ios` lists) has a field name the rule
matches, so nothing a built-in method reports is newly refused.

**Lesson.** A name rule over structured data is asked of every name in the value, not only of the outer one.

## 921. VerifyChain passed unchained values at the start of a device's fact history as rows from before the chain, so anyone who could write the store could add rows there that verified (a repeat in kind of 154 and 854) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 3); fixed on 2026-11-05.
`facts.VerifyChain` counted values with no chain and no provenance at the start of a history as `Unchained` and did
not check them, as rows stored before Phase 41b. `chain_test.go` asserted that behavior. Anyone who could write the
store could put such rows at the head of a device's history, and the verdict still said the chain held.

**Root cause.** An exemption for old rows, inferred from what such a row lacks. Empty fields are what anyone can
write, so the shape that marked a row as old marked a forged row equally well. And there are no old rows: the project
is before 1.0, and nothing deployed predates the chain (the owner's rule is forward only before 1.0), so the
exemption protected nothing.

**Why 154 and 854 did not hold.** 154 is a zero value given a special meaning that a caller can produce without
meaning it; its fix was one field of a test harness. 854's lesson (an exemption is declared by name, never inferred
from a shape that other uses share) was written on 2026-11-03, a day after the chain landed (`462786a6`,
2026-11-02), and nobody went back to the chain with it.

**Fix.** `3e318af1`: a link with no chain is a break wherever it stands. `Verdict.Unchained` is removed, with its
line in the CLI's output (`cmd/pleiades/facts_cmd.go`), its field in `internal/apispec` and the generated OpenAPI.
Test: `TestVerifyChain_AnUnchainedValueAtTheStartIsABreak`. The chain was never in a release (it is not in `v0.3.0`),
so no released output changes.

**Lesson.** An integrity check does not exempt data by what it lacks. Before 1.0 there is no legacy data to exempt.

## 922. The CLI's fact file store renamed its state file into place unsynced, so a crash could leave an empty state file that refused the device's facts until removed by hand (a repeat of 566) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 12); fixed on 2026-11-05.
`writeState` (`internal/facts/file.go`) wrote a temporary file and renamed it into place with no sync of the file and
none of the directory. A crash could persist the rename but not the data: an empty state file, or one filled with
zero bytes on XFS. `readState` refused such a file forever, so `Record`, `Current` and `History` failed for that
device until someone deleted the file by hand. The history append was not synced either, though the state file names
what it holds. `TestFileStore_AnEmptyStateFileIsReadAsNoState` failed on the old code with `dev1.state.json: EOF`.

**Root cause.** A rename makes the change of name atomic, not the content durable. Without a sync before the rename,
a crash can leave the two on disk in the wrong order.

**Why 566 did not hold.** 566 (and 46 before it) writes a key through a synced temporary file. 830 gave this store
its temporary file and rename and left out the sync. A reader that refused an empty file then turned one lost write
into a permanent refusal, which is 566's "refuses forever" again.

**Fix.** `b2f7ff6b`: the temporary state file is synced before the rename, and the directory after it on a
best-effort basis (`syncDir` in `lock_unix.go`; a no-op on Windows, where the read-only directory handle cannot be
flushed, and on other platforms). The history append is synced before the state that names it. A state file that is
empty or holds nothing but NUL bytes reads as no state: the history in `<device>.jsonl` is kept, and what is lost
(last-confirmed times and volatile values) the next run observes again. Test:
`TestFileStore_AnEmptyStateFileIsReadAsNoState` (empty and zero-filled). The syncs themselves cannot be tested
without a real crash; that part rests on reading the code.

**Lesson.** A file written by temporary name and rename is synced before the rename, and its reader decides what an
empty file means rather than refusing it forever.

## 923. A late change stored after a later confirmation ended the history at the late value, so the next run recorded a change nobody saw (a repeat of 831, a case its fix left) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 13); fixed on 2026-11-05. Both
fact stores keep a value confirmed again only as a last sighting, not as a new history row. Run y confirmed value A
at order 11 and was stored first; run x's change to B at order 10 was stored second. The history then ended at B
while `Current` said A. Run z at order 12 found A unchanged and appended A under z: a change that no run saw. The
Crawl file store (`file_store.go`, `Record`) and the Controller's ent store (`entstore/store.go`, `record`) both did
this. The conformance case "a late change keeps a later confirmation in the history" in `factstest`, run for the file
store and for ent on SQLite and on PostgreSQL, was red on all three before the fix.

**Root cause.** 831's fix decides the current value by when each value was last seen, but the history holds only
changes. A late change stored between a value and its later confirmation leaves that confirmation with no row of its
own, so the history's last row disagrees with the current value, and the next run compares against the late one.

**Why 831 did not hold.** 831's tests asked whether a late value replaced the current one, and after its fix it did
not. Neither asked what the history looked like afterward, or what the next run in order would record.

**Fix.** `185e1833`: `facts.Resumed` (`internal/facts/late.go`), used by both stores. After a late change is stored,
the value that was current before it is written again, dated at its last sighting and attributed to that run, when
that sighting is after the late change and no stored value lies between them. Tests: the conformance case above, and
`TestResumed_OnlyAConfirmationAfterTheLateChangeWithNothingBetween` (eight cases). Two older tests asserted the old
history shape and were updated: `TestFileStore_ALateObservationDoesNotReplaceANewerOne` and
`TestStore_ALateBatchDoesNotReplaceANewerValue`.

**Lesson.** A fix for out-of-order arrival is tested by what the next in-order arrival does, not only by the state
just after the late one.

## 924. The run journal and job result consumers handed back for redelivery forever a message whose job or device ID held a NUL, and a result whose reason held one, so a device's own output could lose its result (a repeat of 919 at its sibling sites, and of 208) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the branch's fp-reviewer on 2026-11-05 while 919 was being fixed, and measured on real
PostgreSQL 15 by `TestConsumers_ARefusedValueIsAcknowledgedOnPostgres` (in `internal/facts/entstore`, which has the
PostgreSQL harness). On the old code every case returned SQLSTATE 22021 and asked for redelivery: a journal batch with
a NUL in its job ID, its device ID or a task name, a job result with a NUL in its job or device ID, and a job result
whose `reason` held a NUL. The last is the serious one. A result's reason is free text that can come from the device's
own output, so a device printing a NUL lost its own result: the message was redelivered until its budget ran out, and
the job stayed running until the reaper ended it.

**Root cause.** 919's, in two more places. `journal.Subscriber.Handle` acknowledged only `journal.ErrUnstorable`, which
covers an outcome the store does not know, and `dispatch.ResultConsumer.Handle` only an undecodable message, an unknown
outcome and a negative count. Neither checked an ID before its first query, and neither knew a value the server refuses
from a server that is down. `internal/journal`'s NUL hardening case runs on SQLite, which stores a NUL.

**Why 919 did not hold.** 919's fix was written inside the facts subscriber. LESSONS 244 says a guard added at one
site goes to its siblings in the same change; the three consumers of what a Runner publishes are siblings, and only one
was fixed until the review named the other two.

**Fix.** One package, `internal/poison`, used by all three consumers: `CheckID` before any query (the journal's device
ID is checked when present, since a batch may name none), `Unstorable` (SQLSTATE class 22) acknowledged and logged with
its code only, and `CleanText`, which replaces each NUL in a result's reason with U+FFFD so the result is recorded with
the rest of its text. Tests: `TestConsumers_ARefusedValueIsAcknowledgedOnPostgres` (red on the old consumers, green
now), and in `internal/dispatch` `TestResultConsumer_AnIDThatCannotNameOneIsDroppedBeforeAnyQuery`,
`TestResultConsumer_ANULInTheReasonKeepsTheOutcome` and `TestResultConsumer_ADataExceptionIsAcknowledged`, each red on
the old consumer.

**Lesson.** A fix for how one consumer treats untrusted input belongs to every consumer of the same publisher; put it
in one package they all call, so the next consumer starts from it.

## 925. facts.gather stored a family source it could not read as an empty set, since over SSH a probe's exit status never reached Gather and every family parser read "could not read" as "nothing there", so every item read as removed and came back the next run (a repeat of 13, 451, 723 and 845) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 1); fixed on 2026-11-05 on
`fix/facts-sweep-gatherers`, before push. Every `facts.gather` family (`package.`, `service.`, `port.`, `user.`,
`group.`) stored a source it failed to list as a source that lists nothing. A locked rpmdb, a busy systemd or a broken
Homebrew made every package or service read as removed, and the next good run read them all as added again. On
Windows, a JSON answer that was malformed or had text printed before it read as no items, and an object cut short
after a complete member read as the whole answer. `TestGather_AFamilyIsReadOrTheRunSaysItWasNot`, through the real
SSH harness and a real `/bin/sh` with stand-in tools on `PATH`, failed 5 of its first 6 cases on the old code; the
control (a source that answers) passed on both.

**Root cause.** Two halves that each looked safe alone. Over SSH the run closure in `gather_transport.go` keeps only
stdout, and `pkg/remoteexec`'s `Conn.Run` returns a non-zero exit as `Result.ExitCode` with a nil error, so a failed
listing reached the parser as empty output. And every family parser returned the same nil for "could not read" as
for "nothing there", so nothing downstream could tell them apart.

**Why 13, 451, 723 and 845 did not hold.** 13 says a tool that can return nothing needs a positive control; 451 and
723 each fixed one reader (docker inspect, `wait.routes`) that took a failed look as absence. Each fix lives in its own
code, and the facts families were written later with the same shape. 845 saw this exact path on 2026-11-03: its entry
says "the SSH path reads no exit status for a probe, so the task succeeded". Its fix moved every probe under `sh -c`,
which cured the shell that caused that failure, and left the exit status unread, so any other failure still reached
the store as an empty set. LESSONS 138 (give "I could not look" a third answer) was not applied.

**Fix.** `55ea70bc`, `internal/catalog/facts/gather_outcome.go`. Each family probe runs its listing only where its
source is present (`guarded`, printing `gatherAbsentMark` otherwise), and each listing whose failure matters prints
`gatherFailedMark` when it fails (`orFailed`). `readOutcome` splits a probe's answer into read, absent or failed, and
a per-source check refuses an answer without the structure its source always prints (`checkSystemd`, `checkOpenRC`,
`checkRC`, `checkLaunchd`, `listsSomething` for pkgutil, `checkWindowsArray` on Windows). `familyVerdict` decides the
task: a failed source fails it, whatever else answered, so a failed task stores none of what it emitted; a family no
source answers fails a task that named its subset itself, and is a warning for one reached through `all`.
`parseWindowsObject` needs its closing brace and nothing after it. Tests: `TestGather_AFamilyIsReadOrTheRunSaysItWasNot`,
`TestReadOutcome`, `TestFamilyVerdict`, `TestStructureChecks`, `TestParseWindowsObject_OnlyAWholeObject`. The live
suite (`internal/catalog/facts/live`, real Rocky and Alpine OpenRC containers) passes; its RPM test now asserts that
the dpkg and apk probes say their source is absent there. `2393a634` extends `FuzzGatherParsers` to run each answer
through `readOutcome` and its check first (90 s, about 2.6 million inputs, no failure).

**Found on review.** The branch's fp-reviewer agent, 2026-11-05, before push, found two things the fix left.

(a) The stricter rule broke three callers that named services where no service manager runs. Fixed in `529c032c`
and `9deef5c8`. `cmd/pleiades/facts_release_gate_test.go` runs an Alpine sshd image with no `rc-status` and no
systemd; it now gathers `[packages]`, and asserts that a gather naming `[services]` is refused, saying so, and stores
nothing. `TestCLI_FactsReleaseGate` passes against the real container. `TestGather_PackagesAndServicesMatchThisMachine`
now reaches the families through `all` (`[all, !ports, !users]`), so a test host with no manager warns rather than
fails. The playbook converter's `service_facts` now emits `gather_subset: [all, !hardware, !packages, !ports, !users]`
(`internal/forge/playbook/modules_misc.go`, `serviceFactsSubsets`), so a host with no manager is a warning, as
Ansible's `service_facts` skips there; its note says SysV init's `service --status-all` is not read. Test:
`TestModules_Map`'s `service_facts` case.

(b) Sibling sources still read "could not look" as "none", fixed in `529c032c`. The Windows ports, users and groups
scripts printed `[]` when `Get-NetTCPConnection`, `Get-LocalUser` or `Get-LocalGroup` was missing, which read as no
listeners or accounts; each now prints `gatherAbsentMark` (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_win_items.go`). Test:
`TestGather_AWindowsHostWithoutTheCmdletsSaysSo`, on a modeled host; it has not yet run on a real Windows host. rpm
counts as present only with its database (`rpm --eval '%_dbpath'` and that directory, `gather_packages.go`), so a
Debian host carrying an rpm with no database does not fail the family dpkg answered. A failing `pkgutil --pkg-info`
now fails the macOS probe (`orFailed`, `gather_bsd_items.go`). Linux port sections split only at the start of a line
(`markedSections`, `gather_ports.go`), so a file a local user names with the mark, seen in a root gather's descriptor
listing, cannot fail that gather. Test: `TestStructureChecks`' "linux ports, a mark inside a line" case. The live suite
still passes on real Rocky and Alpine OpenRC containers.

**Lesson.** A reader whose answer is a list has three answers, not two: the items, none, or "could not read". Where
the transport drops the exit status, the probe has to say which one itself, and the parser cannot be the place that
decides.

## 926. facts.gather's systemd probe read a host systemd did not boot, where systemctl lists unit files and no units, so every service read inactive, and a failed list-units read the same (a repeat of 13 and 723; LESSONS 244) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 8); fixed on 2026-11-05 on
`fix/facts-sweep-gatherers`, before push. The systemd probe ran wherever `systemctl` was installed. On a host where
systemd is not PID 1 (a container, or a host booted by another init), `systemctl list-unit-files` still lists the unit
files and `list-units` lists no unit, so every service was stored with no running state. A `list-units` that failed
on a booted host gave the same answer.

**Root cause.** The probe asked only whether the tool exists, not whether the manager it reads is running. Its sibling,
the OpenRC probe, already carried the mirror test (`[ ! -d /run/systemd/system ]`).

**Why 13, 723 and LESSONS 244 did not hold.** 13 and 723 are the empty-read class (925). LESSONS 244 says that when
one of two sibling paths carries a guard, the other is checked too. The OpenRC probe's guard asked the booted question,
and nobody asked it of the systemd probe beside it.

**Fix.** `55ea70bc`: the probe's source is present only when `systemctl` exists and `[ -d /run/systemd/system ]`
(`internal/catalog/facts/gather_services.go`), and `checkSystemd` refuses an answer whose loaded units name no
service, which a booted systemd always has. Test: `TestStructureChecks` (the "systemd, no loaded service" and
"systemd, one section" cases). The booted test itself is a shell condition; it rests on reading the code.

**Lesson.** A probe for a service manager asks whether that manager is running, not only whether its tool is
installed.

## 927. An OpenRC supervise-daemon service's status line, which carries its uptime, was stored whole as its state, so the state was a new value on every gather (a repeat in kind of 870 and 874) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 9); fixed on 2026-11-05 on
`fix/facts-sweep-gatherers`, before push. For a service run by `supervise-daemon`, `rc-status --all -f ini` prints a
status such as `started 1 day(s) 02:13:07 (0)`. `parseOpenRC` stored all of it as the service's state, so an unchanged
service showed a change on every run.

**Root cause.** The parser mapped known state words through `openrcStates` but compared the whole value, so a status
with more than one word matched nothing and was kept as written.

**Why 870 and 874 did not hold.** Both are drift on an unchanged device caused by how a source prints (sockstat's one
line per descriptor, Windows' share mode). Each fix lives in its own probe; nothing asks of every field a family
records whether it moves on an unchanged device. Sweep item 10 (service runtime state and other fields that move on
their own) is the rest of that question and is still open.

**Fix.** `55ea70bc`: the state is the status's first word (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_services.go`). Test:
`TestParseOpenRC_ASupervisedServiceIsRunning`.

**Lesson.** A parser that maps a source's words reads only the word it maps, and a test feeds it the longest status
the source prints.

## 928. FreeBSD with security.bsd.see_other_uids=0 and a non-root login stored a running daemon it could not see as stopped (a repeat in kind of 818) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 11); fixed on 2026-11-05 on
`fix/facts-sweep-gatherers`, before push. Where `security.bsd.see_other_uids=0` hides other users' processes, a
non-root login's `service <name> onestatus` says "is not running" for a daemon that is running as another user.
`parseRC` stored it as `stopped`.

**Root cause.** rc's status answer is built from a process lookup, and the lookup cannot see what the sysctl hides.
"I could not see it" came back in the same words as "it is not there".

**Why 818 did not hold.** 818 fixed a PowerShell guard (`Test-Path`) that answered no for a path it could not read,
and LESSONS 379 says a primitive is measured for what it answers when it cannot look. That rule was written for
existence guards, and rc's status check is the same kind of primitive in another place.

**Fix.** `55ea70bc`: the FreeBSD services probe prints `procsHiddenMark` when the login is not root and `ps -p 1`
fails, and under that mark a "not running" status is left unknown rather than stopped
(`internal/catalog/facts/gather_bsd_items.go`). Test: `TestParseRC_AHiddenDaemonIsUnknown`.

**Found on review.** The branch's fp-reviewer agent, 2026-11-05, before push: the hidden test used `ps -p 1`, and pid 1
never shows inside a FreeBSD jail, so every non-root gather in a jail would have read every stopped daemon as unknown.
Fixed in `529c032c`: the probe prints `procsHiddenMark` only when the login is not root and `sysctl -n
security.bsd.see_other_uids` (which any login may read) says `0`. `TestParseRC_AHiddenDaemonIsUnknown` covers the
parser; the probe's condition is a shell test and rests on reading the code.

**Lesson.** A status that is built by looking for something says "absent" when the look is blocked; ask first whether
the look can see.

## 929. rc-update show -v put its option after the verb, so under POSIXLY_CORRECT glibc's getopt listed nothing and every OpenRC service read disabled (a repeat of 844) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 15); fixed on 2026-11-05 on
`fix/facts-sweep-gatherers`, before push. The OpenRC probe ran `rc-update show -v`. Where `POSIXLY_CORRECT` is set and
the userland uses glibc's getopt, parsing stops at `show` and `-v` is not read as an option, so the listing names
nothing and every OpenRC service read as disabled.

**Root cause.** 844's: an option after the first non-option word is not an option to a non-permuting parser.

**Why 844 did not hold.** 844 fixed the systemctl command and wrote the lesson "put a command's options before its
first operand or verb, always". The OpenRC command in the same probe file was not changed with it.

**Fix.** `55ea70bc`: `rc-update -v show` (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_services.go`). No unit test names this case;
the live suite's real Alpine OpenRC container passes with the new order.

**Lesson.** No new lesson: 844's, applied to every command in the file it touched, not only the one that failed.

## 930. facts.gather's filter matched a family member before gatherNames.distinct told apart a name two databases share, so package.glibc:* matched nothing, and a filter naming a family alone passed the typo refusal and matched nothing (the first a repeat of 849, a case its fix left) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 14); fixed on 2026-11-05 on
`fix/facts-sweep-gatherers`, before push. Where two databases list the same package name, the second is stored as
`package.glibc:i686` (or `@source`, or `#2`). A filter `package.glibc:*` was matched against the key before that
suffix was added, so it matched neither item. And a pattern with no wildcard, such as `package`, passed
`gatherFamilyWanted`, which refuses a filter that can match no fact, and then matched no member. Both cases in
`TestGather_AFamilyIsReadOrTheRunSaysItWasNot` ("a filter matching the key a second database's item is stored under"
and "a filter naming a family alone") were red on the old code.

**Root cause.** The filter read a different key from the one the store keeps. And `gatherFamilyWanted` took the text
before the first wildcard as a prefix even when there was no wildcard, so the whole pattern counted as a prefix of
every member.

**Why 849 did not hold.** 849's fix (`ab881c13`) made names distinct across every probe of a run, and placed that
step after the filter. 849's lesson (a test calls the code the way the run does) was met for the plain run, but no
test ran it with a filter.

**Fix.** `564bbe70`: `names.distinct` runs before the filter, whether or not the filter keeps the item, so the filter
reads the stored key and a key does not change with the filter. A pattern with no wildcard names one key, and is a
member only when it is longer than the family's prefix (`internal/catalog/facts/gather.go`). Tests: the two cases
above.

**Lesson.** A filter matches the key that is stored, so every step that shapes the key runs before it.

## 931. gather_subset was read in order, so [!packages, all] gathered packages (a repeat of 848, a case its fix left) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 16); fixed on 2026-11-05 on
`fix/facts-sweep-gatherers`, before push. `gatherNamed` applied each name in turn, so `all` after `!packages` added
packages back, and the "only removals start from the default" rule did not see the change. Ansible gathers the same
set whatever the order. Two cases of `TestGatherNamed_FollowsAnsiblesRuleInAnyOrder` were red on the old code.

**Root cause.** The list was read as a sequence of edits, where Ansible's `get_collector_names` reads it as sets: what
is added, minus what is excluded and not also named.

**Why 848 did not hold.** 848's fix gave the playbook converter Ansible's order-free rule (`setupSubset`) and left
`facts.gather`'s own reading of the list as it was. Its lesson (map a value's meaning, not its spelling) was applied
to the converter only.

**Fix.** `564bbe70`: `gatherNamed` (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_subsets.go`) follows `get_collector_names`: `all`
adds every subset, a name adds itself, `!name` and `!all` exclude (`!all` every subset but `min`), and a subset is
gathered when it was added and not excluded, or named itself. A list of exclusions alone starts from the default, and
`min` is gathered unless `!min` is named. `gatherExplicit` records which subsets the task named itself, for 925's
verdict. Tests: `TestGatherNamed_FollowsAnsiblesRuleInAnyOrder`, `TestGatherExplicit`.

**Lesson.** No new lesson: 848's, applied to the method itself as well as to its converter.

## 932. itemKey read a byte that is not UTF-8 as the printable U+FFFD, so two names differing only there shared one fact key, and facts.ValidKey accepted such a key (a repeat of 328 and 370) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 16); fixed on 2026-11-05 on
`fix/facts-sweep-gatherers`, before push. `itemKey` ranged over an item's name as runes. A byte that is not UTF-8
came back as U+FFFD, which is printable, so it was written into the key as U+FFFD rather than percent-encoded, and two
names differing only in that byte got the same key: one item overwrote the other. `facts.ValidKey` also ranged over
runes, so it accepted a key holding such a byte.

**Root cause.** Ranging over a Go string replaces each invalid byte with U+FFFD, and the code checked the rune it got
rather than the bytes it was given.

**Why 328 and 370 did not hold.** 328 fixed one argument splitter and 370 one email normalizer; each refuses or keeps
invalid UTF-8 in its own code. 370's lesson (a normalizer that repairs turns a malformed value into a valid key) is
this exact shape, and nothing carries it to new code that builds a key from device text.

**Fix.** `7f7a8ed3`: `itemKey` (`internal/catalog/facts/gather_subsets.go`) decodes each rune with
`utf8.DecodeRuneInString` and percent-encodes a byte that is not UTF-8 as itself. `77a1da13`: `ValidKey`
(`internal/facts/facts.go`) asks `utf8.ValidString` first. Tests: `TestItemKey_ABytesThatIsNotUTF8IsItsOwn`,
`TestValidKey_RefusesWhatIsNotUTF8`.

**Lesson.** Code that builds or checks a key from outside text works on its bytes; a rune loop silently repairs what it
should encode or refuse.

## 933. facts.holdsSecret missed a run's secret holding a byte that is not UTF-8, because the stored text holds U+FFFD where the secret holds that byte, so the fact was stored with the secret in it (a repeat in kind of 918 and 904) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** A security finding, low severity. Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts,
item 16); fixed on 2026-11-05 on `fix/facts-sweep-gatherers`, before push. `facts.Canonical` decodes a value and encodes it again, and `encoding/json`
writes each byte that is not UTF-8 as U+FFFD. A run's secret holding such a byte therefore reaches the canonical text
in a third spelling. `holdsSecret` compared the raw secret and its JSON-escaped form only, found neither, and the fact
was stored with the rest of the secret in it. Measured by `TestPrepare_ASecretThatIsNotUTF8IsStillFound`, red on the
old code. Severity is low: it needs a secret that is not valid UTF-8, and what is stored is that secret with each such
byte replaced.

**Root cause.** A matcher that runs after a conversion compared fewer spellings than the conversion can produce.

**Why 918 and 904 did not hold.** 918's lesson is this one ("a masker that converts a value before matching must match
every spelling the conversion can produce"), and 904's before it. Both fixes are in `internal/redact`'s `Masker`.
`holdsSecret` is a separate matcher in `internal/facts`, and neither fix reached it.

**Fix.** `77a1da13`: `holdsSecret` (`internal/facts/facts.go`) also compares `asStoredText(secret)`, the secret with
each byte that is not UTF-8 written as U+FFFD, as the stored text holds it. Test:
`TestPrepare_ASecretThatIsNotUTF8IsStillFound`.

**Found on review.** The branch's fp-reviewer agent, 2026-11-05, before push, applying LESSONS 244 (check the sibling
path): the same gap was in `internal/redact`. `redact.Value` converts a struct or a typed map through JSON, so a secret
that is not UTF-8 reached a run's report in its U+FFFD spelling, which the raw secret never matches. Measured red on
the old code by `TestValue_ASecretThatIsNotUTF8IsMaskedAfterJSON`, both through the call's own list of secrets and
through the shared literal set. Fixed in `93894ddd`: `withJSONSpellings` (`internal/redact/value.go`) masks that
spelling beside the raw one, `Literals.Add` registers it too, so the shared set and its snapshot carry both, and
`Literals.Forget` removes it with the raw value (`internal/redact/literals.go`).

**Lesson.** No new lesson: 918's, applied to every matcher that runs after a conversion, not only the masker.

## 934. facts.gather's filter matched Ansible's fnmatch patterns with path.Match, which reads [!d] as a class holding ! and d where fnmatch reads every character but d (a repeat in kind of 334 and 848) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Found by the API-model review sweep on 2026-11-04 (facts verdicts, item 16); fixed on 2026-11-05 on
`fix/facts-sweep-gatherers`, before push. The `filter` parameter takes `ansible.builtin.setup`'s patterns, which
Ansible matches with Python's `fnmatch`. The code matched them with `path.Match`, and a comment said the two were the
same. They differ on a negated class: `[!d]` is "not d" to fnmatch and "! or d" to `path.Match`. A filter using one
selected different facts from what it does in Ansible. This was in `v0.3.0` for the single facts.

**Root cause.** Two pattern grammars taken as one because their common cases look alike.

**Why 334 and 848 did not hold.** Both are "equal words taken as equal meanings" for Ansible's interface, and their
fixes checked argument names (334) and `gather_subset`'s meaning (848). Neither looked at the filter's grammar.
