and into `factstest/oracle.go`, the old ent algorithm, comparing Current and History after every observation.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 411.

## 970. A stored fact's device edge had a setter, so an update could move a stored value to another device (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-07, Phase 41h. `TestFact_TheSchemaRefusesEditingAValue` checked three named setters; widened to
refuse every setter on `ent.FactUpdateOne`, it found `SetDevice`, `SetDeviceID` and `ClearDevice`. No code called them,
and nothing deployed.

**Root cause.** The edge was declared `Unique().Required()` without `Immutable()`, and the test listed the setters it
expected to be missing rather than requiring none to exist. The chain hash names the device it was computed for, so a
moved row would break the receiving device's chain at verification; on the sending device it breaks the chain only
when a later row follows it, since a row cut off the end leaves a shorter chain that verifies.

**Fix.** The edge is `Immutable()`; the test refuses any `Set`, `Add`, `Append` or `Clear` method on the update builders
of Fact, FactObservation and FactCoverage, the timestamp mixin's `SetUpdatedAt` alone excepted (only an UPDATE sets
it, which the insert-only trigger test proves never runs).

**Lesson.** A test that something cannot be edited lists what may be edited, not what may not.

## 971. Dropping the fact table's last_seen_at and last_provenance columns was a contracting migration the compatibility check refused (a repeat of 833 and 389) (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-07, Phase 41h. With the columns removed from the schema, the generated migrations dropped them, and
`TestEveryMigrationIsClassifiedAsDeclared` failed: the migration contracts the schema and is not declared, and a new
contract needs the apply-time guard that is not built.

**Root cause.** Removing an unused field from an ent schema reads as a cleanup, and is a column drop the build before
it still writes.

**Why 833 did not prevent it.** 833 was about adding NOT NULL columns; its lesson (expand only) was read as being about
additions. Dropping is the other half of the same rule.

**Fix.** Both columns stay in the schema as `Optional().Immutable()`, written and read by nothing, with a comment that
the 1.0.0 golden image drops them with the squash. The migrations only add `observation_seq` (default 0) and two
tables.

**Lesson.** FAILURE_PATTERNS 389's lesson (expand only) covers removal too: a field no longer used stays until the
squash.

## 972. A state-file test passed only when Go's map order ran its zero-filled case last (fixed before push, a repeat in kind of 962)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-07, Phase 41h. `TestFileStore_AnEmptyStateFileIsReadAsNoState` passed in one package run and failed
in the next with "the state was not written whole again", size 0.

**Root cause.** The test wrote an empty and a zero-filled state file in `range` order over a map, then required the next
stable change to rewrite the state. Phase 41h stopped stable changes from touching the state, so the test now depended
on which case ran last: zero-filled last left 64 bytes and passed.

**Why 962 did not prevent it.** 962 was map order deciding a plan in product code; a test's own map order was not
looked at.

**Fix.** The next gather replaces a volatile value, which is what writes the state now, and the test requires the
volatile value in it. Run 30 times.

**Lesson.** A test that iterates a map must pass in every order; give the cases a slice when the order matters.

## 973. A fact read folded observations read after its values, so a run that replaced a value could read as having confirmed it (fixed before push, a repeat of 528 and 283)

**Symptom.** Found 2026-11-07 by both pre-gate reviews of Phase 41h (Fable and fp-reviewer), never released. Current
and History read a device's values and then its observations in separate reads with no lock or transaction, while a
record writes values first and its observation last. A record landing between the two reads (an unlocked `pleiades
facts` beside a run, or an API read beside a Runner's batch) left the reader with the old value and the new
observation: `facts.Sightings` saw the observation cover the key and write nothing the reader had, and credited the
replaced value to the run that replaced it. Transient; the next read was right.

**Root cause.** Before 41h a confirmation lived on the row it confirmed, so a read was at worst stale. Splitting
confirmations into a second table made the answer depend on two reads, and the reads ran in the writer's order.

**Why 528 and 283 did not prevent it.** Both were reads straddling a write in one store; the fix each time was local
(a lock, one statement). This was a new derived read in the same store family, written without asking what a write
between its two reads would do.

**Fix.** The ent store takes the newest observation number first and folds only observations up to it
(`Store.bound`): each record commits its rows and its observation together and numbers commit in order, so every row
an included observation wrote is visible to the rows read after. The file store reads the observations first, then
the state and values (`load`, `loadAfter`). `TestSighted_ARecordBetweenReadsCreditsNoReplacedValue` and
`TestLoad_ARecordBetweenReadsCreditsNoReplacedValue` put a record between the reads, and each also shows the old order
crediting the wrong run.

**Lesson.** A value derived from two reads is read in the reverse of the order it is written, or in one snapshot.

## 974. An order source longer than the new column would have failed its facts batch on every delivery (fixed before push, a repeat of 208, 919 and 961)

**Symptom.** Found 2026-11-07 by both reviews of Phase 41h. `FactObservation.order_source` has `MaxLen(256)`; a
Runner's order source is a free string in the batch. A longer one failed ent's validator inside Record, which is not a
data exception (`poison.Unstorable`), so the consumer returned the error and the bus redelivered the batch until its
budget ran out, holding up the batches behind it.

**Root cause.** A bound added to a new column for a value copied out of untrusted provenance, with no thought for what
the consumer does with a validation error.

**Why 208, 919 and 961 did not prevent it.** Each fixed one message shape that could never succeed; none asked that a
new column's bound be checked against what the consumer does when it is exceeded.

**Fix.** `orderColumns` stores an order whose source is too long, or whose token is past a signed 64-bit integer, as
an unknown order; `notEarlierThan` always includes unknown orders, so the fast path stays a superset. Conformance case
`unusualOrders` runs both on SQLite, PostgreSQL and the file store.

**Lesson.** A column bound on a value from a batch is a refusal; decide where it is refused before the consumer meets
it.

## 975. The new observations file refused a device's facts over one damaged line, the data a crash-emptied state file had been forgiven for (fixed before push, a repeat of 922)

**Symptom.** Found 2026-11-07 by fp-reviewer. `readSeen` returned an error for any whole line that did not decode,
which failed every Record, Current and History for the device until the file was edited by hand.

**Root cause.** The reader was written like the history file's, where a bad line must stop the read because the
chain depends on every line. Observations hold confirmations only, which the next run makes again.

**Why 922 did not prevent it.** 922 made the state file tolerant when it held these confirmations; 41h moved them to a
new file and wrote its reader from the stricter template next to it.

**Fix.** A damaged line, a digest that does not match its keys, or a line naming a coverage nothing defined is left out
and counted (`seenFile.skipped`); leaving one out can only make a value read as confirmed less recently.
`TestFileStore_ADamagedObservationLineCostsOnlyConfirmations`.

**Lesson.** A reader is as strict as what its data protects, not as strict as the file next to it.

## 976. Six comments and a changelog sentence claimed more than the seen-versus-changed code does (fixed before push, a repeat of 571 and 789)

**Symptom.** fp-reviewer, 2026-11-07: "every gather writes exactly one" observation (a Runner splits a large gather
into batches, and a redelivered batch adds another); a coverage is "written once rather than every hour" (batch splits
move with value lengths); "no field of a row has a setter" (the mixin's `updated_at` has one); "never the reverse" (a
directory sync is a no-op on Windows); "nothing already stored is ever edited" (a volatile value is replaced); the kept
columns "stay so a build from before 41h can still serve this schema" (it can, but what it writes reads as never
confirmed).

**Root cause.** Each sentence described the design's intent, written before the edge it misses was known.

**Fix.** Each now says what the code does, its exception included.

**Lesson.** FAILURE_PATTERNS 228's again: say the exception in the same sentence as the rule.

## 977. commitgate refused a comment-only ent schema edit, which go generate writes nothing for, so the only way through was --no-verify (fixed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-07, Phase 41h. Correcting three schema doc comments the review found overclaiming, the commit was
refused: "this commit changes internal/ent/schema but stages no regenerated file". `go generate ./internal/ent`
produced no change, since ent reads no Go comment, and `git commit --no-verify` was denied by the session's safety
classifier.

**Root cause.** The rule was path-based: any staged schema file needed a staged generated file. Its sibling rule
(`checkEntMigrations`) already said this check "cannot tell such an edit from a comment fix" and that a rule crying wolf
on every schema comment "would be turned off". The regenerate rule had the same blind spot and no escape but skipping
every rule.

**Fix.** `commentsOnly` compares a modified schema file with its parent, each parsed without comments and printed back
with `go/format`; only an identical result is excused. An added file, a rename, a file that does not parse, and a real
edit beside a comment-only one are still refused (`TestCheckEntRegeneratedAcceptsACommentOnlySchemaEdit`, red on the old
rule, and `TestCheckEntRegeneratedStillRefusesACodeChangeBesideComments`).

**Lesson.** A gate whose only exit is skipping every rule teaches skipping; give each rule the precision its sibling
already documented.

## 978. Two new ent tables reached CI with the backup listing fixture still holding the old table count (fixed before the pull request, a third time of a class two recaptures never indexed)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-07, Phase 41h. `make branch-containers` failed shard 6: `internal/backup`'s
`TestParseTOC_ReadsARealBackupOfThisSchema` said "the backup carries data for 38 tables, and this version knows 40".
Deterministic; it failed again alone.

**Root cause.** The test holds a recorded `pg_restore --list` of a real backup (`internal/backup/testdata/toc_migrated.txt`)
to `backup.KnownTables()`, so every new table needs the listing captured again from a real database. The branch added
`fact_observations` and `fact_coverages` and did not. `internal/backup` is a container package that imports the changed
`internal/ent`, so pr-check left it to CI by design, and `make branch-containers` caught it before the pull request.

**Why the earlier two did not prevent it.** The same fixture was recaptured on 2026-09-19 (launchables) and 2026-09-21
(controller_instances) for the same reason, written down only in the test file's header, where nobody adding a table
looks.

**Fix.** Both fixtures recaptured from PostgreSQL 15.19 through the real controller binary (`bootstrap-admin` on a fresh
database, `pg_dump -Fc` and `pg_restore --list` inside the container, the three objects planted for
`toc_planted.txt`); the test's counts are 290 entries, 40 tables, 46 foreign keys. commitgate now warns when a commit
adds an ent schema file without the recaptured listing (`checkBackupListing`, a warning, since the capture needs
PostgreSQL).

**Lesson.** A fixture that every new table invalidates is named at the place a table is added, not only in its test.

## 979. The Controller's check of which facts only a built-in may write kept the old family list when the Runner's floor grew (fixed before push, a repeat in kind of 837 and 749)

**Symptom.** Found 2026-11-07 by fp-reviewer on Phase 136a. The branch moved the loader's fact reservation from
`ReservedFactFamilies` to `collection.FactFloor` (the families plus every first-party namespace as a prefix), but
`internal/facts/entstore/provenance.go`'s `heldByBuiltin`, which drops a built-in's facts from a batch a method outside
the catalog sent, still looped over the families. A batch from an older or development-build Runner carrying
`edge.site` or `kubernetes.version` from a non-catalog method was stored on the Controller while the Runner's loader
refused the same declaration.

**Root cause.** Two tiers enforce one rule, and the rule's data had two readers; the change edited the one in the
package it was writing and missed the other. gopls showed `ReservedFactFamilies` had exactly one other reader.

**Why 837 and 749 did not prevent it.** Both were tiers disagreeing on one decision, each fixed at its site. LESSONS 350
says such a rule is one function every tier calls; here the function existed (`ReservedFact`) and the Controller read
the raw list instead.

**Fix.** `heldByBuiltin` reads `collection.FactFloor()`; `TestSubscriber_KeepsABuiltInFactOnlyFromABuiltInMethod` adds
`edge.site` and is red without the change.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 350 again: before changing a rule's data, list every reader of it (go_symbol_references) and move
all of them in the same commit.

## 980. A new build tag could drop the catalog from a release build through GOFLAGS (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** fp-reviewer, Phase 136a: `cmd/pleiades/catalog_builtins.go` gained `//go:build !nocatalog` for the release
gate, and `tools/release` built with the caller's environment and no `-tags`. A release environment with
`GOFLAGS=-tags=nocatalog` would ship a `pleiades` with no built-in method, the same version string, and a release test
that only runs `version`.

**Root cause.** A tag added for a test changes what every build of the package may produce, and the release path
trusted the environment for flags it never set.

**Fix.** The release build passes `-tags=` explicitly (a command-line flag wins over GOFLAGS).

**Lesson.** A build tag that removes function needs the release build to pin its tags.

## 981. The playbook converter reported a missing native method as a missing parameter (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** Phase 136a's release gate, on a `pleiades` built with no catalog: `ansible.builtin.file` converted to
`file.directory` and the report said "file.directory has no parameter for path" instead of naming the missing method.

**Root cause.** `setParam` looked up the method's parameters, found none for an unregistered method, and blamed the
parameter; the registration check (`checkRequired`) ran later. In a full build every mapped method is registered, so
the order never showed.

**Fix.** `setParam` checks registration first and reports `module.unmapped` with the Collection that holds the method.

**Lesson.** A check that two lookups share should test the outer one first; a build with less linked is the cheapest
place to see the order.

## 982. A new check in the loader's second pass refused a whole collections directory over a file name every earlier entry point admits (fixed before push, a repeat in kind of 823 and 887)

**Symptom.** fp-reviewer on Phase 136b PR 1 (2026-11-07): `programIdentity` held the identity it computed to
`wire.CollectionIdentity.Valid`, which refuses a group with invalid UTF-8 or a control or format character. The group is
the program's file name, which `collection approve`, pass one and `Inspect` all accept. An approved program named
`caf\xe9` or holding a soft hyphen would have stopped every program in its directory from loading (and a Runner from
starting), with `collection list` still showing it approved; the error also printed the raw path.

**Root cause.** A rule meant for readers of a stored identity was applied at the writer, in pass two, which the loader
documents as only repeating rules pass one already checked. The phase promised no behavior change.

**Why 823 and 887 did not prevent it.** Both were two entry points disagreeing on one call; the lesson (LESSONS 244)
names sibling guards, and a new validator added to one stage is the same shape.

**Fix.** The loader no longer holds a program's identity to `Valid`; readers of a stored identity will (later PRs).
The duplicate-method error quotes the path.

**Lesson.** A validation added for a later reader is placed at that reader, not at the writer, unless every earlier
entry point admits the same set.

## 983. A program's own provider text on its capabilities moved its identity digest, then the loader overwrote it (fixed before push, the class of 113)

**Symptom.** fp-reviewer on Phase 136b PR 1: `DescriptionDigest` digested `desc.Capabilities` as decoded, including
each definition's `provider` string, which the program sends and `register` then replaces with the file name. A program
could change its identity by editing text the platform throws away, and a later check rebuilding the digest from what
was registered could never reproduce the loader's.

**Root cause.** The digest was taken over what was received, while the platform keeps what it registers; the two
differed in one field.

**Fix.** The loader digests each definition with `Provider` set to the file name, as register sets it; a test proves a
program's own provider text moves nothing.

**Lesson.** An identity is computed over what is registered, never over what was received.

## 984. The engine journaled an external program's identity as the loader set it, so a name Valid refuses would make the run unreadable to the strict reader 982 planned, and invalid UTF-8 in it was rewritten by encoding/json (fixed before push, a repeat in kind of 982; its UTF-8 half the class of 370 and 932)

**Symptom.** fp-reviewer on Phase 136b PR 2 (`feat/provider-identity-136b-2`, 2026-11-07). `wire.CollectionIdentity.Valid`
(PR #132) refuses a group holding a control or format character or invalid UTF-8. 982 took `Valid` out of the loader, so
an approved program with such a file name still loads, and said readers of a stored identity would hold it to `Valid`.
This branch's engine (`30f1d172`, `internal/engine/journal_identity.go`) then recorded `provider.Identity` as it was. Two
results. A program whose name holds a soft hyphen (U+00AD) would be journaled with an identity the planned strict reader
refuses, and a reader that refuses one line refuses the whole run, which is 959's shape. A name holding invalid UTF-8
(`caf\xe9`) would be rewritten to U+FFFD by `encoding/json` on the way into the file, so the stored group would never
equal the registry's.

**Root cause.** 982 moved the check from the writer to the reader, and the writer added in the next PR wrote every value
the loader admits rather than every value the reader accepts. The writer was not checked against the reader's rule.
The UTF-8 half is a serializer that repairs: `encoding/json` turns a malformed value into a valid one, so nothing after
it can see the difference.

**Why 982 did not prevent it.** 982's lesson places a validation at the reader. It says nothing about the writer, which
from then on is the only place a value the reader refuses can come from. 370 and 932 say a repairing step must be
decided on the raw input; both were fixed in their own code (sign-in, fact keys), and nothing carries that to a new
journal field.

**Fix.** `73c94889`. `collectionIdentity` records only an identity that passes `Valid`. Any other is recorded as zero,
with one slog warning per method per run, and the entry keeps its `ProviderProgram` and `ProviderDigest` columns.
`internal/journal/reader.go`'s `decodeEntry` refuses a line whose identity fails `Valid`. Tests:
`TestJournalEntry_RecordsAProgramsIdentityAsTheLoaderSetIt` (`internal/engine/journal_identity_internal_test.go`, cases
for a name that is not UTF-8 and one holding a soft hyphen) and
`TestReadRunHoldsTheCollectionIdentityToWhatABuildWrites` (`internal/journal/format_test.go`).

**Lesson.** LESSONS 413: when a check moves from the writer to the reader, the writer writes only what that reader
accepts, and the same change tests the writer against the reader's own check.

## 985. The strict journal reader's "refuse anything the writer could not have made" was not extended to format 2's fields (fixed before push, a repeat in kind of 959; LESSONS 408)

**Symptom.** fp-reviewer on Phase 136b PR 2. `internal/journal/reader.go`'s package comment says the reader refuses
anything the writer could not have made, and `decodeEntry` checked `DAGVersion`'s digest shape. Format 2 (`30f1d172`)
added `Collection` and `InverseSpecDigest`, and the reader checked neither: a `Collection.Manifests` or an undo digest
of any shape was accepted, and so was a format-1 line carrying either key, which only format 2 writes.

**Root cause.** The branch extended the writer, the frozen file (`internal/journal/testdata/format-2/entries.jsonl`)
and the decoder's fields, and not the refusals. The refusals are a list of cases in one switch, and a new field gets
none unless someone adds them.

**Why 959 and LESSONS 408 did not prevent it.** 408 says a reader holds a format to the writer's own source and reads a
frozen file of every kind the writer has written. This branch did both halves. They prove the reader accepts what the
writer makes; neither proves it refuses what the writer cannot make, which is the other half of the reader's own
contract. Nothing fails when a new field has no refusal.

**Fix.** `73c94889`. Three new cases in `decodeEntry`: a line of a format before 2 carrying an identity or undo digest,
an identity that fails `Valid` (which checks `Manifests` against `sha256:` and 64 lowercase hex digits), and an undo
digest that does not match `digestPattern`. `TestReadRunHoldsTheCollectionIdentityToWhatABuildWrites` covers each.

**Lesson.** A field added to a strictly read format gets its refusal in the same change: what shapes the writer can put
there, and under which format versions it may appear at all.

## 986. collection.UndoDigest's doc said it covers what decides whether a recorded undo still replays, and it left out a parameter's format, run setting and secret references (fixed before push, a repeat in kind of 885; LESSONS 348)

**Symptom.** fp-reviewer on Phase 136b PR 2. `UndoDigest` (`pkg/collection/identity.go`, `13f4324a`) digested a
hand-picked set of an undo's spec and parameter fields, and its doc said that set is what decides whether a recorded
undo still replays as recorded. It left out `Param.Format` (a recorded path read as a `template_file` replays
differently), `Param.RunSetting` and `Param.SecretRefs`. A build that changed one of them would carry the same digest,
so a rollback could not tell the undo had changed.

**Root cause.** The digest is a projection that names its fields. The fields were chosen by reading the type once, and
nothing held the projection to the type, so a field that decides a replay could be missed at the start and any field
added later would be missed too.

**Why 885 and LESSONS 348 did not prevent it.** 885 added the one missing field to one sealed binding. LESSONS 348 says
a new field is added to a copy that names fields; it is a search done when a field is added, and these fields existed
before the digest did. The repository has reflection guards of this kind (`internal/archtest`'s `journalStringFields`,
the round-trip test from 743), but each covers its own type, and nothing asked a new digest for one.

**Fix.** `73c94889`. `UndoDigest` covers `Format`, `RunSetting` and `SecretRefs`, and its doc lists what it covers and
what it leaves out. `TestUndoDigest_DecidesEveryField` (`pkg/collection/identity_test.go`) walks every field of
`sdk.InverseSpec` and `collection.Param` and fails on one that is in neither the digested list nor the left-out list,
so a new field fails until someone decides it.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 414: a digest over chosen fields of a type lists every field as digested or left out, and a
reflection test fails on a field in neither list.

## 987. The changelog said 0.3 refuses a format-2 journal line by its format version, and v0.3.0 predates the format key (fixed before push, a repeat of 571 and 976)

**Symptom.** fp-reviewer on Phase 136b PR 2. `changelog/journal-collection-identity.added.md` (`30f1d172`) said "a 0.3
build refuses one by its format version rather than reading it". v0.3.0's `internal/journal/reader.go` has no `format`
key at all. It decodes with `DisallowUnknownFields`, so it refuses a format-2 line, but on the unknown key, not by
version.

**Root cause.** The sentence described the format-version mechanism this code has and assumed an older release had it.
Nobody read the tag.

**Why 571 and 976 did not prevent it.** Their rule is to say what the code does, with its exception, and their check is
a review, which is what found this. The code in question was another release's, which a search of the branch's own text
and code cannot reach.

**Fix.** `73c94889`. The fragment now says a build that knows only format 1 refuses format 2 by its version, and that
0.3.0 already refuses any line with a `format` key. Checked with `git show v0.3.0:internal/journal/reader.go`.

**Lesson.** A claim about how an older release behaves is checked in that release's tag (`git show <tag>:<path>`) or its
binary before it is written, as 959 did for v0.3.0's parallel nodes.

## 988. Both fact stores' readers held a stored Collection identity to a rule a minor release may change, so a value stored correctly would have made a device's CLI history unreadable and shown a false chain break on the Controller after such a release (fixed before push, a repeat of 975 and 922; in kind of 959 and LESSONS 397)

**Symptom.** Phase 136b PR 3 (`feat/provider-identity-136b-3`, 2026-11-08). `7bee73af` gave every stored fact a
Collection identity (`facts.Provenance.Collection`) and held it to `Provenance.CheckCollection`
(`internal/facts/provenance.go`) on read as well as on write. `CheckCollection` reads `collection.firstPartyGroups`,
and `tools/schemacompat` lets that list grow on a minor release (`first-party-group-added`, `first-party-method-moved`).
So a value stored correctly under release N, by a program method `acme.gather` or by `net.frr.config` under group `net`,
would fail the rule under N+1 once a group named `acme` or `net.frr` is added. On the CLI, the file store's `readLines`
(`internal/facts/file.go`) refused such a history line, so `Record`, `Current`, `History` and `Verify` failed for the
whole device; `readSeen` skipped such a line and `readState` cleared such a volatile value's identity. On the Controller,
the ent store's `decodeProvenance` (`internal/facts/entstore/rows.go`) cleared it, so `VerifyChain` recomputed the hash
without it and reported a break at that row, which reads as tampering. The branch's own test
`TestFileStore_RefusesAHistoryLineNamingAnotherGroup` asserted the refusal.

**Who found it.** An independent review sent through the Batch API before the branch was pushed (model
`claude-fable-5-1`, high effort; it cost $0.60), confirmed by fp-reviewer. The other review findings taken in the same
fix: the identity cache's doc now names both of its callers and why neither races (`internal/engine/journal_identity.go`);
the Controller's subscriber checks the identity only after a batch is admitted, so a batch it drops is not warned about;
a test that a program's facts carry the identity the loader set, through an engine run
(`TestFacts_AProgramsFactsNameTheIdentityTheLoaderSet`, `internal/engine/facts_identity_test.go`); and
`ErrCollectionIdentity` no longer repeats the `facts:` prefix.

**Root cause.** A write rule was used as a read rule. The rule depends on release data, the first-party group list, so
it answers differently for the same stored value under different releases. A reader that refuses or edits a stored value
by it turns a later release into data loss (the CLI) or a false tamper report (the Controller). The chain already covers
the identity as stored, so the read check protected nothing the chain did not.

**Why 975 and 922 did not prevent it.** Both made a fact file reader tolerant of a line it could not use, and 975's
lesson is that a reader is as strict as what its data protects. The history reader is strict on purpose, because the
chain needs every line, and this branch added a new refusal to that strict reader. Nothing in either lesson asks whether
a new refusal depends on data that changes between releases.

**Why 959 and LESSONS 408 did not prevent it.** 959 was a
reader out of step with what the writer wrote, which made whole records unreadable, and 408's remedy is to hold the
reader to the writer's own source. This branch did that: `CheckCollection` is the writer's own function. But it is the
writer's source as of the reading release, not the one that wrote the value. LESSONS 397 names that mixed-release pair
for a value whose meaning changes; here the value is unchanged and the rule moves.

**Fix.** `df02959e`. `CheckCollection` runs only where a value is written: both stores' `Record`, the engine's
`factProvenance` and the Controller's subscriber. `readLines`, `readSeen`, `readState` and `decodeProvenance` return the
identity as stored, and the chain, which covers it, finds an edited one. `CheckCollection`'s doc says it is a rule for
writing, never for reading. Tests: `TestFileStore_AStoredIdentityALaterRuleRefusesStillReads` (a correctly chained line
the rule refuses still reads and verifies) and `TestFileStore_AnEditedIdentityBreaksTheChainAndReadsAsStored`
(`internal/facts/file_identity_test.go`).

**Lesson.** LESSONS 415: a reader of a hash-chained record hashes and returns what was stored, and a rule that depends
on data a later release may change runs only where the value is written.

## 989. The changelog and the runbook guide said every stored fact names its Collection, the same identity the journal records, and four cases store none (fixed before push, a repeat of 571, 976 and 987)

**Symptom.** Phase 136b PR 3. `changelog/fact-collection-identity.added.md` said "every stored fact now names the
Collection its method came from" and "the same identity the run journal records", and `docs/04-writing-runbooks.md`
said the same. Four cases store no identity: a method in no first-party group, a program whose file name fails
`wire.CollectionIdentity.Valid`, a batch from a Runner before this change, and an identity the Controller clears. The
fact provenance description in `internal/apispec/apispec.go` listed two of the four. fp-reviewer named it a repeat of
571, 976 and 987.

**Root cause.** 228's class: each sentence said the rule and left out the exceptions, though the same branch wrote the
code that makes them (the engine's zero identity for a method in no group, 984's `Valid` check, the subscriber's
clearing).

**Why 571, 976 and 987 did not prevent it.** Their rule (say the exception in the same sentence as the rule) is checked
only by a review. 987 was one day earlier in the same phase, and its lesson is about older releases, not about the
branch's own exceptions. Nothing reads a changelog sentence against the code before the review does.

**Fix.** `79c60df0`. The fragment, the guide and the apispec description name all four cases. The fragment also says
that a build from before this change reads a value stored with an identity without it, so its chain check reports that
value as a break, and that no release before this one keeps facts.

**Lesson.** 976's again: before writing "every" or "the same as" about a stored field, list each path in the branch
that stores it empty and name those paths in the sentence.

## 990. The setup filter's refusals and its wildcard review quoted the playbook's own pattern into the conversion report, and the branch's tests asserted the quoted text (fixed before push, a repeat of 330 and of 968's last case)

**Symptom.** fp-reviewer on `feat/converter-facts-filters`, 2026-11-08, before push. The converter's new translation
of `setup`'s `filter` (`internal/forge/playbook/facts_filter.go`, from `db1b0419`) built its refusals (a pattern that
matches no fact, for one) and its review note on a pattern with a wildcard with `strconv.Quote` of the pattern. The
conversion report is written to be shared and holds names and positions only (330). The branch's own tests asserted
the quoted text (`named: strconv.Quote("nosuchfact")` in
`TestTranslate_ASetupFilterItCannotExpandIsRefusedNamingThePattern`, `"ansible_distribution*" may also match` in
`TestTranslate_ASetupFilterGlobNamesWhatItMayAlsoMatch`), so the leak was locked in, and
`TestReport_RefusedValuesNotPrinted` had no filter case.

**Security.** Information exposure through a report written for sharing, in our own code, found before release. A
filter pattern is usually a fact name, but the report's promise is that no playbook text reaches it, and a mistyped or
pasted value is exactly what a refusal prints. Measured: the guard test, given a refused and a globbed filter, is red
on the old code and green on `6695385c`.

**Root cause.** 330's: a message written for a new refusal is free to quote its input, and the guard test covers only
the paths it lists. A contributing cause, stated plainly: while relaying an earlier review to the building agent, the
main thread told it to leave the quoted patterns as they were. That instruction overrode a recorded pattern, and
nobody checked the pattern before giving it.

**Why 330 and 968 did not hold.** 330's fix is a sentinel test with one case per refusal path. A new path joins it only
when its author adds a case. 968 found the same leak in the converter's fact conditions a day earlier, and its fix
covered those paths only. Neither puts a new refusal under the guard by default. And the instruction to keep the quotes
came from the main thread. It is not in the diff, so a review sees only its result; fp-reviewer's pass over the diff
is what caught it.

**Fix.** `6695385c`. Each finding names the pattern by its place: "setup's filter pattern" when it is the only one,
"pattern 2 of setup's filter", "patterns 2, 3 of setup's filter". `TestReport_RefusedValuesNotPrinted`
(`internal/forge/playbook/translate_test.go`) carries a refused pattern and a globbed one; each row of
`TestTranslate_ASetupFilterItCannotExpandIsRefusedNamingThePattern` asserts the place is named and the pattern is not
printed. The migration guide says a finding names a pattern by its place, never its text.

**Lesson.** A new refusal in the converter adds its case to `TestReport_RefusedValuesNotPrinted` in the same change.
An instruction to keep code as it is gets the same check as a change (LESSONS 416).

**Class.** C7 (secret exposure through logging or output; CWE-532)
**Portable.** yes: any error or report message that quotes the input it refused
**Detector.** sentinel values through every refusal path, asserting none appears in any output; see ~/vuln-corpus/README.md

## 991. A filter of min facts under gather_subset ['!all', '!min'] converted and gathered them where Ansible gathers none, because setupSubset rewrote the subset before the filter's check read it (fixed before push, the class of 848; a sibling guard, LESSONS 244)

**Symptom.** fp-reviewer on `feat/converter-facts-filters`, 2026-11-08, before push. The branch refused a filter
keeping only hardware facts under a `gather_subset` that leaves hardware out. Its twin had no guard: a filter of min
facts (`{filter: ansible_os_family, gather_subset: ['!all', '!min']}`) converted. Ansible's base facts hold none of the
mapped facts, so its filter keeps nothing there, while `facts.gather` always gathers min, so the converted task
gathered and kept them.

**Root cause.** `setupSubset` (`internal/forge/playbook/adjust.go`, 848's fix) wrote its meaning back into the task's
params, replacing the subset as written with `[min]` or `[min, hardware]`. The filter's check read the params after
that, so it could see whether hardware was gathered but not that min had been removed.

**Why 244 and 848 did not prevent it.** 244 says to check the sibling of a guarded path. The sibling here was a case of
the same input, min removed rather than hardware, and the fact its guard needed had been erased by an earlier step.
848's fix computed the subset's meaning correctly for the method and returned it by overwriting the input, which no
later reader of the same params could undo.

**Fix.** `6695385c`. `parseSubset`, `subsetHasHardware` and `subsetHasMin` are factored out of `setupSubset`, and the
filter's check (`facts_filter.go`) reads the subset as written through them. A filter under a subset that leaves out
both min and hardware is refused. Pinned by the row "a min fact with min and hardware left out" in
`TestTranslate_ASetupFilterItCannotExpandIsRefusedNamingThePattern` (`internal/forge/playbook/facts_filter_test.go`).

**Lesson.** A step that turns a shared input into its meaning leaves the input as written for every later reader, and
each reader derives what it needs through the same functions (244's helper rule). When one case of an input is
refused, list its twins (each subset removed alone and together) and give each a row.

## 992. Two documented behaviors of the Windows and non-Windows setup split had no test, so removing either passed: the Windows half keeping the task's gather_subset, and a later read of the split's shared register converting (fixed before push, the kind of 888; LESSONS 213)

**Symptom.** fp-reviewer on `feat/converter-facts-filters`, 2026-11-08, before push. `18ed2ce5` splits a filtered
`setup` into a filtered gather for devices that are not `WindowsShellCapable` and an unfiltered one for those that are
(`internal/forge/playbook/facts_split.go`). Its file comment says the Windows half runs without the filter, its
subsets kept, and that both halves take the task's register, so a later read sees the one that ran (`convert.go`'s
`|| p.split` lets that read convert). Removing either the kept subset or the `|| p.split` left every test green.

**Root cause.** The split's tests held other parts of it, such as which half runs on each host. The two behaviors its
comment promised were reasoned about and never asserted.

**Why 213 and 888 did not prevent it.** 213 asks that a test of a protection fail with the protection removed. It is
applied to the tests a branch writes, and these two behaviors had no test to run that way. 888 found the same kind of
gap (wiring with no test, checks that could not fail), and its check is the review, which is what found this one.

**Fix.** `6695385c`. `TestTranslate_ASplitSetupKeepsItsSubsetAndItsRegisterReads`
(`internal/forge/playbook/facts_split_test.go`) converts a filtered setup with `gather_subset: [hardware]`, registered,
and a later task reading the register. It asserts both gathers carry `[min hardware]` and that the later task converted.
It fails on either mutation.

**Lesson.** Each behavior a comment or doc states about a new transform gets a test that fails when the line making it
true is removed: one mutation per sentence.

## 993. args.value's fixed advice "Quote the value in the playbook" was printed with every setup filter refusal and with refusals already on main that quoting cannot fix (fixed before push, a repeat in kind of 270, 488 and 600)

**Symptom.** Found in the branch review of `feat/converter-facts-filters`, 2026-11-08, before push. The code
`args.value` (`internal/forge/playbook/codes.go`) describes "a value whose meaning differs between Ansible's YAML 1.1
and the runbook's YAML 1.2, or that the native parameter cannot take", and its fix text said only "Quote the value in
the playbook so its meaning is plain." Every setup filter refusal used the code, and so did refusals already on main in
`modules_win.go`, `modules_pkg.go`, `modules_file.go`, `modules_misc.go` and `native.go` (a checksum algorithm with no
native equivalent, `remote_src: true`, and others). Quoting changes none of them.

**Root cause.** A shared code's advice was written for its first use, the YAML meaning. The code's description grew a
second use and its advice did not, and every site that picked the code by its description printed advice for the
first.

**Why 270, 488 and 600 did not prevent it.** Their rule is to follow the advice once before shipping it. Advice in a
shared table is printed by every site that uses the code, so following it where it was written proves nothing for the
others, and a new site is chosen by the code's description, not its advice.

**Fix.** `6695385c`. The advice now reads "Where the YAML meaning is the problem, quote the value in the playbook so
its meaning is plain; otherwise change the value as the finding says, or write the task by hand." The fix adds
no test that holds a code's advice to the messages that use it.

**Lesson.** A code's advice is a claim about every message that carries it. When a code gains a use, read its advice
against the new message, and split the code when one sentence cannot fit both.

## 994. Three comments and the "decides on every host" wording claimed more than the code or its tests show (fixed before push, a repeat of 571, 789 and 976)

**Symptom.** Found in the branch review of `feat/converter-facts-filters`, 2026-11-08, before push.
- `Adjustment.Notes` (`internal/forge/playbook/table.go`, from `db1b0419`) said "one finding each". `a6e708df`, on the
  same branch, joined an Adjust's notes into one finding, since the report keeps one per code and position.
- `facts_major.go` (from `573fd245`) said a comparison with text raises in Jinja. Only an ordering does; an equality
  with text is just never true.
- The migration guide (`5ea9e20d`) and the changelog fragment said `ansible_distribution_major_version | int` decides
  "on every host" what Ansible decides. It is measured against Ansible's output only on the Linux images the fact
  fixtures capture, and reasoned from Ansible's source for Windows, macOS and FreeBSD.

**Root cause.** 228's class. One sentence was made false by a later commit on the same branch (789's shape), and two
stated the rule without its exception or its evidence.

**Why 571, 789 and 976 did not prevent it.** Their rule, say the exception in the same sentence and reread text a
branch's changes touch, is checked only by a review. 976 was the day before, in another phase. Nothing reads a comment
against the code before the review does.

**Fix.** `6695385c`. The Notes doc says they are joined into one finding and why; `facts_major.go` says an ordering
against text raises and an equality with text is never true; the guide and the fragment say what is measured and what
follows from source.

**Lesson.** 976's again, plus one: a claim that a conversion matches Ansible "on every host" names the hosts it was
measured on (LESSONS 404).

## 995. The system Go became go1.27.3 while go.mod's toolchain line named go1.26.10, and GOTOOLCHAIN=auto never switches down, so local builds, tests and scans ran on another Go than CI (fixed on this branch; on main until it merges, live here from 2026-11-08 10:29; a repeat of 552's second trap)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-08, the gate for pull request #135 (`feat/converter-facts-filters`): gosec-check failed on 15
"stale waivers" in files the branch never touched. Diagnosis took about an hour, through two wrong guesses, each
disproven by a rerun: first the 2800M memory cap, then memory in general. The proof came from gosec's own JSON
("cannot decode export data", "export data version 5 is greater than maximum supported version 4") and from
`/var/log/dpkg.log`, which shows `golang-1.27-go` from the longsleep PPA installed at 10:29 that day.

**Root cause.** go.mod named `toolchain go1.26.10`. The Makefile set no `GOTOOLCHAIN`, so Go's default `auto`
applied, and `auto` switches only up to a newer release, never down. Every local make target built, tested and
scanned with the machine's go1.27.3, while CI (`.github/actions/setup-go`, 545's fix) installed go1.26.10. gosec
v2.28.0, built by go1.26, could not decode the export data go1.27 wrote. 996 is what that did to the check.

**Why 552 did not prevent it.** 552 found this trap on the Mac, whose go1.27.2 scanned without `GOTOOLCHAIN` judged
the wrong standard library. Its fix named `GOTOOLCHAIN` only for the Mac's vuln phase (`maccheck -phase vuln`). The
Makefile, where every other local command starts, stayed on `auto`, and nothing compared the Go that built a tool
with the module's. The diagnosis also repeated 552's lesson: memory was the first guess twice, and the answer was
what the run reads that the commit does not fix, here a newer Go (LESSONS 406).

**Fix.**
- `187bd977`: the Makefile exports `GOTOOLCHAIN` from go.mod's toolchain line (`GO_TOOLCHAIN`), so every go command
  a recipe runs uses the release CI installs. `ensure-tool` reinstalls a tool whose build Go differs from that
  release, not only one whose module version differs.
- `edf91629`: a carriage return is dropped from the line, as the CI action drops it, and with no toolchain line the
  value is `auto`.
- `cf8efe74`: `tools/doctor` holds each scanner to the Go release that built it, not only to its pin
  (`TestCheckTools_AToolAnotherGoBuiltIsAFix`), and doctor and `ensure-tool` read that release whatever the
  binary's path holds (`TestBuildRelease_ReadsTheReleaseWhateverThePath`).
- The move itself (`86cbb601`) names `go 1.27.0` and `toolchain go1.27.3`, and gosec is pinned at v2.30.0
  (`187bd977`), since v2.28.0 failed even rebuilt with go1.27.

**Lesson.** A release CI installs from a file is the release every local entry point reads from the same file;
`auto` is not a pin (LESSONS 418).

## 996. gosec-check read gosec's "Golang errors" as no findings, so a gosec that skipped 1,345 packages would have passed a module it had not read (fixed on this branch; on main since 968aac16, 2026-08-04)

**Symptom.** The run in 995. gosec listed 1,345 packages under its JSON's "Golang errors" and made no findings in
them. tools/gosec-check failed only because 15 waivers happened to sit in skipped files, and it reported them as
stale. With no waiver there it would have printed "all individually waived".

**Security.** A fail-open in our own security gate. Whether gosec skipped files in an earlier run, here or in CI, is
not known, because the check never read the field.

**Root cause.** gosec reports a file it cannot type-check under "Golang errors" and goes on. gosec-check decoded only
`Issues`, as it had since it was written (`968aac16`), so a report with nothing read looked like a clean one. LESSONS
138 asks that "I could not look" get a third answer apart from "it is not there"; the check had two.

**Why earlier fixes did not prevent it.** 552's lesson says a scanner killed for memory has said nothing, not
"clean". That scanner printed nothing and failed. This one exited normally and named what it skipped, in a field
nothing read. LESSONS 99 and 138 state the rule, and no check applied it to gosec's output.

**Fix.** `f63e65f5` and `cf8efe74` (`tools/gosec-check/skips.go`, `main.go`).
- gosec's whole-run "-" warning fails the check, telling the reader to rebuild gosec with this toolchain.
- Each skipped file fails unless `gosec-waivers.json` names it under `skips` with a reason. A skip waiver gosec did
  not need is stale and fails, and one with no reason is refused (`TestLoadWaivers_ASkipWithoutAReasonIsRefused`).
  The one file that never type-checks by design, flakegate's container-scan fixture under testdata, is waived by name.
- `TestCheckSkips_ASkipIsNeverAPass`, and `TestJudge_ARecordedSkippingRunFails`, which runs the verdict (`judge`)
  and the decoder (`decodeReport`) over gosec's own recorded JSON (`tools/gosec-check/testdata/gosec-skipped.json`
  and `gosec-clean.json`). It fails when the "Golang errors" tag is renamed or the skip check dropped.
- Run with the old gosec, the check fails naming 1,343 files.

**Lesson.** A scanner that can skip input fails on a skip (LESSONS 417).

**Class.** C9 (fail-open: a check that could not read its input reported a pass; CWE-636)
**Portable.** yes: any gate that judges a tool's findings and ignores the field where the tool names what it skipped
**Detector.** a test over the tool's own recorded output from a run that skipped input, asserting the gate fails; see
~/vuln-corpus/README.md

## 997. Two diagnostic gosec runs ended by timeout left their go list and compile children running, five copies of internal/ent's compile at about 800 MB each, and free memory fell to 1.3 GB (fixed before push by stopping them by PID; a repeat in kind of 340, LESSONS 327)

**Symptom.** 2026-11-08, while diagnosing 995. Two gosec runs were started under `timeout`. After they ended, five
compiles of `internal/ent` at about 800 MB each were still running, with their `go list` parents, and free memory on
this 9.7 GiB machine fell to 1.3 GB. The two oldest `go list` parents were not the diagnostic runs' at all: they dated
from the gate's own gosec run 40 minutes earlier, which had returned its JSON while its loader's children went on.

**Root cause.** Not established beyond this: the signal `timeout` sent ended gosec and did not end the `go list` and
compile processes it had started.

**Why 340 and LESSONS 327 did not prevent it.** 340 says anything a run starts outside the harness survives an outside
kill, and to check for leftovers after one; LESSONS 327 says to stop by process group and confirm with `ps`. Both were
written for tests and an unattended driver, and a short diagnostic run was not treated as either.

**Fix.** The processes were found and stopped by PID (the running comparison by its task), and `ps` afterwards
listed no gosec, `go list` or compile process left; free memory was back at 5.6 GB. No code changed.

**Lesson.** A diagnostic run of a tool that starts the Go toolchain is a run with children: give it no outside kill
shorter than it needs, and after any kill, look for `go list` and `compile` processes before starting the next run.

## 998. hashivault's endpointFor joined reference elements with url.URL.JoinPath, which takes them as already escaped, so %2E%2E in a path reached Vault as `..` and %2F became a separator (fixed on this branch; on main since c6946faa, 2026-08-25, Phase 78b; the class of 72 and 438)

**Symptom.** Found by gosec v2.30.0's new rule G125 during the Go 1.27 bump, 2026-11-08. For a reference path
element written `%2E%2E`, the test's stub server received `/v1/kv/data/../../sys/health`. `%2F` in a mount or a
path became a separator, and a literal `%` sent the request to the base URL. The comment beside the call said
JoinPath escapes each segment, the opposite of what it does.

**Security.** A reference could address a Vault API path outside the secret it named, read with the source's token.
Reasoned by fp-reviewer and not run against a real Vault: on a kv v1 mount, a path of
`%2E%2E/auth/token/lookup-self` with key `id` could return the source's own Vault token, through a ServeMux
clean-and-redirect that keeps `X-Vault-Token`. Our own code; no upstream fix applies.

**Root cause.** `url.URL.JoinPath` treats each element as an escaped path segment. `checkSegments`
(`internal/credtype/lookup/hashivault/reference.go`) refused literal dot segments and judged the text before that
decoding, so an encoded one passed it and was decoded afterward. The wrong comment stated the safety property the
code lacked (228's class), so no reader had a reason to check it.

**Why 72 and 438 did not prevent it.** 72's fix escaped each value with `url.PathEscape` in the API's link builder,
and 438's lesson says a guard decides on exactly the bytes the far side will read. Both fixes stayed in their own
packages, and nothing looked for other URL builders that took input. `checkSegments` judging text that is decoded
later is 438's case exactly.

**Fix.** `e0e8e3cc` and `edf91629`. `endpointFor` passes the mount and each path element through `url.PathEscape`
before `JoinPath`, and the comments in `hashivault.go` and `reference.go` say what JoinPath takes.
`TestAnEncodedSegmentStaysOneLiteralSegment` (`internal/credtype/lookup/hashivault/hashivault_test.go`) holds encoded
dots, an encoded slash in the path and in the mount, and a literal percent to both the path Vault decodes and the
bytes on the wire, and was red on the old code. A G125 waiver stays on the escaped call, because gosec's taint
analysis does not credit `url.PathEscape`. A user-visible change: a path written pre-encoded is now read literally
(`changelog/vault-reference-escaping.security.md`).

**Lesson.** An element taken from input is escaped by the code that builds the URL, every time, and the test reads the
wire bytes as well as the decoded path. When a fix like 72's lands, search the module for the other builders.

**Class.** C4 (path traversal and confinement escape; CWE-22)
**Portable.** yes: any URL built with `url.URL.JoinPath` or `url.JoinPath` from elements taken from input
**Detector.** gosec G125; a test sending encoded dots, an encoded slash and a literal percent through each URL builder,
asserting the wire bytes; see ~/vuln-corpus/README.md

## 999. x/sys v0.49.0, brought in by x/tools v0.52.0, renamed LandlockRulesetAttr.Access_fs to Handled_access_fs and grew the struct, so the loader's confinement no longer compiled (fixed before push)

**Symptom.** `86cbb601`, 2026-11-08. `internal/loader/confine_linux.go` did not compile. It first showed as a skipped
file in the new gosec-check report (996), before any build ran.

**Root cause.** golang.org/x/tools v0.52.0 is the first release whose export data reader decodes go1.27's (ent's code
generation failed with "export data version 5 is greater than maximum supported version 4"). It required
golang.org/x/sys v0.49.0 (from v0.48.0), which names `LandlockRulesetAttr`'s field as the kernel's header does and
adds `Quiet_*` fields. x/sys is a v0 module, so a minor release may rename a field. The archive holds no earlier entry
for a dependency bump changing a field a security control fills; 254 is Landlock, but a threading defect.

**Fix.** `86cbb601`. The field is renamed, and the new quiet fields are left zero. The kernel copies the struct with
`copy_struct_from_user`, which accepts a struct larger than it knows when the extra bytes are zero, so an older
kernel reads the same ruleset. The comment above `restrictThreadAndStart` says so. `internal/loader`'s confinement
tests ran on real Landlock, none skipped.

**Lesson.** A rename fails the build, which is the safe case. The quiet one is a field the struct gains, which takes
its zero value with no error. When a bump changes a type a security control fills, read its diff field by field and
say in the code what each new field's zero value means to the kernel.

## 1000. The Makefile's new comment said every go command uses go.mod's toolchain, but before GNU make 4.4 an exported variable does not reach a parse-time $(shell), so CLEAN_ROOM_IMAGE still took the machine's Go (fixed before push, the class of 686; an outside review confirmed the claim, against LESSONS 392)

**Symptom.** fp-reviewer, before push, measured it with a two-line makefile on this machine's GNU make 4.3. Ubuntu
24.04 ships 4.3 and macOS 3.81. The Fable review through the API had confirmed the wrong claim.

**Root cause.** `187bd977`'s comment said what `export` reaches without measuring it. `CLEAN_ROOM_IMAGE ?=
golang:$(patsubst go%,%,$(shell go env GOVERSION))` (on main since `8e6d7f3e`, 2026-09-29) runs at parse time. Make
before 4.4 passes no exported variable to `$(shell)`, so that go ran with `auto` and named the machine's go1.27.3. On
main, with no export at all, it took the machine's Go too (995).

**Why 686 did not prevent it.** 686 was what make exports reaching a child through `MAKEFLAGS`, and its rule (LESSONS
344) is for a program that runs make. This is what an export does not reach, inside one Makefile, and the answer
depends on the make version. LESSONS 392 says to verify every claim an outside model makes; a review agreeing with a
claim is a claim too.

**Fix.** `cf8efe74`. `CLEAN_ROOM_IMAGE` reads `GO_TOOLCHAIN`, falling back to `go env GOVERSION` only with no
toolchain line, and the comment at the top of the Makefile says what reaches what.

**Lesson.** A claim about what a make variable reaches is measured on the oldest make that runs the file (macOS's
3.81 here), with a makefile small enough to read whole. Agreement from a reviewer is not a measurement.

## 1001. The gosec pin's commit carried the G125 waiver for a line the next commit created, with a reason describing a fix not yet made (fixed before push, a repeat of 685; LESSONS 152)

**Symptom.** Found before push. The commit pinning gosec v2.30.0 carried a waiver keyed to a `hashivault.go` line
that only the hashivault fix (998) created, and its reason described that fix.

**Root cause.** The waivers were written at the tip, where gosec ran, and the change was then split into commits by
topic. A waiver is a `file:line` citation (LESSONS 152) and a statement about the code. It is true only in a commit
that holds that code.

**Why 685 did not prevent it.** 685's lesson asks for `make gosec` and a re-reviewed waiver on each edit to a waived
file. That was done at the tip, which is where gosec runs. Nothing runs gosec on each commit; only the tip is gated.

**Fix.** The history was rebuilt so each waiver lands with its code: `187bd977` carries only the `tlscert` G302
waiver, and `e0e8e3cc` carries the hashivault fix with its G125 waiver. The tip is byte-identical to the tip before
the rebuild. `187bd977`'s message says the G125 finding is fixed and waived in the next commit.

**Lesson.** A waiver is committed with the line it names. When a change is split into commits after gosec ran on the
whole, move each waiver with its code and read each reason against its own commit.

## 1002. Dockerfile.runner and Dockerfile.controller still built from a golang:1.26-bookworm digest after the go line moved to 1.27.0, and no gate the branch ran builds them (fixed before push, the class of 559 and 631)

**Symptom.** Both reviewers (the Fable review through the API and fp-reviewer), before push. The official golang
image sets `GOTOOLCHAIN=local` (checked here in `golang:1.26.8-bookworm`'s config), so the builder stage's `go mod
download` would refuse a module whose go line is 1.27.0. `edf91629`'s message says a 1.26 base "would have fetched
1.27.3 at image-build time"; under `GOTOOLCHAIN=local` it would not, and the build would fail instead.

**Root cause.** Only `tests/e2e`'s packaging gates build these images. pr-check leaves `tests/e2e` to CI (559's
census), and `make branch-containers` runs the container packages a branch changes (631), so the Dockerfiles were
outside every local check. The move to go1.26.10 changed both Dockerfiles in the same commit as go.mod (`7b8ccafc`,
552). This move started from go.mod and the Makefile, and the Dockerfiles were not on its list.

**Fix.** `edf91629`. Both build from `golang:1.27.3-bookworm`, pinned by its index digest.

**Lesson.** A toolchain move lists every file that names a Go release (go.mod, the CI action, the Makefile, each
Dockerfile's builder, the lab's runbooks and README, the scaffold) and changes them together. A file no local gate
builds is checked by reading it (LESSONS 418).

## 1003. The Crawl journal's strict reader held a stored Collection identity to wire.CollectionIdentity.Valid, whose format-character check reads Go's Unicode tables, so a Go release could make a journal one build wrote unreadable to another (fixed on this branch; on main since 73c94889, 2026-11-07, merged in #133; a repeat of 988)

**Symptom.** Phase 136b PR 4 (`feat/provider-identity-136b-4`, 2026-11-08). `decodeEntry` in
`internal/journal/reader.go` refused a line whose identity failed `Valid`, and one refused line makes the whole journal
unreadable. `Valid`'s `controlOrFormat` check uses `unicode.IsGraphic`, category `Cf` and `Variation_Selector`, which
come from the Unicode tables of the Go release that built the binary. go1.26 carries Unicode 15.0.0 and go1.27, which
main moved to in #136, carries 17.0.0 (each toolchain's `unicode.Version`, read here). So a stored identity one build
accepted could fail the same check in a build made with another Go, and its journal would not read.

**Who found it.** An independent review of the PR 4 and PR 5 plan, sent through the Batch API (Fable, the batch named
burn5).

**Root cause.** The class of 988: a reader of a durable record held a stored value to a rule a later release can
change. Here the release is Go's, not The Pleiades'. `73c94889` added the check on read in PR 2.

**Why 988 did not prevent it.** 988's fix and LESSONS 415 looked at rules built on Pleiades release data (the
first-party group list) and treated `Valid` as a shape check that depends on no release data. LESSONS 415's own text
said "the journal's strict reader holds an identity to `wire.CollectionIdentity.Valid`" as the settled choice. Nobody
asked whether `Valid` read data a toolchain upgrade changes, and `unicode`'s tables are such data.

**Fix.** `51ec65eb`. `Valid` is split. `Shape` holds what no Go release can change: byte lengths, UTF-8 validity, NUL
and '/', the fixed C0, DEL and C1 code point ranges (`controlCode`), the digest's pattern, and Program and Version
agreeing. `Valid` is `Shape` plus `controlOrFormat`, for writers. The journal reader holds a line's identity to
`Shape`. Tests: `TestReadRunHoldsTheCollectionIdentityToWhatABuildWrites` (`internal/journal/format_test.go`), red on
the old reader, and `TestControlCodeIsAlsoControlOrFormat` (`pkg/wire/identity_test.go`), which walks every rune to
show `Shape` refuses nothing `Valid` accepts.

**Lesson.** When a reader's check is called release-independent, list what it reads, the standard library's tables
included. A check that reads `unicode`, `time`'s zone data, `mime` types or any table Go updates is a writer's rule
(LESSONS 415).

## 1004. The JSON Schema builder wrote "required": null for an object with no required property, so the published run-report.json, with wire.CollectionIdentity in it, was invalid JSON Schema 2020-12 (fixed before push, the class of 765)

**Symptom.** Phase 136b PR 4, before push. Every field of `wire.CollectionIdentity` is `omitempty`, so
`internal/jsonschema`'s `Builder.Object` built a nil `required` list and wrote it as `"required": null` into
`docs/reference/schemas/run-report.json`. JSON Schema 2020-12 requires `required` to be an array. A consumer that
validates the schema itself (ajv, Python's jsonschema) would refuse the whole contract.

**Who found it.** fp-reviewer, which named 765 as the nearest precedent.

**Root cause.** The builder put `required` in the object unconditionally. The house validator reads null as nothing
required, so every house test passed, and no builder test had an all-optional struct.

**Why 765 did not prevent it.** 765 was a published schema whose field names said more than the code. Its fix
corrected those names, and its lesson was to read a record against its source. Nothing reads a generated schema
against the JSON Schema specification, and the one validator the tests use accepted the invalid form.

**Fix.** `21303261`. An object with no required property leaves the keyword out. The same commit makes an `omitzero`
field optional, as `omitempty` already was, since `encoding/json` leaves a zero value out (the step's new `collection`
field is written with `omitzero`). Test: `TestBuilder_AnAllOptionalObjectNamesNoRequired`
(`internal/jsonschema/jsonschema_test.go`).

**Lesson.** A generator of a published contract is tested on its edge shapes (no required field, no properties, every
tag option `encoding/json` reads), and a validator that is more lenient than the specification is not evidence that a
schema is valid.

## 1005. Three intermediate commits failed their own checks: Builder.Object refused wire.CollectionIdentity for a missing doc comment, because clireport's ModelFiles gained pkg/wire/identity.go only in a later commit (fixed before push, a repeat of 1001 and 685; LESSONS 152)

**Symptom.** Phase 136b PR 4, before push. In three commits short of the tip, `make docs-gen-check` errored:
`internal/jsonschema`'s `Builder.Object` refuses a type whose doc comment it cannot find, and the files it reads doc
comments from are `internal/clireport`'s `ModelFiles`. The commit that put `CollectionIdentity` in the report model came
before the commit adding `pkg/wire/identity.go` to that list. The tip passed.

**Root cause.** As in 1001: the change was written and checked at the tip, then split into commits by topic, and only
the tip is gated. A generator's input list is a statement about which files exist and matter, and it is true only in a
commit that holds the code it serves.

**Why 1001 and 685 did not prevent it.** The writer's brief named 1001, and it happened anyway. 1001's lesson is about
a waiver moving with its line, and this was a generator's file list, which the lesson does not name. Neither lesson
adds a check, and nothing runs a check on each commit of a branch.

**Fix.** The history was rebuilt so each commit carries the `ModelFiles` entry its types need. The tip is
byte-identical to the tip before the rebuild.

**Lesson.** After splitting a change that passed at the tip, run each commit through the checks the tip ran (for
example `git rebase --exec '<check>' origin/main`), or at least the generators and the packages each commit touches.
Naming the past pattern in a brief does not make anything check it.

## 1006. Comments and a guide paragraph the branch made false: two comments said readers hold Valid, the new Valid doc, and docs/13 saying only digests are compared and a same-declaration pair logs nothing (fixed before push, a repeat of 571, 789, 976 and 994)

**Symptom.** Phase 136b PR 4, before push.
- `internal/loader/identity.go` and `internal/engine/journal_identity.go` said readers hold an identity to `Valid`.
  After 1003's fix, a reader holds it to `Shape`.
- The new doc of `Valid` in `pkg/wire/identity.go` needed correcting. As fixed, it says a reader of a delivered or
  stored identity holds it to `Shape`, and a process that stores a received identity (the Controller's facts subscriber)
  is a writer of its store and holds it to `Valid`, which `facts.Provenance.CheckCollection` calls.
- `docs/13-releases-and-stability.md` said only the digests are compared and two builds with the same declarations log
  nothing. The Runner notes different versions at debug level and a built-in method whose Collection the Controller did
  not name at info level.

**Root cause.** 228's class. The branch changed the code these sentences describe (789's shape), and the guide stated
the rule without its exceptions.

**Why 571, 789, 976 and 994 did not prevent it.** Their rule (reread the text a branch's changes touch, and say the
exception in the same sentence) is still checked only by a review. 994 was the same day, on another branch.

**Fix.** In the rebuilt history: `51ec65eb` for the loader's, the engine's and `Valid`'s comments, `36337ef9` for
the guide, which now says the digests decide whether the declarations differ, the versions only choose the warning's
wording, and names the debug and info notes.

**Lesson.** 994's again. When a change renames what a rule is called (here, `Valid` split into `Shape` and `Valid`),
search the comments and docs for the old name before review.

## 1007. The Controller's journal store writes a Runner's batch with no check of its Collection identity, unlike the facts subscriber, so an identity no build writes can be stored and copied into a rollback's steps (open: passed to Phase 136b PR 5; on main since 30f1d172, 2026-11-07)

**Symptom.** Found while building Phase 136b PR 4, 2026-11-08. The journal's ent store (`saveOne` in
`internal/journal/ent_store.go`) and its subscriber (`internal/journal/subscriber.go`) store each entry's
`Collection` as a Runner sent it. Neither calls `Shape`, `Valid` or any other identity check. The facts path checks a
Runner's identity before storing it (`internal/facts/entstore/subscriber.go` calls `CheckCollection`). This branch's
rollback plan copies a stored identity into the steps a rollback's dispatch carries to a Runner (`wire.RollbackStep`),
which decides nothing by it yet.

**Root cause.** `30f1d172` (PR 2) added the identity columns to the journal store's write path, and the check on write
went to the engine, which projects the identity on the Runner. The Controller's store took the Runner's word.

**Status.** Open. Passed to Phase 136b PR 5. The effect of storing such an identity has not been measured.

**Lesson.** Pending the fix. The facts subscriber's rule applies here too: a process that stores a received identity is
a writer of its store and holds it to `Valid` (1006).

**Resolved 2026-11-08 (fixed on `feat/provider-identity-136b-5`, Phase 136b PR 5, `b62e4d37`, with `8b7f1b6e` from
review).** The journal's ent store holds each entry it saves, from the subscriber or any other caller, to what the
engine's projection writes (`identityProblems`, `internal/journal/identity.go`): an identity that passes `Valid`, a
program's identity only on an entry a program ran and a first-party one only on an entry none ran, and an undo digest
of a digest's shape. What fails is stored as none and the entry is kept, as the facts subscriber keeps a fact whose
identity it clears. Since `8b7f1b6e` the store itself logs each cleared identity or undo digest with the job, device,
node, method and reason (1030). Tests, red on the old code: `TestSubscriberStoresNoIdentityTheEngineWouldNotWrite` and
`TestEntStoreSavesNoIdentityTheEngineWouldNotWrite` (`internal/journal/subscriber_identity_test.go`), and
`TestEntStoreLogsToTheLoggerItIsGiven` (`internal/journal/ent_store_logger_test.go`). The store does not hold the
identity to this Controller's group routing, for the reason in 1019. `TestStores_KeepTheSameIdentityForOneTask` holds
the journal store and the fact store to the same identity for one task.

## 1008. httpapi.Join decoded the ref it was given and then cleared RawPath, so a caller's url.PathEscape("r1/mgmt") reached the server as r1/mgmt, one name as two segments; catalystcenter.New did the same to its base path (fixed on this branch; on main since 35f391a1, 2026-09-24, and in catalystcenter since ad1ff164, 2026-08-06; the mirror of 998, the class of 72 and 438)

**Symptom.** Found by the escaping sweep on `fix/url-escaping`, 2026-11-08: a review through the Batch API (Fable,
the batch named burn5) given 82 URL-building call sites with their context. A containerlab node named `r1/mgmt`,
escaped by its caller as `r1%2Fmgmt`, reached a stub server as `.../nodes/r1/mgmt/logs`, and `a%3Bb` went out as a
literal `;`, which a Java server reads as a path parameter. Every `virt.clab` call goes through Join
(`pkg/clabapi.Client.Call`), as do `http.request`'s device paths and onboarding's OpenAPI read.
`pkg/catalystcenter.New` kept only the decoded path of its base URL, so a Catalyst Center behind a proxy prefix
holding `%2F` or `%3B` was called under a different path.

**Security.** Low severity. A name holding `/` could reach another route of the same origin, and the request carried
the device's credential. The dot-segment check held, so a name could not climb above the base path. Shown against a
stub server; not run against a real device. Our own code; no upstream fix applies.

**Root cause.** Join checked `rel.Path`, the decoded form, which is right for the dot check. It then built `out.Path`
from that form and set `out.RawPath = ""`. With no RawPath, `url.URL.String()` escapes Path again, and `/` is the one
character it leaves alone, so the one escape `url.PathEscape` exists for was the one lost. 998 broke the same contract
from the other side: `url.URL.JoinPath` takes its elements as already escaped, and hashivault passed them raw. Here the
callers passed text already escaped, and Join decoded it.

**Why 998, 72 and 438 did not prevent it.** 998 was fixed the same day in hashivault alone. Its lesson asks for a
search of the module's other URL builders, and this sweep is that search. 72's fix escaped values in the API's link
builder only, and 438's lesson stayed in the container engine's guard.

**Fix.** `15e2d5a8` keeps the escaped form beside the decoded one. That first fix built the escaped form from
`EscapedPath`, which falls back to escaping Path whenever RawPath as a whole is not valid escaping, so one raw byte
beside a `%XX` still lost every escape (`/items/a%2Fb c` went out as `/items/a/b%20c`). `556bedef` fixed that before
push: `escapedPathOf` (`pkg/httpapi/escape.go`) keeps each `%XX` as written and escapes only the raw bytes a path may
not hold. `520f18f6` keeps catalystcenter's base path as escaped (then normalized; 1014). Tests, red on the old code:
`TestJoin_SendsTheCallersEscaping` and `TestJoin_KeepsEachEscapeAsWrittenBesideARawByte`
(`pkg/httpapi/join_escape_test.go`), `TestCall_SendsEachNameAsOneSegment` (`pkg/clabapi`),
`TestNew_KeepsTheBasePathAsWritten` (`pkg/catalystcenter`), and `FuzzJoin` (`pkg/httpapi/httpapi_test.go`), which now
varies the base and counts every escaped slash (1016). User-visible: `changelog/url-escaping.security.md`.

**Lesson.** A helper handed text already escaped keeps it escaped to the wire: judge the decoded form, send the escaped
one. As 998's lesson says, the test reads the request line a stub server receives.

**Class.** C4 (path traversal and confinement escape; CWE-22)
**Portable.** yes: any helper that parses an escaped path, sets url.URL.Path from it and clears RawPath
**Detector.** a stub server asserting the request line for a path holding %2F, %3B and a raw space beside %2F; see
~/vuln-corpus/README.md

## 1009. httpapi.Join ran its control-character check on the ref as written and its dot check on the decoded path, so %00, %0A and %7F passed, and so did a "..;" segment, which a Java server reads as ".." (fixed on this branch; on main since 35f391a1, 2026-09-24; a repeat of 438)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/url-escaping`, 2026-11-08, while fixing 1008. `hasControl(ref)` read the raw string, so a
control character written as an escape passed, though the server acts on the decoded path. The dot check compared each
decoded segment with `.` and `..`, so `..;x` passed. A Java server (Batfish is one) drops a `;` path parameter and
resolves the segment as `..`.

**Root cause.** Two guards in one function judged two forms of the same input. 438's lesson is that a guard decides on
exactly the bytes the far side will read.

**Why 438 did not prevent it.** 438's fix and lesson stayed in the container engine's guard (Phase 119b). Nothing held
the module's other URL guards to it, the same gap 1008 names.

**Fix.** `556bedef`. Join refuses a control character in the decoded path too, and `dotSegment`
(`pkg/httpapi/escape.go`) refuses a dot segment followed by a `;`. Tests, red on the old code:
`TestJoin_RefusesWhatTheDecodedPathHolds` and `TestJoin_RefusesADotSegmentInAnyEncoding`
(`pkg/httpapi/join_escape_test.go`).

**Lesson.** Every check in one guard reads the same form of its input, the one the far side acts on. For a URL path
that is the decoded path, read as each kind of server reads it, `;` included.

**Class.** C4 (path traversal and confinement escape; CWE-22)
**Portable.** yes: any path guard that checks the raw text for one rule and the decoded text for another
**Detector.** %00, %0A, %7F and ..;x through each path guard, each expected refused; see ~/vuln-corpus/README.md

## 1010. batfish, gns3 and aiprovider's Google kind appended a path already escaped to url.URL.Path, the decoded field, so every name was escaped twice ("prod west" went out as prod%2520west) (fixed on this branch; on main since b5baafd5, 2026-10-15, in aiprovider, 8444bb5b, 2026-10-22, in batfish, and 3fe90317, 2026-10-23, in gns3; the mirror of 1008)

**Symptom.** Found by the same sweep, 2026-11-08. `pkg/batfish.Client.do` did `u.Path += path` with names escaped
by `url.PathEscape`, so `String()` escaped each `%` again. The network `prod west` was sent as `prod%2520west`, which
Batfish reads as a network named `prod%20west`. `CreateNetwork` sent the raw name in its query, and the work item's
JSON body named it raw too, so a network whose name held a space or a reserved character could be created and then
never given a snapshot, parsed, asked a question or deleted. `pkg/gns3`'s `raw` set `u.Path = path` the same way;
latent, since GNS3 issues project ids as UUIDs. `pkg/aiprovider`'s Google kind asked for a model `a b` as `a%20b` and
for `tunedModels/x` as `tunedModels%2Fx`.

**Root cause.** `url.URL.Path` holds the decoded form, and `String()` escapes whatever is written there. Each client
built its request path itself rather than through one helper that keeps both forms. The archive holds no earlier
double escape.

**Fix.** `335a56d4`, `918db0e2`, `c1145893`. All three send through `httpapi.Join`, which sends an escaped path as
written and refuses a dot segment. Every aiprovider kind now resolves its path through Join, and an endpoint with no
base URL is an error rather than a nil dereference. Tests, red on the old code: `TestDeleteNetwork_SendsTheNameEscapedOnce`
and `TestUploadSnapshot_NamesOneNetworkEverywhere` (`pkg/batfish/client_escape_test.go`),
`TestNodes_SendsTheProjectIDEscapedOnce` (`pkg/gns3`), `TestGoogle_SendsTheModelNameEscapedOnce` (`pkg/aiprovider`).
`TestChat_PostsJSON` holds that every kind still posts JSON after the move.

**Lesson.** Never write escaped text into `url.URL.Path`. A client joins a request path through the one helper that
keeps the escaped form (`httpapi.Join`).

## 1011. url.PathEscape leaves "", "." and ".." as they are, so pkg/cml sent GET /api/v0/labs/.. with the controller's token, and internal/ui's path.Join turned a record named ".." into a link to /ui (fixed on this branch; on main since db3b8b9f, 2026-09-13, in internal/ui, and 654537b1, 2026-10-23, in pkg/cml; a sibling in kind of 815)

**Symptom.** Found by the same sweep, 2026-11-08. A CML lab reference of `..` went out as `GET /api/v0/labs/..`
with the controller's token, which the controller resolves to `/api/v0/` rather than to a lab; `FetchPCAP`'s key took
the same path. In the UI, `path.Join(prefix, resource, url.PathEscape(id))` resolved `..` to `/ui` and `.` to the
record's own list, from a list row, a reference, a section's controls, a live stream and a write's redirect. The API
accepts `..` as a device name. A request with an empty segment (`/ui/devices//edit`), which only a client sending
paths unresolved can make, was routed by chi as `{id} = ""` and rendered that record's edit form with an empty form
action.

**Security.** Low severity, for `pkg/cml`: a lab reference could address a controller path that is not a lab, with the
controller's token. Shown against a stub; not run against a real CML.

**Root cause.** PathEscape escapes characters, and a dot segment is made only of characters it leaves alone. No
escaping makes such an id addressable, since a browser resolves `%2E%2E` too. `path.Join` then cleans what PathEscape
