`TestProjectPatch_AnEchoedRedactedURLNeverReplacesTheStoredOne` (`internal/api`),
`TestProjectsView_SavingTheEditFormNeverReplacesAStoredURLItShowsRedacted` (`internal/ui/resources`).

**Lesson.** As 580: a redacted copy is never accepted where the real value is. A write behind a read that redacts
recognizes the exact text the read showed and keeps the stored value for it.

**Note 2026-11-10 (1127).** The echo rule held only while the stored URL had not changed since the read: a stale form's
placeholder passed the source checks and was saved as a manual project's URL. `RefuseEmbeddedSecret` now refuses the
placeholder text too. Since 1124, an echo that keeps a stored credential URL saves rather than being refused.

## 1088. A manual or archive project stored a source URL carrying a credential in plain text, because entStore.checkSource returned for every type but git before its embedded-secret check (fixed on this branch; on main; a sibling of 458, whose check it skipped)

**Symptom.** Found by the writer on `fix/patch-projects-partial`, 2026-11-09. `POST /projects`, the PATCH and the UI's
project form accepted a manual or archive project whose `scm_url` carried a credential (`https://user:token@host/repo`),
stored it in the unencrypted `scm_url` column, and served it back: redacted for the shapes the detector knew, raw for
the shapes 1089 lists.

**Root cause.** `entStore.checkSource` (`internal/project/ent_store.go`) opened with
`if p.SCMType != SCMGit { return nil }`. That early return was for the source policy (`AdmitsSource`), which is about
where git may fetch from. The embedded-secret refusal, which is about what the column may store, sat after it, so it
ran for git projects only.

**Why 458 did not prevent it.** 458's fix changed what `HasEmbeddedSecret` counts as a credential, not which projects
reach it.

**Shown red first.** `TestStore_RefusesACredentialInTheURLForEveryType` and `TestStore_AStoredCredentialInTheURLIsReadableAndMustBeChanged` (real ent store) returned nil for manual and archive; `TestProjects_ACredentialInTheURLIsRefusedForEveryType` answered 201 for a manual or archive create and 200 for a manual PATCH; the UI form answered 303.

**Fix.** `b9395276`. `checkSource` refuses a credential in the URL first, for every type, and only then returns early
for a type that is not git. The refusal also runs in the UI form. A row stored before the rule stays readable, its URL
shown redacted or withheld, and its next save is refused until its URL changes. Tests:
`TestStore_RefusesACredentialInTheURLForEveryType` and `TestStore_AStoredCredentialInTheURLIsReadableAndMustBeChanged`
(`internal/project`), `TestProjects_ACredentialInTheURLIsRefusedForEveryType` (`internal/api`),
`TestProjectsView_RefusesACredentialInTheURLForEveryType` (`internal/ui/resources`). The refusal is a breaking change,
and its changelog fragment says so.

**Lesson.** A rule about what a store may hold runs for every record the store writes. Placed after an early return
written for a different rule, it inherits that rule's scope.

**Note 2026-11-10 (1124, owner decision).** "Its next save is refused until its URL changes" is reversed: only creation
refuses a stored value. An edit that leaves the URL saves; an edit that changes it, or turns the project git (1125), is
held to every rule.

## 1089. HasEmbeddedSecret and RedactedSourceURL were a list of credential shapes, and three review passes each found shapes the list missed, each one stored in plain text for a manual or archive project and shown raw by GET, the list and the UI (fixed on this branch by an allowlist; a repeat of 458; LESSONS 190 and 277)

**Symptom.** Found across three review passes on `fix/patch-projects-partial`, 2026-11-09, once 1088 let a manual or
archive project's URL reach the detector. Each shape below passed `HasEmbeddedSecret`, so it was stored as written for
a manual or archive project, and `RedactedSourceURL` returned it raw to `GET /projects/{id}`, the list and the UI:

- first: URLs no parser reads (`https://svc:PW@host:badport/x`, a space in the host), `git+https://TOKEN@host`, and a
  scheme-relative `//bot:PW@host`;
- then: a password holding `/`, `?` or `#`; compound schemes with an ssh part (`git+ssh+https://TOKEN@host`); lenient
  slash forms (`https:/user:pw@host`); and tokens in a query string;
- then: an `@` written as `%40`, as the fullwidth U+FF20 or as the small U+FE6B, and query names
  `redact.SecretName` does not match (`sig`, `X-Amz-Signature`, `apikey`).

**Root cause.** The detector named the shapes that carry a credential. A shape nobody listed passed, and each pass of
review could only add the shapes it thought of. Its parse of a URL was also one parser's reading, so a URL that parser
rejects or reads another way than git does fell outside every listed shape.

**Why 458's fix did not hold.** `f5512ff5` fixed 458 by adding positions to the list (any password, any user over http
or https, a colon in an ssh user), as LESSONS 277 advises: list where the protocol accepts a credential and check each.
That kept the detector a denylist, which LESSONS 190 had already said fails open on every shape nobody listed. The first
two review passes on this branch extended the list again, and each next pass found more.

**Fix.** `b9395276` replaced the list with an allowlist, `internal/project/secret_url.go`:

- any `?` or `#` in the URL is refused, for every type, since a repository source needs neither and no list of secret
  parameter names covers them all;
- a URL holding `%40` or a lookalike `@` (U+FF20, U+FE6B, or their percent encodings) is refused;
- a URL with no `@` is clean;
- a URL with an `@` is clean only as a clean `ssh://`, `git+ssh://` or `ssh+git://` login (one `@`, a user with no `:`
  or `%`, parsed cleanly) or an scp-like `user@host:path` as go-git reads it; every other URL with an `@` is refused.

Redaction follows the same rule: a URL is shown as written only when it is clean, its userinfo is cut out only on an
exact structural match, and otherwise it is withheld whole as `(withheld: the URL carries a credential)`. Tests:
`TestStore_RefusesACredentialInAURLAParserMisreads` and the tables in `internal/project/source_test.go` and
`internal/project/source_secret_test.go`, `TestProjects_ACredentialInTheURLIsRefusedForEveryType` and
`TestProjects_ASourceURLMayCarryNoQueryOrFragment` (`internal/api`).

Known limits, written in the file's comment: a token in the path (`https://host/token/abc`) cannot be told from a path
and is not caught; a token used as an ssh login name is allowed by design; and a backup restore (`pg_restore`, or a
SQLite file copy) writes rows without the store's checks, so a row the rule refuses can come back, and every reader then
shows it redacted or withheld.

Over-refusal accepted by design: an `@` in a path (`https://host/org/repo@v1`) and any query or fragment (`?ref=main`,
`#readme`) are now refused. The test rows that pinned them as clean were changed. The owner may revisit this.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 190, with its note of 2026-11-09: after a content detector misses a second time, replace the list
of bad shapes with an allowlist of what is proved clean, rather than adding the shape that was missed.

**Note 2026-11-10 (1123).** "Any `?` or `#` in the URL is refused" held for the literal characters only: the allowlist's
own terms, and its `@` list, were read from the raw text, so `%3F`, `%23`, double encodings and Unicode lookalikes
passed. The rules now check the URL as NFKC and percent decoding leave it, to a fixed point (`revealed`, LESSONS 431).

## 1090. A refused git source and a recorded sync error repeated the caller's URL, password included, because ClassifySource built its message from go-git's parse error and scrubURL could not clean a URL it could not parse (fixed on this branch; on main; a repeat of 457 and 626; in kind of 72)

**Symptom.** Found by the writer on `fix/patch-projects-partial`, 2026-11-09. A source URL go-git cannot parse was
refused with go-git's own error inside the message, and that error quotes the URL:
`parse "https://user:pa/ss@host/r": invalid port ":pa"`. The text reached the API's 400, the UI's form error and a
sync's stored `sync_error`. A sync of a stored URL that may carry a credential recorded its transport error after
`scrubURL`'s pattern scrub, which a password holding a `/` passed.

**Root cause.** A refusal quoted what it refused, through a third-party error that quotes its input, and the scrub meant
to clean it depended on the URL having a shape it could parse.

**Why 457 and 626 did not prevent it.** 457 fixed `kubeapi.checkServer`, and 626 the CML and GNS3 login errors. Each fix
was at its own site; every validator and client writes its own error path, and nothing checks the others. 72 is the
same class in kind: a response that repeats caller input.

**Fix.** `21e76857`. `ClassifySource` refuses a parse failure in a fixed phrase ("that is not a repository address git
can read"). `scrubURL` (`internal/project/git.go`) withholds the transport error whole when the URL may carry a
credential (`HasEmbeddedSecret`, the allowlist of 1089), and otherwise strips only userinfo quoted from elsewhere.
`AdmitsSource`'s refusals are fixed phrases. Tests, shown red on the old code:
`TestProjects_ARefusedSourceNeverRepeatsItsURL` (`internal/api`), `TestSync_NeverRecordsAStoredCredentialInItsError`
and `TestSync_WithholdsATransportErrorQuotingALookalikeAt` (`internal/project`).

**Lesson.** As 457: when the input can carry a secret, an error names the problem and never quotes the input, and a
parser's error is the input quoted.

**Note 2026-11-10 (1128).** `scrubURL` ran only when an error was stored, so an error stored under an older rule kept
what a newer rule withholds. `project.ShownSyncError` applies it again when the error is shown.

## 1091. A project could bind another organization's git credential, and a sync sent it to the host the project named (fixed on this branch on create, PATCH, the UI form and at sync; on main; a repeat of 456; LESSONS 276)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-projects-partial`, 2026-11-09. The API's `checkCredential` and the UI's `usableForGit`
searched `ListAllCredentials` across every organization and never compared the credential's organization with the
project's, and `projectAuth.ResolveAuth` (then in `cmd/controller/main.go`) resolved a credential by its id alone. So a
project in organization A could bind organization B's source control credential, and its sync sent B's secret to
whatever host A's project named. Proven red: the API answered 201 and 200 over the real credential store, the UI
answered 303, and the resolver returned organization B's password.

**Root cause.** The facts that decide where a stored secret goes were taken from the borrowing record. The lookup checked
that the id existed and was usable for git, not whose it was.

**Why 456 did not prevent it.** 456's fix was in `resolve.BorrowedKubernetesSecrets`, the one lookup it found. The
project lookups were separate code with their own search, and nothing holds every credential lookup to the owner's
organization.

**Fix.** `7b717e94`. Create, PATCH and the UI form refuse a credential the project's organization does not own, answered
exactly like an id that does not exist, so a caller learns nothing about another organization's credentials.
`projectAuth.ResolveAuth` (`cmd/controller/project_auth.go`) checks the owner before the resolver runs, so another
organization's secret is never decrypted for the project; a project already bound to one stays readable and its syncs
fail with a fixed message. Tests, shown red on the old code: `TestProjects_BindOnlyACredentialOfTheirOwnOrganization`
(`internal/api`), `TestProjectsView_BindsOnlyACredentialOfTheProjectsOwnOrganization` (`internal/ui/resources`),
`TestProjectAuth_RefusesACredentialOfAnotherOrganization` (`cmd/controller`).

**Limits.** This keeps a project and its credential in one organization. It does not keep a caller to theirs:
authorization is by token scope across the deployment, so a caller holding `project:write` can still create a project
in the victim organization and bind that organization's credential. Who may write a project in which organization waits
on per-organization authorization (98, open; see its note of 2026-11-09). The UI's credential chooser still lists every
organization's credentials, now labelled with their organization, because `view.Field.Options` sees no record and so
cannot narrow the list to the project's organization; that needs a framework hook, and is the owner's decision.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 276 applies to every lookup that lends a stored secret, not only the one that taught it.

## 1092. A NUL in a project's name, description, scm_url or scm_branch reached the store, where on PostgreSQL it would answer 500 (fixed on this branch; on main; a sibling of 371, 919 and 1079)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-projects-partial`, 2026-11-09, beside 1076's bounds. Nothing in the API or the UI form
refused a NUL in a project's text fields. lib/pq sends a NUL in a text parameter and PostgreSQL refuses it, as 371
measured, so the write would fail at the database and answer 500. SQLite keeps the NUL, so the SQLite-backed tests
could not see it. The 500 on PostgreSQL is reasoned from 371's and 1079's measurements; this branch's tests check the
refusal, not a PostgreSQL write.

**Root cause.** As 371: whether a value is legal differs by database, and the check in front of the store did not
cover the production dialect's rule.

**Why 371, 919 and 1079 did not prevent it.** Each fixed its own site (sign-in, the facts and journal consumers, the
kubeconfig import). Nothing holds every text field a caller writes to a NUL check before a PostgreSQL write.

**Fix.** `2392263c`. `project.CheckNUL` (`internal/project/bounds.go`) refuses a NUL with 400 naming the field on create
and PATCH, and the UI form refuses it beside the field. Tests: `TestCheckNUL_NamesTheFirstFieldHoldingANUL`
(`internal/project`), `TestProjects_RefuseANULInATextField` (`internal/api`),
`TestProjectsView_RefusesANULInATextField` (`internal/ui/resources`).

**Lesson.** As 371 and LESSONS 426: the validator in front of a store holds each value to what the production dialect
can store, NUL included.

## 1093. A refused UI project create or edit re-rendered the submitted scm_url raw, so the 422 page held the password just typed (fixed on this branch; on main; low severity)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-projects-partial`, 2026-11-09. A UI form refused for any reason is redisplayed with what
was submitted. A project create or edit refused for a URL like `https://user:token@host/repo` therefore put the
credential back into the page, in the URL control's value.

**Root cause.** The form framework redisplays each submitted value as typed, with no way for a field to say its value
may carry a secret.

**Fix.** `f51df2a1`. `view.Field.RefusedValue` (`internal/ui/view/field.go`), applied at the four refusal re-renders in
`internal/ui/web/resources.go`. The project form's URL field declares it as `RedactedSourceURL`, so a refused form shows
the URL redacted or withheld, as a stored URL is shown. It is not blanked, because a blank would let a second save
clear a manual project's URL. Test: `TestProjectsView_ARefusedFormNeverShowsATypedCredentialURL`
(`internal/ui/resources`).

**Limit.** Every other UI form still re-renders what was submitted; only a field that declares `RefusedValue` is covered.

No earlier entry is this class. The nearest is 226, whose fix refused a prefill for a password control because
`field.templ` writes a password into a value attribute.

**Lesson.** A form that redisplays what was submitted redisplays a secret too; a field whose value may carry one says
how it is shown when refused.

## 1094. The UI harness's fake project store handed out len+1 ids while its Delete compacted the slice, so an id could repeat after a delete (fixed for the project fake on this branch; open: the inventory fake hands out ids the same way, and the announcement fake's Update and Delete keep nothing; a repeat in kind of 1053; LESSONS 424)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-projects-partial`, 2026-11-09. `fakeProjectStore.Create`
(`internal/ui/resources/harness_test.go`) set `p.ID = len(s.projects) + 1`, and its `Delete` removed the entry from the
slice. After a delete, the next create could take the id of a project still stored. The real store never reuses an id.

**Root cause.** As 1053: the fake was written to let the handlers run, not to keep the store's contract.

**Why 1053 did not prevent it.** 1053 swept the device fake and the device retire and inventory delete fakes for
copy-on-read, save under a version check and the store's not-found errors. How a fake hands out ids was not on its list,
and the project fake was not swept.

**Fix.** `b9395276`. The project fake hands out ids from a counter (`nextID`), never reusing one. Test:
`TestFakeProjectStore_NeverHandsOutAnIDTwice` (`internal/ui/resources/fake_projects_test.go`).

**Status.** Open for two other fakes in the same file, found while writing this record, from reading; not run.
`fakeSetStore.Create` sets `set.ID = len(s.sets) + 1` beside a `Delete` that compacts the slice, the same rule.
`fakeAnnouncementStore`'s `Update` and `Delete` answer nil and keep nothing, 1053's shape.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 424. A fake keeps the store's id rule too: an id is never handed out twice.

**Note 2026-11-10 (`fix/patch-inventories-announcements`).** Still open. The branch added `UpdateWith` to both fakes in
`internal/ui/resources/harness_test.go`. `fakeSetStore.UpdateWith` hands its fold copies of the member lists, as the
real store does, and saves through the fake's `Update`. `fakeAnnouncementStore.UpdateWith` answers
`announce.ErrNotFound`. Both clauses of the status above still hold: `fakeSetStore.Create` still sets
`len(s.sets) + 1` beside a `Delete` that compacts the slice, and `fakeAnnouncementStore`'s `Update` and `Delete` still
answer nil and keep nothing. Found while writing this note, by reading, not run: the comment on
`fakeAnnouncementStore.UpdateWith` says the fake "holds none", but `newFakeAnnouncementStore` seeds announcement 1, so
an `UpdateWith` of id 1 answers not found where the real store would fold over it. No UI view edits an announcement
today, so nothing reads that answer yet.

## 1095. A blank credential name answered 500, and a NUL in a credential's or a credential type's text, or in an input source's metadata, reached the store, where on PostgreSQL it would answer 500 (fixed on this branch; on main; a sibling of 1092, 371 and 1079)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09, beside the partial PATCH (1075's note). A blank
credential name passed every check in front of the store and failed ent's `NotEmpty` validator, so create and PATCH
answered 500. Nothing refused a NUL in a credential's name, description or external reference, in an input source
binding's metadata, or anywhere in a credential type: its name, description, input schema or injector document. SQLite
stores a NUL. PostgreSQL refuses one in a `character varying` column and in `jsonb`, which holds a credential's
external references, a binding's metadata, and a type's input schema and injector document, so the write would fail at
the database and answer 500. The PostgreSQL 500 is reasoned from 371's and 1079's measurements; this branch's tests
check the refusals. Neither ent schema bounds these names beyond `NotEmpty` (there is no `MaxLen`), so there was no
length rule to mirror.

**Root cause.** As 1092 and LESSONS 426: a rule the store held with no mirror in front of it, and 371's dialect gap.

**Why 1092, 371 and 1079 did not prevent it.** Each fixed its own site. 1092, one branch earlier, covered projects, and
its entry said nothing holds every text field a caller writes to a NUL check. The credential and credential type writes
were not swept.

**Fix.** `84428cdc`. The rules sit where every writer meets them, so the web UI's forms are held to them as the API
is. The credential store refuses a blank name and a NUL in a credential's name, description or external reference, and
a NUL in an input source's metadata (`internal/credstore/text.go`). `credtype.CredentialType.Validate` refuses a NUL
anywhere in a type (`internal/credtype/text.go`). Each refusal is a `credtype.TextError` that names the field and
repeats nothing the caller sent. The API answers it with 400, and the forms show it beside the box it was typed into.
Tests: `TestCredentialWritesRefuseABlankNameAndANUL` and `TestInputSourceMetadataRefusesANUL` (`internal/credstore`),
`TestValidateRefusesANULAnywhere` and `TestTextErrorSaysABlankNameIsRequired` (`internal/credtype`),
`TestCredentialCreate_RefusesABlankNameAndNUL` and `TestCredentialTypeCreate_RefusesNUL` (`internal/api`),
`TestCredentialForms_RefuseANULBesideTheField` (`internal/ui/resources`).

**Lesson.** LESSONS 426. Put the rule in the store or the domain validator, where a new writer cannot pass it by.

## 1096. Three 403 refusals quoted another organization's credential or credential type by name, so a token holding credential:write without credential:read learned names it had no scope to read (fixed on this branch; on main; the class of 1091 and 72)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09. Three credential store refusals named another
organization's record by its name: a credential of another organization's custom credential type, a template binding
another organization's credential (`PUT /templates/{id}/credentials`), and a credential reading an input through
another organization's source credential (`PUT /credentials/{id}/input-sources`). The API answers each with 403 and the
store's text. `credential:write` does not imply `credential:read`, so a token holding only the write scope learned
names it had no scope to read.

**Root cause.** Each refusal was written in the words an operator of the refused record would want, and the caller was
not that operator.

**Why 1091 and 72 did not prevent it.** 1091 answered another organization's git credential exactly as an id that does
not exist, in the project code it fixed. 72 kept a caller's own path out of a response. Neither swept the credential
store's refusals for text naming a record the caller may not read.

**Fix.** `87e3c529`. Each refusal names the record by the id the request sent, which tells the caller which one was
refused and nothing else, the rule `PATCH /projects/{id}` already keeps for a credential. The API description lists
the 403 on `POST /credentials`, `PUT /templates/{id}/credentials` and `PUT /credentials/{id}/input-sources`
(`e327ef1c`). Test: `TestCredentials_ACrossOrganizationRefusalNamesNothingOfTheirs`
(`internal/api/credentials_cross_org_test.go`).

**Lesson.** A refusal names only what the caller sent or may read. The store's refusals are held to that as a
handler's are, because the API passes their text through.

## 1097. A credential type edit made every stored value of a secret input readable in plain text through GET /credentials/{id} and the UI's edit form: clearing the input's secret flag did it in one request, and removing the input and adding it back as non-secret in two (fixed on this branch; on main; across organizations with the ordinary operator scopes, through 98)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09. A read decides what to redact from the credential
type's current input schema. An edit of a custom type could change that schema under the values its credentials had
already stored, and the API answered 200 each time. Clearing `secret` on an input through `PATCH /credential-types/{id}`
or `PUT /credential-types/{id}/inputs` did it in one request. Removing the input, through those routes or the web UI's
Remove input control, left its values in every credential of the type, and adding it back as non-secret showed them:
two requests. `GET /credentials/{id}` and the credential's edit form then showed the stored secret. These routes need
only the ordinary operator scopes, and authorization is by token scope across the deployment (98), so a caller could
do this to a type, and read its credentials, in any organization. The values a removal left behind also made each such
credential refuse every later update, naming the input its type no longer declared.

**Root cause.** Whether a stored value is secret was read from the schema at display time rather than kept with the
value, and nothing tied a schema edit to the values stored under it. The schema could move from secret to not secret
while the values stayed.

**Earlier entries.** None is this class. Searches of the archive for a secret flag, a non-secret input, redaction from
the current schema and an edit of a credential type found none. 221 is about a managed type's input controls in the UI,
and 120 is masking too much, the other direction.

**Fix.** `50319b68`, in the store (`internal/credstore/type_inputs.go`), so the API and the UI meet it alike. An edit of
a custom type is held to three rules. First, an input the stored type marks secret cannot become non-secret; the 400
names the input and says to remove it and add it again. Second, in the same transaction, every credential of the type
keeps a value, an external reference and an input source only for an input the type declared both before and after
the edit, with one exception: an input added as secret keeps what is stored under its id, read back only as
`$encrypted$`. So a removal deletes what credentials held for the input, an add as non-secret deletes anything stored
under its id, and any edit deletes values an earlier removal left behind, which makes a credential stuck on one
editable again. Third, an edit is refused with 409 while a credential of the type cannot be decrypted, rather than
rewriting its ciphertext blind. The purge pages through the credentials and rewrites each through the same encryption
hook as every write.

Every type edit, and every credential create, update and input-source write, first takes the type row's write lock
inside its transaction (`lockType`) and reads what it checks under it, so a credential write checked against a secret
input is never committed under a plain one. On PostgreSQL the lock is a row lock: read committed reads each statement
afresh, so without it a type edit commits in the middle of a credential write. The type lock tests race type edits
against credential writes, and land an edit inside a write through a seam to prove the edit waits:
`TestTypeEditsRacingCredentialWritesNeverShowASecret_SQLite` and `TestACredentialWriteHoldsTypeEditsOff_SQLite`
(`internal/credstore`), and their `_PostgreSQL` twins (`internal/credstore/locktest`). With the lock removed, the
PostgreSQL run shows a value written as secret in plain text. Other tests: `TestUpdateTypeRefusesMakingASecretInputPlain`,
`TestUpdateTypeRemovingAnInputDeletesWhatCredentialsHoldForIt`, `TestUpdateTypeDeletesValuesAnEarlierRemovalLeftBehind`,
`TestUpdateTypeReAddingARemovedInputFindsNothing` and `TestUpdateTypeRefusesWhileACredentialCannotBeRead`
(`internal/credstore/type_secret_test.go`); `TestCredentialTypePatch_RefusesMakingASecretInputPlain`,
`TestCredentialTypePatch_RemovingAnInputDeletesWhatCredentialsHoldForIt` and
`TestCredentialTypePatch_PurgesValuesAnEarlierRemovalLeftBehind` (`internal/api`);
`TestCredentialTypes_RemovingAndAddingBackAnInputNeverShowsItsSecret` (`internal/ui/resources`). The production guide,
the start-here guide, the API description and the UI's removal confirmation say what an edit now does. The refusals and
the purge are breaking changes, and their changelog fragment says so.

**Cost.** The lock is exclusive, so one type's credential writes queue behind one another across every organization,
and behind an edit's purge. Measured on a SQLite file database and stated in the production guide: a credential write
held it for about 0.35 milliseconds, and a purge read and rewrote a credential in about 35 microseconds, so a type with
ten thousand credentials holds its writers for about a third of a second when an input is removed.

**Checked and not a defect.** Two writers take no lock. Deleting a credential takes none, and a purge running at the
same time skips the deleted credential. Key rotation writes outside the store, as one conditional `UPDATE` on
`updated_at`, so a rotation that read a credential before a purge rewrote it is skipped rather than writing the old
values back. `TestRotate_StaleWriteAfterPurgeIsSkipped` (`internal/credstore/rotate_test.go`) pins that.

**Found while fixing it.** 1098, 1099, 1100, 1102 and 1107, each recorded on its own.

**Limits.** The fix does not keep a caller to their own organization; that is 98, open. A managed type's reconcile
follows the same rules, except that it never deletes what credentials hold for an input it does not ship (1098).

**Lesson.** When a read decides from a schema what is secret, an edit of that schema is a write to every value under
it. Hold it to the rule a value write meets, in the same transaction, under a lock the value writers take, and never
let an input move from secret to not secret.

## 1098. The type-edit rule's first version also ran in a managed type's reconcile, so in a mixed-version window an older build, at startup or through the kubeconfig import, deleted a newer build's input values in every organization (fixed before push; the import's rewrite of a stored managed type is on main; open: an older build still rewrites the managed row to its own schema, and the newer build's re-add then deletes non-secret values; a repeat in kind of 1019 and 1025; LESSONS 163 and 422)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09, before push. 1097's rule, that a credential keeps
values only for inputs its type declares before and after an edit, was first applied to the managed type reconcile
too, in `adoptExistingType`. A reconcile ensures the type with the schema its own build ships. In a mixed-version
window the stored type may be a newer build's, with inputs the older build lacks, so the older build's reconcile
deleted what every credential held for those inputs. A managed type is shared by every organization, so the loss was
too. The kubeconfig import made one import enough: it ensured the managed Kubernetes type with its own build's schema
on every import. Main's `adoptExistingType` deletes nothing, since main has no purge, but its import still rewrites a
newer build's stored type to the older schema.

**Root cause.** A rule on release data, which inputs a type ships, ran in a process whose release did not make the
stored value (LESSONS 422). And the import reshaped shared infrastructure it only needed to read (LESSONS 163).

**Why 1019, 1025 and LESSONS 422 did not prevent it.** 1019 and 1025 were in the facts subscriber and the group
digest, and LESSONS 422 was written from them. The managed type reconcile is the same shape at another site. The purge
was written as a new rule and not checked against 422, and the import was a second caller of the reconcile that
nothing named.

**Fix.** `50319b68`. A reconcile refuses to clear a shipped secret flag, empties an input it adds as non-secret, keeps
what is stored under one it adds as secret, and never deletes what credentials hold for an input it does not ship.
Tests: `TestEnsureManagedTypeHoldsTheSameRule`, `TestEnsureManagedTypeNeverDeletesValuesOfAnInputItDoesNotShip` and
`TestEnsureManagedTypeRoundTripKeepsASecretInputsValues` (`internal/credstore/type_secret_test.go`). The kubeconfig
import uses the managed type as stored and ensures it only when no build has installed it yet (`kubeconfigType`,
`internal/api/devices_kubeconfig.go`; `TestImportKubeconfig_LeavesANewerBuildsTypeAlone`), create-if-absent as LESSONS
163 asks. One credential of a managed type that this Controller cannot decrypt stops that type's reconcile when the
release adds a non-secret input, for every organization; the type is left as it was, the Controller still starts, and
it logs which credential cannot be read (`TestReconcileStopsAtAnUnreadableCredentialAndSaysSo`). A credential holding
values for an input the older build left out stays usable (1103).

**Status.** Open, for one residual. An older build's reconcile still rewrites the managed row to its own schema,
leaving out the newer build's inputs. When the newer build starts again it adds them back, and an input added as
non-secret starts empty, so a non-secret input's values written by the newer build are lost on a roll back and
forward. A secret input loses nothing. The production guide states this. The complete fix is a release ordinal on each
managed row, so a build never rewrites a row a newer build wrote (LESSONS 422); it is queued and not built.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 422 holds for a deletion as for a refusal: a process deletes only what its own release made.

## 1099. Fixing 1098, the kubeconfig import first used whatever type held the managed Kubernetes namespace, so a custom type there could have stored a cluster's token under an input that reads back in plain text (fixed before push; caught in review; LESSONS 244)

**Symptom.** Caught in review on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09, before push. To stop the import
rewriting a newer build's type (1098), the import was changed to read the type stored under the namespace and use it.
Main's path through `EnsureManagedType` refuses a custom type holding the namespace (`adoptExistingType` answers
`ErrExists`). The new read did not ask whether the stored type was managed. A custom type made before an upgrade, or
left by a failed reconcile, would then have been adopted, and its author decides which inputs are secret, so the
import could have stored the cluster's token or key under an input that reads back in plain text.

**Root cause.** The fix replaced a call with a read, and kept the call's purpose but not its guard.

**Fix.** In `50319b68`. `kubeconfigType` (`internal/api/devices_kubeconfig.go`) refuses a custom holder in the words
the reconcile uses for it, naming only the namespace. Test: `TestImportKubeconfig_RefusesACustomTypeHoldingTheNamespace`
(`internal/api/devices_kubeconfig_newer_test.go`).

**Lesson.** LESSONS 244: when a fix moves a path off a call that carried a guard, the new path carries the guard.

## 1100. A credential PATCH or UI form wrote back a record read before the type lock, so a reference a concurrent type edit's purge had deleted came back, and the secret it resolved to would fill an input nothing masks (fixed before push; the class of 1085 and 45)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09, before push. With 1097's purge in place, the
credential PATCH handler and the UI's credential form read the stored credential, folded the change over it, and
handed the whole record to the store, which took the type lock only then. A type edit committed between the read and
the write could remove a secret input and add it back as non-secret. Its purge deleted the credential's external
reference for that input, and the stale record put the reference back. The reference would then resolve a secret into
an input the type no longer marks secret, which a run's masking does not cover. A type had the same shape: a PATCH or
UI control read the type, and a write from that read dropped an input another edit had added meanwhile.

**Root cause.** As 1085: a read-modify-write with the read outside the write's lock.

**Why 1085 and 45 did not prevent it.** 1085 is open, and was recorded as low severity because nothing reads the
field its race can lose. Here the lost write is a deletion that keeps a secret masked, so the same race discloses one.

**Fix.** `50319b68`. `UpdateCredentialWith` and `UpdateTypeWith` take a fold and run it over the record they read under
the type lock, inside the write's transaction. The API's PATCH and PUT handlers and the UI's forms and input and
injector controls use them. Tests: `TestCredentialPatch_NeverRestoresAReferenceAPurgeDeleted` and
`TestCredentialTypePatch_NeverDropsAnInputAddedMeanwhile` (`internal/api/credentials_stale_test.go`). Since `0d88fd85`
a reference on a non-secret input is also refused at the write and at dispatch (1101), a second guard on the same
outcome.

**Lesson.** A read whose result is written back is taken under the lock the write takes. A fold the store runs does
that by construction.

## 1101. A secret resolved from an external source into an input its type does not mark secret was never masked, because CheckValues took a reference on any declared input and checkSourceField returned early for an external-kind source (fixed on this branch; on main; open: the file source's one directory lets a credential in any organization name a file put there for another, owner decision pending with 98; a repeat in kind of 1088; LESSONS 244)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09. A credential's external reference, or an input
source bound to an external-kind credential such as a HashiCorp Vault one, could name an input its type does not mark
secret. The value it resolved to filled that plain input at dispatch. The masking ruleset is built from the type's
secret inputs, so that secret reached the run in plain text. The linked-credential branch of the same check already
refused moving a secret field into a plain input.

**Root cause.** The secret-into-plain check was written for one source kind and placed after an early return for the
other, and the reference check took any declared input.

**Why 1088 did not prevent it.** 1088 was an early return ahead of an embedded-secret check in the project store, one
branch earlier, and its fix was in that function. Nothing swept other functions for an early return ahead of a secret
check, and LESSONS 244's sibling-path rule was not applied to the source kinds.

**Fix.** `0d88fd85`. `CheckValues` refuses a reference on an input that is not secret (400), and `checkSourceField`
(`internal/credstore/ent_store_input_sources.go`) refuses an external-kind source bound into one (409), so credential
create, PATCH, `PUT /credentials/{id}/input-sources` and the web UI's form all meet it. A reference stored before this
is refused at dispatch, before anything is fetched, naming the credential by id and the input by the type's id, in the
string form and the row form alike; the credential stays readable and editable (LESSONS 415). Tests:
`TestCredentials_RefuseAnExternalSourceIntoAPlainInput` (`internal/api`) and
`TestAnExternalReferenceIntoAPlainInputIsRefusedAtDispatch` (`internal/credstore/resolve`). Tests that put references
on plain inputs now use secret ones, and the graph tests' proof that a binding wins over a default moved to a linked
ordinary credential (`TestABindingWinsOverADefault`), the one source a plain input may still read. The refusal is a
breaking change, and its changelog fragment says so.

**Status.** Open, for one stated limit. The `file` secret source reads one directory for the whole Controller, and a
reference names a file by name, so a credential in any organization can name any file in it, one put there for another
organization included. The production guide (`docs/10-running-in-production.md`) now states it as a tenancy limit.
Scoping it is the owner's decision, pending with 98's.

**Lesson.** A secret check runs for every source kind; where one kind returns early, the check comes first.

## 1102. Reads of a credential and its resolution for a run read the credential and its type in two snapshots, so a type edit committed between them paired a value stored as secret with a schema that showed it (fixed before push; the two reads are on main, where 1097 needed no race; found by an outside review; the class of 283)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09, before push, by an independent review of the
type-edit fix (Fable 5.2, through the API), and proven red here; every in-session review pass had missed it. The
credential reads and the resolver read the credential and then its type in separate statements, outside a
transaction. On PostgreSQL read committed gives each statement its own snapshot, and SQLite in WAL mode does the same
for each statement outside a transaction. So an edit committed between the two that removed a secret input and added it
back as non-secret, with 1097's purge in the same transaction, was seen half done: the credential's values from before
the purge and the type's schema from after it. A read then showed the secret, and the resolver would have handed it to
a run unmasked.

**Root cause.** As 283: a decision spread over two statements is only as current as the first one.

**Why 283 did not prevent it.** 283 fixed the project sync sweep, a write that depended on a read. Here two reads
depended on each other, and 1097's fix assumed a reader sees an edit's purge and its schema change together, which only
one snapshot gives.

**Fix.** In `50319b68`. `storage.ReadSnapshot` (`internal/storage/snapshot.go`) runs each read of a credential, and the
resolution that hands one to a run, in one read-only transaction: repeatable read on PostgreSQL, and on SQLite a read
transaction, which already reads one snapshot. Reads take no lock, so no read waits behind a purge. Tests:
`TestReadsTakeOneSnapshot_SQLite` (`internal/credstore`) and `TestReadsTakeOneSnapshot_PostgreSQL`
(`internal/credstore/locktest`); `TestReadSnapshot_ReadsOneMoment`, `TestReadSnapshot_RunsInsideATransactionItIsGiven`
and `TestReadSnapshot_ReturnsWhatReadReturns` (`internal/storage`).

**Lesson.** LESSONS 428. As 283's lesson, for reads: when one read's meaning depends on another, take both in one
snapshot.

## 1103. In a rollback window a credential of a managed type whose input the older build left out could not be updated at all, rotating a compromised token included, and every run binding it failed (fixed on this branch; on main; a repeat in kind of 1019; LESSONS 415 and 422)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09, from 1098. An older build's reconcile leaves out an
input a newer build shipped, and keeps what credentials hold for it. Every update of such a credential then failed,
rotating a compromised token included, because the merged values were checked against the current schema and named the
dropped input. Every run binding it failed too, at the injector, and its reference or source binding failed earlier, at
resolution.

**Root cause.** A rule on release data, the current schema, was applied on the update path to values another release
wrote (LESSONS 422).

**Why 1019 did not prevent it.** LESSONS 422 came from 1019 and 1025 in the facts code. Credential updates were not
swept for it.

**Fix.** `091d7a69`. An update carries the value, the reference and the source binding a credential stores for an
input its type does not declare, neither checked nor dropped (`internal/credstore/carried.go`), and still refuses a
value or a new reference a caller sends for one. Reads already left such ids out, and the resolver now hands none of
them to a run: their secrecy is unknown and the masking ruleset would not cover them. A sealed credential, which would
otherwise be carried as one undeclared key, is refused with 409, and so is an update of a credential this Controller
cannot decrypt. Tests: `TestACredentialWhoseTypeDroppedAnInputCanStillBeUpdated`,
`TestAnUpdateNamingAnInputTheTypeDoesNotDeclareIsRefused` and `TestUpdatingACredentialThisControllerCannotReadIsRefused`
(`internal/credstore`), `TestACredentialWhoseTypeDroppedInputsStillResolves` (`internal/credstore/resolve`), and
`TestUpdatingAnUnreadableCredentialIsAFieldFault` (`internal/ui/resources/credentials`).

**Lesson.** LESSONS 422 on a write path: carry what another release stored, unchecked and unread, rather than refuse
the whole record.

## 1104. A custom credential type of kind vault or database could mark its identifier input (vault_id, name) secret, and refusing to bind two such credentials to one template then quoted the secret value (fixed on this branch; on main; a repeat in kind of 1090)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09. The binding rule tells two vault credentials apart
by `vault_id` and two database connections by `name`, and its refusal quotes the one they share. A custom type could
take either kind, when created or by an edit changing its kind, and mark that input secret. Binding two of its
credentials to one template then put the secret value in the refusal `PUT /templates/{id}/credentials` answered with.
The shipped vault and `pleiades_postgres` types already mark those inputs non-secret.

**Root cause.** The refusal treated the identifier as a label, and nothing held a type to that.

**Why 1090 did not prevent it.** 1090 kept a caller's URL out of an error in the git source classifier. The binding
refusal quotes a stored value, and nothing checked that the value could not be secret.

**Fix.** `fb1cabde`. `credtype.CredentialType.Validate` refuses a vault type whose `vault_id` is secret and a database
type whose `name` is secret (`checkIdentifierPlain`, `internal/credtype/binding.go`), at creation and at every edit,
an edit changing the kind included. A vault's identifier also reaches `ansible-playbook`'s command line as
`--vault-id`. Tests: two new cases in `TestCredentialTypeValidateRefusals` (`internal/credtype/validate_test.go`), and
`TestNoBindingRefusalQuotesASecretInput` (`internal/credstore/identifier_test.go`). The refusal is a breaking change,
and its changelog fragment says so.

**Not covered (from reading, not run).** The rule is checked when a type is written. A custom type stored before it
with a secret identifier is left as it is, and from reading, binding two of its credentials would still quote the
value. Suspected; no test covers it.

**Lesson.** A refusal that quotes a stored value holds every writer of that value to "never secret".

## 1105. A PATCH body naming a field twice, in any mix of case and through the Kelvin sign, was accepted: a later key won for most fields, and a template's survey and a credential's external took both values (fixed on this branch; on main; a repeat in kind of 473 and 486)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09. `encoding/json` matches a key to a field without
regard to case and lets a later key win, and a field decoded by its own unmarshaler into a pointer it already set
decodes the second value into the first. So every PATCH body accepted a field named twice. For most fields the later
value won. For a template's survey both halves were applied, and a credential body naming `external` twice stored both
sets of references. The routes: templates, organizations, teams, contacts, role bindings, projects, credential types
and credentials.

**Root cause.** The strict decode refuses an unknown field, and `encoding/json` has no refusal for a repeated one.

**Why 473 and 486 did not prevent it.** 473 was yaml.v3 decoding into nodes, refused in `pkg/docedit`, and 486 the
build-file reader. Each fixed its own parser. The API's JSON decode was not checked for the same gap.

**Fix.** `bf0e31a7`. `decodePatchObject` (`internal/api/patch.go`), which every PATCH body decodes through, scans the
top level of the object after the strict decode and refuses a field named twice, matching keys to fields as
`encoding/json` does, the Kelvin sign (U+212A) included. `decodeJSON` answers it with a 400 naming the field by its own
tag (`survey.enabled` inside the survey), repeating nothing the caller sent. Tests: `TestPatch_RefusesAFieldNamedTwice`
(`internal/api/patch_repeated_test.go`) and `TestRepeatedPatchField_ReportsNoRepeatForAnUnreadableBody`
(`internal/api/patch_internal_test.go`). The refusal is a breaking change, and its changelog fragment says so. Whether
create and PUT bodies accept a repeated field was not checked here.

**Lesson.** As 473: a decoder that keeps one value of a repeated key is made to refuse it, wherever two readers could
disagree about which value counts.

## 1106. Text claimed more than the code did: the credential type bodies said "one of the twelve kinds" where there are thirteen, the read schema's kind list left out database, and comments said the managed reconcile was the only writer of a managed row once the type lock wrote that row (fixed on this branch; the kind text on main, the writer comments before push; a repeat of 459 and 1074)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09. The create and PATCH bodies of a credential type
said `kind` was "one of the twelve kinds"; `credtype.Kinds` returns thirteen. The read schema's own list of kinds left
out `database`. And once every credential write took the type lock, which writes the type row's `updated_at`,
comments saying the managed reconcile was the only writer of a managed row (`EnsureManagedType`'s doc among them) were
false.

**Root cause.** A hand-written count and list beside the code they describe, and a comment not reread when the code
under it changed.

**Why 459 and 1074 did not prevent it.** 459 was the README's counts, and this count was in the API description, which
nothing compared with `credtype.Kinds`. 1074's class has no check for a comment.

**Fix.** `e327ef1c` builds each kind description from `credtype.Kinds()`
(`TestCredentialKindDescriptionsNameEveryKind`, `internal/apispec/credential_kinds_test.go`). `50319b68` says
`EnsureManagedType` is the only method that changes a managed type's definition, and that the lock's write to
`updated_at` changes nothing a reader sees.

**Lesson.** As 459: a count or list in text is built from the code, or a test holds it equal.

## 1107. UpdateTypeWith handed its fold slices shared with the stored record it compares against, so a fold clearing secret in place would have passed the secret-flag rule (fixed before push; the class of 1053's read by pointer)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09, before push. The new fold methods handed their fold
a record whose slices were the same ones the store kept to check the edit against. A type fold that edited in place,
setting `Secret` to false on each input and returning the record, changed both sides of the comparison, so 1097's
first rule saw no input move from secret to not secret.

**Root cause.** As 1053's device fake, which handed out the stored item by pointer: a caller given state to change
shared it with the copy that judges the change.

**Fix.** `credtype.CredentialType.Clone`, with the input schema's and injector document's own `Clone`
(`internal/credtype/clone.go`), so a fold gets a copy that shares no slice or map with the stored record. Tests:
`TestUpdateTypeWithHoldsAFoldThatEditsInPlace` (`internal/credstore/type_secret_test.go`) and `TestCloneSharesNothing`
(`internal/credtype`).

**Lesson.** A callback handed a record to edit gets a copy that shares nothing with what the caller compares against.

## 1108. The type lock's first PostgreSQL tests shared one database and left their container to the reaper, and put internal/credstore in the container tier (fixed before push; the class of 188 and 423)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09, before push. The first PostgreSQL tests of the type
lock opened one database for every test, so a run of the package twice, or a neighboring test, found the rows an
earlier test left, and they left their container to testcontainers' reaper, which some container hosts run without, so
it could outlive the run. And because they lived in `internal/credstore`, the branch listed that package as a
container package, which would have moved the whole package out of the fast tier.

**Root cause.** Test isolation was taken from one shared container rather than given to each test, and cleanup was
left to a process the host may not run.

**Why 188 and 423 did not prevent it.** 188 found packages whose tests could not run twice in one process, and 423
containers that were never terminated. Both are rules for each new test that nothing checks when one is written.

**Fix.** The PostgreSQL tests moved to `internal/credstore/locktest` (`internal/credstore/locktest/postgres_test.go`),
listed in the Makefile's `DOCKER_DEPENDENT_PACKAGES` with a duration in `tools/testgate/durations.json`, so
`internal/credstore` stays in the fast tier. Each test opens a migrated database of its own on the package's one
container, through `ent.OpenDatabase` as the Controller does, and `TestMain` terminates the container.

**Lesson.** A test that shares a container gets a database of its own on it, and the package that starts the container
also stops it.

**Note 2026-11-09 (branch-containers).** The first `make branch-containers` run failed shard 4 on
`internal/testsupport`'s `TestEveryContainerIsTerminatedWhenItsStartFails`: the new `openPostgres` did not terminate a
container whose start returned an error. The local gate never ran that test, because `internal/testsupport` was unchanged
and pr-check runs only the packages a branch changes, while that test scans every test file in the module (the gap of
FAILURE_PATTERNS 631, which branch-containers exists to catch). Fixed in the commit that added the helper.

## 1109. Credential refusals quoted input values a custom type may mark secret (database port, host, sslmode, name; the Kubernetes host; vault and database identifiers in CheckBinding and Combine; the Vault source's url and api_version), so a secret could reach a job's failure reason or an API error (fixed before push; on main for the pre-branch sites; a repeat in kind of 1090 and 1104; vuln-corpus C7)

**Symptom.** Found by a narrow fp-reviewer pass on `fix/patch-credentials-partial`, 2026-11-09, after 1104 had refused a secret vault or database identifier. That rule named two inputs, and the injection errors quoted others: `port %q is not a number`, the database host and sslmode in `pkg/wire`, the Kubernetes API server host, and the binding conflicts. A custom database-kind type marking `port` secret, with a non-numeric value, put the value into the job's failure reason. A type stored before 1104's rule, with a secret `vault_id`, still had it quoted when two of its credentials were bound.

**Root cause.** Refusals were written to help the person who typed the value, by quoting it, without asking whether the value was a secret. 1104 fixed the two cases it was shown rather than the class.

**Fix.** No refusal built from a credential's input values quotes a value: `wire.ConnectionProblem` names the field, the injector maps it to the input id (`input "port" is not a number`), and the Kubernetes, binding, combine and Vault source refusals name inputs. `checkIdentifierPlain` stays, and nothing depends on it for secrecy. RED for every site listed, and for a pre-rule vault type seeded through the ent client.

**Lesson.** As LESSONS 190: a rule listing the inputs that may not be secret fails open on the next input; the structural rule is that an error never carries a value at all.

## 1110. The binding check read carried, undeclared inputs the run never uses, and carried references and input-source bindings were shown and then dropped on the next binding write (fixed before push; a repeat in kind of 113 and 1087)

**Symptom.** Found by the same pass. `boundFor` read a credential's stored inputs, including values carried for an input its type no longer declares (1103), while the run reads the resolver's declared-only map, so a bind the check accepted failed at run time. Carried references were shown by GET, carried bindings by the input-sources list, a client sending back what it listed was refused, and any binding write deleted the carried binding.

**Root cause.** 1103 carried values through an update but not the other two shapes of the same data, and the two readings of "the inputs this credential holds" (check and run) were written separately.

**Fix.** `credtype.InputSchema.Declared` is the one filter, used by the resolver and `boundFor`; readers hide undeclared references and bindings; an update carries both; `writeInputSources` replaces only the bindings of declared inputs. RED for each.

**Lesson.** When a value is carried rather than checked, carry every shape it takes (value, reference, binding) and have every reader agree on the one filter.

## 1111. Inventory and announcement creates answered 500 for a blank name, title or body or a missing organization, and an unknown organization, an unknown member or a member listed twice reached a database constraint the inventory store read as a taken name, so the caller got 409 "already exists" (fixed on this branch; on main; a repeat of 106; a sibling of 1095)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-inventories-announcements`, 2026-11-10. `POST /inventories` with a blank name or no
organization answered 500: the store returned "inventory: a set needs a name" untyped, and the handler had no mapping
for it. An unknown organization, an unknown device or group id, or a device listed twice reached the foreign key or the
join table's primary key as a constraint error, which the store mapped to `ErrSetExists`, so the caller was told "an
inventory with that name already exists" and asked, in effect, to pick another name. `POST /announcements` with a blank
title or body or an unknown organization answered 500.

**Root cause.** Two shapes. A store rule with no typed error, so the handler could only answer 500 (LESSONS 426's
class, as 1095's blank credential name). And, as 106, one branch reading every `ent.IsConstraintError` as the unique
index on `(name, organization)`, written when a duplicate name was the only constraint a create could hit.

**Why 106 did not prevent it.** 106's fix separated the foreign key reading in `internal/access`'s store, and its lesson
says the fallback is a decision. Nothing swept the other stores' constraint branches, and the inventory set store kept
the one branch on create and on update.

**Fix.** `a74957af`. Typed errors the API maps to 400: `inventory.ErrSetNameRequired`, `ErrSetOrganizationRequired`,
`ErrUnknownOrganization`, `ErrUnknownMember`; `announce.ErrTitleRequired`, `ErrBodyRequired`, `ErrUnknownOrganization`.
The stores check that the organization and every member exist before the write (`checkMembers`, by count,
`internal/inventory/ent_set_store_update.go`), and drop a repeated id first (`distinctIDs`), so a device listed twice is
kept once. The constraint fallback still reads as a taken name. Reasoned, not run: an organization or member deleted
between the check and the write would still reach it, most plainly on create, which runs no transaction. Tests:
`TestEntSetStore_CreateRefusesWhatItCannotSave` and `TestEntSetStore_UpdateWithHoldsTheResultToTheCreateRules`
(`internal/inventory`), `TestEntStore_CreateRefusesAnUnknownOrganization` and
`TestEntStore_StoreFailuresAreReportedNotMisread` (`internal/announce`), `TestInventoryCreate_RefusesWhatTheStoreCannotSave`
and `TestAnnouncementCreate_RefusesWhatTheStoreCannotSave` (`internal/api`).

**Lesson.** As 106 and LESSONS 426. A store that maps a constraint error names the one constraint it means, and checks
the others before the write, so a refusal it does not expect is never read as the one it does.

## 1112. An inventory PATCH wrote back the membership it read before another PATCH committed, so a PATCH naming only the name could put back a device another PATCH had just removed, undoing a revocation on a grant surface (fixed on this branch for the API PATCH; on main; open: the UI's inventory edit form and a PATCH naming a full list from a stale GET still write from an earlier read, 1085; the class of 1085 and 1100; 97)

**Symptom.** Found on `fix/patch-inventories-announcements`, 2026-11-10. The inventory PATCH handler read the Set,
applied the body, then called the store's `Update` with the whole Set. Of two concurrent PATCHes, the second wrote back
the membership it had read before the first committed. A rename-only PATCH racing a PATCH that removed a device put the
device back. An inventory is a grant surface (97), so the lost write is a revocation undone. On main the announcement
PATCH took every editable field from the body and read only its author and organization, which never change, so it had
no stale field to write back; a partial announcement PATCH that read first would have had the race, which is why it
takes the same lock.

**Root cause.** As 1085 and 1100: a read-modify-write with the read outside the write's lock. 1085 recorded the class
as low severity because nothing reads the field its race loses; here the field is who an inventory grants.

**Why 1085 and 1100 did not prevent it.** 1100 fixed the credential routes and stated the lesson; 1085 stayed open for
the other partial PATCHes, and inventories and announcements were then still full replaces, waiting on task 17.

**Fix.** `a74957af`. `SetStore.UpdateWith` (`internal/inventory/ent_set_store_update.go`) and
`announce.Store.UpdateWith` (`internal/announce/ent_store_update.go`) run the caller's fold inside a transaction
(`storage.NewEntUnitOfWork`). They take the row lock by writing `updated_at` first, as credstore's `lockType` does, and
fold over the row read under the lock with the transaction's client. Proven on SQLite
(`TestEntSetStore_UpdateWithFoldsOverTheOtherUpdatesWrite`, `TestEntStore_UpdateWithFoldsOverTheOtherUpdatesWrite`, via
`ent.OpenEmbedded`) and on PostgreSQL in a new container package, `internal/storage/rowlocktest`
(`TestInventoryUpdatesNeverInterleave_PostgreSQL`, `TestAnnouncementUpdatesNeverInterleave_PostgreSQL`), listed in the
Makefile's `DOCKER_DEPENDENT_PACKAGES`. With the lock write removed, measured: the PostgreSQL test fails and the
revoked device comes back (devices `[1 2]`, want `[1]`), and the SQLite test fails with "database is locked".
`TestLockSetRefusesToRunOutsideATransaction` and `TestLockAnnouncementRefusesToRunOutsideATransaction` hold the lock
helpers to a transaction.

**Status.** Open for what the lock cannot reach (1085's note). The lock orders folds; it does not protect a value the
caller read earlier and sends whole. The UI's inventory edit form (`internal/ui/resources/inventories/inventories.go`,
`writer.Update`) calls `Update` with a submission rendered earlier, and a PATCH naming a full member list replaces the
stored one, so either can still put back a member another write removed. There is no version token. The owner decides
whether to add one.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 429. A lock around a fold protects only what the fold reads under it.

**Note 2026-11-10 (`feat/inventory-version`, not yet committed).** The two gaps in the status above are closed on
this branch: the API PATCH by a version column, an ETag and an `If-Match` judged under the lock (1140), and the UI edit
form by a per-element three-way merge under the lock (1141). The owner's version token is the fix 1140 records.

## 1113. A NUL in an inventory's name or description, or in an announcement's title or body, reached the store, where on PostgreSQL it would answer 500 (fixed on this branch; on main; a repeat of 1092 and 1095; the class of 371 and 1079)

**Symptom.** Found by the fp-reviewer agent on `fix/patch-inventories-announcements`, 2026-11-10. Nothing in front of
the inventory or announcement store refused a NUL in a text field. SQLite stores it. PostgreSQL refuses a NUL in a
`character varying` column, so the write would fail at the database and answer 500. The PostgreSQL 500 is reasoned from
371's and 1079's measurements; the branch's tests check the refusal on SQLite, where it now happens before the database.

**Root cause.** As 371: the production dialect's rule had no mirror in front of the store.

**Why 1092 and 1095 did not prevent it.** Each swept its own resource (projects, then credentials and credential
types), and each entry said nothing holds every text field a caller writes to a NUL check. The inventory and
announcement writes were not swept.

**Fix.** `a74957af`. `inventory.NULError` and `announce.NULError` name the field and repeat nothing the caller sent; the
stores refuse a NUL on create and in `UpdateWith`, and the API answers 400. Tests: the NUL cases of
`TestInventoryPatch_RefusesWhatItCannotApply`, `TestInventoryCreate_RefusesWhatTheStoreCannotSave`,
`TestAnnouncementPatch_RefusesWhatItCannotApply` and `TestAnnouncementCreate_RefusesWhatTheStoreCannotSave`
(`internal/api`), and `TestEntStore_UpdateWithLeavesAStoredBlankTitleAlone` (`internal/announce`).

**Lesson.** As 1095 and LESSONS 426. The rule sits in the store, where every writer meets it. A sweep by resource
leaves the next resource out; the open question is a check over every text column the schema has.

## 1114. The store's first blank-name rule was held to the merged record, so an inventory whose stored name was all spaces, which the old PATCH could store, refused a PATCH that only removed a device (fixed before push; caught in review; a repeat of 1103, and of the rule in 1068's fix; LESSONS 415 and 422)

**Symptom.** Found in review on `fix/patch-inventories-announcements`, 2026-11-10, before push. The first version of
`UpdateWith` checked the record as it would be saved against the new rule that a name is not blank. The old PATCH
stored `{"name":"   "}` with 200 (1075's note), so such an inventory exists. A members-only PATCH on it, a revocation
included, answered 400 for a name the caller did not send.

**Root cause.** A writer held a field it was keeping, not changing, to a rule newer than the stored value. The field
was read from storage and written back, so the rule acted on stored data.

**Why 1103 and 1068 did not prevent it.** 1103's lesson says a write path carries what another release stored, and
1068's says a rule that tightens what may be stored runs where the value is created, not where a stored value is
updated. Both were framed by their incidents: release data in a mixed-version window, and names a sync updates. Here
the stored value came from an older code path in the same release, and the update was a revocation, so neither
framing matched. LESSONS 415 and 422 speak of release data, and their rule sentences do not name the fields an update
keeps.

**Fix.** Before push. The text rules hold only the fields the update changes: `checkSetText`
(`internal/inventory/ent_set_store_update.go`) and `checkText` (`internal/announce/ent_store_update.go`) take the stored
record and skip a field whose value is unchanged. Tests: `TestEntSetStore_UpdateWithLeavesAStoredBlankNameAlone`
(`internal/inventory`), `TestEntStore_UpdateWithLeavesAStoredBlankTitleAlone` (`internal/announce`).

**Lesson.** As 1068's fix: a new rule on a write holds only the fields that write changes. A field it keeps is stored
data, however it came to be stored.

## 1115. Doc comments, the route text and the changelog said two UpdateWith calls never interleave, so neither can undo a membership change the other made, but Update and any PATCH naming a full list from an earlier read still replace the list whole (fixed before push; refuted by the claim-refuter agent; a repeat of 1074 and 1106)

**Symptom.** Found by the claim-refuter agent on `fix/patch-inventories-announcements`, 2026-11-10, before push. The
first doc comments on the lock said that two `UpdateWith` calls never interleave, "so neither can undo a membership
change the other made". The first half is what the lock proves. The second is false: `Update`, which the UI form calls,
and any PATCH naming a full member list built from an earlier GET replace the list whole, so either undoes a change
committed after its read (1112's status).

**Root cause.** The claim was written from the fix's own test, which races two folds, rather than from every writer of
the field.

**Why 1074 and 1106 did not prevent it.** Their class has no check for a comment's claim. The review pass that refutes
claims is what caught it, which is the check they ask for.

**Fix.** Before push. The claim was narrowed in `internal/inventory/set.go`, `internal/inventory/ent_set_store_update.go`,
`internal/api/inventories_patch.go`, the apispec schema text
(`internal/apispec/inventory_announcement_write_schemas.go`) and the changelog fragment: folds apply one after the
other; a named list replaces the stored one whole; there is no version check.

**Lesson.** As 1074 and LESSONS 429: a doc claim about a lock names what the lock orders, and says plainly what it
leaves to the caller's read.

## 1116. The first row-lock tests proved the wait only by a 200 ms sleep, and could block forever if the first update failed before its fold (fixed before push; caught in review; a repeat of 211 and 788)

**Symptom.** Found in review on `fix/patch-inventories-announcements`, 2026-11-10, before push. The lock tests started
one update, waited for its fold to signal that it was inside, and started the second. A plain receive on the inside
channel would never return if the first update failed before it reached its fold, so the test would hang to the
package timeout rather than fail. And the only proof that the second update waited was a 200 ms sleep.

**Root cause.** As 211 and 788: ordering taken from a fixed sleep, and a receive with no way out.

**Why 211 and 788 did not prevent it.** Their rule is for each new test, and nothing checks a test when it is written.

**Fix.** Before push, in `internal/storage/rowlocktest/rowlocktest.go`: the test selects on the inside channel or the
first update's done channel, so a failed first update fails the test, and a started channel marks the second update's
start. The sleep stays as a margin. A slow start can only make the test pass without proving the lock; it cannot make
the test fail while the lock holds. The test was shown to fail with the lock write removed (1112).

**Lesson.** As 211: a test's wait names what it waits for and has a way out for every way the waited thing can fail. A
sleep that remains is said to be a margin, with which way it can mislead.

## 1117. Two stub-backed handler tests could not fail once the stub's UpdateWith reset the organization and owner itself (fixed before push; caught in review; a repeat of 54 and 1016; LESSONS 213 and 424)

**Symptom.** Found in review on `fix/patch-inventories-announcements`, 2026-11-10, before push.
`TestInventoryHandler_UpdateKeepsTheStoredOrganizationAndOwner` and
`TestAnnouncementHandler_UpdateCarriesAuthorAndOrganizationForward` (`internal/api`) ran against a stub store. Once the
stub's `UpdateWith` kept the immutable fields itself, as the real store does, the handler had no way to lose them, so
the tests passed with or without the behavior their names claimed.

**Root cause.** As 54 and 1016: a test's fixture did the work the test was named for.

**Why 54 and 1016 did not prevent it.** LESSONS 213 asks for a run with the protection removed. Moving the protection
from the handler into the store moved it out of what the stub test could see, and nobody reran that question after
the move.

**Fix.** Before push. Both were renamed `...UpdateHandsTheStoreTheFieldsTheBodyNamed` and reframed as wiring tests:
they check what the handler passes the store. What the store keeps is held by the store tests against ent
(1112, 1114). The UI fakes' new `UpdateWith` methods were written to act as the stores do:
`fakeSetStore.UpdateWith` hands the fold copies of the member lists, and `fakeAnnouncementStore.UpdateWith` answers
`announce.ErrNotFound` (1094's note, which also records a gap in that fake's comment).

**Lesson.** As LESSONS 213. When a protection moves from one layer to another, recheck that each test named for it can
still fail, and rename the ones that can no longer see it.

## 1118. A background rg with no path read its standard input, which was not a terminal, and waited 40 minutes as the first step of a git rebase -x verification, so nothing was checked (open, as a practice: nothing stops a command in a background shell from reading its stdin; a repeat in kind of 245 and 1082)

**Symptom.** On `fix/patch-inventories-announcements`, 2026-11-10. A background shell ran a `git rebase -x`
verification whose first step was `rg PATTERN` with no path. With no path, rg searches its standard input when that
input is not a terminal, and a background shell's input is not one. It waited for input for 40 minutes. No commit was
checked in that time.

**Root cause.** As 245: a command handed a standard input it should not read. A missing path, which in a terminal
searches the working directory, became a wait when the same command ran in the background.

**Why 245 and 1082 did not prevent it.** 245's lesson ("give every step that must not read input nothing to read") is
in the archive under `make up`, and was not applied to a session's own commands. 1082 found that a tool inside a
`git rebase -x` script can fail silently, and its practice is about PATH and empty test lists, not stdin. The session's
command guard asks for bounded rg output (`-l`, `-c`, `-m`, or a `head`), not for a path.

**Fix.** A practice, not a guard: pass rg an explicit path (`rg ... .`) in every background or scripted command, and
close the stdin of a command that must not read input (`< /dev/null`). Measured while writing this entry: the redirect
must not go on the reader of a pipe. `git show REV:FILE | rg PATTERN < /dev/null` searched the working tree, because the
redirect replaced the pipe as rg's input, and printed the branch's code as though it were the base commit's.

**Lesson.** LESSONS 430.

## 1119. PATCH with an empty body answers the full stored record and changes only updated_at, so a token holding inventory:write or announcement:write without the matching read scope can read any inventory or announcement (open: owner decision; new on this branch for these two routes; reasoned to hold for the earlier partial PATCH routes too; the class of 1096)

**Symptom.** Reasoned on `fix/patch-inventories-announcements`, 2026-11-10, from the code; not run as a scope test.
Since the partial PATCH, `{}` folds nothing over the stored record, writes it back with a new `updated_at`, and answers
200 with the whole record. `Identity.HasScope` (`internal/auth/evaluator.go`) lets no `*:write` scope imply `*:read`:
its only implication is `runbook:check` from `runbook:execute`. So a token holding `inventory:write` alone can read
every inventory, members included, and one holding `announcement:write` every announcement, each without a change a
reader would notice. Before this branch `{}` on these routes answered 500. The same holds, by the same reasoning, for
the routes made partial earlier (templates, organizations, teams, contacts, bindings, projects, credentials and
credential types; 1075's notes), where 1075 recorded `{}` answering 200 as accepted without the read-scope question.
Together with 1111's 400 for an unknown member and 1120, a write-only token can map what exists.

**Root cause.** A write route answers with the record it wrote, which is the ordinary REST shape, and an empty write
makes that a read. Whether a write-only token is a real role here has not been decided.

**Status.** Open, for the owner. Options seen: refuse a PATCH that names no field, answer a write-only caller without
the body, or decide that a write scope implies its read scope and say so in `HasScope`.

**Lesson.** Pending the decision. When a write answers with the stored record, ask what a write that changes nothing
shows a caller who may not read.

**Resolution, on this branch, 2026-11-10 (`fix/patch-needs-read-and-write`, `0882d90b`).** Owner decision 2026-11-10,
after an independent design review (Fable 5.2): a route whose write answers with the stored record needs the record's
read scope as well as its write scope. Measured red through the real token chain (`internal/api/patch_scopes_test.go`,
`TestPatch_AWriteScopeAloneIsRefusedBeforeTheBodyIsRead`): a token holding `inventory:write` alone got `PATCH {}` 200
with the whole inventory, a guessed organization 400, a missing id 404 and a malformed body 400. Each is now one
identical 403.
- `api.Route.AlsoScope` (`internal/api/router.go`), enforced by a second `RequireScope` before the handler.
- `permitted()` in `internal/api/links.go` makes `_links` and the `OPTIONS` `Allow` header require both scopes, with one
  `Permitted` call per scope set, because the HATEOAS generator reads two affordances for one relation as either one
  (`TestPatch_IsNotAdvertisedToAWriteScopeAlone`).
- `apispec.Endpoint.AlsoScope` on 13 PATCH, 5 PUT and 7 POST endpoints (the POSTs are 1134).
  `internal/apispec/patch_scopes_test.go` guards the list, and `TestAlsoScope_EveryDeclaringRouteRefusesTheFirstScopeAlone`
  mounts all 25 through the real router.
- The web UI checks the same declaration (`web.permitsEndpoint`, `view.Descriptor.AlsoCandidates`; 1133).
- The OpenAPI document lists both scopes, and `changelog/patch-needs-read-and-write.breaking.md` names the 25 scope
  additions schema-compat reports as breaking.
- Comments the change made false were corrected: `internal/api/authz.go` ("mounted once per route"),
  `internal/auth/hateoas.go` ("every real attempt is still recorded exactly once"), `cmd/controller/main.go`, and the
  doc of `Route.Rel`.

**Known limits.** Reasoned, not run. A route with `AlsoScope` records two authorization Decisions, so a write-only
caller logs an allowed write and then a denied read. A `Decision` carries no route or request id, so the log does not
tie the two together.

**Still open, for the owner.** Reasoned by the claim-refuter agent, not run.
- Every DELETE answers a write-only token 204 for a record that exists and 404 for one that does not, so it shows what
  exists. This matters most for `DELETE /inventory/devices/{name}`, whose names can be guessed. A template DELETE also
  answers 409 naming a schedule link.
- Action scopes show stored state without a read scope. `POST /jobs/{id}/cancel`, the relaunch route and the launch route
  need `runbook:execute`, not `job:read` or `template:read`. `POST /inventory/devices/{name}/onboard`
  (`inventory:onboard`) returns the `onboard.Result`. `POST` and `DELETE /inventory/devices/{name}/capabilities`
  (`inventory:assert`) return the grant list.
- `PUT /templates/{id}/credentials` needs `credential:read` but reads the template, so it shows a template's existence
  and kind to a holder without `template:read`. A route can carry only one `AlsoScope`.
- Informational: `auth.AllScopes()` leaves out `ScopeAccessRead`, `ScopeSettingsRead` and `ScopeSettingsWrite`, though
  its doc says it covers every constant.

**Lesson, 2026-11-10.** LESSONS 435 for the routes this branch covers. For the routes still open, pending the decision.

**Resolution of the action routes, 2026-11-10 (`fix/action-route-read-scopes`, `8a3449d3`).** Owner decisions
2026-11-10: an action route needs the read scope of each record it reads, and a route may require several scopes
(`AlsoScopes`), rather than answering 204, because a 204 still reads the template first. The `DELETE` 204 and 404 are
left as they are.
- `api.Route.AlsoScope` and `apispec.Endpoint.AlsoScope` became `AlsoScopes []auth.Scope`. The router mounts one
  `RequireScope` per scope (`internal/api/router.go`). `permitted()` in `internal/api/links.go` and the UI's affordances
  (`internal/ui/view/view.go`, `internal/ui/web/handler.go`) ask the HATEOAS generator once per scope position, any
  affordance within one position's list being enough, since the generator reads two affordances for one relation as
  either one.
- The routes 1119 listed now declare what they read: `cancel_job` (`job:read`), `relaunch_job` and `rollback_job`
